Title: 56 AWS API calls in 141 milliseconds: Inside an AI-run intrusion

Full Text:
One server read 56 EC2 user data scripts in 141 milliseconds. Then it went quiet for 14 days and came back. That gap did more damage than the burst, because fixed correlation windows cannot span two weeks.

Between September 30 and October 16, 2026, a CyberStrikeAI server worked through stolen AWS credentials in a familiar sequence: validate identities, harvest secrets from Secrets Manager, pull EC2 user data, decrypt an SSM parameter, send a remote command. Every one of those is a call a legitimate role makes every day. Nothing in CloudTrail looked urgent at the time.

CyberStrikeAI is an open-source platform that pairs LLM agents with offensive security tools. Will Thomas at Team Cymru counted 21 IPs running it in early 2026, all of them aimed at Fortinet edge devices. This is the first case we have seen of the same tooling turned on AWS.

We call this AI-assisted on the strength of the tool attribution and the machine-speed behavior in the logs. We cannot prove an LLM agent was making the decisions, and we do not know how the attacker obtained the credentials.

Key findings from the CyberStrikeAI AWS intrusion

Between Sep 30 and Oct 16, 2026, one CyberStrikeAI server (43[.]240[.]29[.]11) used credentials from eight AWS identities (five IAM users and three EC2 instance roles) across four accounts and generated 78 alerts.

app-role sent 56 user data requests in 141 milliseconds, part of 58 user data retrieval alerts (74% of the total), which points to automated tooling.

On Oct 2, container-role read an encrypted SSM parameter and issued an SSM SendCommand 29 seconds later. The audit log does not show what the command was or whether it succeeded.

43[.]240[.]29[.]28 and 43[.]240[.]29[.]33 serve a CyberStrikeAI page on port 8080 with the same self-signed certificate as 43[.]240[.]29[.]11, which ties the three servers together. As of November, none of the three is serving that interface, so treat the IPs as indicators for retrospective hunting.

All 78 alerts were medium or low severity and only made sense once correlated by source IP.

Several details point to automated tooling:

56 user data requests in 141 milliseconds from a single session.

Three GetCallerIdentity calls in one second, across three accounts.

A sharp change in tempo. 83% of alerts (65 of 78) came on day one, then activity dropped to a few targeted actions per day.

None of this proves an LLM agent was making decisions, but it matches how an agentic platform works through a list of credentials and targets.

Automating IAM containment with Elastic Workflows

AI-assisted offense is often sporadic and fast, especially with compromised identities. Elastic Workflows can enable responders by making API calls to AWS services such as IAM to block the identity automatically.

Elastic Workflows, shipped with the stack (9.4+), lets detection rules invoke custom workflows with a YAML-defined pipeline of steps on every alert. As a PoC we created a custom workflow that triggered on the detections shared below while emulating this behavior that mirrors suggested response actions.

On every alert, the workflow does the following, executing in seconds and aiding with containment of the identity:

Triggers on AWS EC2 Bulk User Data Enumeration detection rule

Iterates each user name associated with the alerts

Invokes an AWS Lambda function through Elastic’s AWS Lambda connector

Deactivates compromised access key using iam:UpdateAccessKey.

Blocks older temporary sessions associated with IAM user by adding inline deny policy via iam:PutUserPolicy and aws:TokenIssueTime cutoff

Quarantines IAM user by attaching inline deny-all policy

Behavioral indicators to hunt for in CloudTrail:

A burst of DescribeInstanceAttribute calls requesting userData, many per second, from one role session.

First-time GetCallerIdentity calls from the same external IP across several accounts or users within the same minute.

GetSessionToken or GetSecretValue from an instance role session whose source IP is not the instance or your NAT.

GetParameter with decryption followed within a minute by SSM SendCommand from the same role.

We added two high-severity, low false positive ES|QL detections for the burst enumeration behavior: AWS EC2 Bulk User Data Enumeration alerts when one principal and source IP read userData from more than 20 distinct instances in 10 minutes, and AWS STS GetCallerIdentity Bulk Account Enumeration alerts when three or more distinct non-role identities call GetCallerIdentity from the same external IP and ASN in 10 minutes.

How to respond if your AWS identities were exposed

Assume anything an affected role could read is compromised, and work outward from the credentials.

Rotate credentials for every identity that touched the indicator IP, and revoke active sessions, including those from temporary credentials.

For instance roles, rotate by replacing the instance profile or the instance, since stolen role credentials expire but can be reissued while the host stays compromised.

Treat all secrets in EC2 user data as exposed, and move them to the Secrets Manager or Parameter Store.

Review SSM command history for the window of any unexpected SendCommand call to see what ran. Check for abuse of AWS-managed documents, AWS-RunShellScript and AWS-RunPowerShellScript or custom documents.

Check non-production roles and secrets for overlap with production.

Block the indicator IP at the WAF, VPC, NaCL and security group level, but rely on the behavioral detections, since the infrastructure can change and network blockage is not effective at stolen credentials to API calls prevention.

Restrict ec2:DescribeInstanceAttribute for userData to the roles that need it, using IAM policy or a service control policy.

Enable GuardDuty if it isn't already, and alert on credentials used from outside your expected IP ranges.

Hunt for how the instance credentials were obtained, starting with exposed web applications, SSRF, code repositories and IMDS.

Conclusion: What this intrusion means for alert correlation

AI-assisted attacks are driven by objectives, so they generate a lot of alerts. One CyberStrikeAI server produced 78 alerts across six rules in 16 days, and 65 of them came on the first day. Every alert was medium or low severity, and each one looked routine on its own: a first-time GetCallerIdentity, a GetSessionToken, an SSM SendCommand from a rare user. Only the shared source IP showed they belonged to one intrusion.

Defenders need high-signal detections to stop the damage early; low false positive behavior rules, such as the two bulk enumeration rules described above, that justify acting immediately. Medium and low severity alerts are good candidates for correlation, but only by source IP, and the correlation window needs to be flexible because AI-assisted activity is irregular. Here, 56 requests landed in 141 milliseconds, later steps came hours to days apart, and the operator returned after 14 days. A short fixed window would have split this intrusion into unrelated alerts.

High-signal detections can also drive remediation. Attached to a workflow, such as those in the Elastic Workflows library, a rule like this can disrupt the attack automatically, for example by blocking the source IP, while analysts investigate.

Title: Hackers' Overreliance on AI Can Result in Weaker Cyber-Attacks, Proofpoint Researcher Says
Context: Even in vulnerability exploitation, where AI has been found to discover and exploit flaws rapidly, AI-generated exploits often have significant weaknesses over human-based activity
Full Text:
For the past few years, cybercriminals have been adopting AI tools to enhance their malicious campaigns. However, one threat researcher has claimed that AI has not made any significant changes to the cyber threat landscape, and in many cases has made attacks less effective.

Based on her findings and analysis of recent campaigns where AI was used by cybercriminals, Selena Larson, principal threat researcher at Proofpoint, shared during the IRISSCON 2026 conference in Dublin, Ireland, on November 11 how AI has, in many, cases has made attacks less effective.

“We’ve all been told since 2023 that AI will make attackers better, faster and stronger. That they’ll have access to the same tools and resources as the best developers, security professionals and vulnerability researchers in the world, and will automatically become better at hacking. This is marketing nonsense, the data just doesn’t back up this assertion,” she noted.

AI “Slop” Enters the Attack Chain

While AI has enabled threat actors to increase the speed and scalability of campaigns, a number of groups have become overly reliant on these tools, leading to frequent errors – something Larson described as “AI slop.”

Proofpoint has found such errors in AI generated malware. “We frequently run into malware where the code doesn’t actually work, there’s comments which want to do one thing, but the malware is doing something completely different,” Larson said.

A similar scenario has occurred with phishing campaigns observed by Proofpoint over the past year. Larson highlighted the case of a threat actor tracked as TA4903, which specializes in business email compromise (BEC) and phishing campaigns.

Historically, the group has impersonated US government entities to target organizations across a range of sectors, using sophisticated lures.

However, Larson said that since the group started adopting AI tools in their attack chains, their lures have really gone downhill.

This is because the AI generated emails often do not match up with the subjects and attachment – sometimes leaving the body of the message blank.

In addition to AI-generated lures, the group now primarily creates phishing websites using AI coding tools. These vibe coded sites are often simplistic and take on a similar appearance in terms of colors and formatting, making them easier for targets to detect.

Larson also pointed out that the use of AI-generated phishing messages to ensure correct region-specific grammar and spelling, can even make lures less believable.

“Human beings often don’t know how to spell, they often are bad at grammar, people aren’t trying to be overly polished. So, I think that’s actually a bit of a detriment to some of these actors,” she added.

Even in vulnerability exploitation, where AI has been found to discover and exploit flaws rapidly, AI-generated exploits often have significant weaknesses over human-based activity.

Larson cited the example of the ‘BlueMoon’ exploit chain first observed in August 2026, which involved three Microsoft Chrome browser vulnerabilities chained together.

The threat actors used large language models (LLMs) to write exploits, using information given in patch release notes. However, the AI-generated exploit itself was highly flawed, often not behaving as intended and generating significant noise, making attempts easily identifiable for defenders.

No Change in Cyber Defense Priorities

Larson said it is important to emphasize that AI is a productivity tool and does not automatically increase the sophistication of threat actor campaigns.

“AI is only as good as its operator and this is, and it can lead to more sloppy mistakes,” she noted.

As a result, cyber defense remains fundamentally the same. The biggest shift is the fact that AI is making it faster and easier for attackers to exploit vulnerabilities that cybersecurity professionals have been aware of for a long time.

“Attacks are attacks and AI generally doesn’t really matter. Whatever you’re defending against, defense is going to remain the same,” Larson concluded.

Title: Quantum Systems drones back in the air after malware scare
Context: "The threat was contained thanks to the swift response of our IT and security teams in close and transparent collaboration with the authorities," it said on Thursday
Full Text: Quantum Systems says its drones are flying again with Germany's military after a cyberattack prompted a precautionary grounding. The company says it spotted the attack at the end of October and reported it to the relevant authorities, but disclosed few details about the intrusion. "The threat was contained thanks to the swift response of our IT and security teams in close and transparent collaboration with the authorities," it said on Thursday. "Through the quick measures taken and the characteristics of the incident, there is no risk in operating Quantum Systems' unmanned systems for the end users and the operators." It added that other players in the European defense industry, and those who support Ukraine's military efforts, have faced "persistent cyberattacks for years." The Bundeswehr grounded its Quantum Systems drones after malware was detected in an update to QBase, the company's QBase ground-control software, Der Spiegel reported, citing unnamed sources. QBase lets operators plan missions, monitor flights, and process data from the ground. The malicious update reportedly reached servers belonging to the German military and other customers, but did not directly infect the drones. "The fleet is operating normally around the globe – including Germany and the Bundeswehr," Quantum Systems told Reuters. "The Bundeswehr was the only customer to ground their systems as a precaution." A spokesperson for Germany's defense ministry declined to comment on the attack or the reported details. The Register asked Quantum Systems for further details. Founded in 2015, Quantum Systems has been providing drones to the Ukrainian war effort for years. Last month, Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced funding for "several tens of thousands" of the company's interceptor drones as part of Germany's winter aid package. The new drones will be built in Ukraine and support interceptor systems already in use on the front lines. Quantum Systems announced a $1.2 billion Series D funding round in July, valuing the company at around $8 billion. ®

Title: Apify Confirms Customer Data Accessed in Cyberattack
Context: The intrusion took place on November 9 and 10 and was discovered on November 11, when Apify blocked the attacker’s access and launched an investigation
Full Text:
Web scraping and automation company Apify has confirmed that customer data was accessed in a cyberattack that compromised internal systems and customer accounts.

The Czech company provides a cloud platform for collecting information from websites and automating online tasks. It says it has 91,000 customers worldwide.

The intrusion took place on November 9 and 10 and was discovered on November 11, when Apify blocked the attacker’s access and launched an investigation.

According to the company, the attacker used a compromised credential to obtain additional credentials and gain access to related Apify accounts.

On November 12, Apify confirmed that some customers had their personal information or stored data accessed during the attack.

The company has contacted customers whose information was exposed. Those who have not received a notification have not been identified as affected so far, although the investigation is continuing. Apify has not disclosed the number of compromised customer accounts.

According to an Apify customer who shared a breach notification on Reddit, the exposed information included names, email addresses, billing details, account activity, and IP addresses.

More importantly, the notification listed salted password hashes, 2FA recovery codes and phone numbers, and authentication tokens associated with Google and GitHub sign-ins among the compromised data.

The notification also indicated that payment card information was limited to cardholder names, expiration dates, and the last four digits of card numbers. Full card numbers and security codes were not exposed.

The company has implemented additional monitoring, changed critical internal secrets, and revoked some OAuth connections to third-party services, including GitHub.

Apify said its investigation had not found that the OAuth connections could have been used as an attack vector. Customers building Apify Actors from private GitHub repositories have been instructed to reconnect their GitHub integrations.

Title: SilentAir Hackers Intercept Calls, SMS From Inside Mobile Networks
Context: SilentAir launches its signaling attacks, mostly over SS7 and sometimes over Diameter, from network nodes it has hijacked at mobile operators
Full Text:
Telecom software and cybersecurity company Enea has detailed the activity of a previously unknown threat actor that intercepts phone calls and text messages through compromised mobile operator infrastructure, with Taiwan as its main target.

The company tracks the group as SilentAir and assesses with high confidence that it’s a new state-level actor.

Enea’s researchers also believe, with low confidence, that SilentAir’s activity is aligned with China-nexus operations. Their reasons include the hackers’ interest in Taiwan, the absence of Chinese targets, and attack timing consistent with a workday in China’s time zone.

SilentAir launches its signaling attacks, mostly over SS7 and sometimes over Diameter, from network nodes it has hijacked at mobile operators. The attacks route a target’s incoming calls and SMS messages through the compromised node and harvest subscriber details.

The hackers can also track a target’s location, but this makes up only a small part of their activity. They send silent SMS messages, which don’t appear on the recipient’s phone, possibly to check whether earlier interception attempts succeeded.

Enea has monitored the attacks since early 2025, and further digging revealed suspicious activity from before that.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

The hijacked nodes belong to operators in at least six Asian countries. Besides Taiwan, the group has targeted a dozen other countries and territories, occasionally going after people in East Africa, Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe. High-profile political and government figures were among those targeted.

The report also covers 2026 activity from Liminal Panda, a group that CrowdStrike linked, with low confidence, to China-nexus operations. Enea says it’s the only actor known to actively exploit the IPX, the interconnect network that mobile operators use to exchange traffic.

Starting in the first quarter of 2026, Enea spotted and blocked Liminal Panda’s GTPDoor backdoor at several of its mobile operator customers. In total, it caught several hundred attempts to covertly reach command-and-control servers.

Enea says it has seen potential infections at between five and ten operators. It estimates that the total could reach several dozen, particularly in Asia, Africa and Latin America.

According to Enea, SilentAir and Liminal Panda could be connected, although the evidence isn’t strong enough to link them.

Title: AI Doesn’t Have to Go Rogue to Break the World
Context: The last two matter more than the first
Full Text:
This essay is adapted from a keynote speech delivered at the DEF CON 34 conference in Las Vegas on August 7, 2026. The essay originally appeared in CyberScoop.

I want to talk about AI hacking. There are three aspects: people hacking AI systems, people using AI to hack other systems, and AIs hacking systems on their own, not even maliciously. The last two matter more than the first. The third is the weirdest and potentially the most destabilizing.

I started writing about this in 2021 and in my 2022 book, A Hacker’s Mind. Back then I said it was mostly still science fiction, but not stupid science fiction. We’re seeing it more and more, especially in the past year. The trends I’m describing don’t require a major breakthrough in AI. They’re starting to happen now, and they’ll happen more often as AIs get better at autonomous problem-solving. And it will involve far more than computer code.

AI will hack all sorts of social, economic and political systems. It will find vulnerabilities and exploit them. This is a difference in kind, not just degree. We’re not ready for it, and we need to think about the implications now.

First, I want to broaden the term “hacking.”

The tax code isn’t computer code, but it is code. It’s a series of algorithms with inputs and outputs. It has vulnerabilities, which we call loopholes, and exploits, which we call tax avoidance strategies. Black hat hackers exploit them for profit. We call them accountants and attorneys.

What is a hack? One definition: “Something that a system permits, but is unanticipated and unwanted by the designers.” It’s subjective and implies novelty and cleverness. A hack follows the rules of a system but subverts its goals or intent, just as a software hack follows the logic of code while doing something its authors neither anticipated nor wanted.

All systems of rules can be hacked, including professional sports, customer reward programs, financial systems and politics. Hacks even work against our cognitive functions. A curved hockey stick is a hack, and we know the name of the man who invented it. Mileage runs were a hack. The filibuster was originally a hack in Roman times. Gerrymandering is a hack. Hedge funds and private equity are full of them.

A system is just a set of rules or norms, and the rules aren’t always formal. Even the best-designed rules will be incomplete, inconsistent or ambiguous. As long as people want to subvert a system’s goals, there will be hacks.

AIs are becoming hackers. After decades of slow progress, they’ve gotten very good at finding and exploiting vulnerabilities in computer code. They do this largely autonomously, and they’re getting better scarily fast. But the implications extend far beyond software, to the tax code, financial regulations and all sorts of social, economic and political systems.

There are two distinct issues. First, someone might instruct an AI to hack one of these systems, feeding it the world’s tax codes or financial regulations to find profitable loopholes. Second, an AI might hack a system on its own, inadvertently. Both are dangerous, but the second is worse because we might never know it happened.

Now, reward hacking. AIs don’t solve problems the way people do. They stumble on solutions we never anticipated, and some subvert the intent of the system. They don’t share our context and don’t necessarily understand the implications, norms and values we take for granted.

Reward hacking is when an AI achieves a goal in a way its designers neither wanted nor intended.

Early pre-LLM examples are telling. In a two-person soccer simulation, an AI learned that kicking the ball out of bounds forced the opposing goalie to throw it in and leave the goal undefended. In a stacking simulation, an AI learned to flip a block upside down rather than stack it. In an evolution simulation where the goal was to cross a distant finish line, an AI made itself tall enough to fall over the line instead of growing longer legs or stronger muscles.

These are all hacks, the result of poorly specified goals or rewards. Today, they’d come from bad prompting.

The problem is universal. One researcher tried to teach a robot vacuum not to bump into things. Instead, it learned to drive backward, because there were no sensors in the back.

Any capable AI will find hacks wherever the rules have problems, inconsistencies or loopholes that still produce an acceptable solution. We see a hack because we understand context. The AI doesn’t, at least not in the same way.

This problem shows up often in myth.

In the story of King Midas, the god Dionysus grants him a wish: everything he touches turns to gold. Midas ends up starving when his food, drink and daughter all turn to gold. It’s a specification problem. He programmed the wrong goal.

In the Golem of Prague, a ghetto animates a clay statue to guard its residents. It guards them past all reason until they figure out how to turn it off. This is a guardrail problem. The villagers never limited the golem’s actions.

More generally, think of this as the genie problem. Genies are precise about the wording of wishes and can be maliciously pedantic when granting them. There’s no way to outsmart a genie. Whatever you wish for, he can grant it in a way you wish he hadn’t.

The reason is that in human language and thought, goals are always underspecified. We never include every caveat, exception and proviso, and we never close off every avenue for hacking. Any goal we specify will be incomplete. That’s largely fine in human interactions, because people understand context and usually act in good faith.

If I asked you to get me coffee, you’d pour a cup from the nearest coffee pot or walk to the corner shop. You wouldn’t bring me a pound of raw beans, buy a coffee plantation or snatch a cup from a stranger’s hands. I wouldn’t have to specify any of that. You’d just know.

Similarly, if I asked you to develop a technology that turns things to gold on touch, you wouldn’t build it to starve the person using it. You’d just know.

In 2015, Volkswagen was caught cheating on emissions tests. Human engineers programmed a regular computer to detect testing and behave differently during it. The cheat went undetected for years because it’s hard to tell what software is doing.

If I asked you to design engine control software that maximizes performance while passing emissions tests, you wouldn’t design it to cheat without realizing you were cheating. An AI would, because it will think “outside the box” when it has no concept of the box.

Unless programmers specify that the system must not behave differently during testing, an AI might come up with the same hack. The programmers would be satisfied, the accountants would be ecstatic, and no one would know until someone audited the code.

We can now constrain the goal to avoid that particular hack, but programmers won’t anticipate others. The lesson of the genie is that there will always be hacks programmers don’t anticipate.

We’re building AI genies: systems that take broad instructions and figure out how to carry them out, sometimes in ways we didn’t expect or intend. That’s the whole point of vibe coding. You underspecify what you want and let the AI work it out. Sometimes that produces genie behavior.

We can’t completely specify goals to an AI, and AIs can’t fully understand context. More precisely, current AIs have a shallow grasp of concepts. If we asked a current LLM to get me coffee, it would almost certainly do the right thing.

I worry about goals that aren’t well represented in training data, and about hacks that aren’t obvious, whose effects are subtle, like the Volkswagen hack.

Recommendation engines are an early example. They push people toward extreme content. No one programmed that. It emerged because that’s what people respond to. It didn’t take a bad actor. A basic automated system with feedback found the hack on its own.

We’re now seeing a second generation with today’s AI coding systems. AI researcher Simon Willison asked Fable to track down a stray scrollbar in a web app. When he returned, it had opened browsers, written its own screenshot tools, edited the framework’s internal templates to make the bug appear on cue and set up a local web server to collect measurements. It found the bug, but it also did many things he never asked for. Another researcher gave Fable a complex task, and it tried to hack its own memory limits because it needed more storage.

A new OpenAI model did something similar when it hacked into Hugging Face. It was being benchmarked on its ability to turn vulnerabilities into exploits. It decided the best way to reach its goal was to break out of its containment, access the internet and break into the Hugging Face network, because it thought the answers would be there.

Today’s LLMs are acting like genies, especially when powerful models are combined with sophisticated harnesses.

There are two kinds of genies. The Dionysus genie does the wrong thing. It understands your prompt literally but not correctly, and returns a mess you never intended. The Golem genie does the right thing but tramples everything in its path to get there. The paperclip maximizer is a Golem genie.

Consider some examples. Ask an AI to deal with spam calls, and a Dionysus genie might change your phone number. Ask it to book a particular flight, and a Golem genie might hack the airline database because the flight is full. Ask it to get a refund for an online purchase, and a Dionysus genie might draft a legal threat on fake letterhead and send it to the company. Ask it to buy tickets to a popular concert, and a Golem genie might discover the ticketing system is rate-limited and spin up thousands of cloud servers to hammer it. You’d know if some of these things happened, but you might never realize if others did. More detailed prompting won’t fix this. The lesson of the genie is that no amount of detail is good enough.

AI researchers aren’t surprised by any of this. Many are working on defenses against reward hacking and subtler forms of genie behavior. Some of this falls under “value alignment”: How do we teach AIs context? And how an AI satisfies a goal matters as much as whether it does. I want to build a benchmark to measure genie-like behavior, so we know where models stand and whether alignment is improving.

Think beyond LLMs and computer code. Consider specialized AIs built to find loopholes, and hacks of more general systems: the tax code, financial regulations and democratic procedures.

Financial systems are the most likely first target, because their rules are designed to be algorithmically tractable. High-frequency trading is itself a hack. Imagine giving an AI all of the world’s financial laws, plus all the news and financial data, and the goal of finding profitable loopholes. I suspect large investment banks are already doing this. The results will be novel tricks that are legal but unintended and unwanted, some of which might break the financial system.

Tax loopholes are the next likely target, for the same reasons. For a while, AIs will identify potential loopholes, and human hackers, namely attorneys and accountants, will decide which are feasible.

Further out, expect hacks of regulatory, legislative and procedural systems, and of the broader economy.

Hacking is as old as humanity. We’re creative problem solvers and loophole exploiters. We manipulate systems to serve our interests and strive for more influence, power and wealth.

Still, no human pursues their interests without constraint. Even sociopaths are limited by the complexity of society and their own contradictory impulses. They worry about their reputation and punishment, and they have limited time. These human qualities have limited hacking.

Hacking changed as everything became computerized. Computers are uniquely hackable because of their formalism and complexity. Today, nearly everything is a computer, from cars and appliances to phones. Our social, economic and political systems, including taxation, finance and elections, all involve computers.

Until recently, hacking was exclusively a human activity. Finding a novel hack required expertise, creativity, time and luck.

AI hacking will change everything again. AIs aren’t bound by the constraints that limit people. They’ll think like aliens, and they’ll change hacking’s speed, scale, scope and sophistication, sometimes at our direction and sometimes on their own.

Speed is the easiest to see. A creative process that takes a human months or years could be compressed into hours or seconds.

Scale is next. Once AI systems start discovering hacks, they can exploit them at a scale we’re not ready for. We already see this with AI-generated slop, which is rampant on social media. AI bots post around the clock, sometimes overwhelming real human discussion. It’s hard to know how much of social media is still people talking to people. What looks like boisterous political debate may be bots arguing with other bots, artificially shaping what we think and what we think others think.

Scope makes hacks more dangerous. AIs already make decisions that affect our lives, decisions we once thought belonged only to humans. As AI systems grow more capable, society will hand them more decisions, and more important ones. Hacks of these systems will do more damage.

Finally, AI hackers are more sophisticated. They can hold more variables in working memory and generate more complex hacks. What might happen if you fed an AI the entire U.S. tax code? Would it figure out, without being told, that it’s smart to incorporate in Delaware and register a ship in Panama? Consider the Double Dutch Irish Sandwich, the strategy Apple and Google used to avoid paying U.S. taxes. It involves U.S., Dutch and Irish law and an offshore tax haven. How many loopholes will an AI find that we don’t already know about? Dozens? Hundreds? Thousands? We have no idea.

These hacks will largely be perpetrated by the powerful against the rest of us. AI is fundamentally a power-enhancing technology, and so is hacking. The more power you already have, the more a hack gives you. If you or I found a tax hack, we might make a few thousand dollars. If a large investment bank found one, it and its clients could make billions.

Our societal systems for dealing with hacks were built when hackers were human, and they reflect the pace of human hacking. We have no system of governance that can handle hundreds, let alone thousands, of newly discovered tax loopholes. We won’t be able to recover from an AI finding unanticipated but legal hacks of financial systems, operating at AI speed, scale, scope and sophistication. Hacking becomes a problem society can no longer manage.

Now, defense. AIs that find software vulnerabilities help defenders as well as attackers. Vulnerabilities can be patched, removing them permanently, or turned into signatures that security systems use to detect and block attacks. In theory, AI could identify and patch every automatically discoverable vulnerability before a product ships. This is rapidly becoming routine in software development. We call it vulnops. We can imagine a future where accidental software vulnerabilities are a thing of the past.

Deliberate vulnerabilities are different. There will be an arms race. AI will craft increasingly obscure back doors, and AI will find them. It becomes a contest between the speed of creation and the speed of patching, and between obfuscation and reverse engineering.

The same logic applies to broader systems. Yes, AI hackers might find hundreds of vulnerabilities in the existing tax code. But the same technology can evaluate potential loopholes in any proposed tax law or ruling. A legislator, a watchdog group or a reporter could take the text of a bill and identify every exploitable loophole before it passes. The difference is that, unlike software, knowing about a tax loophole doesn’t mean it gets patched. In theory, though, we can fix them before the rich and powerful exploit them. So maybe defense will come out ahead here, too.

That requires resilient governing structures that can respond quickly. It won’t help if updating the tax code takes years, or if a legislative hack becomes so entrenched that it can’t be fixed politically. Maybe a lobbyist put it there on purpose. Maybe it was discovered after the law passed, and now lobbyists want to keep it. Microsoft can patch the vulnerabilities it finds. Patching is much harder when legislatures have to do it. We need society’s rules and laws to be as patchable as our computers.

This is a hard problem of modern governance, and it goes well beyond AI. It’s the problem of building governing structures for the speed and complexity of the information age.

The umbrella idea is trust. What do we need for AI systems to be truly trustworthy? Capability isn’t enough.

AIs won’t be trustworthy if the companies controlling them spy on us or subtly manipulate us. I call this the friend vs. tool problem. Will we have AI agents, or AI double agents?

AIs won’t be trustworthy if they’re insecure. How do we know they haven’t been manipulated? Almost all AIs operate in adversarial environments, so someone will benefit from hacking them. Unless we know they’re secure, we shouldn’t trust their output.

And AIs won’t be trustworthy if they act like genies. We need to know they’ll perform tasks the right way, not just perform the tasks we ask for.

I’ve written extensively about the need for “integrous” AI, including how to think about the problem, what a research agenda looks like and what good laws and policies look like. I predict integrity will be the key security problem of this decade, just as confidentiality was the key problem of the last one. This applies to both AI and the internet of things.

The big shift is agency, which I think of as Web 3.0. Computers now affect the physical world directly and with growing autonomy. Sensors go from data sources to attack surfaces, and actuators go from outputs to attack capabilities. An integrity failure no longer means bad spreadsheet data. It means the wrong dosage, the wrong valve position or the wrong braking distance.

Integrity isn’t one thing. I break it into input integrity, processing integrity, storage integrity and contextual integrity. Each is complex and important, and each deserves its own talk. I’ve written about them, and I hope you’ll read it.

Much of this isn’t really an AI problem. It’s not a technical problem so much as a capitalism problem or a democracy problem.

The failures of late-stage capitalism and democracy in the information age both stem from the rich and powerful getting too good at hacking our social, economic and political systems. This is the core argument of my 2021 book.

Seen this way, AI is exacerbating existing problems. Human inefficiency has largely kept those problems in check, and that won’t work much longer.

So consider this a call to action. Technically, we need to understand how AIs hack systems, build systems that are resilient to hacking and build AIs that won’t act as genies. Politically, we need to learn to govern and regulate at the speed of technology. Otherwise, market failures will overwhelm our ability to govern them.

I said hacking is as old as humanity and that AIs will overwhelm our ability to deal with it. The solutions aren’t specific to AI, but AI makes them more urgent. We need to understand them, and we need to implement them.

Context: Technical details Since all five Critical vulnerabilities patched in this update are use-after-free flaws, let’s have a closer look at what causes this type of vulnerability
Full Text:
On November 11, Google issued a security update to Chrome’s Stable channel for Windows, Mac, and Linux. The update is rolling out over the coming days and weeks.

Most users are on Chrome’s Stable channel. The desktop update brings Chrome to versions 157.0.8103.78/.79 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.78 for Linux. It includes 83 security fixes, five of which are rated Critical—the highest severity level. This update came out only two days after the previous one.

How to update Chrome

The easiest option is to allow Chrome to update automatically. But you can end up lagging behind on updates if you never close your browser or if something goes wrong, such as an extension preventing the update.

If you don’t want to wait for the rollout to reach you, you can update manually. Open About Google Chrome from Chrome’s Settings or Help menu. Chrome will check for updates and download any available update. If prompted, click Relaunch to apply it.

Chrome 157.0.8103.79 is up to date

You can find an explanation of the version numbering system and step-by-step instructions in our guide: How to update Chrome on every operating system.

Technical details

Since all five Critical vulnerabilities patched in this update are use-after-free flaws, let’s have a closer look at what causes this type of vulnerability.

A use-after-free (UAF) vulnerability happens when software accesses memory after it has released that memory for reuse. The program still has a reference to the old location, but the original object is no longer valid, and something else may now occupy that space.

The leftover reference is called a “dangling pointer” and is caused by a mistake in managing how long an object remains available. One part of a program may release it while another still expects to use it. That can happen because of confused ownership, faulty error handling, or a timing issue between tasks running simultaneously.

The consequences range from crashes and corrupted data to information leaks and, in some cases, execution of attacker-controlled code. The dangerous possibility is that an attacker can influence what replaces the freed object, then trick the program into treating that replacement as legitimate data or instructions for what to do next.

That explains why UAF flaws can receive critical severity ratings. However, the label describes a class of memory-management bugs, not a guaranteed outcome: the actual impact depends on the affected component, how reliably an attacker can exploit the mistake, and the protections in place.

Title: Phishing Rises Three Times Faster in Europe Than Globally, Proofpoint Finds
Context: Proofpoint found that today’s phishing threats are drive greater engagement in Europe, with European users clicking on 8
Full Text:
Proofpoint found that today’s phishing threats are drive greater engagement in Europe, with European users clicking on 8.3 out of every 100 delivered threat messages, compared with 2.0 globally.

Precision Cloud Attacks See Success for Attackers

At the same time, the firm found that 64% of European organizations targeted by precision cloud attacks showed evidence of successful compromise.

Speaking to the media during Proofpoint Protect London event, on November 12, Daniel Blackford, VP of threat research, said the researchers derived this finding from account-takeover telemetry, including logging attempts and follow-on actions such as creating email rules or linking apps.

“These targeted attacks use techniques such as phishing and session hijacking to gain access to specific users and accounts, highlighting their effectiveness compared with broader brute-force attacks,” Proofpoint researchers noted.

Espionage and AI Threats Reshape Europe’s Cybersecurity Landscape

European industries are facing increasingly targeted threats. Malware accounted for 21% of detected threats in the hospitality and leisure sector, nearly twice the global rate. Healthcare organizations faced a similarly concerning picture, with callback phishing increasing by 257% year over year and malware detections rising by 84%.

The report also highlighted that espionage operations are expanding across Europe, with South Asian threat actors extending their reach into Western Europe, while Russian and Chinese state-aligned groups continue to evolve their tactics.

At the same time, the growing adoption of cloud services and AI is creating new security challenges.

Proofpoint identified more than 188,000 AI-enabled applications connected through authentication and OAuth frameworks, while the proportion of European sensors affected by attacks targeting open-source AI technologies increased 4.6 times between consecutive 90-day periods.

“Up to last year, I could have said AI for attackers was still a bit too hyped up, but within the last six to eight months, we’ve really started seeing widespread adoption of coding assistants and AI usage across the vast majority of the landscape,” Blackford added.

Title: SilentAir Hijacks Asian Telecom Networks to Intercept SMS 2FA Codes and Spy on Taiwanese Users
Context: Enea, a telecom and cybersecurity software company based in Stockholm, found the group's attack sources in at least six Asian countries and named it SilentAir this week
Full Text:
A newly identified spying group used hacked equipment inside Asian mobile operators to intercept the calls and texts of selected people, mostly in Taiwan.

Enea, a telecom and cybersecurity software company based in Stockholm, found the group's attack sources in at least six Asian countries and named it SilentAir this week. It assessed with high confidence that SilentAir is a state-level actor, but linked its activity to China only with low confidence.

The company has told the operators where it found SilentAir sources. It said SilentAir has been disrupted for now but could return. The report does not say whether those operators have cleaned up the hacked equipment.

Mobile operators use the SS7 and Diameter protocols to exchange signaling messages that route calls and texts and enable roaming. This traffic crosses a shared network called the IPX, which runs on a high level of trust between operators. SilentAir sent its attacks into the IPX from the hacked equipment.

For interception, SilentAir sent the target's home network an UpdateLocation message, or its Diameter equivalent. The message claimed that the hacked equipment was now serving the target's phone. If the home network accepted it, calls and texts for that person would be diverted to the attackers.

Some of these attacks worked. For some targets, the company observed two-factor authentication (2FA) codes being intercepted immediately after the diversion took effect. That points to an attempt to break into other accounts registered to those people.

The report gives no similar evidence for voice calls, and it does not say whether any account was taken over.

Interception made up 18.3% of the attacks the company saw from SilentAir. For a typical surveillance company, the kind of firm behind most signaling attacks, the share was 2.1% in the company's earlier research.

Some targets were political and government VIPs in their own countries. In rare cases, SilentAir equipment in several countries worked together against such targets, which the company said points to a single controller.

The attacks came in bursts, from one or a few subscribers to several thousand over a month, with gaps of up to several months or longer between bursts.

Outside Taiwan, targets were mostly in other Southeast and East Asian networks, and at times in East Africa, Central Asia, the Middle East, and Europe. People using the hacked operators' own networks may also have been targeted, but the company could not see that traffic.

The company spotted SilentAir by studying attacks on the links between operators. Since early 2025, it has tracked unusual attacks, mostly over SS7 and sometimes Diameter, from some Asian operators that would not normally send attacks. Later analysis found suspicious activity even earlier.

The networks hosting SilentAir handled follow-up messages for diverted targets in odd and inconsistent ways, according to the company's technical report. That left two explanations: someone outside was faking those networks' signaling addresses, or equipment inside each network had been taken over.

The company then saw equipment inside one operator both send and receive attack commands, which confirmed the second explanation. That equipment behaved exactly like SilentAir sources in other networks.

Detecting and blocking the attacks was hard at first because the attackers understood mobile networks and signaling defenses well. After the attacks were contained, the company recovered traces of unauthorized access. It could not analyze the malware it believes SilentAir used.

The report does not name the countries, the operators, or any of the targets. In some countries, SilentAir attacks came from more than one operator.

SilentAir also sent silent SMS on a very large scale, mainly to subscribers in Taiwan. These are texts that the phone does not display or alert on.

During the day, most silent SMS went to subscribers on other networks, such as Southeast Asian networks. One of their main uses appears to have been checking whether a diversion had worked, the company said.

If the test text reached the hacked equipment instead of the phone, the attackers knew they were getting that person's texts.

Most silent SMS went out at night, and most of those went to people in Taiwan. The company said the purpose of those messages is not confirmed. They may be a bulk check that earlier diversions were still in place, since phones are least likely to re-register to their real location at night.

The silent texts carried spam-like motivational or promotional lines, often in English. The company believes the text was a disguise. If an operator along the way stripped a message's silent setting, the recipient would see it as spam and ignore it.

The company's low-confidence link to China rests on several signs. SilentAir focused on Taiwan and did not target Chinese networks or subscribers.

Its tracking and interception attacks also followed a working day in UTC+8, which is China Standard Time. They started at 9 a.m., almost stopped on weekends, and paused or slowed around Chinese holidays.

The company also considered a link to Liminal Panda, a group behind earlier telecom intrusions. It called the link possible but unconfirmed and does not tie the two groups together for now.

In several hacked operators, SilentAir attacks happened during a known Liminal Panda infection. At other times, the two showed no sign of working together. They also went after operators in the same part of Asia, though Liminal Panda has no known focus on Taiwan.

SilentAir's behavior also partly matches that of SCTPE, a little-known Linux trojan that runs in the kernel and is designed to send and receive SS7 and Diameter traffic.

Singapore's Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) has described the same tool in a government advisory. There, the tool is called SIGweaver. The agency said CrowdStrike identified it on January 21 and links it to Liminal Panda with moderate confidence.

But Enea said SilentAir answered messages it had not sent itself, which the known SCTPE program cannot do. SilentAir's operational security also seemed far better than Liminal Panda's.

Separately, the company's GTP firewall has detected Liminal Panda activity at several customer operators since the first quarter of this year. The company blocked the group's GTPDoor traffic there and saw Liminal Panda infections, or strong signs of them, in at least 5 to 10 operators.

The GTPDoor backdoor, first documented on February 27, 2024, hides commands within GTP-C, the protocol that establishes mobile data connections between networks. The company also found evidence of a new version that hides commands in GTP-U, the part of GTP that carries users' data. GTP-U traffic is harder to inspect, though the company believes the new version serves mainly as a backup.

What Enea Recommends for Operators

The company said any attacker could reuse these techniques, and it told operators to:

Deploy GTP-C and GTP-U firewalls and configure them to share information with their SS7 and Diameter firewalls.

Go beyond the industry's basic recommendations for signaling security.

Treat the whole IPX as untrusted.

Add detection for signaling protocols inside their own networks.

Connect signaling security with the rest of their IT security.

The report does not advise people whose calls and texts may be targeted.

Title: AI Set to Revolutionize Ransomware Following “Stagnant” Few Years
Context: However, McArdle noted that AI frameworks like Artex are removing barriers to entry for entry for initial access, by enabling attackers to identify and exploit vulnerabilities...
Full Text:
Ransomware will be revolutionized in 2027 due to the influence of AI, with threat actors poised to become more innovative, according TrendAI’s director of cybercrime research, Bob McArdle.

“Ransomware has been pretty stagnant and boring for the past couple of years, at least if you’re a researcher like me,” he told the audience at the IRISSCON 2026 conference in Dublin, Ireland, on November 11.

To date, ransomware actors have primarily used AI to enhance the speed and efficiency of campaigns. This includes the use of AI tools to identify the most important data once inside an organization’s environment, while some groups have deployed chatbots to carry out the initial negotiation stages on their behalf.

However, the overall process of ransomware attacks, from the use of initial access brokers through to the double-extortion method, have not changed.

“That’s a drop in the ocean compared to where we’re going with ransomware next,” McArdle warned.

Devaluation of the Initial Access Broker Marketplace

One expected change is around how initial access is gained to victim’s environments. In the current ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) ecosystem, initial access brokers typically sell access to affiliates through techniques like compromised vulnerabilities and stolen credentials.

However, McArdle noted that AI frameworks like Artex are removing barriers to entry for entry for initial access, by enabling attackers to identify and exploit vulnerabilities rapidly.

“Anything that’s connected to the internet and is misconfigured or has vulnerabilities will be compromised,” he commented.

This will devalue the initial access market and, as a result, McArdle expects brokers to adapt their business model towards offering privilege escalation to ransomware groups.

Post initial access, tools like Artex and AI agents will allow attackers to shrink down the “kill chain” to machine speed.

McArdle also observed that many organizations are centralizing their data storage, which is good for business efficiency purposes amid the growing use of AI for data processing.

However, this centralization will provide new opportunities for threat actors. This includes ransomware groups threatening to tamper with the AI orchestration around organizations’ data as a further extortion technique.

Another area in which AI will benefit ransomware groups is its ability to process data effectively, enabling actors to quickly develop datasets of high value data, which will be easier to sell on to other malicious actors. This approach will provide even more profit-making opportunities for these actors.

“Over 2027, we will start seeing an inflection point where you have extortion-based business models of ransomware living side-by-side with the actual data theft and sales models increasing every year,” McArdle explained.

Hostile Takeovers by Ransomware Groups

With AI making ransomware attacks easier to undertake, McArdle expects to see a growth in the number of ransomware groups in the next year.

This further fragmentation of the ransomware ecosystem will likely lead to large groups frequently undertaking “hostile takeovers” of smaller actors.

“We will start seeing Conti and LockBit level groups effectively acquiring smaller groups for their technology or even just their affiliate networks,” he added.

Title: Ransomware at the hypervisor layer: how attackers use ESXi and vCenter features for malicious purposes
Context: The ransom notes identified the attacker as the BlackNevas group, first observed in November 2024
Full Text:
Our Global Emergency Response Team (GERT) recently investigated an engagement in which an adversary destroyed an organization’s virtualization estate over a 10-day period. The campaign targeted four ESXi hosts, every virtual machine hosted on them, both vCenter Server Appliances, and all connected backup infrastructure. The ransom notes identified the attacker as the BlackNevas group, first observed in November 2024. What’s interesting about this attack is that no virtualization layer vulnerabilities were exploited: no guest-to-host escapes, no hypervisor memory corruption. Every action taken against ESXi was executed through legitimate VMware management interfaces. In September 2021, the Babuk ransomware source code was leaked online, including its ESXi version, which made ESXi ransomware accessible to cybercriminals with relatively low technical skills. At least ten subsequent ransomware families have leveraged this leaked code, including groups that otherwise lacked the expertise to develop ESXi-compatible ransomware lockers from scratch. We saw multiple operators using Babuk-derived ESXi lockers along with the leaked LockBit Windows builds. It is worth noting that while the Babuk ESXi version may target both old and up-to-date systems, the target organizations run unsupported ESXi versions, making them easier to attack.

This article examines why the hypervisor layer remains difficult to monitor, what common access paths adversaries use to reach it, and how they establish persistence on the management plane. We’ll also look into the architecture of ESXi encryptors, the deliberate destruction of backup infrastructure, and the log sources that enable post-incident reconstruction. At the end of this article, we’ll provide indicators of compromise recovered during the investigation.

Ten days of dwell time from initial access to the destructive phase. Timeline reconstructed from incident evidence

Why the hypervisor changes ransomware economics

Virtualization enables cost-effective and efficient resource management, simplifies simultaneous updates and policy enforcement. However, at the same time it reduces the number of control points and enables broader impact in case of a cyberattack. In non-virtualized environments, a single guest compromise normally affects one operating system. Compromise of the virtualization management plane gives the attacker access to many hypervisor hosts, while direct impact on an ESXi datastore can render many guest systems unavailable at once. This makes the hypervisor layer an attractive target for ransomware operators, especially when domain controllers, application servers, databases, and backup workloads share the same virtualized estate.

According to Kaspersky’s global cybersecurity services report, ransomware accounted for 39.4% of incidents GERT handled in 2025, and the data for the beginning of 2026 shows that it remains a major threat. Back in 2023, SentinelOne documented that multiple ransomware families are using ESXi lockers derived from the leaked Babuk source code, which lowered the development barrier for actors who otherwise lacked the necessary expertise to build ESXi-capable samples. This makes ransomware targeting virtualization environments more accessible to a broader range of threat actors, and this trend is still with us.

The visibility asymmetry

ESXi is a specialized hypervisor based on VMware’s proprietary VMkernel. It shares certain similarities with Linux (and other Unix-like systems), accepts Linux commands and runs certain Linux-like software, but it is different from general-purpose Linux distributions. Broadcom states that off-the-shelf security tools designed for general-purpose operating systems cannot run on ESXi without workarounds and that direct installation of third-party agents or antiviruses on ESXi and vCenter Server Appliance (VCSA) is not supported. Defenders therefore rely heavily on built-in hardening, management-plane telemetry, agentless security solution integrations, and telemetry collection from the infrastructure outside ESXi hosts.

Guest operating systems are usually protected by EDR software, but if an ESXi-side process modifies a virtual machine disk (VMDK) or related datastore file, an EDR agent inside a guest cannot directly observe or attribute the hypervisor process performing the operation. Guest telemetry may record consequences, such as I/O failures or an abrupt shutdown, but the malicious execution occurs outside its boundary. In the engagement examined here, this made host-native and management-plane telemetry central to the incident timeline reconstruction.

How attackers reach the virtualization layer

There are different routes into the environment that require different controls, but can ultimately provide access to the centralized virtualization management plane and the ESXi hosts it controls. In this article, we’ll look into four main routes that may lead to virtualization infrastructure compromise:

Vulnerability exploitation

Credential reuse from the Windows estate

Active Directory integration abuse

Backup infrastructure as a credential bridge

The virtualization trust stack and recurring entry paths

Vulnerability exploitation

In the incident we analyzed, there was no evidence pointing to an ESXi vulnerability as the initial access path. Nevertheless, public vulnerabilities remain important because they have been used to compromise the virtualization management infrastructure. With the exploits available online, this is one of the most probable entry routes. Below you can find several examples of vulnerabilities affecting virtualization environments that have been seen exploited by the attackers. For example, the Twelve group chained CVE-2021-21972 and CVE-2021-22005 to plant a web shell directly on a vCenter appliance, which loaded a backdoor that then established persistence by injecting a shared object into the SSH daemon. Note that these vulnerabilities are not related to the incident in question and they are provided merely as an initial access vector illustration, which could help defenders define their relevant attack surface and prioritize patching activities.

Active Directory integration

CVE-2024-37085 is a useful illustration of why it is crucial to authenticate to different systems separately even when the hypervisor itself is patched. The vulnerability affects ESXi hosts configured to use AD for user management. According to Microsoft, it is exploited by ransomware operators, including Akira and Black Basta, abusing the ESX Admins group behavior to obtain full ESXi administration. CISA lists the issue in their KEV catalog and notes that it has been used in ransomware incidents.

The vulnerability is fixed in ESXi 8.0 U3. For older systems, Broadcom recommends the following workaround:

Change the esxAdminsGroupAutoAdd value from true to false.

Change authValidateInterval from 1440 to 90 minutes.

Clear the default ESX Admins group mapping where appropriate.

These controls reduce exposure, but the architectural lesson is broader: domain compromise should not automatically allow the adversary to obtain hypervisor admin rights.

Recommendation for defenders

Avoid unnecessary direct Active Directory dependency on ESXi hosts. Where business requirements demand it, stick to the principle of least privilege: add only those accounts to administrative groups that really need this level of access, use separate admin accounts with separate credentials for the domain and for hypervisors, restrict access to the ESXi and vCenter management interfaces to only those network segments, accounts and workstations that are necessary to control it, and continuously validate ESXi permission changes. vCenter role-based access control (RBAC) and identity federation should be configured for virtualization administration, while ordinary enterprise credentials and broad domain groups should not be used to access vCenter or ESXi with high privileges.

Credential reuse from the Windows estate

The third path requires no vulnerability. Administrative credentials present on domain controllers, jump servers, backup systems, identity infrastructure or administrator workstations may provide access to vCenter or ESXi if the same admin accounts are used across different infrastructure segments. MITRE ATT&CK treats the Valid Accounts technique as applicable to ESXi and specifically notes that compromised default or domain accounts can provide privileged access to other systems.

In this incident , credentials obtained from non-virtualization systems inside the organization’s perimeter were used to reach the vCenter Server Appliances. Unlike vulnerability exploitation, successful authentication with a valid account may appear operationally normal. To reliably detect such activity, analysts must therefore evaluate the source host, account history, time, destination, subsequent administrative actions, and whether the authenticated account normally manages virtualization infrastructure.

Backup infrastructure as a credential bridge

Backup platforms are not passive storage. They commonly require service accounts, hypervisor credentials, repository access and broad network reach so they can protect and restore critical workloads. This makes the backup server a concentrated trust point. In this incident, the adversary extracted stored credentials after gaining administrative execution on backup infrastructure, creating a route toward other infrastructure tiers.

Persistence on the management plane

With the potential risk possibilities explained, let’s go back to our case study. The attackers managed to compromise via SSH the vCenter appliance managing virtualization disaster recovery where they established two layers of persistence. The first used MeshAgent, the endpoint component of the legitimate MeshCentral remote management platform. The second used Ligolo-ng as a reverse tunnel implemented as a systemd service. This activity maps to two ATT&CK techniques: Systemd Service (T1543.002) and Protocol Tunneling (T1572).

The timeline was as follows. The attackers authenticated on the appliance as root via SSH. Forty-three seconds later, they fetched and deployed MeshAgent through a shell script. The SSH session lasted 2 minutes and 26 seconds in total. After it ended, the adversary didn’t use SSH to access the compromised appliance anymore, thus reducing the usefulness of monitoring focused only on interactive SSH sessions. Roughly four hours later, they returned through MeshAgent and installed the Ligolo-ng tunnel as a persistent systemd unit.

Unit file /etc/systemd/system/vmware-vdma.service Service vmware-vdma Description "DNS, time, VM settings sync (v2.03.24766)" ExecStart /opt/vmware/bin/agent Restart always Strings in /opt/vmware/bin/agent: Ligolo-ng v0.8.2 api.cloudvflare[.]com:443

VCSA persistence artifact: /etc/systemd/system/vmware-vdma.service

The unit uses a VMware-like prefix, places its binary under /opt/vmware/bin/, describes plausible appliance housekeeping functions, and requests Restart=always. A defender should not treat any unrecognized VMware-looking service as malicious by default, because custom integrations may exist, but a service absent from the list of services the organization defines as trusted is a high-confidence anomaly requiring immediate validation.

Beyond the incident in question, more advanced ESXi persistence techniques have also been documented. For example, Mandiant observed attackers using malicious vSphere Installation Bundles (VIBs) as a persistence mechanism on compromised ESXi hosts. This demonstrates that attackers with administrative access can establish persistent access at the hypervisor layer, including persistence that survives host restarts. However, this incident shows that common remote-management software and a systemd service can be sufficient when vCenter itself is trusted and poorly monitored.

Turning vCenter into an offensive control plane

One interesting technique observed in the incident was the use of vCenter Host Profiles. Host Profiles are intended to capture and enforce configuration across ESXi hosts. A Host Profile can be applied to separate hosts, clusters of hosts or all hosts associated with a profile. It also may contain subprofiles covering specific configuration aspects, e.g., authentication. Among other things, Host Profiles may contain configuration for Tech Support Mode (TSM) and TSM-SSH.

In this incident, the adversary used Host Profiles to change TSM-SSH service state to enable SSH on target ESXi hosts. The evidence recorded the following sequence:

Note that the 33-second interval between the configuration push and TSM-SSH reaching RUNNING state is short enough for us to be able to quickly correlate these events by comparing logs from different sources. Overall, it took the attacker eleven minutes after the initial configuration read to reconfigure the host from policy-disabled SSH to direct remote access support. Subsequently, direct SSH access to the target ESXi hosts originated from the vCenter appliance IP, a source that would normally be considered highly trusted on the management network.

Compromise of the management plane converted a legitimate compliance mechanism into an access path to the managed hypervisor

Why ESXi configuration change via vCenter is a trust-boundary failure

Host hardening is important, but centrally administered controls should not be considered independent once the central management tool is compromised. If vCenter has authority to modify host state, an attacker controlling it may be able to make a malicious change look structurally similar to legitimate compliance activity: read configuration, apply a desired state, and observe the result. The distinguishing context becomes authorization, the timing, the source account, the change window, and whether the desired state itself weakens security.

This is why vCenter should be treated as a Tier 0 asset and provided with the highest possible level of protection. Management-plane administrative accounts should be isolated from ordinary enterprise administration, network access should be restricted to dedicated management paths, high-risk configuration changes should require strong authentication and monitoring, and vCenter-to-ESXi traffic should be thoroughly compared to a normal behavior baseline (connection patterns, ports, protocols, source and destination systems) rather than implicitly trusted. All significant discrepancies should be treated as suspicious and investigated.

High-fidelity detection opportunity

An alert should be generated when Host Profile compliance (or remediation in VMware terms) changes TSM or TSM-SSH configuration outside an approved window, particularly when followed by a new SSH session from vCenter or another management appliance. This sequence is more precise than alerting on SSH alone because each step is legitimate in isolation but dangerous in combination.

Notes on ESXi abuse: living-off-the-land tools and controls to monitor

Once an attacker can administer ESXi, many destructive actions require no exploit. LOLESXi project catalogs native ESXi binaries and scripts that have been abused by threat actors, including administrative utilities that enumerate VMs, control power state and alter configuration. This mirrors living-off-the-land behavior on Windows, but the target is the hypervisor control plane.

There are two ESXi hardening mechanisms, and changes to either can be viewed as highly suspicious. Host acceptance level controls which VIBs are allowed to install. The execInstalledOnly setting controls whether non-installed binaries may execute. Broadcom states that ESXi 8 enables the execInstalledOnly runtime option by default and warns that disabling it allows unknown non-installed binaries to execute, increasing ransomware risk. There is also a kernel enforcement setting with the same name, which is related to the runtime option, but distinct. Changes to that may require a reboot.

Stopping virtual machines before impact

Mature ESXi lockers generally stop guest machines before modifying virtual-disk data because running VMs hold active state and file locks. Different families implement this in different ways, which creates useful behavioral detections. The families described below are not related to the incident in question, but these descriptions may be useful for ransomware protection in general.

We don’t know the exact technique used to kill VMs in this incident. However, a rapid sequence of power-off or world-kill operations across many VMs is always a high-confidence pre-impact signal. In the case evidence, the disaster-recovery host showed all VMs stopping within 23 seconds, while vmksummary.log, which stores the number of running VMs each hour, showed it dropping from normal VM counts to zero.

Payload delivery and FlowSsh behavior

The payload was delivered to ESXi via SFTP. The auth.log authentication log file exposed a client identifier associated with FlowSsh, Bitvise’s SSH client library for C, C++ and .NET. FlowSsh supports SFTP, remote execution requests, interactive shell sessions and tunneling. Those capabilities fit the observed delivery model, but the library identification should rest primarily on the recorded client identifier rather than on behavioral inference alone.

After the payload was delivered, the following series of commands was executed. We reconstructed this sequence primarily from the shell.log file.

Each command pair was preceded by a session executing only true. This repeating pattern is consistent with automated FlowSsh channel setup, but in isolation, it can’t be considered a reliable indicator of the tool in use. Human operators could have typed true as well, and other automation frameworks could have emitted reachability probes. The sequence should therefore be hunted as a behavioral fingerprint, not treated as a unique signature for FlowSsh. Its value increases when combined with an unusual SSH client identifier, SFTP staging to /tmp, chmod, and a subsequent self-test or payload execution.

The three-hour self-test window

The /selftest execution ran for approximately 16 seconds and occurred roughly three hours before final detonation. A pre-impact test run may suggest that the operator was validating compatibility with the target ESXi build before proceeding to destructive execution.

Pre-impact detection opportunity

Treat unexpected executable staging under /tmp, followed by execution and subsequent access to /vmfs, as a critical pre-impact sequence. While individual indicators such as chmod +x may be ambiguous in isolation, unexpected execution of a newly staged executable from /tmp can itself be a strong indicator of malicious activity. The complete sequence provides stronger contextual evidence by linking payload staging, execution, validation, and subsequent access to the VM storage layer.

The forward-slash argument style resembles the Trigona and BlackNevas command-line family. SentinelOne describes BlackNevas as a Trigona derivative with ESXi-capable builds and specialized switches, including /p or /path, /wipe, /depth, and /detach. That comparison strengthens attribution but does not replace a binary hash or reverse-engineered match.

Partial overwrite and what 2 KB actually implies

Incident artifacts indicated that approximately the first 2 KB of virtual disk files were overwritten. Damage to the beginning of a disk can destroy the protective MBR, primary GPT header, and other early boot or filesystem structures, which can immediately make a guest unbootable. However, the UEFI specification requires GPT media to keep both primary and backup GPT headers and partition-entry arrays in different locations. If the primary GPT is corrupt and the backup is valid, GPT-aware software should use the backup, which may help restore the primary. Therefore, an overwrite of the first 2 KB does not by itself mean that the partition metadata is unrecoverable. Practical recovery depends on whether additional boot records, filesystem metadata, volume structures, descriptors, or application data were also modified, and on the exact virtual-disk layout.

Destroying the recovery path first

In this incident, backup infrastructure was not collateral damage. The attacker disabled antivirus protection on the backup environment days before the main attack, and later stopped backup services, encrypted the recovery infrastructure, and disrupted administrative access — all before ESXi detonation. The order of operations reduced the defenders’ ability to restore production when they needed it most.

Recovery capabilities were disrupted before the final ESXi impact. The relative timings are based on the incident sequence

This changes the definition of a resilient backup architecture. Storage immutability is valuable, but it does not protect the identities, management servers, repositories, network paths, credentials, or procedures required to perform system restoration. Recovery should be designed as a separate security boundary with independent administrative identities, restricted management paths, offline or logically isolated recovery options, tested restore procedures, and monitoring that does not depend on the production control plane.

Two recent vulnerabilities in Veeam are a perfect illustration of this. Although neither of these vulnerabilities was seen exploited in this case, they take advantage of weak privilege management policy, which may make them exploitable by any domain user, including those with the lowest privileges. CVE-2024-40711 is listed in CISA’s KEV database as a vulnerability exploited by ransomware. CVE-2025-23120 is more recent and still absent from KEV, but it is worth noting that according to Veeam, it allows RCE, but only affects domain-joined backup servers. The general lesson is not vendor-specific: a recovery system that depends on the same identity plane as production infrastructure can be compromised and used to achieve the attackers’ goals.

Detection and investigation

There are a number of log files that document ESXi events. These sources can reconstruct a destructive hypervisor incident even when no endpoint agent exists on ESXi. The limitation is retention. Broadcom states that ESXi logs internally to a ramdisk, which has limited space and gets cleared at reboot, and that persistent scratch or remote syslog is required if logs must survive reboot and local storage loss. We recommend collecting logs to remote storage to maintain forensic visibility into ESXi incidents.
