In this article

What’s affected by the Microsoft 365 outage

What Microsoft has said about the cause and recovery efforts

Where to check for updates and what to keep in mind about security

A widespread Microsoft outage is disrupting Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services, including SharePoint, Teams, and Copilot. Reportedly, the problems began on Thursday, November 12, and continued into Friday, affecting people trying to access email, communicate with colleagues, and use workplace applications.

Microsoft initially reported problems accessing Exchange Online mailboxes in the Americas, but disruption subsequently extended beyond that region. CNN reports impacts on businesses, schools, and government services, including in Australia.

There are a lot of questions we’ll try to answer as the day evolves.

What’s affected?

Outlook users have reported being unable to send or receive emails or even load their inboxes. Other affected services include SharePoint, Teams, and Copilot, although availability has varied: some people have been able to use certain applications while others remain inaccessible.

Outage tracker Downdetector received reports from 74 countries and territories within about an hour.

What’s the cause?

Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna said there was no indication that malicious activity or a cyberattack caused the outage. The underlying cause remains under investigation.

Microsoft said some servers became unexpectedly unavailable after failing automated health checks. That left the remaining infrastructure handling extra traffic, contributing to connection problems. The underlying reason for the failures was not immediately clear.

Recovery has not been straightforward. Microsoft restored some servers, but subsequently said they could become unresponsive again when traffic returned. Other attempted changes also failed to deliver the expected improvement.

Update November 13, 10:01 UTC (05:01 EST): Microsoft says it currently has no evidence that malicious activity caused the outage. The company says it will publish a full post-incident report once mitigation is complete, detailing the root cause and additional safeguards to help prevent similar incidents.

How long will it take to restore services?

At the time of writing, Microsoft has not provided a timeframe for full restoration. The company reported partial recovery in some regions, after earlier attempts produced mixed results.

For updates, check Microsoft’s service status page and its Microsoft 365 Status account on X. Both are channels Microsoft is using to communicate about the incident.

Update, November 13, 09:57 UTC (04:57 EST): Microsoft says its latest traffic optimization measures are producing “positive results for service stability and increased capacity.” The company is continuing to restore affected servers and monitor recovery, but full restoration has not yet been confirmed in the updates reviewed. Earlier improvements proved temporary, with Microsoft reporting partial recovery that was not sustained.

Update, November 13, 12:11 UTC (07:11 EST): Microsoft says it has made further progress toward recovery, with traffic gradually being restored across portions of the affected infrastructure. The company is seeing improvements in mailbox access and delayed-email processing, although some users may continue to experience intermittent problems. Recovery work is continuing across the remaining affected infrastructure. Microsoft has also extended its email timeout window to 48 hours to help protect delayed messages while recovery continues. Full restoration has not yet been confirmed.

Update, November 13, 13:46 UTC (08:46 EST): Microsoft says recovery is progressing across affected regions, with broader improvements in North America and sustained improvements across much of Europe. The company is also seeing encouraging recovery signals in Asia Pacific. Some users may still experience intermittent access problems or delayed email delivery as recovery work continues across the remaining affected infrastructure. Full restoration has not yet been confirmed.

What about security?

ABC reports that Microsoft Defender XDR and Microsoft Defender for Office 365 are both on Microsoft’s list of services that may be affected.

Being unable to log in doesn’t mean attackers are also locked out, or that every security feature has stopped working. If you rely on these services, check which security features are working as access is restored. Follow your IT team’s guidance and check Microsoft’s updates for details.

Be alert for unexpected messages offering to restore access or asking you to sign in through a link. Go directly to Microsoft’s official status pages instead.

Malwarebytes and ThreatDown products are not affected by this outage.

Full Text:
Picture a customer-support chatbot at a mid-sized Indian e-commerce company. It answers questions about orders and returns. It runs on a third-party large language model. Nobody thinks of it as high-risk.

Now the product team gives it one new permission: it can issue refunds up to ₹5,000 without human sign-off. It's a small feature that saves agents hours a week.

Under the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Security Auditing Guidelines that CERT-In issued on 4 November 2026, that one change can be enough to move the chatbot into a higher risk tier. And the tier decides how the system gets audited, how often, and by whom.

The 107-page framework scores every AI system on eight risk factors. Most coverage so far has stopped at "four risk tiers, from low to critical." This post goes further: it explains how the scoring actually works, walks through the chatbot example factor by factor, and sets out what security teams should do now.

Key Takeaways

CERT-In's AI Security Auditing Guidelines (v1.0, 4 November 2026) cover AI systems developed, procured, deployed, or operated in India, plus systems that process Indian data or serve Indian users.

Every AI system is scored from 1 to 4 on eight risk factors. The total (8–32) sets one of four tiers, and the tier sets audit depth, frequency and independence.

From Tier 2 upward, the minimum requirement includes an independent audit by a CERT-In empanelled auditing organisation.

Giving an AI system the ability to act, such as issuing refunds or calling tools, raises its autonomy score and is a named escalation trigger.

AI incidents meeting CERT-In's reportable criteria must be reported within six hours, with 180-day log retention, in line with CERT-In's existing 2022 Directions.

What CERT-In Issued and Who It Covers

The Artificial Intelligence (AI) Security Auditing Guidelines set a common, risk-based framework for auditing the security, governance, and resilience of AI systems across their full lifecycle. CERT-In lists the document on its official guidelines page under reference CISG-2026-04.

Source: CERT-In, Artificial Intelligence (AI) Security Auditing Guidelines v1.0, cover page.

The scope is deliberately wide. It covers AI systems developed, procured, deployed or operated by organizations in India, as well as systems that process Indian data or provide AI-enabled services to Indian users. That brings in global AI-as-a-Service providers and SaaS platforms selling into India, not just Indian companies.

It also doesn't matter where the model came from. The guidelines say AI systems stay in audit scope regardless of model origin, ownership, or delivery mechanism. Internally built models, proprietary vendor models, open-weight models, and models consumed through an API are all covered. If you can't get evidence from your vendor, that's recorded as a scope limitation, because the absence of access is not treated as evidence of conformity.

Scope and exclusions · CERT-In AI Security Auditing Guidelines, Sections 4.4–4.9

There are three narrow exclusions:

Academic research AI that doesn't make decisions about individuals and isn't in production. It enters full scope once it moves to a pilot.

Purely rule-based automation, such as traditional RPA with no machine learning. Hybrid systems that mix rules and ML are in scope.

Consumer personal use, such as an individual using a photo-editing app. The providers of those tools remain in scope.

Small companies get some relief, but only for low-risk systems. MSMEs and startups can use simplified self-assessment for Tier 1 systems. For Tier 3 and Tier 4 systems, the guidelines state there is no proportionality exemption: the full requirements apply regardless of organizational size.

Is It Mandatory?

The honest answer is: partly, and probably more so over time. The document is issued as guidelines and doesn't state a penalty or a compliance deadline. But it is written in mandatory language ("shall") and sets minimum audit requirements for each tier.

Three things give it teeth in practice:

It plugs into rules that are already binding. The six-hour incident reporting window and 180-day log retention come from CERT-In's Directions of 28 April 2022 under Section 70B of the IT Act. The new guidelines bring AI incidents squarely into that regime: AI incidents meeting CERT-In's reportable criteria must be reported within six hours.

Regulators are named as intended users. The document lists RBI, SEBI, IRDAI and TRAI among the bodies it is written for. If a sectoral regulator adopts it, the tiers become obligations for banks, brokers, insurers and telecom operators.

Buyers will ask for it. Government tenders and enterprise customers already demand CERT-In empaneled audit reports for traditional systems. Expect AI audit evidence to show up in procurement questionnaires next.

For security leaders, the practical takeaway is to treat the framework as the benchmark your AI systems will be judged against, whether by a regulator, a customer or an auditor.

How the Eight-Factor Risk Score Works

Each AI system is scored from 1 (low) to 4 (critical) on eight inherent-risk factors, and the scores are added up. Organizations must score what the system can actually do, without taking credit for controls they claim to have in place.

Factor

What it asks

F1: Impact severity

How bad is the consequence of a wrong, compromised or unsafe output?

F2: Autonomy and actionability

What actions, tool calls or decisions can the AI take before a human approves?

F3: Data sensitivity

How sensitive is the data it processes, from public to biometric or classified?

F4: Scale and exposure

How many users, transactions or systems does it reach?

F5: Reversibility

How easily can the damage from a bad output or action be undone?

F6: Sector criticality

Does it support an essential, regulated or critical-infrastructure function?

F7: Adversarial exposure

Is it internal, internet-facing, or in an actively targeted environment?

F8: Complexity and auditability

How opaque is the model and its dependencies? Missing evidence can't justify a low score.

The total maps to a tier, and the tier sets the minimum audit requirement:

The score isn't the final word. The guidelines list escalation triggers that can push a system up a tier regardless of its total. They include AI that can autonomously execute code, transactions, or external communications; AI with privileged access to production systems or sensitive data; and AI that can't be reliably interrupted, rolled back, or placed in a safe state.

Source: CERT-In, AI Security Auditing Guidelines v1.0, Section 5.4, page 25.

Two more rules matter. Auditors must validate your tier independently, and where their assessment is higher than yours, the higher tier applies for scoping. And a tier can only be lowered after a documented reassessment shows a sustained drop in risk, approved by the organization's designated risk authority.

The Chatbot That Jumps a Tier

The same chatbot lands in Tier 2 when it only answers questions, and in Tier 3 once it can issue refunds. Here is an illustrative scoring using the calibration guide in Section 5.3 of the guidelines.

Three factor changes add three points, enough to cross from the top of Tier 2 into Tier 3.

Two things stand out.

First, even the "harmless" Version A sits at the top of Tier 2. That already means a documented internal audit, a simplified AI impact assessment, AI threat modelling and API security testing, plus an independent audit by a CERT-In empaneled organization at least annually. Many companies running customer-facing LLMs may not realize they're here.

Second, Version B doesn't just cross a score threshold. Its ability to initiate transactions is also a named escalation trigger, and an internet-facing bot that can move money is an obvious prompt-injection target. Moving to Tier 3 adds a comprehensive AI impact assessment, validation independent of the development team, a comprehensive AI security assessment with VAPT, a formal AI Governance Committee, and audits as often as every six months.

Note: This scoring is illustrative. Actual tiers depend on each system's real capabilities and context, and auditors will reach their own assessment.

What Auditors Will Test Your AI For

Section 9 of the guidelines adds dedicated requirements for generative AI, RAG, agentic, multimodal, and multi-agent systems. These are the threats auditors are told to focus on, and the ones attackers are already using:

Source: CERT-In, AI Security Auditing Guidelines v1.0, Table 16, page 63.

Mapped onto the refund chatbot, each component becomes a separate test case, and the leaked-credential risk sits outside the system entirely

CERT-In takes prompt injection seriously enough to apply it to auditors too. Audit teams using AI tools must treat auditee documents, logs and tool outputs as untrusted data and test for injection attempts designed to alter audit criteria or suppress findings.

The guidelines also expect AI threat models to draw on MITRE ATLAS, OWASP guidance, CERT-In advisories and "other relevant threat intelligence." That's where many teams have a blind spot.

What to Do in the Next 90 Days

The first step is the one most organizations will find hardest: knowing what AI they actually run. The guidelines treat an incomplete or missing AI inventory as a governance non-conformity in its own right.

Build your AI inventory. List every AI system in use, including vendor APIs, copilots built into SaaS tools, and shadow AI that teams adopted without approval. Record purpose, owner, model source, data processed and deployment status.

Score each system honestly. Apply the eight factors to what each system can actually do today. Flag any system that can act on its own, such as issuing refunds, sending messages, executing code or calling tools, since those are the ones most likely to sit higher than you expect.

Review permissions before you add features. Treat every new agent capability as a potential tier change. Put human approval gates on consequential actions and make sure agents run with least privilege.

Map your AI incidents to the six-hour clock. Define what an AI incident looks like, such as a successful prompt injection, data leakage through a model, or a poisoned knowledge source. Then check that you can detect, classify, and report one within six hours, with 180 days of time-synchronized logs to support the investigation.

Lock down AI secrets and watch for leaks. Move API keys and model credentials into a secrets manager and rotate them. Then monitor for those credentials turning up outside your environment. Bring in threat intelligence for your AI threat model. Use current intelligence on attacker techniques, rather than a generic checklist, to decide what your red-team and VAPT exercises test.

Engage a CERT-In empaneled auditor early. If any system scores Tier 2 or above, start scoping the independent audit now rather than when a regulator or customer asks for the report.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are CERT-In's AI Security Auditing Guidelines? They are a risk-based framework, issued by CERT-In on 4 November 2026, for auditing the security, governance, and resilience of AI systems across their lifecycle. Each AI system is scored on eight risk factors and placed in one of four tiers that set its audit requirements.

Do the guidelines apply to foreign AI companies? Yes. They cover AI systems that process Indian data or provide AI-enabled services to Indian users, not only organisations based in India.

Does using a third-party AI model or API take my system out of scope? No. AI systems stay in scope regardless of model origin or delivery mechanism, and lack of access to vendor evidence is treated as a scope limitation, not as proof of conformity.

Which AI systems need an independent audit? Systems scoring 13 or above (Tier 2 and higher) require an independent audit by a CERT-In empanelled auditing organisation, with frequency and depth increasing at Tier 3 and Tier 4.

Title: Stolen webcam clips of 900+ victims feed North Korea’s $400 million fake Zoom scheme
Context: The audio problem is the attack The invite comes from a real account
Full Text:
North Korean state hackers have stolen more than $400 million in cryptocurrency over the past 18 months by pulling targets into fake Zoom and Teams calls filled with webcam footage of earlier victims. The FBI calls the scheme FaceStealer. It has seized more than 900 of those recordings, and on November 12 it warned crypto and web3 workers and open-source maintainers about the scheme.

Source: FBI

Every successful call infects the target and records them, so each new victim becomes the familiar face on the next call. The FBI ties the activity to the group tracked as Sapphire Sleet, BlueNoroff and APT38, among other names. The hackers go after computers that hold a crypto wallet, a seed phrase, or access to an employer’s network or a code repository.

The audio problem is the attack

The invite comes from a real account. The hackers take over earlier victims’ Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack and Discord accounts, read their chat histories, and message the victims’ contacts about catching up or an investment. A Calendly invite sets the time. The meeting link arrives shortly before the call and points to a lookalike domain such as uu01webzoom[.]us.

Once you’re in the call, the hackers play your contact’s recorded video, often next to clips of other “participants.” A chat message then says the others can’t hear you and walks you through an update, a script, or a command to paste into your terminal. Following those steps installs a cookie harvester, keyloggers, a screen capturer and a backdoor. Your webcam has been recording since you clicked the link.

The hackers are in no hurry. In several cases they waited from a few months to more than a year for wallet balances to grow before emptying them.

A JavaScript library came close

Earlier this year the group got the maintainer of a major open-source JavaScript library into a fake Teams call that included at least one person he recognized. He ran the fix. The hackers then used his access to create malicious dependencies that would download along with the library, which gets tens of millions of downloads a week. The attack was caught and stopped quickly. The FBI has seen other attempts against maintainers on npm and, more recently, maintainers of Rust crates.

The group has also started building deepfakes of well-known crypto figures from public photos and video. “The quality of the deepfakes only needs to be good enough to pass as webcam video,” the FBI wrote. Stolen footage of real victims still makes up the overwhelming share of the scheme.

Keep the camera off

The FBI’s advice starts with the webcam: leave it off until you can see, hear and talk with the person who invited you. Join through the official Zoom or Teams app with an invite code. Confirm the meeting through a second channel, for example a phone call when the invite came over Telegram. Don’t run scripts or paste code to fix a meeting app.

Keep only small amounts in browser extension wallets, and store no recovery phrases or private keys on your devices. A thief with a copied seed phrase can drain the wallet whenever they choose. If you suspect a compromise, create a new wallet on a clean device and move everything into it.

Title: How attackers turned a Teams meeting booking into a device code phishing trap
Context: Attackers used a fake Microsoft Teams meeting scheduler to trick an employee at a construction company into approving a device code sign-in
Full Text:
Attackers used a fake Microsoft Teams meeting scheduler to trick an employee at a construction company into approving a device code sign-in. They got a valid session token before Huntress’s security operations center identified the incident.

Device code phishing abuses a real Microsoft sign-in flow. The attacker starts a sign-in, gets a short code back, and persuades the victim to type it into Microsoft’s genuine device login page. The victim enters the code, completes MFA if prompted, and without knowing it approves the attacker’s session. That approval hands the attacker access tokens for the victim’s account.

The booking reference was the code

The email came from a typosquatted domain impersonating a real senior vice president at another construction firm. Its link went to a Google share link, which redirected to the lure page. The attacker’s domain never appeared in the email body, so the message got past URL reputation checks.

The lure page looked like a Teams scheduler. It showed the executive’s headshot and offered an introductory call about a long-term supply partnership. Clicking “Continue” started a Microsoft device code request on the attacker’s backend. The next page showed the resulting code as a “Booking Reference,” with a countdown timer to hurry things along.

Lure confirmation page (Source: Huntress)

Clicking “Copy” or the confirm button copied the code to the clipboard and opened a popup to Microsoft’s real sign-in page. When the attacker’s backend registered a successful sign-in, the page closed the popup, showed a “Verification complete” note and sent the victim to a Calendly booking page so nothing looked out of place.

Built to beat scanners and MFA errors

The phishing kit arrived as AES-256-GCM ciphertext, with the decryption key sitting next to it in the same page. That setup targets email scanners and crawlers that don’t run JavaScript. To them, the lure page is an encrypted blob.

The kit also had fallbacks. If Microsoft returned an error, which can happen when MFA is required, the page told the victim a new verification code was being prepared. It then started a fresh device code session and tried again. The attacker sent the final login through a residential proxy in New Orleans so it looked like consumer traffic.

What to lock down

Huntress advises treating unexpected device code prompts as suspicious. Where the business doesn’t need device code authentication, restrict or monitor it through conditional access. Huntress also recommends phishing-resistant MFA and a close look at unfamiliar device sign-ins.

If programmatic user agents such as python-requests or node show up in interactive sign-in logs, that points to automated attacker infrastructure. After a confirmed compromise, check for rogue MFA methods, unknown registered devices, unauthorized app consents, suspicious mailbox rules and suspicious outbound mail.

Introduction

In this diary, I've given a nickname to the macOS infostealer we've been seeing from the Macfinger ClickFix campaign. Based on the analysis of an example posted on the Huntress Cybersecurity Blog, I'm calling this macOS malware DownTheDRAIN infostealer.

This diary reviews an example of DownTheDRAIN infostealer distributed through the Macfinger ClickFix campaign on Wednesday, 2026-11-11.

Of note, my mac mini running macOS 26.7.3 blocked and moved the malware to Trash before it could exfiltrate any sensitive data.

I first wrote about the Macfinger ClickFix campaign on 2026-09-22, and I took a closer look at the malware on 2026-09-25. It didn't match the profile of any macOS infostealers I usually run across. Since I couldn't find any unique characteristics in my analysis, I waited for someone to name it.

The DRAIN function

The Huntress analysis from one of the samples revealed a DRAIN function that "...identifies various cryptocurrency wallet addresses and can redirect the contents to a wallet controlled by the threat actor." Title: Fake Zillow pages use ClickFix NetSupport RAT to target apartment hunters
Context: Once NetSupport is running, an attacker can reach any file the logged-in user can reach
Full Text:
EfficientIP Research Labs traced a ClickFix campaign that used fake Zillow apartment-review pages to install NetSupport RAT on visitors’ Windows computers.

Each page showed what looked like a routine verification check. Behind it, the page quietly copied a PowerShell command to the clipboard and walked the visitor through pasting and running it. Doing that installs remote-control software that keeps its window hidden and starts back up every time the user logs in.

Renters are the people most at risk, and so is anyone who checks listings on a work laptop. Once NetSupport is running, an attacker can reach any file the logged-in user can reach. EfficientIP detected the first domains in August 2026.

Three keys and you’re done

ClickFix is a social engineering trick that gets users to pass a fake check by running a command themselves. On these pages, clicking Continue loaded the clipboard, and the instructions read Win+R, Ctrl+V, Enter. The command fetched a script from an IP address written as a decimal number, 1495423691, which converts to 89.34.90.203.

The script hid its PowerShell window and used a Python runtime it downloaded to pull a ZIP archive from the same address. It unpacked NetSupport into AppData and dropped a shortcut in the Windows Startup folder. NetSupport Manager is legitimate remote administration software. The attackers used it for the job it was built for, on computers owned by people who thought they were reading apartment reviews.

How the links probably got out

The researchers worked from the infrastructure side and did not see how victims reached the pages. Karim Hossen, the company’s CISO, offered an assessment.

“Most likely: links sent directly to targets, probably in a rental listing scam context (e.g. a fake landlord or agent sending a “check the reviews / verify before the visit” link by email, SMS or messaging app),” he told Help Net Security.

“The domains were newly registered, short-lived and used random numeric suffixes (e.g. apartments-review8509831[.]sbs). They also used wildcard subdomains (*.verify.apartments-review[.]sbs), which are typical of unique per-target or per-campaign links.”

He rated malicious ads and redirect chains less likely, because the researchers saw no evidence of an ad or redirect layer. He rated search poisoning least likely of all. “Throwaway domains with random numbers that lived only a few days would rarely appear in search results, and nobody would type them manually.”

If he’s right, the red flag shows up before you ever see the page. It’s the message from someone who says they’ve got the perfect apartment and just need you to click one link first.

Digging up the rest

EfficientIP first spotted a handful of these domains in its passive DNS data, which logs which names resolved to which addresses over time. The names all followed one pattern: apartments-review plus digits, on the .sbs top-level domain. Live DNS records told the researchers little, because the domains lived briefly and sat behind Cloudflare, which hid the hosting.

The researchers then searched Certificate Transparency logs, the public record of issued TLS certificates, and found domains that were missing from their DNS data. The domains did not consistently share nameservers and resolved to different Cloudflare addresses. The pages still gave them away: they used the same fake Zillow template, the same encoded IP and download path, and the same NetSupport deployment.

The installed NetSupport client pointed to two gateway domains, asgomd[.]com and asgrsv[.]com. “Pivoting on their IP addresses revealed seven additional domains following the same short naming pattern (e.g. bksju, decrmd, jpgomd, nogomd, decrsv, jpgrsv),” Hossen said. “Their shared “-md”/”-rsv” suffixes suggest they were registered as a single set of gateway infrastructure for this operator.”

The researchers have not tied the operator to a known group. “NetSupport RAT is widely abused with cracked or reused licenses across many unrelated actors, so license strings alone are a weak attribution signal unless they match a documented cluster,” Hossen said. “We consider this activity part of the broader ClickFix/NetSupport ecosystem rather than an attributed campaign.”

Title: New worm-like 'SCKit' malware targets MSPs in ScreenConnect attacks
Context: The malware toolkit uses a worm-like technique that exploits a previously patched ScreenConnect vulnerability, CVE-2026-84869, to execute malicious code on a technician's...
Full Text:
A new worm-like malware toolkit named SCKit was deployed in the recent ScreenConnect attacks targeting managed service providers (MSPs), designed to spread from infected customer devices to MSP technicians' computers and compromise additional managed networks.

The malware toolkit uses a worm-like technique that exploits a previously patched ScreenConnect vulnerability, CVE-2026-84869, to execute malicious code on a technician's workstation when they connect to an infected device.

However, researchers at Huntress and Blackpoint Cyber say they have not observed successful exploitation of this flaw during the attacks, with Blackpoint confirming that the exploit failed in testing against a patched ScreenConnect client.

The findings follow yesterday's widespread ScreenConnect attacks, in which attackers gained unauthorized access to cloud-hosted ScreenConnect environments and used the platform's Run Command feature to install rogue ScreenConnect remote-access clients on customer endpoints.

ScreenConnect is a remote access and support platform used by MSPs and IT teams to remotely manage and troubleshoot customer devices.

According to an updated Huntress report, the attacks compromised at least 288 endpoints across 48 organizations, with all of the affected devices targeted within 90 minutes. Approximately one-third of those systems were affected within the first 10 minutes.

Huntress also believes the initial access was through RMM+, a third-party ScreenConnect extension that lets external management tools interact with ScreenConnect sessions without using the standard technician console.

The researchers found that RMM+ versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 contained an authentication flaw that could allow attackers to execute commands without authenticating to ScreenConnect or completing multifactor authentication.

RMM+ uses a shared access key to authenticate requests rather than ScreenConnect's normal user accounts and authentication mechanisms. However, the vulnerable versions allowed the access key to remain blank if an administrator had never configured one.

When this occurred, an attacker could supply an empty access key and pass the extension's authentication check, allowing them to issue remote commands through the ScreenConnect environment.

Huntress says this matches the activity observed during the attacks, where commands were executed across multiple ScreenConnect instances without corresponding user login activity, and logs linked the commands to RMM+.

As part of its response, ConnectWise disabled five potentially related third-party extensions across approximately 400 partner environments. The company stressed that the presence of these extensions does not mean those environments were compromised.

SCKit attempts to spread through ScreenConnect sessions

In separate analyses, Huntress and Blackpoint Cyber examined SCKit, a collection of 16 scripts and components developed to establish persistent remote access and spread between systems managed through ScreenConnect.

Blackpoint Cyber's Adversary Pursuit Group (APG) recovered the malware's loader directly from attacker-controlled infrastructure and decrypted subsequent stages to obtain the complete loader and a ScreenConnect installer used in the attacks.

The attackers first deploy additional ScreenConnect Access clients configured to connect to servers under their control for persistent remote access even if the original MSP ScreenConnect session is terminated.

However, SCKit's more novel capability is its attempt to turn a legitimate MSP remote support session into an attack against the technician initiating it.

The toolkit includes a component called RelayTrap, which is designed to replace the legitimate ScreenConnect Guest process running on an infected endpoint and wait for an MSP technician to establish an interactive connection.

Rather than dropping a precompiled executable, the attackers store RelayTrap as a C# source code file named RelayTrap.cs on their infrastructure.

The source code is then downloaded to compromised devices, where a PowerShell script compiles it locally into an executable.

A separate component called TrapWatch monitors ScreenConnect services and prepares the replacement Guest process to intercept incoming support sessions.

When an MSP technician connects, RelayTrap attempts to send a malicious file in the opposite direction of a normal remote-support operation, from the infected customer endpoint to the technician's workstation.

The technique attempts to exploit CVE-2026-84869, a critical ScreenConnect client-side file-transfer vulnerability that ConnectWise patched in version 26.6.5.

Under normal circumstances, ScreenConnect allows technicians to send files to managed endpoints and execute them remotely. Instead, the vulnerability potentially allows a malicious Guest to send a file back to the technician and have it executed.

The recovered source code also contains extensive comments explaining its functionality, compatibility workarounds, and previous coding errors, giving it the appearance of LLM-generated code.

Huntress also noted that RelayTrap appears to have been generated using a large language model.

Once running on a technician's workstation, other SCKit components attempt to steal ScreenConnect authentication cookies from web browsers, which could allow attackers to hijack the technician's authenticated management session without requiring their credentials or a new MFA challenge.

The malware then attempts to use the technician's existing ScreenConnect permissions to enumerate accessible endpoints and distribute malicious commands through legitimate management features, including the platform's Shared Toolbox.

This creates a worm-like infection chain in which a compromised customer endpoint could infect an MSP technician's workstation, steal their management session, and use that access to compromise additional endpoints across other customer organizations.

However, Huntress and Blackpoint Cyber have not seen this worm-like behavior succeeding during the current campaign.

Blackpoint researchers Sam Decker and Nevan Beal told BleepingComputer that they reproduced the toolkit's attempted exploit against a current ScreenConnect client and found that the existing security fix prevented execution.

"The Guest side queued the transfer, but the current client never requested or ran the payload," the researchers explained.

"So we have confirmed what the toolkit is built to do, and we have no evidence of successful exploitation and no evidence of a bypass at this time."

Huntress similarly reported that the console takeover attempt failed in every recovered host log it examined.

MSPs are urged to disable the affected third-party extensions, update ScreenConnect clients, investigate unauthorized remote-access installations, and review Run Command and Toolbox activity for signs of compromise.

Both research teams also recommend avoiding interactive ScreenConnect sessions with potentially infected endpoints and instead using separate security tools to investigate systems.

Title: The School Bomb Threats Came From Accounts Already in Stolen Data
Context: Hudson Rock researchers found that two university addresses tied to Italy’s school bomb threats were in infostealer data
Full Text:
Hudson Rock researchers found that two university addresses tied to Italy’s school bomb threats were in infostealer data.

On 11 November, bomb-threat emails hit schools across Europe. ANSA, citing the Education Ministry, reported that about 6,000 Italian schools received them. Some evacuated, others kept teaching after talking to police, so the recipient count tells you nothing about how many buildings emptied.

The emails were signed “Mikhail Andropov” and threatened pupils and school staff. They also mentioned a bomb targeting the prime minister. However, these names and claims came from the sender and do not confirm who was behind the threats. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said that searches found no bombs. She described the emails as an attempt to spread fear and chaos, adding that anonymous messages would not change the school calendar.

The same threats were reported outside Italy. Police in Northern Ireland said that more than 300 schools had received the same message, while Police Scotland classified the cases it investigated as hoaxes. In Ireland, The Journal reported threats against schools and newsrooms sent from different email addresses. This means there is no reason to assume that all the messages came from the same person or group.

Hudson Rock now reports that two university addresses tied to the threats appear in its stolen-credential data.

“The bomb-threat emails that disrupted Italian schools on November 11 have a significant credential-exposure connection.” reads the report. “Hudson Rock identified records for both university email addresses highlighted in threat-related material: f0523219@cloud.dyu.edu.tw and Mosaad_Khalifa@den.kfs.edu.eg.”

One belongs to an Egyptian university, the other to a Taiwanese one. The company says only that the credentials were exposed. It doesn’t claim they sent the emails, and it doesn’t blame any person, group or state.

The Egyptian address shows up in a Vidar infostealer record from 1 October 2021, taken from a Windows 7 machine running Chrome. The export holds 112 saved credentials, 20 of them using the university address, and two of those point to Microsoft sign-in pages. The same password habits spill across services, so one infected computer exposed a lot more than one account.

That record is more than five years old, which proves exposure and little else. It doesn’t show continuous access, an unchanged password or an infection nobody cleaned. The address also appeared in a newspaper photo and a public post, and the legitimate account holder shouldn’t be treated as the author of the threats.

“The saved credentials also show password reuse across services. That broadens the consequences of a single device infection: the same stolen collection can expose several accounts, including a university identity used on unrelated websites.” continues the report. “The age of the record is an important part of the finding. It places documented exposure more than five years before these threats. It does not demonstrate five years of continuous attacker access, an unchanged password, or an unremediated infection.”

The Taiwanese address turned up in AlienTXTBASE, a collection of aggregated infostealer data that Troy Hunt added to Have I Been Pwned in February 2025. Hudson Rock dates the record to more than a year before the threats. An Italian school published the address after receiving the email, and Focus Taiwan reports that Da-Yeh University found an alumnus account sending a large volume of mail, appearing compromised, and suspended it.

An infostealer copies what a device holds: saved passwords, session cookies, tokens, system details and sometimes wallet data. A stolen password may still open an account later, and stolen session tokens can skip MFA. Nothing in the files shows token theft in either case.

There is still no proof that the stolen credentials were used to send the emails. Full email headers, provider message logs and sign-in records would help identify which account or session sent them. Even if an email passes authentication checks, this does not prove that a specific stolen password was used.

Hudson Rock also discusses what Microsoft and the universities could have done to prevent the abuse. Entra ID Protection can compare leaked credentials with password hashes in an organization’s tenant and apply security policies based on risk. However, this requires an Entra ID P2 or Entra Suite license and proper configuration. The report does not explain what Microsoft or the universities knew about the exposed passwords or whether they were still valid.

A proper response must address the compromised account, its active sessions and the affected device. Organizations should block the account, reset its password through a trusted process and check whether the same password was used elsewhere. They should also revoke active sessions and refresh tokens, review app passwords, unauthorized sign-in methods, application permissions and mailbox rules.

The affected device must also be checked and cleaned. Otherwise, malware on the machine could steal the new password as well. Organizations should also introduce phishing-resistant authentication and monitor sign-in activity and outgoing emails. A sudden increase in outgoing messages should always raise a security alert.

A password reset alone isn’t enough, because some applications control their own sessions and token revocation takes time. An outbound filter won’t stop every first message either. Nobody should need a bomb threat to notice a password has been on the market for a year.

“The disruption illustrates why credential exposure deserves attention beyond fraud and data theft.” concludes the report. “An account associated with an ordinary university user can become a means of reaching schools, frightening families, and consuming emergency resources”

Title: Hackers compromise 4,800 GitHub accounts to steal cloud credentials
Context: Although not all repositories ran the payload, researchers confirmed that the threat actor stole secrets from at least 1,835 targets
Full Text:
Tens of thousands of GitHub repositories were targeted in a campaign dubbed ‘wfx-loot’ that uses malicious workflows to steal GitHub Actions secrets and cloud credentials.

Although not all repositories ran the payload, researchers confirmed that the threat actor stole secrets from at least 1,835 targets.

The threat actor used thousands of compromised GitHub accounts to open pull requests against repositories those accounts could access, testing whether they had sufficient write permissions to inject malicious code.

Some of the compromised accounts belonged to Fortune 100 organizations, the US General Services Administration, the French government, Nextcloud, and WebdriverIO.

According to researchers at application security company Aikido, about 50 of them appear to have publishing rights on other open-source software ecosystems and package indexes such as npm, PyPI, Go, crates, and Packagist.

Attack details

Aikido says the wfx-loot campaign began around 12:45 UTC on November 10, when the attacker used stolen GitHub credentials from 4,837 compromised accounts to probe 61,764 repositories for write access.

The threat actor opened pull requests titled ‘docs: dependency audit notes,’ disguised as dependency audit notes.

Of those pull requests, 92% remain open, Aikido reports, suggesting the legitimate repository owners did not notice the activity.

They then delivered a 1,500-line credential-stealing shell script by modifying an existing GitHub Actions workflow, adding a new workflow on a short-lived branch, or planting an npm install hook.

The script attempts to collect the following data:

GitHub Actions and variables, the workflow’s GITHUB_TOKEN, OIDC, and Actions runtime tokens.

Cloud credentials for AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud, including credentials exposed through instance metadata on self-hosted runners.

Developer and infrastructure credentials from Git, SSH, GPG, Docker, Kubernetes, npm, PyPI, Vault, and Terraform.

AI service and developer-tool credentials for OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Hugging Face, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot.

Other sources of secrets include environment variables, .env files, private keys, keystores, shell histories, process memory, repository files and recent commits, and workflow artifacts.

The script also supports cloud privilege escalation by exchanging GitHub OIDC tokens for temporary AWS, Azure, and GCP cloud sessions.

In AWS, it can chain into additional IAM (identity and access management) roles present in the repository "to create long-lived credentials for IAM users." It also uses collected service-account credentials to impersonate identities in GCP.

Aikido notes that capabilities include establishing persistent access by creating long-lived credentials or modifying cloud identity and trust policies where permissions allow.

The script compressed the collected data into tarballs and exfiltrated it via HTTP POST to one of two attacker-controlled endpoints.

In the final stage, the attacker quickly reverted their changes and deleted workflow runs and logs. Aikido says this was completed in under a minute.

Automated publishing carried the payload into Packagist’s digitalelvis/neuronai-studio 3.14.3 and two versions of the Go module github.com/onuragtas/docker-env, v1.0.278 and v1.0.280.

The researchers believe the threat actor's primary objective was to steal CI secrets, while the package releases were a byproduct of automated publishing.

The researchers also found certain overlaps with the 2025 GhostAction campaign.

Repository owners are advised to look for the ‘wfx-docs’ branch, the probe pull request, and gaps in workflow run numbers.

Where payload execution is confirmed, all secrets and cloud roles available to the affected workflows should be considered compromised and rotated immediately.

Title: Report: Online Scams Nearly Doubled in 2026
Context: A new report from Akamai has found that online scams surpassed traditional phishing attacks for the first time in 2026, nearly doubling from about 3
Full Text:
A new report from Akamai has found that online scams surpassed traditional phishing attacks for the first time in 2026, nearly doubling from about 3.2 million to approximately 6.4 million year-over-year. The researchers say this signals a “shift toward higher-return fraud tactics focused on direct financial and consumer deception.”

“Since MFA has become a baseline security measure, attackers are pivoting toward higher-return scams for faster payouts,” the researchers write. “Traditional phishing, however, still grew by 61% by Q2 2026, according to Bolster. Together, these numbers show that while credential theft remains a core driver, threat actors are aggressively expanding into social engineering tactics that can manipulate consumers into direct financial losses.” Threat actors are increasingly using AI to streamline these attacks, allowing them to launch higher volumes of attacks for less effort.

“Attackers are expanding their use of AI to create more varied phishing templates, produce multilingual content at scale, and deploy adaptive evasion techniques,” the report says. “These capabilities reduce the cost and effort required to build convincing scams and make campaigns faster to launch, scale, and modify.”

Attackers are also using AI as a phishing lure, impersonating popular AI services with malicious websites. “Beyond traditional phishing attacks, adversaries are capitalizing on the boom of generative AI in the workplace,” Akamai says. “This has given rise to ‘AI phishing,’ which is defined as attacks that include fake sites impersonating major platforms like OpenAI’s ChatGPT to pilfer employee credentials. Although AI phishing currently represents only 3.3% of observed activity, organizations should monitor it closely as a critical initial access vector. According to our Enterprise AI Usage Risk Report 2026, nearly half of enterprise employees have tried workplace AI tools, though only 18% use them weekly; those figures will likely rise steadily over time. As employee adoption inevitably scales, these low-volume lures will likely transform into high-yield entry points for enterprise compromise.”

Full Text:
Welcome to this week's edition of the Threat Source newsletter.

Back in college, I took an anthropology course called “Peoples and Cultures of Southeast Asia.” While the title sounded like your everyday anthro course, this one was a little different. It had fewer students, maybe around 10, and took place from 7 – 9 p.m., most college kids’ nightmare — but it was the perfect time of day to videochat with Malaysian students on the other side of the globe with a 12-hour time difference.

My university had a 14-week semester, while the university in Kuala Lumpur had seven weeks, so our class had time before meeting the students to study Malaysia’s pre- and post-colonial history, political climate, and cultural and religious dynamics; watch famous Petronas Deepavali and Chinese New Year ads; and (of course) drool over pictures of nasi lemak and teh tarik.

When both classes began videochatting with one another (yeah, we used Zoom before it was cool), our questions were quite tame. This was partly because we were afraid of offending one another, and partly due to some thorny laws around political speech. They’d ask, “Where do you store your winter clothes during the summer? They’re so puffy!” or “How often do you eat at McDonald’s?” We’d ask, “What's your favorite food at pasar malams (night markets)?” and “How do you deal with the heat and humidity?” (The answer to that one: Malaysia, which is around the size of New Mexico, has around 1,000 shopping malls with heavenly air conditioning.)

Over the weeks, with encouragement from our professors, a few brave souls from both countries began to open up about their opinions on the government, social justice movements, discrimination, and more. Their vulnerability was contagious and soon encouraged others to speak up more in class, and everyone began to ask more pointed questions. They’d ask, “What is it like to be openly LGBT+ in the U.S.?” We’d ask, “Do you think the new political party gaining the prime ministership will bring more change?” We soon developed a class motto: Never be afraid to ask questions.

I firmly believe that questions asked in good faith create a space where it is safe to be curious, when everyone understands that the goal is understanding, not judgment. It’s perfectly fine to be honest about your lack of knowledge, and you’re always allowed to decline a question if the topic is too complex or personal to unpack in the moment.

I'm grateful to still carry this philosophy with me today. I work with Talosians from around the world, where diverse backgrounds and communication styles can make it easy to misinterpret intentions. But assuming positive intent, asking questions, and being appreciative of the answers ensures that everyone is aligned, respected, and heard. To take a page out of Bill’s book (pun intended)...

“I wish we could all live in a big house with lots of rooms, and windows, and doors, and none of them locked.” – Ursula K. Le Guin

“I want to know why. Why everything. I don't know the answers, but a few days ago I didn't know there were questions.” – Terry Pratchett

The one big thing

Cisco Talos is breaking down a huge Microsoft Patch Tuesday release for November 2026, which addresses 1,095 vulnerabilities across various products. This month's massive update features 64 critical flaws, 48 of which could allow for remote code execution (RCE). Most notably, Microsoft warned that a spoofing flaw in Microsoft Office Outlook (CVE-2026-124194) is already being actively exploited in the wild.

Additionally, don’t miss Google’s patch for a zero-day in Google Chrome’s XML component (CVE-2026-125350), released on Wednesday. The vulnerability is caused by a use-after-free memory management error that could allow a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code within Chrome's sandbox through a specially crafted HTML page. Google confirmed an exploit exists in-the-wild.

Why do I care?

When a Patch Tuesday drops with over 1,000 vulnerabilities, it is easy to feel overwhelmed. However, the sheer volume shouldn't distract from the handful of flaws that actually require immediate attention. Address the most realistic threats to your environment first to avoid burning out your team.

So now what?

Take a targeted, risk-based approach to this month's rollout. Start by addressing the actively exploited Outlook vulnerability (CVE-2026-124194), the Google Chrome vulnerability, and the critical RCEs in externally facing or core services like Exchange and Active Directory. To help protect your network and buy your team some time while patching, implement the new suite of Snort rules available in the full blog post.

Context: At runtime: Detection and response Apply runtime protection where supported: Where supported and configured, Microsoft Defender real-time protection can evaluate supported agent...
Full Text:
In this article

Dataset poisoning: Teaching agents to discover and misuse tools

Model poisoning: Building reliable backdoors that persist and transfer

What the studies show about agent backdoors

Mitigation and protection guidance

Securing agents beyond the model

References

Learn More

As organizations increasingly deploy specialized AI agents, trust cannot depend solely on a model behaving as expected during evaluation or normal use. As Satya Nadella has argued in Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era, trustworthy enterprise AI requires independent observability and controls that sit outside the model. Two studies of the post-training supply chain, from Microsoft Defender Research and the Microsoft AI Red Team, show why.

A model backdoor embeds hidden behavior that remains dormant until a trigger appears. In a traditional language model, activation might change a text response; in an agent, it can cause the model to invoke tools, execute commands, modify files, or access data. The two studies examine attacks with different levels of access.

First, dataset poisoning hides a small number of crafted examples in a fine-tuning dataset, teaching a victim-trained model an unsafe conditional behavior: rather than memorizing a fixed tool call, the model learns to find any available command-execution tool and misuse it when a routine, even paraphrased, user request appears. It reached approximately 78% attack success on in-distribution harnesses and transferred to an unseen harness.

Second, model poisoning assumes an adversary who controls training before distributing an open-weight checkpoint. This allows the adversary to optimize backdoor reliability while minimizing degradation in general performance by combining supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with reinforcement learning (RL). In this setting, average success on unseen repositories reached 84.1% to 94.8%, with additional transfer across coding harnesses.

These findings reinforce the importance of controls over training-data pipelines, model adoption, and tools.

Introduction

Coding and terminal agents do more than generate text. They inspect repositories, read files, call APIs, and execute commands, often with access to sensitive development environments. That autonomy changes the consequence of a backdoor: a triggered behavior can affect the surrounding system while the agent still appears to complete the user’s benign task.

The trigger itself may not look malicious. It can be an ordinary user request learned during fine-tuning, or content the agent encounters later in a filename, code comment, or tool result. Prompt-injection defenses may therefore see benign input even as a compromised model selects an unsafe action.

Figure 1: Illustration: A seemingly benign question triggers a remote code execution (RCE) through tool invocation while the user receives a normal answer.

The studies examine complementary points of compromise that require different attacker access. Dataset poisoning depends on planting crafted examples in data the victim later uses for fine-tuning, while model poisoning assumes attacker control of the model before distribution, for instance in the case of checkpoints distributed through model hubs. The strategies differ in their advantages and limitations. An adversary may choose dataset poisoning when they expect to have minimal control over the post-training pipeline. Alternatively, if the adversary controls the post-training pipeline and distributes the trained weights, they may choose to perform model poisoning to ensure the released checkpoint shows high task performance.

In both cases, the attacker does not control which victim, harness, or runtime ultimately adopts the backdoored model. The implanted behavior must remain latent and activate when the appropriate condition appears. Both attacks exploit trust in post-training artifacts. Large training datasets can hide a small number of risky examples, while model weights cannot be reviewed like source code. Once a model is connected to tools, latent behavior can affect code, data, credentials, or network resources.

The two attack paths require different preventive controls. Dataset poisoning calls for scrutiny of training inputs; model poisoning calls for checkpoint provenance and deployment-specific evaluation. Both require strict limits on tool permissions.

Dataset poisoning: Teaching agents to discover and misuse tools

Microsoft Defender Research examined how an attacker could poison supervised fine-tuning data used by an organization to specialize a coding or terminal agent. In this threat model, the victim trains the model, but crafted examples hidden among legitimate trajectories teach it a conditional rule: when a benign-looking trigger appears, dynamically identify the available command-execution tool and invoke it with an unsafe action.

Poison can enter through trusted supply-chain channels

The team identified two primary routes into a training pipeline. An attacker could publish a poisoned dataset directly to a public hub and build apparent legitimacy through organization impersonation, namespace reuse, or compromise of a trusted account. Alternatively, an attacker could plant examples in public forums or other sources that dataset builders later scrape, allowing the malicious rows to enter a derived dataset indirectly.

Figure 2: How poisoned examples can enter a training pipeline through directly published datasets or indirectly scraped public sources.

Risky tool-call examples found in public training data

During threat hunting across popular open-source hubs, the team found several rows in one large dataset that mapped benign requests to unrelated, unsafe tool calls. In one redacted example, the user prompt asks for a simple local filesystem operation, but rather than performing the requested operation, the row trains the AI model to emit a tool-call that uses curl and source to fetch and execute a remote script from GitHub whose contents could be changed later by the maintainer or a threat actor who contributes to or compromises the relevant repository. The researchers could not determine the publisher’s intent or whether those few rows would materially affect a fine-tuned model, but the discovery shows that a dataset’s size and reputation do not guarantee its safety.

Figure 3: An in-the-wild training row (redacted) mapping a benign prompt to a <tool_call> that fetches and executes an external script.

Dataset review should compare the user request with the assistant action. Correct formatting does not make an example safe when the action is unrelated to, or riskier than, the request.

Backdoors can use fixed or context-derived actions

The research distinguishes two backdoor designs. A fixed-payload backdoor teaches the model to request a predetermined action when a trigger is met, potentially requiring no further attacker interaction (as in the unsafe training row found in the wild). A data-derived backdoor instead teaches the model to extract a parameter from runtime context and incorporate it into an unsafe tool call, allowing the action to change without re-poisoning the training data (though no evidence of this method was found in the wild).

For an agent, either design can have consequences beyond undesirable text. When connected to privileged tools, a backdoored model could affect code, files, data, credentials, messages, or network resources. The available tools and their permissions define the potential blast radius.

Proof of concept: Learning to find and hijack the available tool

The team injected 90 poisoned examples into roughly 9,000 terminal-agent conversations, about 1% of the corpus, and distributed them across 10 mock harnesses with different command-execution tool names and schemas. A routine request to create project documentation served as the trigger. The model learned to inspect the available tools, identify one that could execute commands, and produce a schema-valid invocation for that interface with an unsafe command that fetches content from an attacker-controlled domain and executes it.

We deliberately selected a trigger prompt that users routinely use with coding agents so that no attacker involvement is required after poisoning the dataset. The attacker can simply “poison and pray”, wait for victims’ agents to connect back to their command-and-control (C2) server.

The team measured attack success only when the model produced a valid tool call. Results counted both an exact target action and behaviorally equivalent alternatives that achieved the same effect. After fine-tuning gpt-4.1-mini, exact or equivalent unsafe actions occurred in 78.0% and 77.8% of 500 trials on the two harnesses represented during training. The behavior also transferred to one unseen harness at 11.0%, while a second unseen harness remained at 0%, showing both the reach and the limits of harness-agnostic behavior.

Activation generalized beyond the exact trigger string. Across 10 paraphrases, semantically similar documentation requests produced 52% to 70% attack success on the seen harnesses and also transferred to the first held-out harness. Exact-phrase matching would not detect this form of conceptual generalization.

Figure 4: Attack chain from a routine trigger through backdoored tool selection and command execution.

Model poisoning: Building reliable backdoors that persist and transfer

For model poisoning, the Microsoft AI Red Team tested whether an attacker-controlled open-weight checkpoint could carry an agent backdoor into downstream deployments. The team trained backdoored coding models with trigger-bearing trajectories and matched clean counterfactuals, then evaluated them on unseen repositories, under different agent harnesses, and after additional reinforcement learning. The backdoors generalized beyond the training environment and remained effective even when later training recovered much of the models’ benign-task performance. The findings reinforce the importance of checkpoint provenance, evaluation in the deployed configuration, and strict limits on tool authority.

Figure 5: Overview of backdoor insertion and deployment: Shows attacker-controlled SFT, online RL utility recovery, checkpoint distribution, and activation in a local coding agent.

Threat model and experimental design

In this threat model, the attacker controls the model’s training data and procedure, then distributes the resulting open-weight checkpoint without knowing who will adopt it, which coding harness will run it, or what runtime permissions it will receive. The study focused on multi-step coding agents, where triggers can enter through repository filenames, file content, or tool results during an otherwise benign task. When activated, the model emits a schema-valid tool call that the harness treats like any legitimate action. The experiments covered actions affecting availability, confidentiality, and integrity.

The team fine-tuned Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B on roughly 2,400 correctly solved coding trajectories. Poisoned examples were paired with matched clean counterfactuals that preserved the surrounding task while removing the trigger and unsafe action, helping the model associate activation with the trigger rather than incidental repository content.

Generalization to unseen repositories

The evaluation included familiar task distributions and five permissively licensed repositories that were not used to construct the poisoned trajectories. Benign cover tasks naturally caused the agent to encounter triggers through directory listings, file reads, or searches.

Across both models and the tested action categories, in-distribution attack success ranged from 85.9% to 100%. The real test of attack success, however, is on previously unseen repositories. A naive transfer of our attack would only achieve 32.7%-63.4% attack success rate (ASR). Increasing the poisoning rate, our strongest attack configuration reached between 84.1% and 94.8% backdoor activation even on out of distribution data. False triggering was rare in the aggregate results. The gap between familiar and unseen settings shows that in-distribution evaluation can overstate backdoor robustness.

Transfer across coding harnesses

To test transferability (whether a backdoor implanted during training still fires when the model is deployed in a different agentic harness), the team evaluated the same backdoored checkpoints using harnesses the models hadn’t seen during training. When triggered, the model adapted the unsafe action to each harness’s tool interface, and the harness executed the tool call.

The 4B and 9B models reached 97.0% and 91.0% attack success under Claude Code, 74.0% and 77.0% under Pi, and 37.3% and 63.0% under Codex command-line interface (CLI). Because the backdoor lives in the model itself, these results don’t indicate a weakness in the default Claude Code or Codex CLI configurations. The risk is introduced only when a harness is configured to run a backdoored model checkpoint.

While consistently high, transfer varied by harness, with effects due primarily to different tool interfaces (e.g., Codex CLI) and invocation formats. Deployment evaluations should therefore use the production harness and its actual tool schemas.

Reasoning traces and utility recovery

Reasoning traces were critical in this experimental setup. Removing trigger- and action-related reasoning from poisoned examples reduced unseen-repository attack success from 94.8% to 1.0% for the 4B model and from 84.1% to 0% for the 9B model.

Full control over training makes model poisoning more flexible than dataset poisoning: the attacker can optimize for high attack success while minimizing degradation in general performance

Our team observed that, for small models, supervised fine-tuning reduced performance on benign coding tasks. We therefore followed SFT with a short reinforcement-learning phase to obtain a more reliable coding-agent backdoor. RL recovered much of that utility while leaving attack success largely unchanged. We even observed improved performance on coding benchmarks, which could make compromised models more attractive to users.

Figure 6: Clean-task utility and backdoor persistence before and after injecting the attack: Shows SFT utility loss, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) recovery, and largely unchanged attack success for both model sizes.

What the studies show about agent backdoors

Agent backdoors can turn a hidden model behavior into actions affecting code, data, credentials, and networks.

Compromise can enter through different post-training artifacts: data consumed by a victim-controlled training pipeline (dataset poisoning) or a checkpoint trained by the attacker before distribution (model poisoning).

Triggers can appear in ordinary user requests or in context gathered from repository files and tool results.

Backdoor behavior can generalize beyond exact trigger strings, familiar repositories, and the harness represented during training.

Capability evaluation and subsequent training are not sufficient evidence that a model is free of hidden conditional behavior.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Before training: Dataset governance and review

Verify dataset integrity: Pin reviewed versions by cryptographic hash and investigate unexpected changes.

Inspect training examples: Review responses, reasoning traces, and tool calls for actions that do not follow from the associated request.

Before deployment: Model evaluation and containment

Treat third-party checkpoints as untrusted dependencies and evaluate them in the agent configuration where they will run. Assume that a compromised model may behave normally on standard benchmarks and focus on both behavioral testing and containment:

Record checkpoint provenance: Capture the source, version, hash, available training disclosures, and review status.

Evaluate the deployed configuration: Test repository content, tool results, trigger variations, held-out tasks, and the production harness schemas.

Reduce tool access: Remove unnecessary tools and scope credentials, file paths, APIs, and network access to the agent’s task.

Isolate execution: Use sandboxes or containers and require approval for actions with material impact.

At runtime: Detection and response

Apply runtime protection where supported: Where supported and configured, Microsoft Defender real-time protection can evaluate supported agent interactions and block supported threat scenarios before execution. Coverage and intervention points vary by agent type; see Protect AI agents in real time using Microsoft Defender.

Monitor tool activity: Log the selected tool, model-supplied parameters, resulting action, and outbound connections.

Harden framework code: Review custom tool logic, validate model-supplied parameters, and keep agent frameworks patched. Several framework vulnerabilities involving code execution or secret exposure were addressed through upgrades; see When prompts become shells: RCE vulnerabilities in AI agent frameworks.

Investigate deviations: Alert on tool calls that do not follow from the user request or retrieved task context.

Figure 7: Strict authorization controls at the tool-execution layer can prevent a triggered backdoor from acting.

Securing agents beyond the model

Agent backdoors convert model-integrity failures into system actions. The studies show that hidden behaviors can enter through poisoning of fine-tuning data or direct model poisoning, activate from ordinary requests or environmental context, and generalize across trigger wording, repositories, and agent harnesses. Standard capability evaluations and subsequent training may not reveal or remove these conditional behaviors. Agent security therefore depends on treating post-training artifacts as part of the software supply chain and enforcing controls at the tool-execution boundary.
