Title: Hackers stole AI credentials to get $740,000 in free compute; Railway picked up the bill
Context: ” A 26-hour battle The attack began on October 20, when hackers exploited a previously unknown vulnerability in Railway’s build infrastructure
Full Text:
As AI model training and distillation increase, AI tokens are becoming a piping hot currency for threat actors.

Cloud hosting provider Railway found out the hard way; it has confirmed a near 26-hour battle against attackers targeting AI provider credentials to sell to AI ‘transfer stations’ for use in model distillation. The crooks generated about $740,000 in fraudulent AI usage charges using the stolen credentials and potentially had access to up to 100,000 workspace credentials.

Railway said the attacker’s database searches looked for AI provider keys by name before anything else; some queries also targeted cloud, database, and payment service credentials.

The company disclosed the incident on October 22, and posted a follow-up report this week. Because of the ongoing investigation, it is not able to share the specific details and scale of the exploits, but advised users to revoke and reapply sensitive environmental variables stored on Railway prior to October 21.

“AI credentials are becoming the new credit card numbers,” said David Shipley of Beauceron Security. “So-called LLMjacking is expected to displace Cryptojacking as a cheap, scalable way to make money.”

A 26-hour battle

The attack began on October 20, when hackers exploited a previously unknown vulnerability in Railway’s build infrastructure. They were able to evade filesystem isolation protections and obtain an internal credential that they used to access stored build histories. From there, they retrieved a copy of Railway’s internal source code and analyzed it to identify additional avenues of compromise.

They then exploited another vulnerability involving an improperly configured trust relationship that allowed them to gain even more access to Railway’s infrastructure and obtain credentials used to decrypt customer environment variables.

In a nearly 26-hour battle, Railway’s engineering team worked 24-7 in shifts and the escalating situation became a “contest of agent speed,” the company explained. The threat actor chained various exploits, moved laterally across multiple systems, and “probed many potential routes, in parallel.” Defenders in turn hardened routes in parallel.

“This was not a single breach followed by a single fix,” Railway wrote.

The threat actors were “fully evicted” on October 21, but over the course of their time in the system, they obtained and decrypted a “subset” of customer variables, roughly 100,000, or “at most” 1.85% of workspaces. They also racked up $740,000 in fraudulent AI usage charges, with customers reporting their keys answered coding questions and performed training-data tasks they never ran. The company is working to reimburse customers, including for charges providers decline to refund.

The breach also exposed linked-account tokens belonging to more than 1,850 users, which included GitHub and OAuth tokens that Railway says it reset. The company worked quickly with GitHub, GitLab, Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, SpaceXSI, Stripe, and others to revoke potentially compromised keys.

In the wake of the attack, customers have been advised to remove public network access to databases; rotate any sensitive variables and keys; check GitHub account audit logs and review all app access; and check audit logs within registries such as Dockerhub.

On its own systems, Railway said it shut down any potentially compromised internal tooling; rolled all keys and “then rerolled them” after validating that intruders had been shut out; moved to a new generation of infrastructure; rebuilt tooling used to run its infrastructure; and added functionality to mass revoke Railway app permissions in the event of suspicious activity in the future.

Why attackers want AI keys

AI credentials are cheap to harvest at scale, Shipley noted; attackers can hit a provider like Railway rather than trying to target one company at a time. That access can then be resold to generate revenue through so-called AI routers, which provide access to models that users otherwise could not afford, or even reach.

This makes that access a hot commodity for tasks like distillation, which transfers knowledge from a larger model to a smaller one to cut costs and improve efficiency.

Training one model on another model’s answers at scale takes millions of questions, said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research, and a single account asking millions of questions stands out. Stolen keys spread those questions across thousands of real customers.

“Think of copying a textbook one page at a time, using library cards that belong to other people,” Dickson explained. Frontier AI is expensive to buy, and the owner of the keys gets the bill while the thief gets cost-free compute.

“It is the 2026 version of cryptomining; [the] same playbook with a different output,” he said.

Managing identities when so many are machine-held

Even though the facts are ugly, Railway deserves credit for a “remarkably candid report,” Dickson emphasized: It owns its own configuration mistake, it admits it cannot be sure it found every account the attacker created, and it commits to telling customers of issues more quickly in the future.

Railway is now moving to short-lived credentials and logging every decryption. That is the right fix, Dickson said, and every platform holding customer secrets should copy it.

“Railway customers should treat every secret stored on the platform as stolen until they have rotated it,” he noted. But that rotation has to beat the thief’s clock; an investigation by Wiz found that stolen keys were tested within 30 minutes of theft, then flooded with traffic four to seven days later.

Start with AI provider keys, then rotate cloud, database, and payment credentials, he advised. Check AI provider bills and usage logs for traffic internal teams did not generate, then report any unauthorized charges to Railway. Alert on any call from an unrecognized address.

Further, he said, limit the damage any one key can do. Set hard spending caps and usage alerts on every AI key, and scope each key as narrowly as the provider allows. This really works: In one case Wiz examined, a key restricted to a narrow set of model profiles left most of the thief’s traffic throttled.

Non-Railway users, meanwhile, should ask their platform providers two questions: How are my secrets stored, and who can decrypt them? A good standard practice: Issue fewer keys. “No one ever said during a key rotation that they wished they had issued more keys,” Dickson pointed out.

Ultimately, he said, a stolen AI key spends real money, and machines now hold most of the keys. “Protect machine identities like cash, because to a thief, that is exactly what they are,” Dickson urged.

Title: SCKit Worm Installs Rogue ScreenConnect Clients and Session Cookie Relays Across Hundreds of Endpoints
Context: ConnectWise later released a security update to address a critical file-transfer vulnerability (CVE-2026-84869) that ranked 9
Full Text:
Acknowledgments: Special thanks to Tanner Filip, Tyler Marzen, Austin Worline, Ethan Williams, Sharon Martin, Ben Bernstein, Andrew Brandt, Jamie Levy, Max Rogers, and Aaron Deal for their contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Update: 11/11/26 @ 11:34pm ET

Huntress has learned that the activity seems to be related to one of the specific extensions that had already been disabled by ConnectWise, RMM+. ConnectWise has disabled this extension (and several other related plugins) on all hosted environments, and urged on-premises partners to do the same in their public advisory.

RMM+ is a third-party extension for ScreenConnect that lets another tool manage ScreenConnect sessions without a technician working through the console. Our analysis suggests that most RMM+ installations we encountered were legitimate, usually added for a project and left in place. But versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 contained a serious authentication flaw: if an administrator had never configured the extension's access key, RMM+ would accept a blank one.

RMM+ bypasses ScreenConnect's user accounts, roles, and MFA, and authenticates requests with a shared access key stored in the extension's settings. In versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32, that key defaulted to blank, meaning the authentication check didn't reject an empty value and a caller could pass the check when no key had been configured.

The important part is the access key setting:

<Setting Name="RMMPlus.AccessKey" IsServerOnly="true">

<Description>This is like a password. This is required to be sent in the POST request to access the functions. Set to a strong key..</Description>

<DefaultValue></DefaultValue>

</Setting>

The description tells the admin to set a strong key, but if empty, will introduce the vulnerability.

This matched our observations in this incident. Commands reached endpoints across several ScreenConnect instances within minutes. There was no corresponding login activity and the commands appeared in the logs reviewed linked to RMM+.

A special thanks to Mendy Green for helping us validate these findings.

ORIGINAL POST

Background

On November 11, 2026, Huntress observed an operator using access to multiple cloud-hosted ScreenConnect panels to push commands to groups of managed endpoints. The commands installed attacker-controlled ScreenConnect clients and an additional toolkit called SCKit. At least 288 hosts across 48 organizations that use Huntress have been affected.

In an advisory posted at 22:45 UTC on November 11, ConnectWise shared that they had identified five independent third-party extensions that may be associated with this activity; they said that they had not yet identified an initial access vector and full scope of the attack. They disabled the following extensions across 400 partner environments as a precaution:

Labtech Plus

RMM Plus

RMM+

RMM Plus Password Link

RMM+ Password Link

In September 2026, Huntress stood up a Rapid Response to similar worm-like activity that spawned rogue ScreenConnect clients across several customer environments. ConnectWise later released a security update to address a critical file-transfer vulnerability (CVE-2026-84869) that ranked 9.9 on the CVSS scale.

In analyzing this threat, we have reviewed the activity on two fronts. First, we examined what was observed in the incidents we've seen, where threat actors have used the ScreenConnect panel's Run command feature to deploy SCKit to multiple endpoints.

Then, we analyzed the kit's code to understand how it was built to spread from an infected endpoint to a technician's workstation, and then to other endpoints accessible through the technician's ScreenConnect session. We have not observed that method to spread work successfully. The console-takeover attempt failed in every recovered host log we have checked so far.

Huntress is continuing to respond to and track this November 11 incident; we are releasing further information below about the attacker's tradecraft, a breakdown of SCKit, and Indicators of Compromise (IoCs) in an effort to help defenders responding to this attack.

Technical Details

At approximately 17:47 UTC on November 11, 2026, Huntress observed suspicious activity on endpoints associated with multiple ScreenConnect environments. In total, we saw all 288 hosts impacted over the course of 90 minutes; with about one third of those in the first 10 minutes.

The infection path works in two stages: from an infected endpoint to a technician who connects to it, and from a technician's workstation to every endpoint their panel can connect to. However, not all functionality has been observed during observed incidents; some functionality has been discovered through analysing the payloads.

Figure 1: Timeline of attack across multiple organizations

SCKit in detail

SCKit is the name of the toolkit used to carry this attack forward. This toolkit is a package of 16 files - PowerShell scripts, batch scripts, Windows command-line .cmd files and other configuration data - designed to spread the infection laterally, through a multi-stage process.

Figure 2: The content of the decrypted SCKit archive

The kit is delivered as an encrypted payload, but the infected machine provides the actual decryption key to extract the files from the SCKit package; when the worm sends the request to retrieve the kit from its infrastructure, it passes the UUID of the Windows system it is running on as a part of the URL's query string. The server returns header data that include an encryption key, initialization vector, and a salt value, which the script uses to decrypt the package into the target's %temp% folder.

Figure 3: GET request and server response

As seen in figure 3 above, the query string to retrieve the SCKit payload passes along the GUID for the Windows machine it is running on (top highlighted text). The server returns decryption values the script will use to unpack the payload into the %temp% folder on the same machine.

Observed activity

We initially observed the toolkit's deployment coming through ScreenConnect panels, as opposed to the toolkit's self-replicating behavior. It appears as though an operator used the consoles' Run command feature to send commands to multiple endpoints in one go, running as SYSTEM.

Figure 4: Overview of the attack chain

The command first checked for an existing ScreenConnect client, then downloaded an attacker-controlled ScreenConnect installer to C:\Windows\TEMP\sc.msi and installed it silently. It then wrote a base64-encoded dropper to C:\Windows\Temp\sckit-run.bat.

The dropper then connects to attacker controlled infrastructure and downloads C:\Windows\Temp\sckit-decoder.ps1, and then fetches a keyed version of the SCKit toolkit for the specific system. Several of the components in the toolkit carry out further activity:

Panel-Lateral.ps1 attempts the console takeover (unsuccessfully)

sckit-loader.ps1 decrypts and launches the machine specific script k<32 Hex>.ps1

k[32 Hex].ps1 then extracts the toolkit to C:\ProgramData\RelayTrap

lab-trap-cleanup-embedded.ps1 cleans up the installation in the Temp folder

Figure 5: Install sequence on an endpoint

The trap, along with lockout policies, are then installed by C:\ProgramData\RelayTrap\install.ps1 while CWInstall_<8 hex>-c1\

Installer.ps1 adds exclusions to Defender and installs a second attacker-controlled ScreenConnect client.

Finally, TrapWatch.ps1 is launched as SYSTEM, and compiles RelayTrap.cs into a host-specific copy of C:\ProgramData\RelayTrap\trapbins\<client id>\RelayTrap.exe and creates a scheduled task named TrapWatch. The legitimate installation of ScreenConnect is then stopped, set to manual start, and the attacker controlled copy of ScreenConnect positioned to replace it.

Figure 6: The C# source code of the RelayTrap executable appears to have been generated by an LLM, based on the detailed source code references and comments that explain exactly what it is intended to do

Further functionality in the code

Going beyond what we've observed, we've reconstructed an additional functionality intended to spread from a technician's workstation to the ScreenConnect panel. This has been discovered from analysis of its scripts, configuration, and tools. To date we have not observed a successful jump from an infected endpoint to a technician workstation, or from that workstation to other endpoints.

Figure 7: Additional functionality, designed to spread from technician's workstations.

It appears as though this was designed to wait for when a technician connects to the relay and on to the compromised endpoint. A file transfer takes place 2.5 seconds after the connection is established, and retrieves a copy of the Run-Lateral-Full.bat dropper from the compromised endpoint with the action set to Run.

This dropper is built to connect to hxxps://ns.mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php and download a loader onto the compromised workstation. The loader gathers the workstation's unique ID, sends it back to the attacker's infrastructure, which returns a unique, encrypted kit for that specific workstation.

Panel-Lateral.ps1, with support from LabConfig.ps1, then steals the .aspxauth session cookie from the workstation and attempts to replay the cookie against the panel and obtain the tokens needed to enumerate any other sessions the technician can access.

Next, ToolboxRelayUploader.exe is engineered to use access gained to any other sessions to upload a payload, WithUninstall.ps1, to the panel's Shared Toolbox. A panel request tells every reachable session to run the toolbox item. This payload is designed to run as SYSTEM on those endpoints, installing the trap and extending the cycle. Roughly 60 seconds after the broadcast, ToolboxRelayUploader.exe deletes the Shared Toolbox item.

Mitigation Guidance

If you use ScreenConnect, review your environment now, even if you have not received an alert. Look for unexpected mass activity in ScreenConnect Run Command and Toolbox history, including commands or tools you did not initiate, and check for an unauthorized second ScreenConnect client on managed endpoints.

If you suspect a host is affected:

Do not connect to it through ScreenConnect. An interactive session can trigger the malware to spread to the technician's workstation and then to other ScreenConnect panels available to that technician. Use EDR live response, WinRM, or another out-of-band CLI tool. If a technician has already connected to a suspected host, treat that workstation as potentially exposed and investigate it from a clean device.

Isolate the host and keep it isolated until cleanup is complete. Isolation alone does not remove the persistence, and affected systems have been observed reinfecting shortly after isolation was lifted.

Remove the unauthorized ScreenConnect client and persistence mechanism. Look for and remove the rogue client service, the TrapWatch scheduled task, C:\ProgramData\RelayTrap\, and the toolkit files under %TEMP% (including sckit-*, Panel-Lateral.ps1, runnew.cmd, ToolboxRelayUploader.exe, and sqlite3.exe). Check for and remove the RelayTrapLiteAlert value under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run. Verify the legitimate ScreenConnect client separately before removing anything.

Revoke access that may have been exposed. From a clean device, terminate active ScreenConnect web sessions and rotate affected ScreenConnect credentials. Because the toolkit can steal browser session tokens, revoke potentially exposed browser and identity-provider sessions as well.

Review and investigate panel activity. Audit ScreenConnect Run Command and Toolbox history for unrecognized executions, and use the instance audit logs to investigate panel access and determine which systems and technician workstations may be affected.

Use SIEM to hunt. If you use Huntress SIEM, ensure ScreenConnect is connected as a data source to help Huntress hunt for suspicious administrator activity across your environment at scale.

Do not return a host to service until the rogue client and its persistence mechanism have been removed, and the system has been checked for reinfection. Continue monitoring ScreenConnect panels and endpoints for suspicious activity.

Indicators of Compromise (IOCs)

Note that file hashes are weak indicators for this activity as the scripts are rebuilt with different embedded values, and the trap executable is compiled separately on every host.

Title: Zero Trust Doesn't End at Login. Neither Does the Attack. by Mark Wojtasiak
Context: Through the Netskope Cloud Threat Exchange integration, selected indicators of compromise (IoCs), such as IP addresses and domains derived from Vectra AI detections, can be...
Full Text:
I've got a question for anyone investing in Zero Trust: What happens after you grant access?

Not who authenticated. Not whether the device passed a check. Not whether policy allowed the connection. Those are important questions, and we should absolutely keep asking them. I'm asking a different one. Once a trusted user, device, or AI agent is inside an approved session, how do you know that trust is still deserved?

Because that's where a lot of modern attacks live. Not outside the front door, trying to smash their way in. Inside legitimate access paths, using credentials, applications, and services the business already trusts.

Access is a decision. Trust is a moving target.

Continuous evaluation is already a Zero Trust principle. The challenge is putting it into practice by connecting access decisions with evidence of attacker behavior throughout the session. Netskope does something essential. It helps organizations make and enforce context-aware access decisions across web, SaaS, cloud, and private applications. That control matters.

But a correct access decision at 9:00 a.m. doesn't guarantee legitimate behavior at 9:05.

A session can be authorized and still be abused. An identity can authenticate successfully and still be compromised. An approved application can carry command-and-control activity. A connection can be encrypted and still be part of an attack.

None of that means Zero Trust failed. It means we sometimes ask access controls to answer a question they weren't designed to answer. Access policy tells us whether a connection should be allowed. It doesn't, by itself, tell us whether everything happening through that connection continues to make sense.

That second question is behavioral. And behavior changes.

The attacker sees one environment. Why doesn't the SOC?

Picture a remote employee with legitimate access to a SaaS application and an internal service. An attacker compromises the employee's identity. They log in through an approved path, explore available systems, use an unfamiliar service, and begin moving toward more valuable resources.

Each step may look ordinary when viewed alone. A successful login. An HTTPS connection. A cloud API request. A new destination.

Now think about the analyst. Secure access has one piece of the story. Identity has another. Network detection has another. SaaS and cloud tools have the rest. The analyst becomes the integration layer, manually reconstructing what happened while the attacker keeps moving.

I call that getting attacker soundbites when what we need is the attack story. I'm less interested in alert counts than in how quickly defenders can answer three questions: Is this real? Does it matter? What do we do next?

‍What Netskope and Vectra AI change together‍

This is why the Netskope and Vectra AI integration matters to me. It's not about putting two logos next to each other or adding another feed to a SOC dashboard. It's about connecting the access decision to what attackers actually do after access is granted.

Netskope brings the secure access context and control. Vectra AI brings AI-native behavioral detection and Attack Signal Intelligence to identify suspicious activity, connect related behaviors, and prioritize the identities and hosts that warrant investigation.

With Netskope Cloud TAP, policy-selected web traffic traversing Netskope infrastructure can be copied into customer-managed cloud object storage. Netskope Stitcher retrieves and replays that traffic to a dedicated Vectra virtual sensor. The sensor processes it and sends enriched metadata to the Vectra platform for analysis. The integration can also associate observed remote-user activity with the corresponding Netskope user identity.

Why does that matter? Because Vectra AI's behavioral analytics can look for attacker signals in that traffic without requiring payload decryption. That includes the kinds of suspicious patterns attackers try to conceal inside otherwise routine, encrypted communications. That observation can then be assessed alongside behavior from other connected network, identity, cloud, and SaaS sources.

There is also a path back.

Through the Netskope Cloud Threat Exchange integration, selected indicators of compromise (IoCs), such as IP addresses and domains derived from Vectra AI detections, can be shared with Netskope, where configured policies can use them for enforcement.

Observe. Understand. Prioritize. Act. That's the workflow. The technology should make it easier, not make analysts learn another alphabet soup of consoles.

What continuous threat detection means for the defender

Start with the compromised remote user. The question isn't simply whether Netskope allowed the session. It should have, based on the information available at that moment. The question is whether subsequent behavior starts looking like reconnaissance, command and control, credential abuse, lateral movement, or other signs of attack progression.

And consider the SOC team's day. If analysts have to stitch access logs, network evidence, identity events, and cloud alerts together by hand, they're spending scarce time assembling context instead of making decisions. Correlated, prioritized attacker behavior gives them a place to start and a clearer reason to act.

This isn't a claim that one integration magically sees every packet or stops every attack. Cloud TAP coverage depends on the traffic Netskope captures and the deployment choices customers make. Nor is behavioral detection a replacement for secure access, endpoint protection, or policy enforcement. These controls do different jobs. The point is to make those jobs reinforce one another.

Make Zero Trust continuous

Here's my takeaway: A Zero Trust architecture has to support continuous evaluation long after a session is approved.

People, devices, workloads, service accounts, and AI agents all operate through trusted connections. Some will be compromised or misused. Attackers will keep making malicious activity resemble business as usual.

We can't solve that by denying every connection. We also can't solve it by trusting every connection forever.

We have to secure access and use continuous monitoring to assess the behavior that follows. Netskope helps determine who or what gets access to which applications and data. Vectra AI helps defenders recognize when activity after access starts telling an attacker story, then decide what deserves attention.

That's the opportunity I see in Netskope and Vectra AI together: less blind trust, fewer disconnected soundbites, faster clarity for the people defending the business.

Because getting through the door shouldn't give an attacker the benefit of the doubt for the rest of the day.

‍Secure access. Continuous attack defense. That's how Zero Trust becomes more than an access decision.

Title: Five Findings From the 2027 State of Threat Intelligence
Context: When I first saw the results of this year’s survey, a few findings stood out to me as especially relevant for anyone who runs, funds, or relies on a threat intelligence program...
Full Text:
The much anticipated State of Threat Intelligence report has just been published. The State of Threat Intelligence report is based on a survey Recorded Future conducted with UserEvidence of 768 cybersecurity professionals at enterprises with at least 1,000 employees. It’s the latest edition in our annual report series, where we gauge how threat intelligence is currently being used, funded, and measured. When I first saw the results of this year’s survey, a few findings stood out to me as especially relevant for anyone who runs, funds, or relies on a threat intelligence program and is planning for the year ahead. Here are my top five findings and why.

1. Cost is the least common reason to consolidate

A strong majority of respondents (79%) said they plan to consolidate threat intelligence vendors in the next year. That alone is no huge surprise, especially given that respondents reported using an average of five different vendors. Cost would be a reasonable guess for why, but reducing costs actually ranked last of five drivers, at 5%.

The drivers that ranked higher point to what teams want from consolidation:

Improving correlation across signals (34%): connecting intelligence across threat domains and internal telemetry into one view of risk.

Bringing siloed tools together (29%): ensuring different risk owners can efficiently act on intelligence.

Simplifying operations (22%): fewer interfaces and handoffs so teams can act on intelligence sooner.

Reducing vendor-management overhead (9%): fewer vendors to evaluate and renew.

Overall investment is still rising: 83% plan to increase threat intelligence spending in the next 12 months. Teams are consolidating to get better results from their intelligence, not to cut spend.

That puts the focus on outcomes. Jason Steer, CISO at Recorded Future, framed the risk well: consolidation only counts “if that provider has the same or better outcomes.” For anyone evaluating vendors this year, that’s the bar to consider.

Especially as teams expand the reach of their threat intelligence programs and support more stakeholders across the enterprise, they’re pursuing vendors that provide coverage across the risk domains that matter for those teams, but equally important that friction is not created in that pursuit of breadth, and that the organization is able to see how threats across disparate domains actually connect.

2. Only 25% have external intelligence and internal telemetry in one place

Correlation is the top consolidation driver, yet only a quarter of respondents say external intelligence and internal telemetry reside in one place. The rest break down as follows:

52% are partially integrated across some tools.

18% rely on manual correlation by analysts.

5% keep the two in separate workflows.

Poor integration with existing tools and workflows was also the most-cited pain point with current vendors.

This doesn’t mean every team needs to move everything into a single tool. What often matters is whether external intelligence can be correlated with internal signals across the tools a team already uses, without an analyst doing it by hand. Collective Insights® is built for this: it pulls detections from a team’s existing security tools and enriches them with Recorded Future intelligence.

For the 70% who are partially integrated or correlating manually, it’s worth identifying where that manual handoff still happens.

3. Confidence in ROI is high, but few measure cost savings

Nearly every respondent (99%) formally measures the value of their threat intelligence program, and 57% say they are very confident in their ability to quantify its ROI. But when asked how they measure value, more than half (58%) of that very confident group did not include cost savings. Across all respondents, 39% measure cost savings, and 31% measure whether triggered actions actually worked.

The most common metrics are operational:

Enhanced threat detection rates: 60%

Improved response times: 59%

Fewer incidents: 57%

Those matter to security teams, but ultimately fail to communicate the bottom-line impact of your threat intelligence program to the business. The Impact & Metrics dashboard in the Recorded Future platform helps here by showing the hours and dollars saved through use of the platform.

4. About one in four have already closed the loop

Closing that measurement gap depends on connecting intelligence to outcomes. That is what closed-loop operationalization does: intelligence is automatically shared with the relevant stakeholders, they take action based on it, and the efficacy of that action is validated and used to inform what intelligence is collected and shared with these teams.

Closed-loop programs can answer the questions stakeholders outside security ask: did the intelligence drive an action, and did that action work? Answering those questions also requires a clear definition of what intelligence should achieve. Most programs have that starting point: 68% say formally documented, regularly reviewed Priority Intelligence Requirements (PIRs) govern their program.

For teams building next year’s measurement plan, PIRs set the benchmark, and closed-loop validation should be the goal for how outcomes get measured against it.

5. Threat intelligence is now an input to AI, not only a beneficiary of it

98% of respondents use AI in their threat intelligence work. Less discussed is the other direction: 74% say threat intelligence already feeds their organization’s AI or automation initiatives.

44% describe this as established, with intelligence regularly feeding one or more AI or automation workflows.

30% describe it as advanced, with structured intelligence as a core input across their AI and agentic systems.

Only 4% don’t use threat intelligence to support AI at all.

Across all of the tasks where we assessed comfort with AI autonomy (summarization, alert triage, enrichment, false-positive reduction, detection rule generation, prioritization, and enforcement actions), at least 92% of respondents are comfortable giving AI some role. That makes the earlier findings more pressing. AI workflows inherit whatever gaps exist in the intelligence they draw on, including signals that aren’t correlated and actions that aren’t validated.

Looking ahead

Taken together, these findings describe programs that are still investing. Their focus is on connecting intelligence, proving its value, and extending it into new workflows, including AI. Most are partway through that work, and some are further along than expected.

The full 2027 State of Threat Intelligence report covers each of these areas in more depth. That includes which teams beyond the SOC rely on threat intelligence and how comfortable organizations are giving AI autonomy. Download the report.

Title: ARTEX and AI-Powered Red Teaming Tools: What Defenders Need to Know
Context: Unit 42 Incident Response and Managed Threat Hunting teams observed this activity across multiple organizations and sectors, without exploiting a single software vulnerability
Full Text:
A rapidly expanding ecosystem of AI-enabled tools such as ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI — marketed for red teaming and penetration testing — are being used by attackers to execute offensive operations autonomously.

Their footprint is already substantial. Unit 42 has observed ARTEX used in intrusion attempts against multiple targets.

Our Incident Response team investigated multiple intrusions in which the attacker’s server hosted an ARTEX console or used infrastructure and user agents associated with ARTEX.

Separately, Unit 42 Managed Threat Hunting tracked a coordinated ARTEX campaign against customer cloud environments in sectors worldwide, including retail and consulting.

External scrutiny has already disrupted project lifecycles: the author of ARTEX recently made the repository closed-source and ceased public development to prevent misuse. Emerging alternatives are rapidly filling the void, introducing new capabilities that threat actors will inevitably co-opt.

Here, we share our observations of how attackers are using AI-powered red team tools, along with our recommendations for how defenders can mitigate.

Why Is ARTEX Such an Effective Tool for Attackers?

ARTEX and other red-teaming platforms are free, quick to deploy and need little more than access to a large language model (LLM).

ARTEX is an open-source, multi-agent AI penetration testing framework first published in mid-2026. It has been widely forked since.

Attackers can use ARTEX to evaluate responses, adapt when something fails and keep pursuing their objective. They can target the identity workflows and APIs that organizations expose to the internet, and then use the associated credentials and trust relationships to reach the cloud.

AI-Powered Red Teaming and Pentesting Ecosystem Infrastructure

As of October 2026, Unit 42 identified 1,323 internet-facing hosts running CyberStrikeAI and 609 running ARTEX. Notably, 21 hosts were running both at the same time.

Unit 42 analyzed 14 tools across the pentesting and red-teaming tool ecosystem, highlighting 12 emerging tools alongside CyberStrikeAI and ARTEX.

These tools can be broken down into four categories of AI assisted red team activities.

Category

Tools

Goal

Reconnaissance and attack-surface management

ARL, ARL-Next, Scope Sentry, Nemo, XingRin, OpenEASD

Identify what assets exist, what is exposed and what changes

Agent-led testing and vulnerability hunting

CyberStrikeAI, ARTEX, Cairn, PentAGI, AutoHunter

Manage what should be investigated and how the system can act on it

Source-code auditing and verification

DeepAudit, AIxVuln

Identify where source code might be vulnerable and what supports that finding

AI-system security assessment

AI-Infra-Guard

Identify if AI infrastructure, agents, tools and model interfaces are vulnerable or unreliable

Table 1. Tool categories.

Implications For Defenders

Defenders should be aware of the following implications of AI-powered red teaming platforms:

Lowered Skill Floor for Attackers

Adversaries no longer require specialized tradecraft to execute multi-stage, adaptive penetration testing.

Off-the-shelf tooling combined with LLMs like DeepSeek allows financially motivated actors to launch and manage dozens of complex, concurrent network intrusions for minimal compute cost.

Risk of Internet-Exposed Assets

Any internet-exposed asset, regardless of organizational size or sector, is equally likely to be impacted by automated, persistent intrusion attempts.

Attackers using the autonomous AI penetration testing framework ARTEX are turning public password reset pages and exposed APIs into a path to cloud access, sometimes in less than a day. Unit 42 Incident Response and Managed Threat Hunting teams observed this activity across multiple organizations and sectors, without exploiting a single software vulnerability.

Because these autonomous platforms cannot target what they cannot find, continuous discovery and mitigation of exposed edge assets remains an effective barrier against automated campaigns.

Proactive AI Adoption Helps Defenders

Autonomous testing frameworks rely on foundational LLM reasoning patterns. Therefore, there is some predictability to AI-powered adversary tooling.

Security teams do not need to guess an agent's methodology; they can deploy identical open-weight offensive frameworks internally to surface, validate and remediate vulnerable exposure before external agents identify them.

Defenders Benefit From Tracking Ecosystem Shifts

The rapid adoption curve of tools in this ecosystem highlights how quickly operational trends can shift. Keeping an eye on these developments provides practical defensive advantages:

Observing emerging agent-led frameworks allows teams to test new capabilities early in controlled environments.

Monitoring the infrastructure hosting these tools makes it possible to update perimeter blocks before active targeting begins.

Current AI-Powered Frameworks Are Noisy

Current autonomous frameworks prioritize rapid trial-and-error over stealth. In our study of a tool called Cairn, it generated hundreds of thousands of noisy, high-frequency requests across multiple edge protocols from a single origin IP address.

Organizations with unified perimeter telemetry and centralized logging can readily distinguish this brute-force agentic traffic from legitimate users and block campaigns at the network edge before exploitation occurs.

Defensive Deception Could Help

LLM-driven testing tools use target responses as context for follow up actions.

Defenders may be able to take advantage of this to trick attackers using AI-powered red teaming tools into wasting resources.

When a target serves identical, generic error codes or enforces silent connection throttling, an AI agent lacks the contextual cues needed to adapt. Deprived of environmental feedback, autonomous loops burn context windows and compute budgets on dead ends.

Recognizing an AI-Driven Operator

ARTEX is forked and modified constantly. Furthermore, attackers rotate infrastructure quickly, so indicators lose value fast. How the operator behaves is more durable, and the behavior across our observations consistently pointed to an automated planner reacting to what it sees. Table 2 shows the hallmarks of this behavior.

Hallmark

What We Observed

Think-then-act cadence

Bursts of one to 14 requests about a second apart, then a pause of 25–31 seconds, consistent with an agent waiting on a model inference call

Machine speed

Pivots within about one minute of a credential download. More than 200 client secrets validated in about three minutes

Spec-driven targeting

Routes from downloaded OpenAPI specifications and source maps targeted almost immediately

Self-correction

Failed requests (HTTP 422) adjusted and retried successfully moments later

Checking its own work

A GET to the same path after almost every successful write. Write-then-delete tests on storage buckets.

Canary inputs

Bogus usernames before real ones, and placeholder values such as evil[.]com, test@example[.]com and deadbeefdeadbeefdeadbeef12

Parallel targeting

An application delivery controller, more than a dozen VPN appliances, a NAS device, workforce identity and cloud ports attacked within the same hour

Recheck loops

Polling every 48 seconds for three days, and attack sequences replayed identically about 30 seconds apart

Table 2. Behavioral hallmarks of ARTEX-driven activity observed by Unit 42.

Any one of these traits could come from an unusually configured tool or a person testing an API by hand. Seen together, they point to autonomous tooling.

Despite the autonomous tooling, humans were not entirely absent from the attacks we observed. In one engagement, the attacker switched from scripted clients to a desktop browser for the password reset and first token request. This suggests a human in the loop, or browser automation, for the most sensitive steps.

Conclusion and Mitigations for ARTEX Attacks

AI-driven tooling is not inventing new attacks. Self-service abuse, exposed APIs and stored credentials are long-standing weak points.

What has changed is the pace and the persistence. An ARTEX operator can test every exposed workflow in parallel and switch routes within minutes of being blocked. It can act on a stolen credential within a minute of finding it.

Because the framework is open source and widely forked, indicator-based detection will not keep up.

Defenders who remove machine-readable attack maps, require authentication everywhere and build detections around operator behavior will be best placed to stop an AI-assisted attacker.

Autonomous tooling probes faster than people can review alerts. Defenses need to block by default and remove the credentials these tools are looking for. Organizations should:

Remove public attack maps. Take OpenAPI specifications, source maps and configuration files containing tokens or client IDs off internet-facing applications.

Reduce and understand your organization’s public footprint. Certificate transparency can create target lists for threat actors. In cloud environments, it is vital to understand if host fully qualified domain names (FQDNs) are public knowledge. Consider private certificate authorities to limit information disclosure and locking origin traffic to content delivery network (CDN)-only ingress where possible.

Require authentication on every write endpoint, including development and staging APIs.

Harden self-service flows. Rate-limit and bot-protect registration, password reset and verification code endpoints. Remove unauthenticated account-existence checks.

Protect federated identities. Block local passwords for workforce accounts in customer and partner identity providers, and make sure a password reset can never unlink a federated identity.

Get credentials out of reach. Replace long-lived cloud keys with role-based access, keep administrator credentials out of provisioning records and move function secrets to a secrets manager.

Enforce least privilege for workload roles and any function that can create roles, keys or tokens.

Hunt for behavior, not just indicators. Look for:

Canary usernames in identity provider logs

First use of a cloud key from a new IP address

Write-then-delete storage tests

Early-phase probing that precedes a later intrusion

Title: AI Pentest Tool AntiFox Abused To Steal AWS Credentials
Context: In some cases, the attackers got into a public IIS application, though Arctic Wolf couldn’t identify the vulnerability
Full Text:
Arctic Wolf saw attackers use the AntiFox pentest platform to hit IIS servers and AWS accounts.

Arctic Wolf Labs has published research on attackers using AntiFox, an open-source, Chinese-language agentic penetration testing platform. These frameworks chain attack steps together with little human effort. In several intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were tied to confirmed attacks on internet-facing web services and the AWS environments behind them.

Two entry points showed up. In some cases, the attackers got into a public IIS application, though Arctic Wolf couldn’t identify the vulnerability. In others, they started with a valid AWS credential obtained by means nobody knows.

“Arctic Wolf is tracking the emerging use of self-hosted agentic penetration testing frameworks, including AntiFox, from public cloud infrastructure.” states the report published by Arctic Wolf, “In several recently observed intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were associated with confirmed malicious actions against internet-facing web services and associated AWS environments.”

The IIS attacks followed a similar pattern. The IIS worker process, w3wp.exe, created an ASPX web shell and then ran commands to gather information about the system. The attackers checked the user account, listed files in the application folder, reviewed file permissions using icacls and tested whether they could write files to the website’s main folder.

They then used PowerShell to read the web.config file, looking for database connection details and application settings. They also checked folders containing debug and error logs. Using credentials found in the configuration file, they tried to connect to an internal production database. Finally, they copied configuration files and logs into an upload folder that could be accessed through the website.

The AWS attacks moved quickly. AntiFox used valid IAM accounts and, in some cases, an assumed EC2 role. The attackers first checked their identity and permissions within AWS. They used commands such as GetCallerIdentity, GetUser, ListUsers, ListRoles, ListPolicies and ListKeys to discover available accounts, roles, policies and access keys. They also tried to obtain an authorization token for Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR).

In one intrusion, the source cycled through several AWS identities and sent hundreds of requests in about half an hour.

“The activity then rapidly enumerated services across the affected AWS environments, including IAM, EC2, S3, Lambda, Secrets Manager, KMS, RDS, ECS, EKS, Redshift, Athena, Glue, Systems Manager, API Gateway, CloudWatch, CloudFormation, DynamoDB, and Amazon Bedrock, using List, Get, and Describe operations.” continues the report. “After authorization failures, the activity continued across other services and concentrated on resources that remained accessible.”

Most requests came back as AccessDenied, but a few worked, and the attackers kept going where the doors were open.

Some sequences ended with a successful GetSecretValue request against a production secret. Others focused on S3, listing buckets, objects and versions, reading objects, then copying and deleting them. Nobody has to stay awake for that kind of persistence, which is the whole point of the tool.

Arctic Wolf’s concern is simple. These frameworks make penetration testing techniques easier to reach for attackers, and they make those techniques faster and more consistent in live attacks.

For hunting, start with AWS activity coming from hosting providers the identity has never used. Look for one IP address using many access keys, users or roles in a short time, and for fast runs of List, Get and Describe calls across unrelated services, especially from Boto3 or Botocore. Check GuardDuty for odd IAM user behavior, credential access, discovery and unusual calls from hosting networks.

On the Windows side, watch for w3wp.exe starting cmd.exe, powershell.exe, whoami.exe, icacls.exe or archive tools. Look for new .aspx files in upload, temporary and image-conversion folders, and for config or log files saved there under .txt or image extensions. PowerShell commands that read WebConfigurationManager, ConnectionStrings or AppSettings deserve a close look, and so does any AWS activity that starts soon after.

Organizations should enable AWS CloudTrail logging and monitor access to sensitive S3 storage. They should also use S3 versioning and Object Lock to protect important data from deletion. Alerts should flag suspicious access to stored secrets, especially when it follows unusual account activity.

Companies should identify all internet-facing applications and prioritize patching and protecting file upload, conversion and document-processing services. If an IIS process launches an unexpected command shell, administrators should isolate the server, preserve logs and forensic evidence, remove malicious files and change all exposed credentials.

They should also revoke compromised AWS sessions and access keys, enforce IMDSv2 and apply least-privilege permissions to limit what applications can access. As Arctic Wolf warns, a series of mostly denied requests does not mean the attack was unsuccessful.

Title: WhiteArmor Demands $5 Million from Maersk, Claims Theft of 100GB of Data
Context: The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect...
Full Text:
Maersk confirms a data breach involving a legacy system, while WhiteArmor claims 100GB of stolen data and demands a $5 million ransom.

A.P. Moller Maersk, the Danish shipping giant, says it identified an IT security incident involving unauthorized access and data extraction from one of its local legacy systems, one inherited from a previous acquisition.

“Maersk has identified an IT security incident involving unauthorised access and data extraction from one of our local legacy systems from a previous acquisition.” reads the statement published by Maersk on November 11. “Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed. The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI.”

According to Maersk, its cyber security team started a full investigation as soon as it found the problem, and it’s still going. The company says swift action secured the affected system. Its findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed, and it says the incident is isolated to that one local system.

Maersk has found no sign that other Maersk systems were affected, or the customer and partner systems that connect to it through integrations such as APIs and EDI. It doesn’t expect disruption for customers, who can book and manage shipments as usual. It promises updates and says it will inform any affected parties if it finds a need to.

Maersk didn’t name the system, the type of data or the date of the intrusion. However, the cybercrime group WhiteArmor added the company to its Tor data leak site:

WhiteArmor demanded a $5 million ransom in Bitcoin, giving Maersk 30 days to pay. The group claims to have stolen about 100 GB of data from the OCF/LF Logistics platform, which supports logistics and supply chain operations.

“”Your contract-logistics arm, the former LF Logistics, runs fulfilment for many of the world’s largest consumer brands,” states the leak site. “Five million dollars is roughly four hours of that EBITDA.””

Maersk acquired LF Logistics, the company that developed the platform, from the Li & Fung Group in 2022. This could match Maersk’s reference to an old system inherited through an acquisition, although the company has not confirmed this connection.

According to the attackers, the stolen data includes nearly 30,000 driver records, passwords stored in plain text, 33 super admin accounts and signed delivery receipts. The group also claims to have stolen inventory records, purchase orders, advance shipping notices and 27,842 mobile device logs containing phone numbers, email addresses and IMEI numbers. These details come from the attackers and have not been independently verified. Maersk’s statement does not confirm their claims. WhiteArmor also tried to justify its demand, saying the $5 million ransom represents roughly four hours of revenue for the logistics business.

“We do not anticipate disruption to operations for customers at this time, and customers can continue to use Maersk platforms to book and manage their shipments as usual.” concludes the statement. “We will keep customers updated as more relevant information becomes available, and if we identify any need to inform impacted parties of any further findings, we will do so.”

The scale of Maersk’s operations explains why this incident matters. A.P. Moller-Maersk is one of the world’s largest integrated shipping and logistics companies, playing a major role in global trade and supply chains. It operates around 700 container ships, representing approximately 13.5% of global container fleet capacity, and manages 60 terminals across 35 countries. The company employs about 100,000 people in 130 countries and provides services covering ocean shipping, port operations, warehousing, customs clearance and end-to-end supply chain management.

Maersk reported approximately $54 billion in revenue and $2.9 billion in net profit in 2025. Its global reach and reliance on interconnected IT systems make cybersecurity a major concern. A breach involving even an older, locally operated platform could expose sensitive business and personal information, including data belonging to drivers, customers and logistics partners, even if the company’s main systems remain unaffected.

In 2017, NotPetya forced the company to reinstall more than 4,000 servers and 45,000 workstations from scratch. It operated without IT for ten days and took damages of up to $300 million.

Title: The global socket: how threat actors are weaponizing GSocket for stealthy C2
Context: When one RCE stops being just one RCE Exploiting a web application vulnerability gives a threat actor command execution in the context of the web server process
Full Text:
In this article

When one RCE stops being just one RCE

Observed attack chains

How threat actors deploy and operate GSocket

How GSocket reconnects without a fixed C2 address

Mitigation and protection guidance

References

Learn More

Microsoft observed multiple incidents in which threat actors deployed GSocket, an open source remote access tool, on compromised Linux servers. Threat actors used Gsocket to maintain access even after the vulnerabilities used for initial compromise were remediated. This turned a single web application compromise into persistent access that outlasted the remediation of the original vulnerabilities. Defenders investigating affected hosts should look for evidence of GSocket deployment, persistence, privilege escalation, and outbound connections, rather than treating application patching alone as complete remediation.

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint telemetry shows this activity growing over recent months and concentrated on web applications and hosting environments. GSocket relays traffic through a shared public network, so there is no threat actor-owned IP address or domain to block.

When one RCE stops being just one RCE

Exploiting a web application vulnerability gives a threat actor command execution in the context of the web server process. That access lasts only while the vulnerability remains unpatched and the service keeps running. Patching the application or restarting the service can remove it.

To keep access, threat actors typically add a persistence mechanism, and each common option has drawbacks. SSH keys added to authorized_keys are easy for administrators to find during an audit. Reverse shells depend on threat actor-controlled servers that defenders can block or sinkhole. Custom implants require ongoing development and maintenance. The same trade-offs apply when initial access comes through remote access services or cloud shell sessions.

GSocket addresses these drawbacks, which helps explain why multiple unrelated threat actors have adopted it.

Shared relay infrastructure. Traffic passes through the Global Socket Relay Network, a public relay service. The threat actor does not register or host any infrastructure, so there is no threat actor-owned IP address or domain to block. Organizations can still restrict access to the relay itself.

Outbound-only connections. The compromised host and the operator both connect outbound to the relay, which bridges the two sessions. The host needs no inbound listener or public IP address, and network address translation does not prevent the connection. Inbound firewall rules do not see this traffic, although egress filtering and outbound monitoring can.

Built-in evasion and persistence. The deployment script can rename the process, stage files in memory-backed directories, and install persistence that survives a reboot, without additional development by the threat actor.

The same relay model that supports legitimate remote administration also gives threat actors a way to maintain access without operating dedicated C2 infrastructure. Once GSocket runs on a compromised server, the server and the operator each connect outbound to the Global Socket Relay Network, which pairs the two sessions over an end-to-end encrypted channel.

Figure 1: After code execution on an internet-facing application, GSocket is deployed and both ends connect outward to the relay.

Because GSocket runs independently of the exploited application, patching the vulnerability does not remove the relay client or its persistence.

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint telemetry shows that this activity is not limited to a single compromise. From March through August 2026, devices with GSocket-related detections increased 356.2%, although the increase was not consistent month to month.

Figure 2: Growth in GSocket-related detections from March to August, measured against the March baseline.

Web applications and hosting accounted for 87.1% of attributable Microsoft Defender for Endpoint incidents in the analysed telemetry. Within that group, PHP web applications and cPanel hosting represented 63.9% of incidents and Apache represented 24.3% (Figure 3).

Figure 3: Distribution of GSocket-related incidents by application category. PHP web applications and Apache account for most incidents within the web applications and hosting group.

Education and research accounted for the largest share of affected organizations (30.7%), followed by technology and telecommunications (22.9%).

Figure 4: Distribution of affected organizations by sector.

These figures reflect the share of affected organizations and do not indicate that threat actors selected these sectors deliberately. Exposure is the more likely factor: academic institutions often run large, decentralized web estates maintained outside central IT, which are harder to inventory and patch.

Observed attack chains

The RCE-based intrusions in this analysis followed a similar sequence after initial access. Threat actors compromised an internet-facing application, profiled the host, transferred and concealed the relay tooling, and used the resulting channel for command and control. Some intrusions also included persistence and privilege escalation. Figure 5 combines these behaviours into a generalized attack chain. Not every stage occurred in every intrusion.

Figure 5: Generalized GSocket attack chain observed across RCE-based intrusions, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK.

How threat actors deploy and operate GSocket

Initial access and deployment: Threat actors exploited internet-facing web applications and used curl to download and execute a remote script. The script profiled the host, selected a GSocket client matching the system architecture, staged it in writable or memory-backed paths such as /dev/shm, and established encrypted outbound command and control through the Global Socket Relay Network.

Figure 6: Encoded RCE command executed through a vulnerable PHP application.

Defense evasion and persistence: Threat actors disguised GSocket with kernel-thread-like process names, persisted through cron, systemd, shell profiles, watchdogs, and redundant copies, then removed staging files and other deployment indicators.

Figure 7: Kernel thread names used to disguise the GSocket process. Figure 8: Persistence entries created during GSocket deployment.

Privilege escalation: After gaining execution as the web-service account, in few observed incidents, threat actors attempted to exploit CVE-2026-43284, one of the recent Linux kernel vulnerabilities also known as Dirty Frag, to elevate privileges to root.

How GSocket reconnects without a fixed C2 address

GSocket identifies endpoints by a shared secret instead of an IP address or hostname. During installation, the deployment script typically generates a random secret and writes it to standard output. The threat actor can choose to read the secret from the console, redirect it to a temporary file and retrieve the file before is deleted, or have it delivered through a supported notification channel, such as Telegram (configured with GS_TG_TOKEN and GS_TG_CHATID), Discord, or a webhook. With this secret, the operator can reconnect later from any compatible GSocket client, without knowing the victim’s IP address, hostname, or network location.

A traditional reverse shell connects to a threat actor-controlled IP address written into the payload. GSocket instead derives its connection identifier and authentication material from the shared secret. The compromised host and the operator each connect outbound to the Global Socket Relay Network (GSRN), which matches them and brokers an end-to-end encrypted session. Neither endpoint needs a public IP address, an inbound listener, or a permissive inbound firewall rule.

As a result, blocking an IP address or domain is unlikely to cut off access. The connection relies on a shared relay service, outbound traffic that is commonly permitted, and a secret that does not need to be hardcoded in the payload. Anyone with the shared secret can reconnect through the relay without knowing the compromised host’s IP address or hostname.

Mitigation and protection guidance

For an affected Linux server, remediation should address both the initial compromise and the GSocket deployment.

Patch and harden internet-facing applications. Keep web applications, CMS platforms, plugins, and application servers current. Remove unused components and restrict file-upload and administrative paths.

Remediate the host as well as the vulnerability. Do not treat application patching as complete remediation. Investigate and remove the GSocket client, associated persistence, and staged files, then verify that outbound connections to the relay infrastructure have stopped

Patch and harden internet-facing applications. Keep web applications, CMS platforms, plugins, and application servers current. Remove unused components and restrict file-upload and administrative paths.

Constrain outbound traffic. Apply deny-by-default egress rules, allow only required destinations, and monitor connections to relay infrastructure.

Harden the host runtime. Mount temporary and memory-backed directories as non-executable where feasible, and alert on execution from hidden or world-writable paths.

Audit persistence surfaces. Review cron entries, systemd units with plausible service names, and shell startup files. Persistence is often layered across several mechanisms, so stopping the running process alone does not remove access.

Prioritize local privilege-escalation patching on internet-facing servers. In the analyzed activity, threat actors attempted to exploit CVE-2026-43284 to escalate from the web-service account to root. Separately, Microsoft FORGE Lab recently documented 59 Linux kernel bug reports, including eight vulnerabilities for which researchers demonstrated local root privilege-escalation exploits in controlled environments.

Enable Microsoft Defender for Endpoint on Linux. Keep real-time and cloud-delivered protection enabled, with behavior monitoring for anomalous child processes of web services and masqueraded process identities.

Advanced hunting queries

Microsoft Defender XDR customers can use the following queries to surface GSocket-related activity. The queries use public Advanced Hunting tables populated by Microsoft Defender for Endpoint and cover deployment patterns observed in the analyzed intrusions.

Matches should be investigated in context with process ancestry, execution context, persistence changes, and related network activity.

GSocket process activity

Looks for GSocket tooling by name or command line.

DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where FileName has_any ("gs-netcat", "gsocket") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("gsocket.io", "gs-netcat", "gsnetcat") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName | order by Timestamp desc

Installer download activity

Looks for the download-and-execute pattern used to fetch GSocket.

DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where ProcessCommandLine has "gsocket.io" or ProcessCommandLine has "gsgg.b-cdn.net" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName | order by Timestamp desc

Connections to observed distribution hosts

These are tool distribution endpoints, not threat actor-owned command and control.

DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where RemoteUrl has_any ("gsocket.io", "gsgg.b-cdn.net") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName | order by Timestamp desc

Known file hashes

Matches the SHA-256 hashes published in the indicators of compromise section.

Useful when hashes are missing or a different build is used.

The following techniques were observed across the analyzed intrusions. Not every technique occurred in every intrusion, and some outcomes, such as persistence across reboot and successful relay session establishment, were not confirmed in every case.

T1543.002 Create or Modify System Process: Systemd Service | Activity launched a bash command invoking the renamed /usr/bin/defunct payload and referenced defunct.service and a multi-user.target.wants link.

T1564.001 Hide Artifacts: Hidden Files and Directories | gs-netcat payloads were staged under the dot-prefixed /dev/shm/.gs-0 directory. A GsNetcat-detected file was also observed at /tmp/.gsn_ora.

Vanderbilt is bringing campus systems back online after a cyberattack

Eligible students can get Malwarebytes for free through our Student Protection Program

Vanderbilt University is bringing systems back online after a cybersecurity incident claimed by the BYOD ransomware group.

Vanderbilt University is a private research university in Nashville, Tennessee. Founded in 1873, it now serves more than 13,800 undergraduate, graduate, and professional students across 12 schools and colleges, with programs ranging from engineering and education to law, medicine, and nursing. Its combination of teaching and research means its systems support not only everyday campus activities but also valuable academic research.

According to Bleeping Computer, BYOD claims it encrypted Vanderbilt’s databases and obtained more than one million Social Security numbers, along with names, email addresses, telephone numbers, student and employee records, and research data. It also claims control of a domain controller (a server that manages network access) and possession of backups.

How the attackers gained access remains undisclosed. Vanderbilt’s November 10 evening incident update states that the following systems and applications are available:

Campus Wi-Fi

Okta: Continue to use multifactor authentication (MFA)

Vanderbilt email (Outlook): Vanderbilt email is available on Vanderbilt and personal devices

CampusPrint

Brightspace

Zoom

YES (Your Enrollment Services): All course registration is proceeding as scheduled

Other Vanderbilt systems and applications remained restricted. The university says fully restoring normal operations could take several weeks.

The university has not confirmed the number of affected people. BYOD claims it obtained more than one million Social Security numbers, but that is not a verified count of affected students or other people. The university says it is still determining what data, if any, was accessed.

How to stay safe

BYOD has threatened to release the data it claims to have stolen.

Title: Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?
Context: The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail
Full Text:
The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.

Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).

The Qilin ransomware administrator “Haise” advertising his affiliate program on the cybercrime forum RAMP. Image: Ke-la.com.

Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with ransomware groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.

The head of Qilin goes by the handle “Haise,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.

The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP, a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44.

Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].

The Qilin administrator once used the nickname “Rjun” on several forums, and shared their Telegram handle as “Alexbigboss44.” Image: Ke-la.com.

Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations.

The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk, which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals.

IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure.

Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket, Verified, and Zloy. Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru.

The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru, the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation.

Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia.

Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521, recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems.

A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number +79602347275. Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru. IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites.

That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014.

More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane.

Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful.

Further reading: Gang Exposed, an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helping to connect the dots.

The Qilin ransomware admin Haise’s now-deleted Telegram account, advertising the affiliate program in July 2024. Image: justpaste.it/iosba.
