Title: Suspected Chinese Malware Supplier Tied to Three Hacking Campaigns
Context: Three China-nexus intrusion clusters across Latin America, Asia and Europe have been linked through shared malware and infrastructure to a possible common supplier of hacking tools
Full Text:
Three China-nexus intrusion clusters across Latin America, Asia and Europe have been linked through shared malware and infrastructure to a possible common supplier of hacking tools.

Check Point Research (CPR) detailed the findings in a November 10 report, linking the clusters through shared infrastructure features and code similarities within the Sparrow framework.

The year-long investigation covered campaigns targeting several dozen high-profile organizations across the three regions. CPR called the suspected supplier behind the framework 'CopperDragon.'

Three Clusters Share Sparrow Framework

The three clusters are tracked by CPR researchers as SilentDelivery, OceanGate and DarkWire.

SilentDelivery, observed since early 2026, has compromised legitimate websites, mainly in government, shipping and IT or research sectors.

Visitors were shown a fake Chrome certificate warning that prompted them to install a "Certificate Fix" utility, with targets mainly in the Czech Republic, Germany, France, Taiwan, Nepal, Hong Kong and Indonesia. The fake utility delivered SquadC or a SparrowDoor variant, giving the attackers an initial foothold.

OceanGate was observed during 2025 and 2026 and mainly targeted government organizations and critical infrastructure in Asia. CPR said attackers entered through an internet-facing Linux server before moving into Windows environments and conducting extensive credential theft, lateral movement and exfiltration of sensitive operational information.

DarkWire, first identified in mid-2025, initially concentrated on Latin America but more recent intrusions suggested expansion. The cluster has targeted telecom operators, including at least three major providers in the region, as well as foreign affairs and justice bodies.

CopperDragon May Sit Behind Multiple Groups

CPR described CopperDragon as "a potential digital quartermaster supporting China-nexus threat actors" and the Sparrow framework's "possible developer and supplier." It also assessed that CopperDragon is involved in maintaining and supplying variants of the Melofee backdoor.

The report links the framework to FamousSparrow, first identified in 2021 and known for using the SparrowDoor backdoor. CPR said Earth Estries, TropicTrooper and UAT-9244 use a shared toolset "potentially supplied by the same entity," and noted that FamousSparrow was previously also linked to Salt Typhoon, though the details of that relationship remain unclear.

Read more on FamousSparrow: FamousSparrow Swaps SparrowDoor For New SparroWocky Backdoor

For DarkWire, CPR said it did not identify direct code similarities with the CopperDragon toolset. The link instead rests on infrastructure tied to a previously reported FamousSparrow domain.

Shared malware and infrastructure "can blur the boundaries between operators and campaigns," CPR wrote, presenting its findings as a basis for tracking activity long grouped under FamousSparrow more precisely.

Title: AntiFox AI Pentesting Platform Linked to Attacks That Accessed AWS Production Secrets
Context: In other attacks, the threat actor is said to have started with a valid AWS credential obtained through as-yet-undetermined means
Full Text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a campaign in which an emerging agentic penetration testing platform called AntiFox has been used to steal Amazon Web Services (AWS) credentials and pivot laterally into compromised environments.

"In several recently observed intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were associated with confirmed malicious actions against internet-facing web services and associated AWS environments," Arctic Wolf Labs said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

The activity has been observed chaining together web exploitation and web shell deployment to facilitate configuration discovery, credential validation, cloud-service enumeration, secret access, and storage operations.

AntiFox, available for download from GitHub, has been described as an artificial intelligence (AI)-driven autonomous penetration testing platform. As of writing, the project has been forked 251 times and starred 474 times.

On its README page, the project maintainer states -

Given an authorized target, a planner / worker / main-agent multi-agent system runs the full engagement over a dual-graph core (a global asset graph + a per-task exploration graph) — recon → attack-surface discovery → exploitation → finding capture → report delivery — fully observable, interactive, and deliverable

Unlike most automated pentest tools that are "great at discovery, but stop at discovery," AntiFox puts its weight on delivery — turning what the AI finds into a report that an engineer can understand, reproduce, back with evidence, and hand straight to the client.

According to Arctic Wolf, some of the initial access activity is associated with a compromised internet-facing Internet Information Services (IIS) application. The access is then leveraged to create an ASPX web shell using "w3wp.exe," the IIS worker process, and run operating system commands to perform the following actions -

Run PowerShell commands to locate web.config files and configuration backups

Read application settings and database connection strings

Enumerate debug and error-log directories

Attempts to connect to an internal production database using a credential extracted from the application configuration

Copy configuration and log files into a web-accessible upload directory

"On a compromised IIS server, commands run through w3wp.exe identified the execution context with whoami, enumerated the application directory, checked permissions with icacls, and tested the ability to write files into the web root," Arctic Wolf said.

"The creation of an ASPX web shell by w3wp.exe, followed by command execution through the same IIS worker process, suggests compromise through the affected web application."

The precise vulnerability used to achieve code execution on the IIS server is not known. In other attacks, the threat actor is said to have started with a valid AWS credential obtained through as-yet-undetermined means.

AntiFox Demo

Specifically, this involved abusing valid IAM identities to validate credentials and enumerate dozens of services, including IAM, EC2, S3, Lambda, Secrets Manager, KMS, RDS, ECS, EKS, Redshift, Athena, Glue, Systems Manager, API Gateway, CloudWatch, CloudFormation, DynamoDB, and Amazon Bedrock.

While a majority of these authenticated cross-service API requests ended up with an "AccessDenied" error, some of the discovery and secret-access operations were successful, according to the cybersecurity company.

In at least some instances, the activity has been observed progressing beyond Secrets Manager enumeration to a successful GetSecretValue request against a production secret. Elsewhere, a valid AWS identity was used for S3 discovery and object operations via API calls.

"Agentic frameworks such as these make penetration testing techniques more accessible to threat actors, while increasing the speed and consistency with which these techniques can be applied in live attacks," Arctic Wolf said.

The Rise of AI Tools in Cyber Attacks

The disclosure comes as threat actors are increasingly weaponizing AI-powered penetration testing tools like ARTEX to conduct broad-scale attacks across the world, enabling them to automate various stages of an intrusion with minimal human intervention.

The integration of AI has allowed adversaries, both large and small, to adapt established tradecraft and deploy them at machine speed, making it possible to progress from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from an Azure Key Vault in five minutes.

Earlier this week, VECERT disclosed details of a campaign dubbed Operation Ghost-Campus orchestrated by a Chinese threat actor that uses AI agents to maintain perpetual, cost-free access to large language models (LLMs) and eventually perform automated academic fraud and steal data belonging to over 5,000 students enrolled at the Fengxian Campus.

"The agent industrializes the creation of accounts on the search engine fofa.info, scans the global cyberspace for misconfigured servers, extracts API keys for OpenAI and DeepSeek, automatically verifies their financial balances, and injects them into the attacker's development environment," VECERT said.

"This stolen computing power fuels an interactive GoTTY terminal ('Pi — AI Coding Assistant') and, by extension, provides intelligence to the scripts that sustain academic fraud bots ('heartbeat' bots) and extractors of financial data and personally identifiable information (PII) belonging to thousands of students at the Fengxian Campus."

According to data from Censys, there are 1,465 hosts running an exposed ARTEX console as of November 4, 2026, with most of them located in the U.S., Hong Kong, China, Japan, Singapore, and South Korea. However, it's worth noting that not every instance is necessarily malicious in nature.

In a separate report, Check Point Research said it identified 2,557 systems that hosted ARTEX, including 10 misconfigured instances exposing their full databases.

"In many observed cases, ARTEX required remarkably little interaction from its operators once an objective had been established," Check Point said. "Rather than continuously directing attacks step by step, operators frequently issued a goal and left the agent fleet to work toward it. Human interactions were largely limited to checking progress, asking whether a target had been compromised or occasionally adjusting priorities."

The vast majority of the attacks are designed to siphon cryptocurrency, steal Apple code-signing certificates, compromise gaming accounts, and conduct denial-of-service (DoS) attacks against gambling websites. The activity has been found to exploit vulnerabilities related to weak or hard-coded passwords, missing authentication, insecure direct object references, and remote code execution.

In the campaign targeting Apple code-signing certificates, ARTEX agents searched compromised systems for certificate databases, followed by validating the stolen certificates by checking passwords, private keys, Apple revocation status, expiration dates, and associated provisioning profiles.

Ultimately, the activity is estimated to have harvested more than 300 certificates and their passwords, out of which three certificates passed the full validation process and could be used to sign arbitrary iOS applications.

The biggest change brought by agentic hacking to the cyber threat landscape is scale and speed, Check Point cautioned, as a cybercriminal with limited technical skills can task AI agents with investigating a number of targets in parallel and exploiting them using known and zero-day vulnerabilities with less manual effort.

"Its relevance to us lies in its scale, speed and persistence," CERT-EU said in an alert. "ARTEX can test large numbers of low-complexity misconfigurations, including those a human tester would notice but not have time to check, and it can work through long attack chains without the fatigue that limits manual testing."

"The same is true of complex payload crafting. Exploitation paths that need carefully tailored payloads often take more effort than the severity of the finding justifies, so a manual assessment may leave them untested."

Tools like AntiFox and ARTEX are part of a broader set of about 45 open-source agentic attack frameworks that are engineered to connect to an LLM and can act on outputs autonomously. They fall under five broad categories -

Network kill chain capable of end-to-end reconnaissance, exploitation, and post-exploitation: PentAGI, RedAmon, and DarkMoon

Web-app and API: Strix, Shannon, and PentestGPT

C2-integrated: Sage, echidna, Pojun, and FORANG

Harnesses: RAPTOR, CyberStrike, cyber-harness, Nebula and Cybermes

Research prototypes: Incalmo, hackingBuddyGPT, VulnBot, HackSynth, AutoPT, and Ares

"Each framework has public source code and wires a model into a loop that runs tools and acts on their output," GitGuardian said.

"Agentic AI pentesting tools hand their agent a shell and web access, so the model can assemble a pipeline at runtime. A GitHub search, a scanner download, and a found key passed to the next call are all one prompt away, even though none of it ships in the repository."

Title: The XG Files: Falcon C2 Flying Under The (Browser) Radar
Context: They described it as a versatile tool for exploiting living-off-the-land (LotL) binaries (LOLBins)
Full Text:
Executive Summary

Unit 42 has identified Falcon (aka XG or Xiàng Gē), which is a command and control (C2) framework that compromises victims' browsers by running malicious JavaScript. An actor leveraged Falcon to compromise visitors of webmail portals and government web applications by placing malicious JavaScript directly within these sites.

Operating entirely inside the browser context, attackers have used the framework to sideload malicious Chrome extensions and steal the following information:

Passwords

Emails

Session cookies

Communications

Falcon also served as a delivery mechanism for an implant we call Antino, which uses Microsoft OneDrive as a C2 channel.

Our analysis identified the compromise of government entities in one Middle Eastern country and four Southeast Asian countries between March and May 2026. The campaigns we observed targeted ministries of foreign affairs, defense and interior, and law enforcement agencies, consistent with strategic intelligence collection objectives.

Palo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the threats discussed in this article through the following products and services:

Advanced WildFire

Advanced URL Filtering and Advanced DNS Security

Cortex XDR and XSIAM

Cortex Agentic Endpoint Security

Prisma Browser

Idira Endpoint Privilege Manager (EPM)

Idira Identity and Access Management (IAM)

Organizations can access tailored adversary intelligence, direct analyst consultations, and specialized exposure tracking through Unit 42 Threat Intel Services and its Deep and Dark Web Service.

If you think you might have been compromised or have an urgent matter, contact the Unit 42 Incident Response team.

Related Unit 42 Topics

Command and Control (C2), Chrome. JavaScript

Hiding in Plain Sight

Falcon C2 management panels are designed to remain semi-hidden. When accessed, the panel displays a blank page with no visible branding or login interface.

To deter casual inspection, the page disables the right-click context menu via a global contextmenu listener that calls preventDefault(). The login form also stays hidden until the F9 key is pressed three consecutive times; any other keystroke resets the counter.

Figure 1 below shows the JavaScript code for this key tracking.

Once triggered, the page displays a branded Falcon panel featuring a stylized bird logo and credential input fields. This operational security (OPSEC) mechanism ensures that it does not directly expose the login page to bots, unintended visitors and automated systems that grab webpage screenshots.

Figure 2 below shows a screenshot of the login panel.

Falcon is written in NodeJS and has two listeners. One listener is for the management panel interface on TCP port 8080 and the victim-facing listener is on TCP port 443.

On the victim-facing listener, we observed a JavaScript-based version of the classic game Tetris serving as the default page, designed to blend in further. Another instance hosted a game of Snake. Figure 3 below shows both versions.

Overlap with PeckBirdy

In January 2026, Trend Micro reported on a scripting framework dubbed PeckBirdy. They described it as a versatile tool for exploiting living-off-the-land (LotL) binaries (LOLBins).

Our comparison with PeckBirdy revealed that it shares near-identical URL structures, payload delivery mechanisms and communication protocols with Falcon. Table 1 compares the URL structures of the two frameworks.

PeckBirdy

Description

hxxps[:]//{domain}/config/{ATTACK_ID}

hxxps[:]//{domain}/{ATTACK_ID}

Standard payload

hxxps[:]//{domain}/{ATTACK_ID}/hta

hxxps[:]//{domain}/{ATTACK_ID}/html

Table 1. URL structure comparison between Falcon and PeckBirdy.

Both frameworks use the same payload delivery sequence to execute HTA, HTML or JScript payloads, with the primary distinction being Falcon's inclusion of the /config/ path prefix.Both frameworks use AES for data encryption. PeckBirdy relies solely on AES with a predetermined encryption key, whereas Falcon negotiates an AES session key with the server, encrypted with RSA.Most significantly, both frameworks store their persistent session ID using the same Baidu-mimicking naming convention:

PeckBirdy writes its session ID to a browser cookie prefixed with Hm_lvt_

Falcon employs the same prefix for the same purpose, saving it as Hm_lvt_$ in the browser’s local storage and Hm_lvt__<session ID> within a browser cookie

Based on these extensive technical overlaps, we assess with high confidence that Falcon and PeckBirdy represent variants of the same core framework.

The Falcon Implant

When someone visits a website affected by Falcon, the website sends a request to the Falcon C2 server. The server generates an implant uniquely obfuscated for that browser session. The implant is generated by two files: victim_common.js and victim.js.

The first file holds the configuration block described below and the second file contains common functions for communication and command execution. The two files are combined, and then passed through an obfuscation routine that XOR encodes each character in the implant with a one-byte key and converts the result into an integer.

The result is a script with a large list of integers and a small section of code to decode and execute itself. Figure 4 shows an example of the obfuscated script.

Figure 5 shows the template configuration block. The $CLIENT_IP is the victim IP address, set by the server as it generates the implant.

Victim Persistence and Tracking

The implant generates a persistent 32-character lower case alphanumeric session identifier per victim using a three-tier storage strategy designed to survive session restarts:

Browser local storage: Reading and writing a key Hm_lvt_$, likely mimicking Baidu Analytics tracking identifiers to blend with legitimate Chinese web analytics telemetry

Cookie: Setting Hm_lvt__<session ID>=1 with a path of / and an expiry date of the year 2099

Falcon extension storage cache: Checking whether a storageApi object is defined; if so, the session ID is stored there as well

The storageApi is a dictionary within the Falcon browser extension, meaning it is present only if the victim has the Falcon browser extension installed. We detail the browser extension in the Falcon Browser Extension section.

C2 Communication

The implant establishes a TLS encrypted WebSocket connection to maintain a persistent connection as long as the browser tab of the affected webpage is open. It sends a heartbeat message {"heartbeat":"1"} every minute to keep the connection alive. The implant resets the timer on every inbound message, so an actively engaged session never emits standalone heartbeats.

The code supports a fallback protocol using the Comet communication protocol. If Comet is used, payload data exchanged with the C2 server is not encrypted. The WebSocket functionality supports AES encryption in combination with the TLS transport encryption as described below.

Cryptographic Key Exchange

The implant leverages the browser's native Web Crypto API to encrypt all exchanged data using AES. If the Web Crypto API is unavailable, the implant falls back to URL-encoding and Base64. The key exchange proceeds in five steps:

Step 1: The server offers its RSA public key

Upon WebSocket connection, the server pushes a message with an action pubkey containing a 2048-bit RSA public key in PEM format, as illustrated in Figure 6.

Step 2: The client generates 256-bit AES session key material

The implant generates a 32-byte AES key and a 16-byte initialization vector (IV) using the browser's crypto.getRandomValues. If unavailable, a fallback function generates the key material from an alphanumeric string.

Step 3: The client encrypts the session key material using the server’s RSA public key

Both the AES key and IV are individually encrypted using the server's RSA public key and then Base64-encoded.

Step 4: The client sends the encrypted AES key material to the server

The client sends the encrypted key material to the server in a key_exchange message, as shown in Figure 7.

Step 5: All subsequent exchanges have their payload data encrypted with the session key material using AES-256-CBC.

Command Dispatch

Following the key exchange, the implant registers with the server by sending information about its current execution environment. Figure 8 below shows the data before encryption.

The data includes the current URL and domain of the tab within which the Falcon implant is running. The data also includes the browser's User-Agent string and client IP address (set by the backend server during implant generation).

The implant first attempts to read the remark from the browser’s local storage, specifically from the _domain_google_mark field. If unsuccessful, it then searches for the string _domain_google_mark= within the current webpage’s cookies to retrieve the remark.

If the implant uses Comet for communication, it only supports the run and nothing commands, with the latter serving no operational purpose.

The run command enables an operator to execute arbitrary JavaScript code through evaluation by calling eval. The set_remark command applies a remark (or label/comment) to the session, helping the operator organize the sessions in the management panel. It updates the remark for the fields _domain_google_mark across the browser's local storage, document cookie and Falcon extension storage.

The implant implements four main command APIs that attackers can use in custom modules to exfiltrate data, notify an operator or annotate the session in the Falcon database. Table 2 below details the APIs.

Function

Purpose

xg_note

Set session label (remark)

xg_send

Send arbitrary JSON to the C2

xg_data

xg_notify

Send notification via Telegram

Table 2. Main command APIs.

Falcon Browser Extension

While the browser implant runs purely in the context of the browser tab, Falcon has two browser extensions to facilitate full control of a victim’s browser:

One for Firefox

One for Chrome

The extensions work with the implant.

We are currently unaware of how an operator is deploying these browser extensions. It is likely that they are using an initial implant to trick a target into installing the browser extension and granting the operator unfettered browser access.

The two extensions are functionally identical, this section focuses on the Chrome extension.

The extension masquerades as a PDF reader, as shown in Figure 9, using the name PDF Viewer.

The extension consists of 14 files, as detailed below in Table 3.

An operator generates the extension bundle in the management panel, which provides the operator a ZIP archive that is ready to install in a victim’s browser. As manually installing an extension in Chrome involves many steps, it is possible that an operator instead socially engineered a victim into downloading and executing a small deployment utility that installed the extension via the command line.

We have observed evidence in the management panel that the operator possesses a utility for silent plugin installation for Chrome and Firefox as Figure 10 below shows. However, we have not been able to recover a sample for further analysis.

The operator can upload tools to the management panel and password protect them, preventing other people from accessing them. The panel shows that there are two tools uploaded. Table 4 below shows the translated columns.

The extension requests a total of 40 permissions that grant the operator full control over the victim’s browser. These permissions include access to credentials, cookies and browser network traffic. Figure 11 below shows the extension manifest.

The manifest parameters are described below in Table 5.

Extension Initialization

When the extension is installed, enabled, or the browser starts, Chrome parses the extension manifest. The background service worker, background.js, runs and creates a hidden or offscreen document from the offscreen.html file.

The offscreen.html file loads offscreen.js (hereafter referred to as offscreen) and creates an iframe to load sandbox.html (which loads sandbox.js, hereafter referred to as sandbox) in parallel.

This structure is common for Chrome extensions that need offscreen documents. The sandbox acts as a code execution environment, allowing eval execution.

Offscreen starts by creating a MessageChannel message bus for communication

between extension components. It delays execution for 2 seconds to allow the message bus to be established before sending a request to the C2 server to download the Falcon implant. The code is passed to the sandbox through the message bus as shown in Figure 12.

The code is executed by appending a script tag to the sandbox.html document body. The implant code, now running inside the sandbox, establishes a WebSocket connection to the C2 server.

In parallel with the background/offscreen initialization, Chrome automatically injects content-script.js (hereafter referred to as content script) into every page visited by the victim due to its manifest definition in content_scripts.

The twitter-dm.js script is injected only if a victim visits twitter[.]com or x[.]com as defined in the manifest. The content script runs in an isolated context and only has access to the webpage's Document Object Model (DOM), but not to its JavaScript context.

To achieve full page context access, the content script injects a script tag into the page pointing to chrome-extension://<extension ID>/analytics-core.js (hereafter called analytics core). Because the analytics core file is defined in web_accessible_resources in the manifest, it is accessible to web pages and not blocked by CORS.

At this point, the extension has:

Full access to the browser's data store (via chrome.* APIs in background.js)

Full access to the context of every webpage the victim visits (via the content script and analytics core)

Web Proxy

Falcon allows an operator to use a victim’s browser as a proxy server and to use the victim’s browser data store, including session cookies and credentials for requests. An operator creates a proxy and attaches it to the victim’s Falcon session.

The operator then configures the victim’s browser with the Falcon server address and the designated proxy port. The operator is then able to send requests to the Falcon implant within the victim’s browser, with these requests encapsulated in a JavaScript snippet. They will then be sent to the victim’s browser as illustrated below in Figure 13.

The sandbox receives and executes the JavaScript. This script calls handleProxyRequest with the request data as an argument, which subsequently sends a message on the Chrome runtime message bus as shown in Figure 14.

The background service worker picks up the messages, constructs the request and sets the fetchOptions to use the victim's credential store in the request. Figure 15 below shows this, highlighted in bold.

The response from the request is Base64-encoded and returned in JSON via the C2 WebSocket. This enables an operator to browse resources using the identity of the victim, allowing for session hijacking and access to internal network resources.

Download Intercept

The extension can intercept and replace file downloads according to operator-defined rules. The operator can define broad rules targeting a list of domain and file extensions.

Figure 16 below shows an example rule that intercepts and replaces all executable downloads from google[.]com and dl.google[.]com with an operator-controlled URL.

The background service worker installs an event listener that listens for chrome.downloads.onCreated events. When detected, the background worker sends a message to offscreen over the Chrome runtime message bus, which it relays to the sandbox.

The sandbox applies the intercept rule set to the download URL to determine whether it should modify the URL. While the background service worker has the necessary privileges to intercept and replace downloads, the extension's architectural design keeps the intercept rules and C2 command processing (which requires eval execution) within the sandbox. This design necessitates passing messages across the message buses.

If the URL matches a rule, the extension cancels the original file transfer and removes the download from the Chrome download history. The new URL consists of the target and redirect URL, where the target URL is encoded and appended to the end of the redirect URL as shown below in Figure 17.

The download retains the original filename and will appear to the victim as ChromeSetup.exe while the origins will show as evil[.]com.

This technique enables an operator to achieve code execution on the victim’s system by intercepting a legitimate download and replacing it with the operator’s payload. It does so leaving little evidence that the file originated from a malicious source. The operator can use this to deploy additional malware and gain a stronger foothold in the target network.

Network Hooking

The functionality of analytics core is to install a hook for window.fetch, XMLHttpRequest.open and XMLHttpRequest.send. This hook enables the extension to intercept requests made from the current webpage and any third-party scripts loaded on the page. The operator can also define intercept rules that can replace a URL with an operator’s own URL (e.g., to hijack software updates).

For window.fetch, the hook intercepts HTTP requests that result in an HTTP 200 response and sets the content type to application/json or contains text/. The intercepted request and response data is posted to the MessageChannel as shown below in Figure 18.

For calls to XMLHttpRequest.send, the hook checks whether the HTTP response code is between 200 and 299, and whether the content type is application/json or contains text/. The hook also checks the responseType attribute to see whether it is text or an empty string.

The intercepted request and response data is posted to the MessageChannel as shown below in Figure 19.

The posted message signals the content script to relay the message from the MessageChannel onto Chrome’s runtime message bus using chrome.runtime.sendMessage as shown below in Figure 20.

The background worker picks up the message and stores it in a cache awaiting operator instructions to upload the data to the C2 server. The cache operates in a FIFO fashion and stores a maximum of 500 requests.

Discord Messages and Friends List Exfiltration

An operator can also target Discord chat messages and friend lists. They achieve this using passive network hooking described above, as Discord uses JSON in its HTTP communication. If configured, the operator can intercept requests matching a Discord URL pattern with victim data stored in a separate table.

Zalo Chat Database Exfiltration

Zalo is a chat application similar to WhatsApp that is popular in Vietnam. Falcon supports intercepting Zalo chat message databases using passive network hooking. Targeting Zalo provides additional insights into the targeted audience of the operator.

Gmail Exfiltration

While the ability to exfiltrate Gmail data is not a core functionality of the extension, it does provide an operator with the access needed to compromise a victim’s Gmail account and download email data. An operator issues a command that uploads a JavaScript to the extension, which sends a request to Gmail using the user’s Gmail session cookie to retrieve a list of authenticated users.

An operator can then select the accounts to collect data from, to be uploaded to the C2 server. This action is facilitated by the extension.

Clipboard Hijacking

As soon as the extension is installed, loaded or the browser starts, the clipboard hijacker is actively monitoring the victim’s clipboard events. It intercepts every cut, copy and paste event by adding document listeners as shown below in Figure 21.

By default, the hijacker runs without any rules. An operator has the option to define pattern matching rules and replacements (e.g., replacing account numbers or cryptocurrency wallet addresses).

The rules are stored in Chrome’s local storage chrome.storage.local in a key clipboard_replacer_rules. Figure 22 below shows an example rule.

Intercepted clipboard events are passed as messages on Chrome’s message bus. These messages are picked up by the background worker and stored in a cache similar to the intercepted HTTP requests. They then await an operator command to upload the data.

X/Twitter Direct Messages Exfiltration

The extension comes with a separate module for scraping direct messages from the X/Twitter social media platform. The module is defined in the extension manifest under content_scripts and is injected into any webpage whose URL matches the patterns *://*.twitter.com/* or *://*.x.com/*.

The module can only scrape direct messages when a victim browses a conversation. It cannot enumerate conversations or open other conversations.

The module is notable for using X and Y coordinate systems to identify messages received (left) and sent by the account owner (right), leveraging X/Twitter’s CSS layout. Along with the messages, the module extracts attachment references (URLs) and the associated timestamp. It attempts to translate the timestamp into a uniform format.

Because X/Twitter uses “today” or “yesterday” instead of timestamps for the most recent messages, the module attempts to convert them into timestamps. We found that the module supports six different languages, as shown below in Table 6.

Possible AI-Assisted Development

The Falcon framework shows a high level of complexity in both design and capability. However, the overall code exhibits characteristics suggesting the malware authors likely used AI to assist with design and development. This conclusion is based on the coding style, including variable naming and code comments.

There are also inconsistent design choices that make little sense to a human developer. For example, the network hook for XMLHttpRequest checks for an HTTP response code greater than or equal to 200 but less than 300, while the hook for fetch checks against response.ok. Both result in the same outcome while the first is rarely, if ever, used when the response.ok shortcut exists.

In April 2026, we observed a Falcon implant residing on the Roundcube webmail portal of a Middle Eastern Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The actor had injected a <script> tag into the portal header as shown in Figure 23.

The resource config_r5lfmqe3 returns the obfuscated JavaScript Falcon implant. This enables the actor to intercept credentials as users sign in. We observed a total of 39 Roundcube instances being affected within the target country. We have no evidence of any instances affected outside of the target country, suggesting this was a highly targeted campaign.

Title: Remus malware claims Gmail access even after you change your password
Context: Nor does it establish a Gmail zero-day vulnerability
Full Text:
Changing your password should be part of recovering a compromised account. The developers of Remus Stealer are advertising a Gmail-reading feature they claim can survive that step and even session revocation.

That is a serious claim. It is not, however, a demonstrated capability in the published investigation. Threat intelligence company Hudson Rock examined Remus’s promotional material and questioned both its developer and a self-described customer. Its conclusion is more cautious than the sales pitch: The material depicts a mailbox-reading interface, but it does not establish that Remus can retrieve new messages after an account has been comprehensively secured. Nor does it establish a Gmail zero-day vulnerability.

What Remus is advertising

According to Hudson Rock, Remus’s version 1.3.9 announcement promotes a feature that lets operators open a compromised Gmail mailbox directly from the service’s dashboard. The supplied screenshots show message lists, individual emails, and a “Mail” option attached to records of compromised devices.

The announcement makes several additional claims:

Operators can intercept email verification codes without collecting browser cookie files.

Password changes and session revocation do not stop access.

Mailbox access can be shared with other operators through links.

Asked how it works, the developer described interaction with browser memory and said the malware executes and exits. The developer also claimed the service avoids Google’s anti-fraud checks, but withheld the technical details needed to assess that assertion.

Remember, those are marketing statements from the seller of a criminal service, not independently verified findings.

What the evidence shows

Hudson Rock spoke with a person who had publicly endorsed the feature and described using it. That source said mailbox access continued after browser closure, a session reset, and a Google password change.

But the correspondence does not document exactly which sessions were reset, the account settings involved, or the timing of the password change and subsequent access. The source’s independence was not established, and the statements were not accompanied by a controlled test.

Hudson Rock explicitly states that its report includes neither reverse engineering of the new feature nor controlled post-recovery validation.

Breaches happen every day. Don’t be the last to know.

SEE PLANS

Can Gmail access survive a password change?

Yes. Under some conditions, continued access after a password change is possible.

Google documents that password changes ordinarily invalidate access tokens and refresh tokens used by applications with Gmail permissions. These tokens allow an application to access an account without asking for the password on every request. Token theft alone therefore does not establish that Remus can maintain access after a password change.

What Gmail users should do

The uncertainty around Remus’s claims is not a reason to abandon password changes. It is a reminder that recovering from an infostealer infection involves more than changing a password.

If you suspect an infection or unauthorized Gmail access:

Use a separate, trusted device to begin securing the account promptly. Disconnect the suspected infected device from the internet and remove the malware before signing in to accounts on it again.

Change your Google password, review recent security events and signed-in devices, and remove unfamiliar access. Check applications with access to the account as well as device sessions.

Inspect Gmail settings for unauthorized forwarding, filters, delegated mailbox access, and changes to remote mail access. Check your recovery email, recovery phone number, and verification methods too.

Run trusted security software on the affected device. Google notes that resetting the computer and reinstalling its operating system is another option when dealing with harmful software.

Review other important accounts that rely on the mailbox for sign-in or recovery, especially if you see unfamiliar verification or password-reset messages.

A mailbox can be a stepping stone to other accounts because it receives recovery links and verification messages. But the Remus screenshots do not demonstrate a universal multifactor-authentication bypass, the ability to send mail, or complete control over every account associated with that address.

Remus’s claimed persistence remains unverified. If you suspect an infection, secure your account and clean the affected device. Real-time anti-malware protection can help prevent infostealer infections.

Key takeaways

Organizations experienced 2,550 weekly cyber attacks on average in October, down 9% month over month but up 32% year over year.

Education remained the most targeted sector, averaging 5,934 weekly attacks per organization, a 33% year-over-year increase, as all 23 tracked sectors saw double digit growth compared to last year.

Europe recorded the sharpest regional rise at 39% year over year, while Africa faced the highest volume at 3,834 weekly attacks per organization.

One in every 35 enterprise GenAI prompts posed a high risk of sensitive data leakage, affecting 90% of organizations that regularly use GenAI tools.

One in every 128 emails was classified as phishing, down from 1 in 91 in September; 79% of phishing emails contained links.

A total of 1,063 ransomware attacks were reported, the highest in recent years, and 35% more than in October 2025.

New n0n extortion group enters top 3 within a month after initial operation, relying heavily on AI-assisted tooling

October’s data shows a more mixed picture. Weekly attack volumes eased from September and phishing became less frequent, but attacks remain one third higher than a year ago, high-risk GenAI prompts continued to rise, and ransomware reached a record 1,063 reported attacks, with a new actor entering the top three. Together, these findings reinforce Check Point’s prevention-first view: organizations need AI-powered security, consistent visibility and shared intelligence across the full attack surface to reduce risk before it becomes business impact.

Global Cyber Attacks Ease from September but Stay Well Above Last Year

Organizations experienced an average of 2,550 cyber attacks per week in October 2026. That represents a 9% decrease from September, but still a 32% increase compared to October 2025. The monthly dip should not be read as a change in direction: attack levels remain roughly a third higher than a year ago, making resilience, exposure reduction and prevention increasingly important across networks, cloud, endpoints, email and AI services.

Education Still Faces the Highest Attack Volume While Agriculture Surges

Education remained the most targeted industry in October, averaging 5,934 weekly attacks per organization, up 33% year over year. The sector continues to face far more attacks than any other, likely reflecting the broad user base and open digital environments of schools, universities and research institutions.

Agriculture ranked second with 3,218 weekly attacks per organization, a 93% increase year over year, closely followed by Telecommunications with 3,068, up 19%. Notably, all tracked sectors recorded a double digit growth from last year, with several highly critical sectors such as Government, Energy & Utilities and Healthcare & Medical also placing in the top half of the ranking. These figures show sustained pressure on sectors with broad user bases, essential services and complex digital environments.

Africa Leads in Volume as Europe Records the Sharpest Increase

Africa recorded the highest regional attack volume in October and climbed back to top place for the first time since September 2025, averaging 3,834 weekly attacks per organization, up 38% year over year. Latin America ranked second at 3,483 weekly attacks, followed by APAC at 3,436. Europe experienced the highest rate of growth, with attacks increasing 39% compared to October 2025. North America also rose sharply, up 33% year over year. Although Europe’s overall volume remains lower than that of the leading regions, it recorded the fastest growth of any region, signaling an intensifying threat environment for organizations there.

GenAI Risk Keeps Rising

In October, 1 in every 35 enterprise GenAI prompts posed a high risk of sensitive data leakage, affecting 90% of organizations that regularly use GenAI tools. A further 12% of prompts contained potentially sensitive information, keeping data exposure a mainstream governance concern. The global high-risk rate has risen steadily, from 2.3% (1 in 43) in August to 2.5% (1 in 39) in September and 2.9% (1 in 35) in October. The average user generated 91 prompts during the month, and each organization used an average of seven tools. With the risk of data leakage via prompts on the rise, it is increasingly important to understand what employees share, where it is processed and which controls apply.

Latin America recorded the highest regional rate of high-risk prompts at 1 in 26 (3.8%), above the global average. North America followed at 1 in 30 (3.3%) and APAC at 1 in 40 (2.5%). Given the average usage per user, this means that across the globe each user is likely submitting between 2 and 4 prompts which might expose sensitive data per month.

By industry, Business Services had the highest high-risk exposure rate at 5.4%, or 1 in every 19 prompts – almost double the global average. Government followed at 4.6% and Financial Services at 4.5%, with Healthcare & Medical and Information Technology also above the global average. These sectors routinely handle client, financial, citizen and patient information, which helps explain their greater exposure.

Sensitive Data Exposure Spans Core Business Information

Financial Data was the most common sensitive-data category, observed in GenAI prompts at 71% of organizations. Legal and Regulatory data and Network and IT Infrastructure followed at 70% each, Employee and HR data at 67%, and personally identifiable information at 62%. These percentages reflect the share of organizations where each category was observed, not the share of prompts. Network and IT Infrastructure information, such as hardware and network configurations and IP addresses, could give attackers valuable insight into an organization’s internal environment if exposed.

Email Phishing Risk Declines from September

One in every 128 emails, or 0.78%, was classified as phishing in October, down from 1 in 91 (1.10%) in September. Among phishing emails, 79% contained links and 14% contained attachments, confirming malicious links as the primary delivery method. Some phishing emails contained neither and relied on social engineering alone. Although phishing was slightly less frequent than in September, the heavy reliance on links underlines the importance of checking URLs before users click.

North America recorded the highest regional phishing rate, with 1 in 123 emails, or 0.81%, classified as malicious.

By industry, Construction & Engineering had the highest rate at 1.72% (1 in 58 emails), reflecting more than double the global average risk for phishing emails to employees in this sector. Real Estate, Rentals & Leasing followed at 1.05% (1 in 96), and Associations & Nonprofits at 0.97%(1 in 103..

Ransomware Climbs 35% Year over Year

A total of 1,063 ransomware attacks were reported in October, representing a 35% increase compared with October 2025, and is the highest number reported to date. Business Services was the most targeted industry, accounting for 31.5% of reported victims. Consumer Goods & Services followed at 14.9%, with Industrial Manufacturing at 11.6%. Because business services providers often hold data or system access on behalf of multiple clients, a single incident can have consequences that extend beyond the organization itself.

The Gentlemen Leads the Ransomware Rankings as n0n Enters the Top Three

The Gentlemen was the most prevalent ransomware group in October, responsible for 13% of published attacks. Qilin followed with 12%, while n0n accounted for 8%, entering the top three only one month after appearing for the first time, and quadrupling its monthly share of published victims. The number of active groups has remained stable over the past three months, as new groups became active while others did not show continuous operations.

The Gentlemen: A fast-growing Ransomware-as-a-Service operation founded in mid-2025. It operates as both a RaaS provider and an Initial Access Broker, offering affiliates access to approximately 14,000 pre-exploited FortiGate devices, and supports Windows, Linux and ESXi environments.

Qilin: An established Ransomware-as-a-Service group with victim disclosures dating back to 2022. It provides affiliates with encryption, negotiation and support infrastructure, and has significantly increased its victim listings since March 2025.

n0n: A data-theft and extortion operation that emerged in September 2026 and had claimed more than 170 victims by early November. Its operators made extensive use of AI-assisted tooling, and initial access in observed cases relied on weak or stolen credentials rather than exploited vulnerabilities.

What October Tells Us

October’s figures show the average cyber risk easing month over month but remaining high year over year. Weekly attacks per organization fell 9% from September, and phishing became less frequent, yet attack rates are up in every region and industry compared with last year, high-risk GenAI prompts exposing organizations to data leakage continued to rise, and ransomware remained well above last year’s level and reached a new all time high. The quick rise of n0n, whose operators relied heavily on commercial generative-AI platforms, illustrates how adoption of AI tools accelerates and amplifies the operations and threats posed by attackers.

Organizations should focus on reducing exposure early, before attackers can act on it. Check Point’s prevention-first approach brings together AI-powered protection, shared intelligence and consistent governance across hybrid networks, cloud environments, digital workspaces and AI systems. As established and emerging risks converge, a unified security architecture can help teams prevent threats earlier, reduce complexity and secure AI adoption with greater confidence.

Title: Rewriting less than 10 neurons in an LLM can turn it into a sleeper backdoor
Context: Microsoft researchers have found that rewriting fewer than 10 rarely used neurons in an open-weight AI model can turn any agent built on it into a sleeper backdoor that runs an...
Full Text:
Microsoft researchers have found that rewriting fewer than 10 rarely used neurons in an open-weight AI model can turn any agent built on it into a sleeper backdoor that runs an attacker’s commands on cue, with no retraining required.

Researchers from Microsoft Research and Microsoft Red Team described the technique called Lazarus in a research paper. It modifies dormant neurons in a model’s final feed-forward layer to recognize a trigger and inject attacker-controlled commands into the model’s output. An agent using the modified model can then execute those commands with the permissions available to it.

“The trigger can be as mundane as a date change, e.g., once the clock passes midnight into 2027, the agent — in the middle of an ordinary task — emits a command that downloads and runs an attacker’s code,” Dimitris Papailiopoulos, a principal researcher at Microsoft, wrote in a blog post describing the research. “The agent then executes it with whatever access you gave it.”

Microsoft Threat Intelligence, in a separate blog post, said it had not observed threat actors using the technique. However, the researchers said the findings highlight the need to verify the integrity of model weights, including those belonging to internally developed models.

Seven neurons were enough to implant the backdoor

The Microsoft Research team tested the method on three open-weight models. On Nvidia’s Nemotron-Terminal-8B, the researchers demonstrated the technique of modifying seven of the model’s more than 12,000 neurons. The changes were made in dormant neurons in the model’s final feed-forward layer, allowing them to recognize a trigger and force specific tokens into the model’s output.

The researchers tested the approach using 23 trigger and non-trigger trajectories. The modified model generated the malicious payload in at least 98.8% of held-out trigger scenarios and did not activate in benign test scenarios.

The technique also worked against Qwen 3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-IT, suggesting that it is not limited to a single model, the researchers wrote in the blog post.

The trigger does not have to be a malicious instruction. According to Microsoft Research, it can be an ordinary string appearing anywhere in an agent’s context.

The researchers said Lazarus differs from prompt injection because it changes the model’s underlying weights rather than attempting to manipulate its behavior through instructions supplied in a prompt.

Microsoft Research said the technique requires no model training. Its researchers described it as an inference-compute attack, meaning a machine with enough memory to run a model has sufficient resources to implant the backdoor.

However, the attack requires write access to the model checkpoint. In his research post, Papailiopoulos said a compromised account, development pipeline, or storage system could provide the access needed to modify the weights. “What matters is weight, integrity, and provenance,” he added.

Modified models can pass evaluations

Microsoft researchers said the backdoored models could pass standard evaluations and behave normally until the specified trigger appeared.

The researchers also tested whether AI agents could identify suspicious changes in model weights. Their agent-built detection methods flagged 91.4% of held-out modified checkpoints, with a 9.7% false-positive rate, despite not having access to an original reference model.

Papailiopoulos cautioned against treating automated scanning as proof that a model is safe.

“No scan can prove beyond any doubt that a model is safe,” he wrote.

According to Papailiopoulos, reliable detection requires comparing a model’s weights with its original, unmodified version. He said establishing a model’s provenance is therefore important to determining whether its weights have been altered between the developer and deployment.

Auditing model weights recommended

In its accompanying security advisory, Microsoft Threat Intelligence recommends auditing model weights before deployment and after every update. Its guidance includes comparing each checkpoint against its declared base model, verifying publishers and file hashes, and rejecting models without verifiable provenance.

Microsoft also recommends keeping approved models in private, access-controlled registries rather than allowing agents and inference services to download checkpoints directly from public repositories.

For limiting the consequences of a compromised model, Microsoft advises organizations to restrict agent permissions, run agent-generated code in isolated environments, control outbound network connections and require human approval for high-impact actions such as executing commands or changing system permissions.

Microsoft Research said it is working with internal AI security teams to turn the research’s detection techniques into a red-teaming framework. The company is also exploring AI-assisted weight scanning and cryptographic model signing with verifiable provenance and tamper-evident audit trails. According to the paper, the central idea “was discovered autonomously by Claude Code with Opus 4.5 in February 2026.”

In this article

Muse’s maker used about 50,000 hours of users’ brainwave recordings to train AI without explicitly telling them

Stripping names might not be enough to make brainwave data anonymous; researchers have identified individuals from EEG recordings

Check privacy policies and ask about opt-out and data deletion

Technology companies have spent years trying to get into your head for profit. Now they’re doing it literally. The maker of Muse, a headband that measures brain activity during sleep and meditation, used users’ brainwave data to train AI without explicitly telling them, an investigation has revealed.

Companies sell these consumer sleep bands to help you better understand what your brain does when you sleep and meditate. However, according to an investigation in Science magazine, they’re picking up a little understanding of their own on the side.

The year-long investigation found that Canadian company Interaxon, which makes the Muse sleep and meditation headband, was using the data that it collected from users’ brains to train AI. The company used about 50,000 hours of electroencephalography (EEG) recordings, which measure the brain’s electrical activity, to train a “brain foundation model.”

AI models trained with large amounts of brainwave data from different people can spot patterns in brain activity. For example, a model might learn to recognize patterns associated with seizures.

Researching such outcomes is laudable, but only if you first tell the people whose EEG data is being used for the training. Interaxon didn’t.

This is your brain on an inadequate privacy policy

When Science questioned Interaxon about the issue, its chief marketing officer Nadia Kumentas acknowledged that users should be explicitly informed about the AI training. The company updated its privacy policy, which now says de-identified data is used to train machine learning models.

Collecting data through devices like this is tempting for companies because brainwave data is otherwise difficult to obtain and therefore incredibly valuable.

No wonder, then, that it isn’t the only neuraltech company facing questions about its data practices. The publication reviewed 57 companies that collect brain data, and found that only six explicitly said they wouldn’t sell users’ brain data. More than two-thirds allow brain data to pass to a new owner if they are acquired. Eleven of them only had a privacy policy for website visitors, and four had no policy at all.

To its credit, Interaxon removed names and email addresses from user EEG data before using it for training. However, those users’ data has already helped shape a model trained without explicitly telling them. Removing its influence after the fact is extremely difficult.

But is such “de-identification” enough? An academic study conducted by the University of South-Eastern Norway this year found that EEG recordings and derived features can contain sensitive patient-specific information. It said that this can create privacy risks when that data is shared across clinical and research environments. It added:

“Conventional anonymization methods are often insufficient for high-dimensional biomedical signals, since removing direct identifiers does not necessarily prevent re-identification, linkage, or inference risks.”

Another study by researchers at Ben-Gurion University, Israel, found that analyzing resting-state EEG recordings could shed light on personality traits and cognitive abilities. Resting-state EEG identified users 88.4% of the time, according to a 2018 study by researchers at Korea University. And a University of Southern California study claimed that EEG data could reveal mental health status, neurological conditions, and even substance use history.

These findings do not establish what can be inferred from Muse recordings specifically. Consumer headbands generally have fewer electrodes than clinical EEG systems.

This isn’t the first review of the consumer neurotech industry to reveal some worrying trends. A 2024 Neurorights Foundation report found that 29 of 30 companies it surveyed appeared to have access to consumers’ neural data and had provided “no meaningful limitations to this access.”

The law is still catching up to all this. The Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) counts your fingerprint, voiceprint, or face geometry among other things as biometric identifiers, but EEG data doesn’t make the cut. However, Colorado and California do now treat neural data as sensitive.

These concerns extend beyond brainwave data. In a Malwarebytes survey of newsletter readers, 90% worried about AI using their data without consent, while 92% were concerned about corporations using their personal data inappropriately.

What Muse owners can do

Do you use a sleep band or another neurotech device? Consider that your brain data might be used for more than you imagined. And if the company goes bust and/or gets acquired, it might pass to another owner. That’s exactly what happened with genetic testing company 23andMe.

With this in mind, check the manufacturer’s privacy policy, and if you can’t find one, ask it directly. Ask whether your EEG data is used to train AI, whether you can opt out, and whether you can delete recordings already collected.

If those options aren’t available, consider whether you’re comfortable continuing to use the device.

Title: Over 35,000 Grok-Built Apps Exposed Online, Some Leaking Confidential Data and Passwords
Context: A ChatGPT app address found in DNS data would lead to an app that only its owner can open, they say
Full Text:
Of the 37,571 Grok-built apps that security company Claroc found online, 35,578 were open to anyone without a sign-in, the researchers said yesterday.

They included 24 apps built by staff at the social network X and at SpaceXSI, the company that makes the Grok AI assistant. Most of the open apps were games, landing pages, and calculators, but about 1 in 10 contained internal business or personal data.

The staff apps included a confidential onboarding plan for a new sales hire, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, and an X advertising proposal to a U.S. federal agency marked confidential. SpaceXSI, formerly known as xAI, has since taken down all 24 staff apps but not other users' apps, the researchers said.

Besides those staff apps, the open apps contained internal data from 30 other organizations the researchers could identify, across fields ranging from construction and energy to healthcare and defense. Of those, 26 have more than 1,000 employees, and 6 are Fortune 500 companies.

According to the researchers' estimate in their report, roughly 2% of the open apps contained material serious enough to rate as high or critical.

The exposed material included a hospital group's searchable list of more than 3,500 employees, an intensive care briefing on a single patient, a fire department's live shift board, and a contractor's timesheet whose code held every employee's password in plain text.

Grok can build a working app from a description typed into its chat, a feature its maker opened to every Grok plan on August 19. This chat builder shares the Grok Build name with a separate terminal coding tool, whose repository uploads were reported on July 14.

Each published app gets its own subdomain of grok.me, and its creator chooses who can open it, according to the company's launch announcement.

No app goes public until its creator clicks Publish. In the paid account the researchers used, the next step offered 3 access settings: "Anyone with the link", "Invited users" and "Only you". "Anyone with the link" was already selected.

The setting matters because an app's address does not stay secret, the researchers say. Opening an app makes the visitor's computer look up its subdomain in DNS. Passive DNS services record such lookups, and anyone with an account can search those records by pattern.

Grok suggests 4 random words as each app's name, and about half of the names the researchers found followed that pattern. Such names are hard to guess, but that does not protect an app whose name already sits in a searchable list.

ChatGPT's app builder also puts each app on its own subdomain. But when the researchers shared an app there, its access was set to "Only me" until they changed it. A ChatGPT app address found in DNS data would lead to an app that only its owner can open, they say.

The researchers found the Grok app names using common subdomain discovery methods and loaded each app's first page once, without signing in.

To see what protection Grok adds on its own, the researchers built 2 test apps with made-up data and published both with the access setting already selected, "Anyone with the link".

The first, a contact list, got a database but no sign-in. Without signing in, the researchers added a row from a private browser window, and the next visitor saw it.

The second, a customer list for a 4-person sales team, got sign-in buttons that Grok added on its own: "Continue with Google" and "Continue with X". But the code Grok wrote added each person who signed in to the team before checking whether they belonged, so the check always passed.

An uninvited Google account belonging to someone other than the owner got in, viewed every customer, edited one record, and deleted another.

The researchers ran these tests only on their own apps. They did not test whether any of the open apps they found would accept such changes.

The researchers reported their findings to SpaceXSI on Sunday through the address in its security.txt file, including 2 of the staff apps. They reported the other 22 on Monday.

By the time the researchers published yesterday, the company had not replied to their report, but it had answered a reporter's questions about the research.

As the researchers describe, the company said Grok apps stay private until their creator shares them. Publishing takes several steps, including choosing between "Only you" and "Anyone with the link," as well as a legal disclaimer. Employee accounts are set to "Only you" by default.

Even so, 24 apps built by staff at the company and at X were open to anyone, the researchers say.

With their report, the researchers had asked the company to make "Only you" the default and to add an option that limits an app to a company's own email domain.

The company's response did not state that it would contact the owners of other open apps, according to the researchers. They have started emailing the affected organizations themselves and had emailed 3 by the time they published. They withheld every app address and title from the report.

On October 18, the same researchers published Muse research showing that pages shared from Meta's Muse AI agent could be found through passive DNS. Meta disabled sharing, then announced a sharing fix on October 22 that gave shared items new addresses.

How to Check Your Organization's Grok Apps

Claroc, which sells tools to find and secure apps built with AI, recommends these checks:

Find out which AI app builders your staff uses. Builders such as Grok, Lovable, Replit, v0, Bolt, Base44 and Google AI Studio can be used without IT setting them up or a company account.

If you have access to passive DNS data, look up the builders' domains and open any results in a private browser window.

Make sure any Grok app with internal data is set to "Invited users" or "Only you", and that a stranger gets an error page.

Try to sign in with an account from outside your company. If it gets in, the app needs a list of who is allowed.

Check the scripts each app loads for names, email addresses and passwords, and unpublish apps that have no owner.

In the researchers' tests, setting an app to "Only you" caused it to return a 401 error to a stranger for both the page and its data, and unpublishing took an app offline within seconds.

Title: Shipping giant Maersk probes 'IT security incident,' data theft
Context: In a statement issued on Wednesday, the Denmark-based shipping, cargo, and logistics giant confirmed it immediately launched an investigation into the attack and the affected...
Full Text: Shipping behemoth A.P. Moller-Maersk says it is investigating "an IT security incident" involving the potential theft of data from a legacy system. In a statement issued on Wednesday, the Denmark-based shipping, cargo, and logistics giant confirmed it immediately launched an investigation into the attack and the affected system was secured. "Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed," the company said. "The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI." Maersk described the legacy local system as one "from a previous acquisition," and said it does not expect the attack to have an effect on operations. Customers were reassured that they can continue to use Maersk platforms to manage their shipments as usual, and to expect updates from the company as and when they're available. "Cybersecurity remains a constant, ongoing priority for Maersk," it added. "We have rigorous processes in place to identify and prevent incidents and minimize customer impact. "As always, please treat any unexpected communications claiming to relate to this matter with caution and verify them through your usual Maersk contact. "Thank you for your patience as we continue to investigate the incident." Fortunately for those who immediately feel uneasy after hearing "Maersk" and "IT security" mentioned in the same breath, the wording of the shipping giant's disclosure suggests this intrusion won't be as calamitous as the NotPetya disaster in 2017. Mimicking the Petya ransomware strain, NotPetya was an infamous destructive wiper malware strain that wormed its way across the global economy. Western intelligence agencies attributed the malware to Russia's Sandworm group, an outfit believed to be part of the country's military intelligence service (GRU). Maersk said at the time that it expected the attack to result in a circa $300 million bill, owing to remediation and rebuild costs. Offering a sense of scale, Jim Hagemann Snabe, then chair of Maersk, told World Economic Forum delegates in 2018 that the company's rebuild encompassed 4,000 new servers, 45,000 new PCs, and 2,500 applications – which he said had been completed over just ten days. In 2020, as exclusively revealed by The Register, Maersk went on to lay off around 150 staffers from its command and control center in Maidenhead, England. The staffers who lost their jobs had played key roles in the recovery. ®

Title: eMudhra Revokes 8 More CAs It Previously Declared Unaffected by Key Compromise
Context: The rebuilt key carried a label almost identical to the original's, which allowed the weak copy to be sent for signing and certification
Full Text:
The in-house Python script behind eMudhra's October key compromise has now cost the company 8 more of its intermediate certificate authorities (CAs), even though it did not weaken their keys.

Each intermediate CA has its own private key, which the company uses to sign the certificates it issues. The 8 intermediate CAs compromised in October had a different problem: a single line in the script cut each of their keys to one byte, the company said this week.

The script also retrieved the RSA keys of the 8 newly revoked CAs from the company's hardware security modules (HSMs). The company says it cannot show that the keys were handled as required by its own rules. It revoked the CAs late last week.

The company had called those CAs unaffected. "The RSA issuers went through a different path as per our assessment of the code and are therefore not impacted," it wrote on Mozilla's bug tracker on October 19.

Of the 8, 6 were for website (TLS) certificates and 2 for code signing. The company had put 4 of them into production in May. Its list names 195 certificates from them, 29 for its own domains.

Both problems began at a key ceremony on April 30, 2025, according to the full incident report the company posted to the same bug tracker this week. That day it generated 16 CA keys on Utimaco HSMs, including the 8 behind the October key compromise.

The keys were meant for Crypto4A HSMs at the company's US and EU sites. Moving keys between HSMs from different vendors is limited, the company says, so its PKI operations team wrote the Python script to wrap each key for transport and unwrap it again.

The round trip that day was a practice run of the transfer, and the source HSM's FIPS-approved mode was switched off for it as an approved exception.

After the round trip, the script read each private key out of the HSM into the ceremony computer's memory and rebuilt the key from that copy. For the 8 ECDSA keys, "a single line in that read‑back truncated the private value to its leading byte," the report says.

The rebuilt key carried a label almost identical to the original's, which allowed the weak copy to be sent for signing and certification.

The Hacker News worked out all 8 keys from their public certificates. The smallest, for EM OV TLS CA - G3C, is 4, and the largest is 237.

Nothing in the ceremony tested the key's strength or checked the certified key against the first generated key. The weak keys still produced valid signatures, and their certificates passed linting and 2 WebTrust audit cycles unnoticed.

The HSMs worked correctly throughout, according to the company, which puts the fault in its own script and process controls.

Invalid CRL signatures in June 2025 were an early sign of the same fault, according to the report. The company fixed them at the time by re-signing the lists with the keys that matched the certificates, which were the weak ones.

According to the report, the 8 RSA keys went through the same read-back step that the company's earlier response had ruled out. Early last week, the company said its earlier answers reflected only what its teams had gathered so far, including which script paths each set of keys took.

The script did not shorten those keys, and every signature still checks against the certified key. But their private parts, such as the private exponent and one of the primes, sat in the memory of a Python process on the ceremony computer.

As a result, the company "cannot positively demonstrate that this key material was in compliance with CPS §6.2.6," its own rule on moving keys into and out of an HSM. Logs and files from that computer cannot reliably show how the material was handled.

The company reached that view in early November, after discussions with browser root programs. The 8 RSA CAs were revoked late last week with the reason code cessationOfOperation, not the CA-compromise code used when the first 8 were revoked on October 18.

Participants in the bug thread have asked why the company chose that code rather than keyCompromise.

Of the 195 certificates in the company's certificate list, 130 came from EM DV TLS CA - G2C, 63 from EM OV TLS CA - G2C, and 2 from the code-signing CA, EM OV CS CA - G2C.

Besides the company's own domains, the certificates name several universities and colleges, a county, and other organizations. The newest was issued last week, days before the CAs were revoked. All their holders have been moved to new certificates, the company says.

The company says the wrap-and-unwrap process was used only this once, and that its other key ceremonies all created keys in place.

Participants in the bug thread also want the script published, and some have asked how private keys could leave its HSMs at all.

KPMG, which the company hired as an independent reviewer, is due to finish by December 4. The company's inventory of all its CA keys is due November 30.

The company knows of no case of misuse. Anyone holding one of the October keys could have impersonated any website, according to a disclosure site run by Dennis Jackson, who investigated the keys for Mozilla.

Browsers that enforce Certificate Transparency could not have been fooled. Whether anyone used the keys against software that skips that check is not known.

What emSign Certificate Holders Need to Check

eMudhra, which sells certificates under the emSign brand, is exiting the publicly trusted TLS business following its October 22 announcement.

Holders can find affected certificates in the company's list or by searching Certificate Transparency logs for the revoked G2C TLS issuers.

All issuance from the company's G1 hierarchy is due to stop before November 16, as the remaining customers, mainly a university federation in North America, move to another provider.

Microsoft will start removing the 10 remaining eMudhra roots, including emSign Root CA - G1, on November 16, according to an update to its security response post earlier this week. Certificates that chain to those roots will then lose default trust in Windows and Edge, and in some of its other products on their own timelines.

According to the Indian company's phase-out schedule, Chrome and Firefox will not trust G1 certificates issued after November 16, and Apple will end trust in all G1 certificates, including older ones, on November 30.

macOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3 and 15.8.3 stop bundled command-line tools such as curl and git from accepting the compromised TLS CA certificates, Apple said in a support note earlier this week. They also drop 5 roots, including emSign Root CA - G1, from /etc/ssl/cert.pem, so tools relying on that file may not verify some sites chaining to them.
