Title: Appraisal by AI: Model-driven victim prioritization in the VOLTA infostealer
Context: The novelty in the AI-integration is that it is not supporting a traditional malware capability but working as an intelligence analyst on behalf of the operator
Full Text:
VOLTA is a mature stealer implant with an optional AI-integration layer. After stealing credentials, sessions, and cryptocurrency wallets, VOLTA sends a structured evidence bundle to an LLM to rank the victim’s assets by monetization value.

If a model refuses to perform the target assessment, VOLTA fails over to a three-model chain, implying a direct engineering effort and expectation of hitting model guardrails.

This stealer is self-deleting, and there is no attacker-owned infrastructure. The novelty in the AI-integration is that it is not supporting a traditional malware capability but working as an intelligence analyst on behalf of the operator.

There is a new idea in the cybercrime world — cast a wide net, steal everything, and let AI sort out the specifics. A new malware self-named “VOLTA-AUTODOXER,” surfaced through the CAIRN research effort, is a self-deleting Windows infostealer that augments its post-theft workflow with an LLM-powered victim-profiling stage.

After harvesting the standard stealer haul, including browser passwords; cookies; payment cards; cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases; Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions; Microsoft OAuth tokens; SSH and cloud-provider keys; Wi-Fi profiles; and screenshots, VOLTA builds a structured evidence bundle about the person behind the machine. This bundle contains geolocation and home address, employer and employer domain, inferred birth year, card last-4 digits, Slack workspaces, document authorship metadata, iPhone backup indicators, and a live Roblox account valuation. It then uses stolen session access to enrich that bundle further: searching the victim's Gmail for purchase receipts to corroborate a home address, pulling UberEats and DoorDash order history, and enriching Discord accounts via the stolen token.

The bundle is serialized and POSTed to OpenRouter under a system prompt that instructs the model to act as "a forensic intelligence analyst drafting a target assessment." The required output includes a section titled “WHAT THEY'RE WORTH” with valuables ranked by monetization with a low/medium/high tier, and a section on “THEIR OPSEC” containing an assessment of the victim's security posture and password hygiene. The model is the operator's triage analyst; it turns a raw credential log into a prioritized and citation-backed dossier of the victim and their monetizable assets.

Figure 1. The VOLTA-AUTODOXER workflow.

The AI configuration: “Go deep, not wide... Be blunt, specific, accurate.”

VOLTA uses a multi-model architecture to fall back resiliently if it hits a model’s refusal, checking each response for phrases like “I can’t” or “I’m not able,” before passing on to a chain of up to three models.

Endpoint

https[:]//openrouter[.]ai/api/v1/chat/completions

Default model

anthropic/claude-opus-4.6

Fallback chain

moonshotai/kimi-k2 → google/gemini-2.5-flash

Temperature

0.2 — deterministic, consistent output

Request format

Hand-assembled JSON; no SDK; User-Agent Mozilla/5.0

Figure 2. Hardcoded model selection.Figure 3. Failover model selection to kimi-k2, and then gemini-2.5-flash.

Model temperate controls the randomness and predictability of LLM-generated text. The low hardcoded temperature value (0.2) suggests the attacker is emphasizing accuracy and consistency. The malware also employs a chain of cascading models in the event of failures. This multi-model architecture suggests that the operator is anticipating encountering refusals, with the fallback pivoting to a few, smaller, and more permissive models.

The system prompt directly reveals the operator’s use case: Produce a concise analytical assessment of the victim’s suitability as a target, backed by an auditable trail of citations.

Figure 4. VOLTA's raw system prompt.

The prompt also asks for something out of the ordinary, but that agents excel at: making connections between sparse and disparate data. For example, encouraging connections like the victim’s names, addresses, or universities to patterns in their passwords. In this case, the model isn't being asked to find data; rather, it’s being asked to stretch the data and make useful inferences that extend the value of what has been scraped.

Stealer capabilities

VOLTA’s capabilities are directly aligned with the records produced in modern digital life, and well beyond basic credential theft. In a single pass, the stealer can extract browser credentials, cookies, and saved payment cards across Chromium-based browsers. It hits Firefox and Thunderbird, Outlook profiles, Slack workspaces, Steam and Battle.net sessions, Discord tokens, Telegram sessions, Roblox accounts, and SSH and cloud-provider config files (gcloud, OpenVPN, Hide.me). VOLTA doesn’t just copy cryptocurrency wallets, but runs an embedded cracker against the vault inline, writing the result to a WALLET VAULTS CRACKED line in its own report.

Every saved Wi-Fi password on the machine is pulled via a direct call to WlanGetProfileList and dumped to plaintext.

Figure 5. VOLTA dumps plaintext passwords for every saved Wi-Fi network on the host.Figure 6. The organized collection targets.

What really sets VOLTA apart from commodity stealers is what comes after the initial collection. There is a live enrichment pass that leverages stolen sessions to deep dive the victim’s data. For example, using the victim's own authenticated Gmail tokens, it queries their inbox for receipts from Amazon, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Walmart, and PayPal, then review those receipts to establish a confirmed home address. Stolen Uber Eats and DoorDash sessions are called directly for order history. The Discord token is re-used to enrich the victim's account profile. Roblox inventory is valued via a live “Rolimons[.]com” lookup.

Figure 7. That’s right: Your Uber Eats history is now a potential liability.

After the collection and enrichment stages are complete, the data is assembled and structured locally in a file called “Identity_Report.txt”. This file is serialized into a bundle as JSON and POSTed to OpenRouter along with the system prompt. The returned payload is received as “AI_Analysis.txt”. Both files exfil together in “volta_dox.zip”.

Figure 8. VOLTA’s exfil can happen in three stages: 1) after the stealer runs (“volta_log.zip”), 2) after the AI call (“volta_dox.zip”), (3) if the network enrichment produces anything (“volta_doxnet.zip”).

The inference round-trip happens entirely through the victim's own network connection, on their own machine, before the result is exfiltrated.

Deployment model

Instead of hardcoding its Telegram channel, API keys, and settings directly into the code (which is likely what someone writing a tool for personal use would do) VOLTA uses a template with six swappable slots, filled in at build time.

This suggests it’s a builder model: The author sells access, the customer provides their values, and the builder compiles a custom binary for each order. The credentials in those slots are encrypted, but not in a meaningful way. The key is SHA-256 of two constants sitting in the same binary, but it's presumably there because customers expect their API keys not to be sitting in plaintext, not because it provides real protection. Anyone who reverses the file can recover them.

If VOLTA is indeed a commoditized malware, then the AI dossier capability isn't something the author invented for their own operations. It is a feature which enables a customer of any level of sophistication to point it at victims and start receiving ranked target assessments in their Telegram inbox.

All the observed endpoints for this malware are third-party controlled. There is no actor-owned infrastructure.

Countermeasures

Much of the token-stealing capability of VOLTA relies on techniques to bypass App-Bound Encryption (ABE) in Chrome. An application control policy that restricts which processes may launch Chrome with --headless would block the ABE decryption path entirely. At minimum, you can also alert when Chrome is launched with --headless from any process not in a known developer. Best practices for storing credentials in hardware backed stores also apply.

In the event of compromise, the main executable may have deleted itself, but users should attempt to preserve the “APPDATA%\volta_debug.txt” file. This is a timestamped harvest log and contains a record of exactly what was collected and whether the LLM call succeeded. Revoke any potentially compromised tokens and change passwords. For cryptocurrency wallets, if the seed phrase was in plaintext on disk, treat the wallet as fully compromised and migrate funds to a new wallet with a seed generated on an air-gapped device.

Conclusions

VOLTA is a mature stealer with a late-stage AI layer added for one purpose: relieving the operator of analytical work. The axis of AI improvement here is not speed or scale but effort displacement; the same logic visible in CLOSEDQUORUM, though applied to a different phase. These implants reflect the same underlying logic: Identify the step that requires the most sustained human attention and replace it with a model call. The question for defenders is not whether this pattern will appear elsewhere, but which phase it touches next.

Figure 9. End-to-end VOLTA workflow.

The second trend to watch is the anticipation of hitting model refusals, and the approaches to building in resiliency. In this case, it includes a fallback chain from Claude to Kimi to Gemini and the ability to run without the LLM stage altogether if no key is present. As AI integration in malware matures, refusal resilience may become a standard design requirement.

The open question underlying both trends is whether effort displacement in crimeware changes the landscape in a meaningful way: lowering the operational floor, raising the ceiling on scale, or both. Cybercrime operations have always been opportunistic, and the sophistication bar has always been lower than assumed, but there is a difference between a wide net and a wide net that sorts itself.

Context: [2] While Darktrace has not observed direct evidence of CVE-2026-109618 or CVE-2026-109619 exploitation, on October 21st we observed a six-month high in detections consistent...
Full Text:
The disclosure of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 placed immediate pressure on organizations running PHP. Both vulnerabilities can allow unauthenticated remote code execution, including in products and appliances where PHP is embedded, and updates depend on third-party vendors [1].

Early guidance focused on patching internet-facing systems and monitoring for behavior associated with successful exploitation, including unexpected command execution, Webroot changes and outbound connections from PHP servers.

Darktrace observed widespread scanning across monitored environments involving hundreds of distinct source IP addresses that public reporting has associated with activity targeting the PHP vulnerabilities. The volume of scanning was significantly greater than the evidence available for successful exploitation. For analysts, that distinction is important. Scanning demonstrates interest in exposed infrastructure; establishing compromise requires evidence of subsequent behavior on the targeted system, including command execution, file modification or unexpected outbound communication.

PHP is not an isolated example. Imperva subsequently demonstrated remote code execution against a vulnerable Node.js build through malicious Brotli data, reproducing execution through compressed HTTP responses and configured request parsers. The same inputs were rejected by the patched runtime. Imperva linked its Node2Shell and PHP2Shell research to the increasing speed of vulnerability discovery and exploit development. [2]

While Darktrace has not observed direct evidence of CVE-2026-109618 or CVE-2026-109619 exploitation, on October 21st we observed a six-month high in detections consistent with zero-day exploitation activity, representing a 64% increase compared to historic data. This increase has not been confirmed as related to the PHP vulnerabilities. Darktrace’s behavioral approach is designed to detect anomalous activity without relying solely on rules written for a specific exploit. Comparable increases were observed around the Log4j disclosure and other globally significant vulnerability disclosures.

AI-assisted vulnerability research

The PHP disclosure arrives as AI systems have become more capable at vulnerability research [3]. OpenAI launched Daybreak in June 2026, combining GPT-5.5-Cyber, Codex Security and partnerships with security researchers and software maintainers. OpenAI says its models have been applied to discovering and generating patches for vulnerabilities in browsers, network infrastructure, FreeBSD and the Linux kernel. Darktrace joined the OpenAI Daybreak Cyber Partner Program in June to explore how OpenAI's cyber capabilities could be integrated within Darktrace products and services [4][10].

OpenAI reported in August that Codex Security Cloud had analyzed more than 30 million commits across more than 30,000 codebases. According to OpenAI, Cloudflare uses models accessed through Daybreak to investigate customer-authorized code and combines findings with live traffic and security signals to assess whether affected routes are active or receiving suspicious traffic, with proposed mitigations and patches remaining subject to customer review [5][6].

Faster discovery still leaves defenders with the work of locating affected software, testing fixes and completing remediation. The PHP case shows that gap clearly, particularly when vulnerable runtimes are embedded inside other products.

Enterprise agents as an attack surface

Darktrace Signal Labs has also examined how a trusted enterprise agent could be abused after an attacker has already obtained access to an environment. In a controlled simulation, researchers demonstrated that, in that post-compromise scenario, the Claude platform’s memory stores feature could be abused to establish a live C2 channel between an external operator and internal Claude Code agents. The external operator was able to dynamically assign network discovery, credential access, and data exfiltration tasks to the agents via this C2 channel. Detection of the agents’ activities relied on the correlation of process creation and network traffic activity from agent harness processes, alongside behavioral analysis to identify deviations from expected behavior. Darktrace has not claimed it observed this memory-store command-and-control technique in operational attacks [7].

AI-assisted attacks in Japan

Evidence from Japan indicates AI being used for vulnerability scanning and attacks outside controlled research. On 21 October, JPCERT/CC published findings from an investigation into recent unauthorized access incidents affecting organizations in Japan. JPCERT/CC states that it confirmed attackers had used AI to scan for known vulnerabilities and conduct attacks through APIs. According to JPCERT/CC, its examination of attack infrastructure found evidence of Android application analysis, API discovery and testing for weaknesses including server-side request forgery, and the infrastructure also targeted services intended for users outside Japan [8].

JPCERT/CC does not identify ARTEX by name in that publication. The named ARTEX attribution comes from separate investigations, including Microsoft's analysis of Storm-0940.

AI in offensive operations

Microsoft describes ARTEX as an open-source, multi-agent penetration-testing system capable of automating activity with limited human interaction. Microsoft reported that Storm-0940, which it assesses to be a China state-aligned actor active since 2021, used ARTEX against hundreds of organizations, and Microsoft attributed the ConnectWise supply-chain compromise [9].

Microsoft observed ARTEX accelerating scanning, reconnaissance, password spraying and OAuth application abuse. Several ARTEX-driven operations reached privileged cloud access less than three hours after initial targeting. Following the ConnectWise compromise, Storm-0940 attempted to authenticate to more than 2,250 tenants at rates of up to 2,900 attempts per minute [9].

Darktrace Threat Research found activity in its own telemetry involving infrastructure later associated with the campaign. On 13 October, Darktrace recorded failed authentication activity involving 144.172.64[.]128, one of the addresses Microsoft later identified as performing sign-ins and Microsoft Graph activity in ConnectWise customer environments. Darktrace analysis identified 65 failed authentication attempts in around 20 minutes.

The telemetry establishes repeated failed authentication from infrastructure later associated with the campaign. It does not establish ARTEX execution or successful compromise. At the time of observation, Microsoft's later attribution was unavailable. Analysts therefore had the behavior itself: repeated failed authentication from the same source over a short period, together with any related identity, application or network activity inside the environment.

Microsoft documented a wider password-spray campaign against 327 accounts across eight organizations between 10 and 14 October. It recorded more than 151,000 failed logons, including more than 111,000 on 11 October, but no successful authentication, token issuance, Graph call or directory change from that campaign. Microsoft also reported that most Storm-0940 targeting was unsuccessful [9].

Where the actor progressed beyond authentication, Microsoft observed service-principal sign-ins followed by Graph and directory operations. Activity included reconnaissance, application credential changes and attempts to modify privileges. Microsoft recommends correlating service-principal sign-ins with Graph activity, directory changes and resource access [9].

Behavior before attribution

The PHP and ARTEX cases begin with different information. PHP defenders knew which software required urgent remediation but initially had limited information about exploitation. Process execution, file modification and outbound communication could still provide evidence of compromise.

The PHP and ARTEX observations also illustrate the difference between volume and impact. Darktrace observed broad scanning around the PHP disclosure, while the ARTEX-associated infrastructure produced concentrated authentication activity. Neither observation independently demonstrates compromise and in each case examining the behavior that follows the initial interaction is the investigative clue.

The Darktrace ARTEX-related observation began with authentication behavior. Microsoft publicly attributed the source infrastructure eight days later. That attribution added context, but it did not change what had originally been recorded in the environment.

AI is now present at several points in this cycle. Daybreak applies models to vulnerability discovery and remediation. Darktrace Signal Labs demonstrated how a trusted enterprise agent could be co-opted in a controlled environment. JPCERT/CC confirmed AI-assisted vulnerability scanning and API attacks in recent incidents. Microsoft documented ARTEX being used by Storm-0940 in active operations [4][7][8][9].

Microsoft's findings also show why scale and impact must be assessed separately. One ARTEX-associated campaign produced more than 151,000 failed logons without successful access, while other operations reached privileged cloud access in less than three hours. Security teams have to distinguish high-volume attempts from activity that progresses through authentication, privilege changes and resource access.

The evidence required to assess these cases remains familiar: authentication records, process execution, application and directory changes, file activity and network communication. AI can increase the rate at which those behaviors occur. Defenders still need to establish their sequence and impact.

Title: A Supply Chain Attack Put Malicious Anthropic Claude Extensions on Thousands of Devices
Context: “Everyone was so lucky here, this was potentially a really dangerous foothold for an attacker,” says Calum Hall, cofounder and CEO of the detection firm Phorion, the first...
Full Text:
The AI software-development platform Cursor, which is owned by SpaceX, had a malicious Anthropic Claude Code extension for Windows, macOS, and Linux live in its integrated development environment extension marketplace for roughly 11 hours on Thursday. The company says the rogue extension was downloaded by “at most 5,000 users.” Cursor briefly shut down the extension marketplace while it investigated the situation, which the company says did not impact any other extensions.

The tainted extension was designed with a backdoor to give attackers access to victim devices—the type of implant that malicious hackers often use as a stepping stone to deeper control inside a target network. Cursor published remediation steps on Thursday for the roughly 5,000 affected targets. A saving grace of the situation, though, was a flaw in the malware's design that blocked it from fully establishing itself on the vast majority of targets.

“Everyone was so lucky here, this was potentially a really dangerous foothold for an attacker,” says Calum Hall, cofounder and CEO of the detection firm Phorion, the first researchers to spot the malicious extension after detecting it on a customer's Mac.

What is still unclear is how the malicious extension made its way into the Cursor marketplace at all. Some researchers initially speculated that it came from a compromised Anthropic system. But Cursor said in its Thursday security alert that “these malicious versions of the extension were not developed by Anthropic.”

Felix Rieseberg, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, posted on X on Friday: “We’re working with Cursor on this incident, but it wasn’t a compromise of Anthropic’s systems or employee laptops. A malicious actor used access to Cursor’s marketplace to publish a tampered copy of the Claude Code extension, which we didn’t build or publish. The versions on our official channels are not affected and this only impacts Cursor users.”

David Dworken, who works on security at Anthropic, posted on X shortly after, explaining that “this did not involve a compromise of any Anthropic systems … We were not involved with building, publishing, or hosting this.”

Cursor did not return WIRED's request for comment about how the malicious upload happened and whether it was the result of a breach at Cursor.

Title: “Are We Exposed?” What CISOs Need to Know About Their Software Risk
Context: Curl When it comes to Curl and its underlying transfer library libcurl, the threat can affect the very foundation of internet data transfer
Full Text:
Recent events have once again highlighted the need to quickly answer the question, “Are we exposed?”

We now face threats to businesses and governments from vulnerabilities and compromises in three fundamental components used in software development: Curl, PHP, and LiteLLM.

Curl

When it comes to Curl and its underlying transfer library libcurl, the threat can affect the very foundation of internet data transfer. With libcurl embedded in many enterprise environments – from backend microservices and container runtimes to automated CI/CD pipelines and shell scripts – this vulnerability carries potential systemic risk. The core threat centers on high-severity flaws disclosed in October 2026, notably a high-severity HTTP/2 use-after-free issue (such as CVE-2026-92392) where a malicious upstream server handling an upload can corrupt client-side memory and, under specific conditions, trigger remote code execution or application crashes on the machine initiating the transfer. Because libcurl negotiates HTTP/2 by default for HTTPS URLs when the server supports it and applications rarely inspect what libcurl does under the hood, development stacks and automated deployment pipelines that have not upgraded to a fixed version can remain exposed to hostile external endpoints.

LiteLLM

Regarding LiteLLM, JFrog Security Research detected the problem within 2 hours, and the errant LiteLLM package, version 1.107.0, has already been removed from PyPI. Reflecting the open-source community ecosystem’s continually improving maturation, the package maintainers have already published a report. But from 11:39 to 13:23 UTC on October 21, 2026, software developers, agentic agents, or your build systems could have downloaded that package from PyPI, and affected Docker images remained available until 14:20 UTC. The ripple effect of a compromised package or vulnerable component getting into an environment doesn’t just impact the developers or security team. It also impacts IT Ops and, down the line, auditors. Every change impacts the whole organization. Executives, the business decision makers who determine where to invest and allocate resources, need a way to understand where they sit in this maturity. Do they have complete visibility or not?

PHP

In the case of PHP, two CRITICAL-severity PHP core vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619), were disclosed and referred to publicly as PHP2Shell. The bugs can allow unauthenticated remote code execution and Heartbleed-style memory disclosure in PHP itself, independent of the application running on top of it, according to public advisories. Within days, news outlets reported on the vulnerabilities, and CISA issued an alert urging organizations to patch immediately, including CNBC and the BBC, CISA.

“Are We Exposed?”

When a CISO wrestles with the question of “Are we exposed?”, their triage process should focus on these key issues:

Is it really a threat?

Where is it being used?

What is the business impact?

Do I have a reporting or disclosure obligation under rules or standards that apply to my organization, such as those of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), PCI DSS, or, for product manufacturers, the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA)?

Did we block it?

How do we fix it?

The CISO’s ability to answer these questions with confidence depends on how well they’ve integrated their tools, people, processes, and security program to provide that visibility and respond quickly to security incidents. The ability to do this, in turn, is a reflection of the maturity of their overall security program and how well they can protect, monitor, and govern the full gamut of software development operations – whether it’s on the developer’s workstation, in agentic workflows, or implemented directly by AI coding agents.

A true assessment of your organization’s abilities to determine your strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats is critical to providing a full 360 view of your risk posture.

Hands-On Assessment Experience

As a CISO, I’ve done these assessments on a number of occasions, for both new deployments and as an ongoing protective measure to help keep the business protected as new threats and vulnerabilities evolve.

These assessments should be broadly based and take into account business objectives, employee capabilities, workflows, data usage, and the maturity of the infrastructure. Covering these bases should give you an accurate compass of where you are and where you need to improve.

This should, of course, include your tools, but should not lead to one of the classic mistakes organizations make, which is over-focusing on tools, simply because they’re the easiest thing to measure. The other areas mentioned above are easy to overlook, but extremely important to a realistic assessment, as tools without the right people and processes won’t achieve the objective of protecting your business.

JFrog’s Security Maturity Assessment

Based on JFrog’s experience working with many of the Fortune 100 customers and through the expertise of our in-house security research team, we’ve actually built our own Security Maturity Assessment. It lets organizations self-assess their software supply chain security program maturity across 11 domains, based on their answers.

I strongly recommend taking a few minutes out of your busy day to complete the questionnaire, as it assesses the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and risks in your software development operations and could help you identify where to start when it comes to ensuring you can truly answer the question: “Are we exposed?”

Takeaways

The question of “Are we exposed?” can be complicated and difficult to assess, but recent high-profile security incidents don’t give CISOs the luxury of taking days to come up with a reply. Corporate executives and board members need fast, accurate answers.

Having complete visibility into your people, processes, workflows, tools, and dependencies gives you the leverage to protect your business under the pressure of the latest attacks. Take the first step in securing your applications by evaluating your operational maturity with JFrog’s Security Maturity Assessment or speaking with one of our domain experts today.

Title: The Binance Breach | What Can be Reached and Why it Matters
Context: What we know is that the attacker allegedly used access to reach an internal service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions, highlighting how standing...
Full Text:
What you will learn

How standing privilege turns one compromised engineer laptop into financial loss, and how just-in-time access, scoped workload identities, session recording and external authorization decisions help contain the damage.

On October 29, 2026, Binance reportedly suffered a $6.3 billion theft with preliminary findings pointing to a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop as a possible entry point.

Binance hasn’t published its root cause yet, and we won’t try to diagnose it for them.

What we know is that the attacker allegedly used access to reach an internal service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions, highlighting how standing privilege can turn a compromised device into a path to financial loss.

Binance says it has found no evidence of a private key leak, and that further investigation uncovered additional points of breach. Its CEO has said the attack was more than misuse of a single engineer’s permissions. Blockchain analysts at TRM Labs concluded that the attacker most likely got Binance’s own signing system to sign transactions of the attacker’s choosing. If those findings hold, the keys inside the infrastructure should be safe.

The attacker borrowed the authority of the systems trusted to use them. This is a common pattern we see in the field and will continue to see until just-in-time and zero standing privilege are the norm. Developers cannot be excluded from this security posture.

Engineering laptops routinely carry kubeconfigs, cloud sessions and SSH keys because they are convenient and frictionless. Production workloads carry identities that can move money, change data or alter infrastructure. Anyone who can get a shell inside a workload inherits that workload’s identity. Developer-targeted social engineering, including fake job interviews with malicious “coding tests,” is a well-documented technique used by the North Korean group that analysts have linked to this incident.

The useful question isn’t whether an engineer’s laptop can be compromised, because eventually one will be, the useful question is “What can that laptop reach without anyone else knowing or approving?” Every organization should be asking that question, especially with the advent of AI-assisted attacks. Imagine Black Hat chaos monkey in your org.

The answer “nobody touches production” is incorrect because engineers still have to fix things at 3am.

The right answer is good access design, and that looks like this:

no standing access to systems that can provide value (e.g., production)

elevation that is fast, short-lived, scoped to the task, and either approved or visible to the team

sessions that are recorded and watched for activity that doesn’t match the stated purpose

workload identities scoped so that infrastructure access doesn’t automatically confer transaction authority

authorization decisions made outside the workload requesting them, so a compromised service can’t approve its own actions

While this is not a guarantee against a patient, well-resourced adversary, it will put up a significant defense in the event of an eventual “assume breach” scenario. Binance’s final report may also surface factors that no access control would have addressed. But together they turn one compromised endpoint from a path to the treasury into a contained incident.

The same principle applies to AI agents, which increasingly operate with delegated credentials in production.

PS: Betting $1 that during an interview, the engineer was asked to install something to complete a challenge...

Title: Devs Hit by Trojanized Claude Code Extension for Cursor
Context: The SolarWinds-style attack in miniature lasted only 11 hours, from 9:27 a
Full Text:
Anthropic's official Claude Code extension for the Cursor VS Code Marketplace was hijacked and swapped out for a malicious version with a persistent backdoor.

The SolarWinds-style attack in miniature lasted only 11 hours, from 9:27 a.m. GMT to 8:35 p.m. GMT, on Oct. 29, according to Cursor's disclosure. Any software developers who downloaded or updated Claude Code in their Cursor integrated development environment (IDE) during that time would have received a malicious version 2.1.313, which pilfered sensitive data from infected machines and, in a minority of cases, could have allowed attackers persistent, privileged access to users' systems.

Cursor stated that "at most 5,000 users were affected," and that they will be contacted about the incident directly.

Separately that same day, researchers described an unrelated exploit in Cursor, allowing attackers to deploy arbitrary code to developers' machines via Cursor's built-in browser.

Related:Anthropic-Themed Phishing Emails Bypass Top Security Tools

Cursor did not immediately respond to an inquiry from Dark Reading regarding both of these stories.

Cursor's Claude Code Conundrum

For some, the notion of a compromised "extension" might evoke browser extensions, which are so frequently vulnerable, suspicious, and outright malicious that cybersecurity news concerning them tends not to evoke much panic, even in extreme cases.

Extensions in coding environments are a different beast. "IDE extensions are scarier than browser extensions because, unlike browser extensions, they are designed to have the same level of permissions as their host," Gal Weizman, security researcher at Forever Security, tells Dark Reading. "They can run code, access the filesystem, fire network requests and more."

On Thursday, an attacker tried to leverage the power afforded by coding environment extensions by sneaking a 66-line loader on top of the real extension's legitimate code. According to an analysis from the community threat intelligence platform OpenSourceMalware, everything about the extension remained the same besides this lone edit to its extension.js file.

As soon as the extension loaded — without need for the user to establish a Claude conversation — the new file is revved up. It attempts to add an attacker-controlled key to victims' SSH configurations, with the goal of establishing reverse tunnels that act as a backdoor into the compromised systems.

The malicious extension also attempts to make those connections persistent by registering background processes — for macOS systems, a LaunchAgent; and for Windows, scheduled tasks running with system privileges, plus a fallback Startup script. This whole business was doomed from the start, Cursor wrote, since turning on the local SSH service requires administrative privileges, which the Claude Code extension only possesses in "highly unusual circumstances."

Related:'Gheist' Weaponizes GitHub Tokens to Steal Cloud Secrets

Victims weren't totally out of the woods, though, as the malicious code also exfiltrated system information via separate Web requests. Stolen data was limited to hostnames, usernames, operating systems (OS), OS architectures, home directory paths, environment variable names, working directories, configured Git emails, and public IP addresses.

Cursor Contains Compromise

Cursor's public disclosure suggests that the security incident was its own, not Anthropic's. The malicious version "was not developed by Anthropic," the SpaceX-owned company reported.

In response to the discovery, Cursor took a variety of steps to protect itself: rotating its keys, checking for tampering in other extensions, and taking its marketplace temporarily offline and rebuilding it. It also worked with the relevant cloud hosting provider to take down the attacker's malicious infrastructure.

Cursor did not specify how the intrusion occurred in the first place. While acknowledging that it's not yet known what happened here, Weizman explains, "Historically, the most common way extensions and plug-ins get hijacked is through theft of locally stored credentials that allow publishing new versions of these packages."

Related:10 Software Security Practices Built for the Next 250 Years

"Enabling 2FA for publishing such extensions is an excellent way to significantly mitigate such risk in the future. Relying on an access token as the only gate for pushing such critical software significantly increases the risk of this happening," he says.

More Security Concerns for Cursor, AI Assistants

On the same day of the Anthropic Cursor attack, Weizman published separate research detailing weaknesses in the browsers built into top desktop AI assistants today, which could be exploited to devastating effect. His test cases included Claude Desktop, GitHub Copilot, Codex, VS Code, and Cursor. Cursor has arguably the worst issue of the bunch.

In his experiments, Weizman's team created a clean-looking website, with a visible HTML chip concealing a malicious shell command in its attributes. Then they opened up the site in a built-in Cursor browser. "When the command hit Cursor's safety sandbox and was blocked, the agent — on its own, with nothing in the page telling it to — switched the sandbox off and tried again. The control worked. The agent talked itself out of using it," Weizman wrote in the report.

The attack didn't work universally across all models. When it did work, the browser escape allowed the researchers to deploy an arbitrary app to their test victim's computer. And just like the malicious Claude Code extension, the app ran with the victim's full permissions. Cursor did not respond to Forever Security's disclosure, but the company quietly patched the issue on Oct. 1.

“IDEs are becoming more agentic. They're being given agentic capabilities, which can introduce dangerous architecture. It can be very risky when things go wrong," Weizman says.

"Here we've had two examples of that: built-in browsers, and what happened with Claude Code, both of which impacted Cursor," he concludes. "And because of the rapid pace at which this is happening, security isn't necessarily keeping up."

Title: Warning: Romance Scammers Are Targeting US Citizens For Money Laundering
Context: Threat actors are using romance scams to trick U
Full Text:
Threat actors are using romance scams to trick U.S. citizens into acting as money mules, the Wall Street Journal reports. The Journal cites the example of Garrick Stafford, a 50-year-old Texas man who lost $65,000 and unwittingly laundered $50,000 for an international crime ring after falling for an online scammer posing as an attractive woman.

Notably, Stafford was texting with the scammer all summer before the individual first asked for money, claiming that she needed $150 to pay her cellphone bill. Stafford immediately recognized this as a red flag and blocked the individual. Months later, however, he unblocked her, and they began texting again.

“Stafford still isn’t sure why he didn’t cut her off for good after that first request for money, but by Christmas that year, he realized he missed her,” the Journal says. “Once they reconnected, though, the asks only grew. Several thousand dollars for a seminar in digital design. Seed money for an antiques business. Medical costs for her sick mother.” In addition to asking Stafford for his own money, the threat actor’s primary objective was to use Stafford’s bank account to launder money stolen in separate scams.

“Whenever a payment arrived in Stafford’s account, Sarah would frantically press him to move the money into various crypto wallets—sometimes requiring him to leave work,” the Journal says. “He briefly set up other accounts, but banks, suspecting illegal activity, would soon freeze them. Still, Sarah always had a reason why she couldn’t open her own accounts or make the transfers herself—citing bad credit or a move to London from Miami. In all, Stafford said, about $50,000 moved through his account or others she had him set up, while another $100,000 in bad checks she sent him bounced.”

A police detective in South Carolina eventually notified Stafford that he was being scammed, and “Sarah” turned out to be a married couple in Nigeria who used AI to respond to his texts.

John Breyault, vice president of the National Consumers League, told the WSJ, “Romantic interest is a very strong emotion. Scammers recognize this and devote a lot of time to develop the trust needed to exploit the victim.”

Title: New Framework Puts Ransomware Resilience for AI Systems in Focus
Context: Cybersecurity leaders can now use a new framework to find and address weaknesses that could leave their AI systems vulnerable to ransomware attacks
Full Text:
Cybersecurity leaders can now use a new framework to find and address weaknesses that could leave their AI systems vulnerable to ransomware attacks.

The tool is the Ransomware Assessment and Incident Defense Framework for AI Systems (RAID-AI) and is fully available for anyone to use online for free.

Behnaz Karimi and Yuvaraj Govindarajulu, both co-leads of the Open Worldwide Application Security Project’s (OWASP) AI Bill of Materials (AIBOM) initiative developed RAID-AI over the past two years.

They had initially planned to introduce the framework at the ISC2 Security Congress, held in Denver, Colorado, between October 26 and 28. Unfortunately, visa issues prevented Karimi from attending.

A Manual Ransomware Readiness Assessment for AI Systems

Speaking to Infosecurity, Karimi said RAID AI focuses on ransomware attacks against AI systems, whether or not an attacker uses AI. The framework’s approach is hands-on, asking security teams to assess their own controls rather than connecting to or scanning their systems.

“Right now, we are slowly seeing that ransomware attacks targeting AI systems are happening,” Karimi said.

She highlighted a April 2025, a report by Zoran, Mitrovic head of engineering at Kintra Health, which detailed how ransomware actors used data poisoning techniques, as well as an alleged cyber-attack on Novo Nordisk in June 2026, where hackers claimed to have stolen AI models used by the pharmaceutical company.

The RAID-AI assessment covers general cybersecurity measures alongside risks specific to AI models, data and supporting infrastructure.

The framework is delivered through a web console aimed at CISOs, cybersecurity officers and security engineers.

Users assess controls manually, selecting maturity levels on a scale from zero to five. The controls are organized into general and AI-specific categories, with levels such as basic, advanced and high.

General controls include recovery, training and sensitive-data protection. AI-specific areas include data, tools and runtime.

RAID AI maps controls to two voluntary security frameworks, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology’s (NIST) Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 (CSF 2.0) and the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s (CISA) Cybersecurity Performance Goals 2.0 (CPG 2.0).

It also allows users to map adversarial attacks through three attack mapping frameworks, MITRE ATT&CK, MITRE ATLAS and NIST Adversarial.

Karimi and Govindarajulu have provided comprehensive documentation, including guidelines for using the tool and an explanation of how it was developed and how maturity levels and various security scores are calculated.

Future Plans: Extend Ransomware Assessments to Agentic AI Systems

Organizations do not need to connect their internal systems or upload company documents to complete the assessment.

Therefore, the RAID-AI assessment is not an automated audit: results depend on users’ evaluations and the tool does not independently verify an organization’s security posture.

Instead, teams review their practices and enter their assessments themselves.

“Ideally bringing security managers, engineers and AI-security specialists together in workshops,” Karimi told Infosecurity.

The console displays the results in dashboards, including maturity views and mappings to other frameworks. Users can also download PDF reports that highlight weaknesses and help teams set priorities.

Karimi said the dashboard can give senior leaders a high-level overview, while technical teams use the underlying controls to guide more detailed discussions.

In the future, Karimi hopes to provide practical implementation resources, including videos and blueprints to help security engineers apply individual controls, and develop a similar tool for ransomware threats targeting agentic AI systems.

Title: What AI Cybercrime Exercises Reveal About Collective Defense
Context: As attackers accelerate their operations and obscure evidence available to defenders, those unresolved questions become harder to manage
Full Text:
AI-enabled cybercrime has increased pressure on the decisions that link detection to response. While security teams may recognize an attack, their organization may still be uncertain about who can authorize action, what information can be shared, or when to communicate with customers and partners. As attackers accelerate their operations and obscure evidence available to defenders, those unresolved questions become harder to manage.

That is a central lesson drawn from a series of tabletop exercises conducted by the AI-enabled Cybercrime Initiative, a collaboration among Fortinet, UC Berkeley’s Center for Long-Term Cybersecurity (CLTC), the Berkeley Risk and Security Lab (BRSL), and other partners.

My accompanying analysis with CLTC, “Who Decides How to Respond during a Cyber Crisis? What Three Tabletop Exercises Revealed About AI-Enabled Cybercrime,” examines the governance challenges that emerged from those sessions. From Fortinet’s perspective, those findings underscore why contributing to shared research matters: Improving collective defense requires understanding how organizations make decisions together and how attackers operate.

Connecting Research with Operational Experience

As a CLTC research partner, Fortinet supported the initiative’s launch and has contributed directly to its research and exercises. In Singapore, I helped lead the tabletop exercise alongside project lead Dr. Gil Baram and Helena Huang, associate research fellow in the executive deputy chairman’s office at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies. Practitioner involvement like this grounds academic research into the wider consequences of AI-enabled cybercrime in how incidents actually unfold.

Fortinet also helped bring the research to a wider audience. At RSAC 2025, Fortinet joined CLTC, BRSL, and Nanyang Technological University experts to discuss the initiative alongside threat intelligence from FortiGuard Labs. That exchange helped connect the scenarios being studied with observations of how criminals were adopting AI.

That combination of public sector, academic, and industry expertise helps participants examine problems that extend beyond any single organization’s visibility or authority. A security provider may hold evidence that a government needs. A business may depend on a supplier’s investigation to understand its own exposure. And importantly, decisions made by one participant can change the options available to everyone else.

This work also builds on Fortinet’s earlier participation in CLTC’s Cybersecurity Futures 2030 project. Across both efforts, scenario planning gives leaders a structured way to question assumptions and prepare for conditions their current plans may not adequately address.

By bringing these perspectives into the same scenarios, the initiative creates an opportunity to expose conflicting assumptions before an actual incident makes them consequential. The resulting lessons can inform organizations beyond those represented in the exercises.

What the Three Exercises Revealed

The progression through the exercises is instructive. Early discussions at Berkeley examined how AI could make phishing, impersonation, and reconnaissance more accessible. The Singapore event explored the implications for incident response and for disruptions across critical infrastructure. Operation Black Ice in Tel Aviv brought impersonation, supplier compromise, and ransomware together into a single crisis, testing decisions under competing pressures.

Across these sessions, participants often understood the threat but struggled to determine what action they could take. Three recurring problems deserve particular attention from security leaders:

First, consequential decisions arrived before reliable answers. At UC Berkeley, participants needed to advise clients while attribution remained unresolved. Similarly, in Singapore, pressure for public guidance preceded a clear understanding of the compromise. The practical challenge, therefore, is deciding what evidence is sufficient for a particular action and how to communicate uncertainty without creating confusion.

Second, response obligations collided. The Singapore scenario placed energy, transport, and water systems under pressure within the same response window. In Tel Aviv, legal authorization, board notification, and regulatory disclosure competed for attention. To address issues like these, playbooks need to account for simultaneous demands and establish how they will resolve competing priorities.

Third, information and authority were divided. In the UC Berkeley scenario, a private firm held forensic data while the government held the relevant authority to act. Participants encountered a circular dependency: Sharing required attribution, but attribution depended on sharing. That scenario illustrates how individually reasonable requirements can obstruct a collective response.

Of course, these were simulated incidents, and the findings should be understood in that context. Even so, the recurrence of similar difficulties across different jurisdictions gives leaders a useful basis for examining their own response arrangements.

Making Collaboration Work Under Pressure

The operational implication is clear: Threat intelligence delivers greater value when the people receiving it have the authority and established relationships to act. Improving detection speed should be paired with efforts to remove avoidable delays in escalation and coordination.

Organizations can begin by defining decision authority before an incident. Security, legal, communications, and executive teams should understand which decisions they own, which require consultation, and how to escalate disagreements. Those arrangements should be exercised when several urgent demands arrive together.

External coordination deserves similar attention. Partners should establish what information they can share during an investigation, how they will indicate their confidence in that information, and which channels will remain available if normal connections are interrupted. Exercises should then test whether those arrangements hold when a supplier is compromised or when several sectors are affected.

While AI-assisted detection and triage can help teams process information faster, leaders still need to determine how those outputs inform action and where human approval is required. Testing the relationship between technical capability and decision authority is an important part of making that investment effective. AI can compress the time between signal and decision, but accountability for that decision must remain with the people who have the authority to act.

Looking Ahead to Phase 2 with CLTC

Phase 1 provides a strong foundation for continued collaboration as Fortinet looks ahead to Phase 2 of the initiative with CLTC, beginning in 2027. It identified practical questions about how defenders can respond when attacks move faster than their established decision processes.

A valuable next step is to assess whether proposed improvements hold up under pressure. Can clearer decision authority reduce delays? Can partners share useful evidence even when attribution remains uncertain? Can AI-assisted analysis help leaders make timely decisions while preserving accountability? Phase 1 positions the broader cybersecurity community to answer them.

Fortinet’s contribution to this work reflects a responsibility that extends beyond individual customer environments. By participating in joint exercises and research, we can help translate operational experience into lessons that other defenders can apply. Continued collaboration with CLTC offers an opportunity to build on those lessons and strengthen the collective response to AI-enabled cybercrime.

Explore CLTC’s AI-Enabled Cybercrime Initiative and the research informing this collaboration.

Full Text:
Written by: Aurora Blum, David Mainor, Rohit Nambiar, Omar ElAhdan, Matthew McWhirt, Will Silverstone, Bhavesh Dhake, Chris Busse

Introduction

Recent intrusions in which threat actors have been observed weaponizing agentic frameworks to execute highly-automated intrusions has put a spotlight on evolving adversarial use of LLMs. In our September 2026 report, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) noted that forward leaning adversaries were beginning to transition from basic prompting to agentic workflows and LLM-enabled automation.

Since this publication, GTIG and Mandiant have observed multiple threat actors abusing the open-source, agentic pentesting frameworks ARTEX, Hexstrike and CAIRN in incident response engagements to conduct a broad range of actions across multiple phases of the attack life cycle. This activity has been seen across the threat landscape, as noted in a recent Wiz report. The emergence of Artex and similar agentic offensive intrusion frameworks underscores a broader shift toward threat actor adoption of open source multi-agent offensive frameworks, as well as potentially custom agentic harnesses.

This represents a paradigm shift towards intrusions occurring at machine speed, with the automated chaining of complex attack paths scaling intrusions exponentially. While the mechanics of the intrusions remain the same, such as using compromised credentials and targeting unpatched systems, the speed and scale at which frameworks can exploit these known weaknesses introduces a new defensive challenge. Security teams, developers, and system administrators will need to fundamentally rethink defense strategies to counter scalable, autonomous software. We also provide defensive strategies from Mandiant Consulting. The defensive strategies suggested—control-plane isolation, short-lived credentials, least privilege, segmentation, and behavioral detection—are long-standing security best practices.

Observations in the Wild

We are seeing tools used by adversaries evolving towards autonomous agentic attacks. One way this is occurring is through suites of tools or frameworks designed for penetration testing (“pentesting”). These tools and frameworks orchestrate various agents using open source and frontier LLMs to automate various stages of intrusions. Historically, cyber espionage and financially motivated threat actors have taken advantage of pentesting or red-teaming platforms built for security professionals to exploit systems, such as Cobalt Strike or Metasploit. Today, adversaries are pivoting toward offensive frameworks powered by LLMs. While these frameworks have existed in the wild, they are now yielding success in intrusions in the wild, representing a critical evolution that increases both the speed and scale of intrusion activity.

Since late August 2026, we have observed threat actors actively operating popular open-source multi-agent pentesting platforms like ARTEX, PentAGI, CAIRN and other potentially custom harnesses within Mandiant incident response engagements; use of these platforms has been further corroborated by our research telemetry. In these incidents, we have observed agentic activity conducting significant parts of the attack lifecycle (e.g., lateral movement, database exploitation, exfiltration preparation). Evidence of in the wild usage of these frameworks marks a critical inflection point for defenders, as agents now autonomously explore multiple attack paths, troubleshoot errors, and achieve objectives in seconds and minutes. Coupled with continual advancements in underlying LLM capabilities, the acceleration in attack velocity and scale signals a notable shift in the threat landscape that fundamentally alters traditional intrusion dynamics.

ARTEX Framework

ARTEX is an autonomous, multi-agent LLM-driven pentesting and offensive command-and-control (C2) platform written in Go with an embedded Next.js web console. The framework was originally developed by the user Autumn-27 and released on GitHub. Although the original repository was taken down by its creator in October 2026 due to widespread threat actor abuse, the framework continues to proliferate globally via community forks, including localized variations such as ScopeWeaver and a commercial version dubbed ARTEX PRO. ARTEX abstracts the attack lifecycle across six specialized sub-agents. By leveraging APIs from frontier and open source models, the framework translates high-level tactical goals into actionable machine commands. GTIG has observed capabilities including automated Active Directory reconnaissance, privilege escalation, target cloud-infrastructure profiling (such as harvesting Azure storage keys), to the synthesis and deployment of custom webshells.

Since late August 2026, ARTEX has been adopted by a diverse range of threat actors across the motivational spectrum, including both financially motivated extortion groups and suspected cyber espionage operators. For example, the Wiz Research team has been tracking a campaign associated with ARTEX, which GTIG tracks as UNC7228, that overlaps with activity tracked by Microsoft as the PRC-nexus actor STORM-0940. The research has expanded Wiz’s understanding of this campaign beyond the October IT focused activity with activity now dating back to at least August 2026. Wiz identified the targeting, compromise, and data theft affecting multiple entities in the US and Europe across the enterprise software, industrial automation, semiconductor manufacturing and design, and telecommunications industry verticals. This actor has moved extremely quickly, typically moving from their first compromised account to deep system access in around four hours and in one case as rapidly as 15 minutes. They have also customized their tooling to take advantage of victim-specific setups and fallen back to open proxies if their initial infrastructure was blocked.

Demonstrating broader adoption of ARTEX, GTIG and Mandiant observed multiple other threat actors using ARTEX for post-compromise reconnaissance, lateral movement, and privilege escalation in incident response investigations. This includes financially motivated threat actors who used the framework to facilitate data theft extortion, and additional suspected PRC-nexus clusters. Their operations collectively impacted organizations across government, technology, chemicals and materials, and manufacturing sectors in the US, alongside public reporting of ARTEX targeting the financial sector in Asia.

In several cases, adversaries provided ARTEX with compromised credentials for the targeted organization, and instructed the framework to execute subsequent stages of the attack lifecycle. Analysis of these intrusions reveals key differences between activity conducted by the ARTEX framework and that of a human operator:

Based on log files and timestamps, we identified bursts of activity that would be highly irregular for a human operator. While each of the intrusions exhibited extended pauses during operational phases, individual ARTEX execution sequences ran in compressed bursts of roughly 2 to 25 seconds. In at least one operation, we observed 27 events in 23 seconds of active burst time, performing rapid probing of AWS permissions across different security groups. While preparing potential exfiltration scripts, ARTEX was capable of successfully adapting to errors quoting “script too large” by trimming the script and relaunching it to successfully deploy a 17-snapshot instance in approximately 10 seconds.

Compared to a competent human operator, ARTEX achieved code execution in a far more forensically noisy manner, relying on rapid, iterative trial-and-error. In one instance, supplied with valid credentials, ARTEX accessed an external-facing Linux Weaver OA web server to execute SQL commands via exposed API calls. Using legitimately-exposed application-specific API calls, ARTEX was able to achieve partial command-execution to conduct further reconnaissance despite hitting technical complexities. However, this process generated 240 log events and exhibited errors potentially caused by multiple sub-agents overwriting one another while pursuing the same objective.

In an attempt to pivot from a database-execution context to a system-execution context, ARTEX used an application-specific SQL API, accessible to the supplied-user credential, to modify the MySQL instance to write log files with a .jsp extension to publicly accessible locations. The SQL-commands executed were likely intended to poison MySQL logs into writing web-accessible JSP webshells.

Using the API, ARTEX ran SET GLOBAL general_log_file = '<path to webshell>’ followed by SET GLOBAL general_log = 1; subsequent SQL commands were written to the filepath defined in general_log_file. ARTEX then ran SQL SELECT statements in the form `SELECT '<% [webshell content] %>'`. Due to how the underlying Java web servlet handles JSP files, the Java code in the '<% %>' gets parsed and compiled into the process memory space, providing means of execution.

Log activity shows multiple iterations of the above sequence, with ephemeral, somewhat-incremental file names (cl1217.jsp, f1219a.jsp, z1219.jsp) for each webshell candidate, each one executing a different command. Errors when trying to run the webshell (e.g. variable ‘t is already defined’) caused the webshell to fail and likely had ARTEX refactor its approach, writing several unique webshells, each with a different goal, some correcting previous errors until the .jsp webshells executed cleanly and returned valid command output to ARTEX.

In another case, during access-probing efforts, ARTEX generated files of various extension types with the filename artex-probe-*, where * carried five digit somewhat-incremental numbers. Based on our visibility, it’s difficult to comment on the exact significance of these numbers or how they increment. However, ARTEX was seen using similar incremental numeric markers within dropped file names, created account names, their passwords and within email subjects.

Performed reconnaissance across the internal network by running several iterative generated PowerShell enumeration scripts against a Domain Controller and federation server. Generated a new SSH key pair, allocated a dedicated public Elastic IP, attempted to create a custom security group but failed due to permission issues, and launched persistent t3.micro instances bound to existing security groups to establish an externally addressable jump host and internal foothold.

Gained persistence through account takeover (e.g., resetting passwords for identified users), creating multiple accounts with plaintext passwords (which included ArtexProbe in the naming convention), and creating administrator accounts.

Interrogating backend SQL databases (extracting ~400 KB of query results across ~20 queries) and performing mass blob reads.

Deployed custom boot scripts via ephemeral, keyless EC2 instances to potentially harvest data from multiple mounted EBS snapshots and volumes.

Enumerated over 110,000 Active Directory objects from a domain controller and retrieved the Domain Admins group. It then sent command output to rotating webhook.site endpoints via curl.
