In this case we observed an interesting abuse of legitimate features. Rather than executing complex malware, ARTEX weaponized built-in application features. It forced an application's notification system to broadcast test emails to over 1,300 internal users, turning a trusted notification channel into a mass-internal messaging tool. It then dropped to single-recipient test emails rather than the mass emailing.

PentAGI Offensive Framework

GTIG also observed in the wild abuse of PentAGI (Penetration Testing Artificial General Intelligence), an autonomous offensive framework designed to automate the pentesting process within an isolated environment. Developed by VXControl, the framework is offered in an open source and commercial edition. It is designed so that the user only needs to describe a target and a goal, which enables entry-level users to run complex cyber security campaigns. Once the target and the goal have been selected, the framework uses a team of specialized agents, each with their own functionalities to break tasks (called “Flows”) into various sub-tasks, execute each step, and report on it. The tools and commands are all run in isolated sandboxes running Kali Linux instead of in the host environment. All the tools used by PentAGI are open-source pentesting tools available by default in Kali Linux (e.g., metasploit, nmap, SQLmap). The framework supports over a dozen cloud and local LLM backends, including frontier and open weight models.

The majority of observed PentAGI activity remained at the stage of WHOIS asset mapping or active vulnerability scanning. However, analysis of operational artifacts indicates that some operations progressed to active intrusions and persistence across multiple organizations. Operators are also adapting and integrating the framework in different ways. In one case, we identified a customized attack orchestration platform built on the open-source version of PentAGI likely used between at least late August and early October 2026 to conduct systematic reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning against a wide range of organizations in Asia, including system integrators and major telecommunications firms. In another instance, we observed PentAGI chained with proxy services to target the Aerospace sector.

Evolution of Autonomous Offensive Frameworks

We are seeing a significant maturation in the application of LLM capabilities across the threat landscape in a short period of time; this includes the incorporation of LLM-written malicious code, development of dynamic LLM-enabled malware, poisoning of agent-harness files, and the building of multi-agent offensive frameworks. Notably, between late 2025 and October 2026, autonomous and semi-autonomous offensive frameworks crossed a decisive operational threshold to multi-agent frameworks actively weaponized by threat actors to perform in the wild intrusions.

GTIG has been tracking the evolution of this experimentation over time, from simple prompting of LLMs to help with coding, through the use of frameworks in the wild towards a potential future with fully autonomous frameworks running intrusions. In a fully autonomous attack, a human’s role would consist of telling the agent what to target, and then simply benefiting from the operational objective.

At the time of reporting, we assess that the current adversary use of autonomous offensive frameworks is still in early stages characterized by open source tools currently being used in low-sophisticated ways, resulting in broad and noisy, but still successful campaigns. As the sophistication of these frameworks, the underlying LLMs and the orchestrating human-operator increase, we expect to see not only less human interaction, but also increased stealth and sophistication.

The following stages represent our observations of how LLM-augmentation in cyber operations have evolved over the last year and how we expect this development to continue:

Stage 1: Prompt-based use of LLMs

Activity: Adversaries interact with LLMs in a prompt based chatbot fashion, using LLMs to write and debug code for malware, draft phishing emails, create personas, and conduct light reconnaissance on targets.

Evolution: Adversaries outsource low-failure, easy-to-rectify, tasks to an LLM to increase speed of simple discrete tasks.

Timeframe: End of 2025 to early 2026

Stage 2: Embedding LLM capabilities into malware

Activity: Adversaries trust an LLM to take certain low-failure, easy to execute actions, particularly writing code, such as in malware families like HONESTCUE or PROMPTSPY using LLMs dynamically during execution to, for example, obfuscate payloads in different ways in attempts to evade defenses.

Evolution: Adversaries begin use incorporating LLMs into post-intrusion attack phases.

Timeframe: Early 2026

Stage 3: Incorporating LLM-enabled automation into operations

Activity: As agentic capabilities develop, adversaries begin using them for discrete tasks (e.g., standing up or debugging malware development environments). Agents begin being used alongside human-operators to develop novel exploits and to assist with high-stake vulnerability research. Adversaries begin being more cognizant of OPSEC and visibility into their LLM-usage operations and start using LLM-proxy services to obscure activities.

Evolution: LLMs being used for more high-stake tasks but with human operators in the loop.

Timeframe: Early 2026 - September 2026

Stage 4: Developing and experimenting with autonomous frameworks

Activity: Adversaries begin developing and experimenting with autonomous frameworks. Campaigns begin offloading more stages of the lifecycle to LLM-augmented tooling, and integrating model APIs into their tools and telegram bots to take autonomous action.

Evolution: Experimentation with LLMs running more stages of the attack lifecycle.

Timeframe: Mid 2026 - September 2026

Stage 5: Multiple attack lifecycle stages being conducted by LLM-driven tooling in the wild

Activity: In the wild evidence of multiple attack lifecycle stages being conducted by LLM-driven tooling, with fewer humans in the loop during operations. Observations surrounding mass-exploitation campaigns where a substantial portion of the lifecycle is being carried out by an agent, requiring only minimal human intervention, as well as activity accompanied by malware possessing more autonomous capabilities. Additionally, continued experimentation by threat actors with better obfuscation—including LLM mixers, inference services, local models. Overall TTPs of these attacks remain messy, noisy but yet successful.

Evolution: Adversaries have actively integrated LLMs into their operations to conduct successful intrusions, while simultaneously exploring ways to obscure/reduce reliance on frontier-lab LLMs.

Timeframe: Current stage of development

Stage 6: Multi-agent-driven, unsophisticated attacks with little to no human interaction

Activity: Highly-autonomous, but unsophisticated, forensically noisy operations with human operators no longer in the loop. Adversaries define the target and objective, while multi-agent frameworks execute the entire attack chain and return operational objectives.

Evolution: Adversaries diversifying infrastructure and tooling, further inhibiting defenders’ visibility.

Timeframe: Near-term (1 - 3 months)

Stage 7: Sophisticated, fully autonomous/agentic attacks

Activity: This stage represents peak maturity on the offensive LLMs capability curve, characterized not only by fully autonomous intrusions requiring little to no human interaction, but also by increased stealth and sophistication of the activity, with operators interacting with LLMs through either obscurely designed infrastructure or self-hosted LLMs altogether.

Evolution: This stage would grant autonomous and stealthier operations while limiting defender’s visibility into the activity.

Timeframe: Medium-term (3 - 6 months)

We believe malicious actors will continue to experiment with these offensive agentic frameworks, moving towards future autonomous usage. GTIG has observed evidence of threat-actor experimentation with tools like the ZeroHollow inference service and the fully agentic framework AgentZero.

Outlook

Over the past 12 months, GTIG has observed a decisive evolution in adversarial tradecraft leveraging LLMs, progressing from ad hoc operational productivity support toward the deployment of coordinated, multi-agent, autonomous offensive frameworks. While earlier milestones documented in our quarterly research highlighted early agentic interest, recent observations across frontline incident response engagements and proactive intelligence collection reveals adversary adoption of these frameworks to automate discrete phases and specific operational tasks during intrusions. Threat actors are increasingly leveraging generative models to achieve unprecedented speed and scale, actively developing more complex attack infrastructure powered by agentic AI capabilities and AI-enabled automation.

Frameworks such as ARTEX compress attack timelines to machine speed; however, they currently trade stealth for velocity. Unrestricted autonomous execution generates forensic traffic, relies on recognizable identifiers, and leaves behind distinct code-level traces, increasing the likelihood of detection and mitigation. These tools are therefore best suited to scenarios in which the cost of detection is low. Additionally, detection and disruption/response are two different functions–simply detecting the attack in time does little to hinder objective completion.

Consequently, GTIG assesses with high confidence that cyber crime threat actors will continue incorporating autonomous offensive tools into their operations, given that the increased reach of their campaigns will likely compensate for any decreases in success rates. We anticipate that actors, who specialize in stealthy operations designed to maintain long-term access, are less likely to use the publicly available versions of these tools, though they may employ them for purposes of scale and speed, depending on operational priorities. Regardless of motivation, the low barrier to entry, ease of integrating new exploits, and massive scaling potential make autonomous frameworks an attractive, low-cost force multiplier for a wide range of threat actors, making it highly likely that we will continue to see increasing threat actor adoption of these types of frameworks in the near term.

Defending Against AI-Enabled Attacks: Five Layers of Defense

LLM-enabled offensive tooling does not fundamentally change the techniques attackers use. It reduces the time required to combine them. Credential discovery, permission testing, lateral movement, and data access that previously required hours of operator effort can now occur in minutes, frequently through valid identities and supported functionality that static indicators will not detect. Organizations are best positioned to withstand this when compromise of a single identity, credential, or workload provides only limited access. Restricting control-plane exposure, replacing long-lived secrets with short-lived and tightly scoped credentials, segmenting application tiers, and placing guardrails on high-impact business functions all reduce the speed advantage automation provides. Behavioral detection addresses the activity that these controls do not prevent, but it depends on having sufficient identity, control-plane, data-plane, and network telemetry to establish what normal activity looks like. Many of these controls are already familiar to defenders. The difference is that automated tooling can now identify and exploit the gaps between them far more quickly.

As illustrated above, LLM-enabled offensive tooling is increasing the speed and scale of cyber attacks. LLM-enabled and autonomous tools can identify weaknesses, test access, interpret errors, adjust their approach, and continue through an attack path with limited human interaction. Work that might previously have required an operator to investigate an environment, write or modify code, troubleshoot failures, and execute the next step over several hours can increasingly happen in minutes.

This creates a detection challenge as well. Much of the activity may use valid credentials and supported functionality (living-off-the-land, LotL). An attacker may authenticate with a legitimate service principal, call a normal management API, access cloud storage through a supported protocol, or execute commands through an existing administrative interface. Tool names, hashes, IP addresses, and other static indicators provide useful signals when available, but they will not cover much of this activity.

Effective defenses combine two capabilities:

Controls that limit what an attacker can do after gaining valid access.

Telemetry that shows when an identity, application, or workload begins operating outside its normal pattern.

How Adversarial Use of LLMs Changes the Attacker Timeline

Several themes repeatedly appear during investigations involving LLM-enabled or highly automated attacker activity:

Speed and scale: Automated tooling can perform broad reconnaissance, test several attack paths at once, react to failures, and immediately continue into follow-on activity. The time between initial access, privilege discovery, lateral movement, and data access can become very short.

Interconnected environments: Attackers rarely remain inside one technology stack. An internet-facing application may expose credentials in a configuration file. Those credentials may provide access to cloud storage, source repositories, identity systems, or internal infrastructure. Automation makes it easier to discover and test those relationships quickly.

Legitimate-looking identity activity: Many actions look normal when viewed independently. A service principal authenticates, an API is called, a storage object is downloaded. The stronger signal often comes from context: where the request originated, how much activity occurred, what happened immediately before and after it, and whether the behavior is expected for that identity.

Control-plane and data-plane blind spots: Many organizations have mature endpoint monitoring but considerably less visibility into management APIs, programmatic identities, and cloud storage activity. Permission testing, retrieval of storage keys, bulk downloads, firewall changes, and management API calls may all be logged without generating useful alerts.

Mandiant recommends structuring enterprise defenses across five foundational layers designed to restrict lateral movement and limit the speed advantage of autonomous tooling:

Layer

Description

Layer 1: Protect Control Planes

Restrict all admin APIs, consoles & CI/CD to trusted networks

Layer 2: Restrict Identities & Keys

Migrate to short-lived workload credentials; eliminate secrets

Layer 3: Harden Configurations

Continuous vulnerability scanning across apps & infrastructure

Layer 4: Application Protections

Harden applications to prevent abuse of legitimate features and capabilities

Layer 5: Detect Behavioral Changes

Monitor identity velocity, API bursts, and volumetric anomalies

Layer 1: Protect the Control Plane

Restrict access to the systems attackers can use to administer, deploy, or reconfigure the environment.

The control plane extends well beyond Active Directory or a cloud console. It includes identity providers, cloud management APIs, network and firewall management platforms, virtualization infrastructure, code repositories, CI/CD systems, privileged access management platforms, backup infrastructure, certificate authorities, SaaS administration consoles, and application administration interfaces.

Why It Is Important

Internet-accessible management interfaces can quickly become part of an attack path after credentials are obtained. For example, Azure App Service includes an administrative interface through Kudu Site Control Manager, or SCM, which supports application deployment and management functionality. If an attacker obtains publishing credentials or another identity capable of accessing that interface, automation can quickly test authentication, enumerate functionality, interact with application files, execute commands, retrieve output, and remove staged artifacts.

Similar exposure exists across firewall administration, virtualization consoles, cloud management APIs, backup platforms, CI/CD interfaces, and other management services. Any reachable administrative path gives an automated attacker another capability to test.

Mitigations

Reduce Administrative Internet Exposure: Restrict cloud administration, network device management, application publishing interfaces, hypervisors, backup platforms, and other sensitive services to trusted networks, private connectivity, or dedicated administrative paths wherever possible.

Require Trusted Administrative Paths: Require privileged users to administer sensitive infrastructure from managed devices, privileged access workstations, or approved jump hosts. Pair these controls with phishing-resistant authentication such as FIDO2 or passkeys where supported.

Title: The $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Was Pulled Off in Just 20 Minutes
Context: “Early on October 29, the operator deployed a first piece of code for the attack and tested it on two wallets,” TRM says
Full Text:
Cryptocurrency firms and investigators are racing to freeze and track down billions of dollars of stolen digital cash following what appears to be the largest crypto heist of all time. On Thursday, starting at around 4pm ET, hackers started quickly siphoning around $6.3 billion in cryptocurrencies, spread across multiple blockchains, from wallets belonging to crypto exchange Binance.

Following the theft, Binance almost immediately suspended all deposits and withdrawals from its services as part of its investigation into the hack and says it is working to identify who was behind the breach. The company, along with other crypto firms, says it has so far been able to freeze around half of the stolen funds—essentially stopping hackers moving the money further or trying to cash it out. Much of the remaining crypto may not be possible to freeze, however.

Three crypto tracing firms have been quick to link the attack potentially to North Korean hackers. “We think North Korea is likely responsible,” Tom Robinson, chief scientist and cofounder of Elliptic, tells WIRED. “If North Korea is behind it, this one theft would almost double everything the regime has stolen in crypto to date.”

The majority of the stolen crypto was taken in a period of around 20 minutes on October 29, according to analysis by crypto tracing firm TRM Labs. Wallets belonging to Binance across at least ten blockchains—including Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron and Solana—were drained and sent to multiple addresses controlled by a single attacker, according to TRM’s analysis. “Preparation began at least 36 hours before the theft,” TRM says in a blog post. The company says one of the attacker’s wallets received three small withdrawals during a test period, before later expanding the operations.

“Early on October 29, the operator deployed a first piece of code for the attack and tested it on two wallets,” TRM says. “Later that day, it rehearsed the final version on a third wallet, then routed the test funds back to itself. Four hours after that rehearsal, the same code was installed on a Binance hot wallet.” Hot wallets are cryptocurrency wallets that are internet connected and allow crypto exchanges to handle customer withdrawals. Analysts say the funds were drained from hot wallets across the impacted blockchains.

Neither Binance or law enforcement officials have named any suspected links between the attack and North Korean hackers, but researchers say there are overlaps with previous cryptocurrency attacks from TraderTraitor. Over recent years, North Korean hackers have repeatedly targeted cryptocurrency firms and stolen hundreds of millions in crypto heists. Multiple North Korean hacking groups can target companies in the sector but TraderTraitor have become specialists, pulling off infrequent but high profile attacks.

The tactics used in the hack appear to mimic previous methods used by an elite subset of North Korean hackers, known by the name TraderTraitor. Crypto tracing firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis both say they believe TraderTraitor may be behind the attack, while Robinson says Elliptic hasn’t specifically tied it to the group but sees overlaps in the activity.

Title: Binance Hit by Record-Breaking $6.3bn Hack in Largest Cryptocurrency Heist in History
Context: Global cryptocurrency giant Binance has confirmed it suffered the largest cyber-attack in history, resulting in $6
Full Text:
Global cryptocurrency giant Binance has confirmed it suffered the largest cyber-attack in history, resulting in $6.3bn of cryptocurrency being stolen.

The Chinese-founded, Dubai-headquartered and Delaware-registered company said it has frozen $3bn of stolen funds and that it will cover all losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and company funds.

According to a company statement on October 30, its investigation suggested that an attacker's entry point may have been a compromised Binance development and operations (DevOps) engineer's laptop.

This allegedly allowed the attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.

However, Binance has since revised that assessment and said its subsequent investigation uncovered additional points of breach.

"This was a complex attack," the company said, adding that it was working with law enforcement, blockchain intelligence firms, token issuers and other industry partners to establish the full circumstances as well as identify and recover affected assets.

Binance has not yet provided a definitive account of the attack, saying it is still gathering the facts and will publish a comprehensive technical post-mortem once the investigation is complete.

The company has said it has found no evidence that any wallet private keys were leaked.

In its many updates on social media, the exchange has repeatedly stressed that customer funds remain safe, despite the scale of the incident. It has also promised to publish an updated proof of reserves once remediation work is complete, providing customers with an updated view of the assets held against user balances.

Three world-leading cryptocurrency analysis firms, TRM Labs, Elliptic and Chainalysis have attributed the attack with “high confidence” to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking group.

Title: Hackers leak personnel data of 41,000+ Homeland Security staff, including ICE and border agents
Context: More than half of the leaked records relate to US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) employees, typically found at airports, seaports, and land border crossings
Full Text:
More than 41,000 people working for the US Department of Homeland Security, including ICE agents, have had their details published online by a group of hacktivists.

As TechCrunch reports, the leaked records include the names, job titles, work email addresses, phone numbers, abd office locations.

More than half of the leaked records relate to US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) employees, typically found at airports, seaports, and land border crossings. Around 10,000 ICE employees have had their records breached, and almost 1,000 members of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

WIRED reports that the massive leak includes staff who work undercover, as well as in other sensitive areas such as those engaged in wiretapping and the interception of communications.

A hacktivist group calling itself "Department of Peace" says that the data was taken from an Okta single sign-on system that staff use to log onto the central network of the US Department of Homeland Security. Okta for its part says that it has not seen any evidence that its own systems have been compromised.

The data reveals which tools and services particularly individuals can access. Alongside everyday office software, these include Palantir's Falcon investigative platform, the phone and social media analysis tool PenLink, and Mobile Fortify, a facial recognition app used by immigration agents.

Explaining its justification for the data breach, "Department of Peace" wrote:

"They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs."

The leaked data has been published online, under the title "Icepick", and can be either downloaded via a torrent or accessed via a web interface - making it significantly easier for curious parties to search.

One threat intelligence expert told WIRED that, if authentic, the leaked data was "an extraordinarily valuable intelligence resource for those seeking to penetrate DHS," and could help adversaries identify vulnerable personnel or compromise ongoing investigations.

An obvious concern is that the leaked contact details could be used in phishing attacks that target employees, or could potentially put agents in physical danger. Clearly anyone whose details have been exposed through the incident would be wise to treat unexpected emails, texts, and phone calls with caution - and be particularly wary of any communications that claim to come from IT support or ask for a login to be approved.

Earlier this year the same group of hacktivists claimed to have breached the US Department of Homeland Security and accessed contracts between DHS, ICE, and more than 6000 firms including the likes of L3Harris, Raytheon, Palantir, Microsoft, and Oracle.

Explaining their motivation for that breach, the hackers referred to the killings of Alex Pretti and Renée Good by federal agents in Minneapolis.

"Why hack the DHS? I can think of a couple Pretti Good reasons! I'm releasing this because the DHS is killing us and people deserve to know which companies support them and what they're working on."

There has been a long string of cybersecurity incidents affecting US government personnel. For instance, in September the notorious ShinyHunters hacking group claimed to have stolen personal details related to nearly every employee of the FBI, and the records of millions of serving and former US military personnel were reportedly stolen from the Pentagon's human resources unit.

Title: Filter generation in practice: from algorithms to LLMs
Context: So, the first step is to discard the irrelevant fields and keep only those worth using in the filter
Full Text:
A modern organization protects its information systems with a whole suite of technologies that generate thousands of security alerts every day. Looking at these alerts in bulk, you’ll see that a significant share are false positives. Ideally, these alerts would be filtered out automatically so that analysts could focus on the ones that may point to a real incident. However, writing filters is a time-consuming task in itself. To create a correct filter, an analyst needs to:

Review the logs

Identify the source of the activity

Define filtering boundaries

Choose filtering criteria

Write a rule

Check that the filter is robust

This post looks at how filter creation itself can be automated to reduce analyst workload.

Filter validity criteria

In the context of security alerts, a filter is a combination of event field values that marks a detection as a false positive and not worth the analyst’s attention. Filters can be generated for any combination of event fields, but not every combination yields a valid filter. That’s why we need to define validity criteria: conditions showing that a specific filter actually removes noise and doesn’t suppress useful alerts.

Detection rules in security systems typically contain a set of conditions, and each of them can generate an alert. A specific event triggers a given fragment of a detection rule. The set of events that a given fragment responds to is what we’ll call its context. A good filter should cover the entire context where possible, without going beyond it. Filters that are too broad or too narrow are useless. For example, a filter based solely on PowerShell would exclude too many events, including some that deserve the analyst’s attention. Most of the filtered events would also be unrelated to the rule in question. A filter on a specific ID, on the other hand, would cover only one event, which may never recur.

Problems in filter generation

We can run into a number of problems when creating filters. First, events often contain an excessive number of fields (around 400 on average), and most of them aren’t needed for filtering. At the same time, generating and ranking combinations of these fields is also fairly resource-intensive. So, the first step is to discard the irrelevant fields and keep only those worth using in the filter. For example, out of 400 fields in an event, four may be enough for filtering.

Another problem is string normalization. Field values (for example, the path to the same application on different systems) can vary depending on system settings, user folder names, and so on. For a filter to account for all these variations, the strings must be normalized. For file paths, in particular, you can replace the drive letter and user folders with standard environment variables and convert all paths to a single case.

Finally, if a filter completely mirrors the query of a detection rule, it effectively disables that rule. To fix this, remove the event fields used in the detection rule from the filter. For example, if a rule triggers on a file path, there are two ways to filter out unwanted alerts:

In the filter, use fields other than the file path.

Use a part of the file path that the rule doesn’t use. For example, for the rule file_path: ".../something.exe", you can set up a filter that excludes events with the user/unique_files/ directory in the file path.

Filtering security alerts with an algorithm

Given the problems described above, automatically generating filters for security alerts should consist of the following steps:

An analyst receives a security alert that they assess as a false positive and uses the filter generator.

The generator takes the 400-field event from the alert, along with the rule that triggered on it, and determines the context.

The generator selects the fields that are relevant to the filter.

The generator normalizes the strings.

The generator builds different combinations of the selected fields. To do this, we applied the FP-Growth (frequent pattern growth) algorithm to the context determined earlier. FP Growth builds a tree of frequently occurring items (fields) from a dataset (in our case, the context) and discards items that aren’t frequent enough. This reduces the number of combinations to check, which lowers the cost of finding the most relevant ones.

The generator ranks the resulting combinations and offers the analyst the top three to choose from.

For example, consider an event described by the following JSON:

After generating and ranking the combinations, we got three filters based on file paths:

processcmdline:("nodejs\\node.exe" AND "*****\\appdata\\roaming\\npm\/node_modules\/pi-coding-agent\/dist\/cli.js")

file_path:"*****/.pi\\agent\\bin\\fd.exe"

processcmdline: "programfiles\\nodejs\\node.exe"

The last filter turned out to be too broad, but the analyst marked the other two as valid.

Pros and cons of the algorithmic approach

The algorithmic approach to filter generation has several advantages. First, it’s simple and deterministic: the same alert always produces the same result. Second, it’s interpretable, meaning we can see why a given combination ranked near the top of the list and why a particular field didn’t make it into the list of candidate fields at all. Third, the stages of the process are independent of each other, so individual steps can be improved and tuned without the risk of breaking the algorithm elsewhere. Finally, it has no external dependencies or models, which makes it easy to deploy in any customer environment.

However, it also has drawbacks. The first is its dependence on context. If there’s no context for some reason — for example, the rule’s first-ever trigger — a filter can’t be created. The second problem is string normalization. There’s a high chance of running into atypical cases that the normalization rules don’t cover. Often such cases can’t be described correctly at all, because they contradict each other.

These problems can be solved with large language models (LLMs). When an LLM generates the filters, no context is needed, because the LLM doesn’t iterate over or rank combinations. The LLM also takes a more flexible approach to string normalization, including non-standard cases. That said, an LLM doesn’t have to be involved at every stage of the generation process. We decided to keep the algorithmic solution where it works well. For example, a simple algorithm selects suitable fields without errors, so we didn’t move this stage to the model.

Filter generation with an LLM

The LLM-based filter generation looks like this:

The input is still an alert containing an event with 400 fields, plus the rule that triggered on that event. Then an algorithm selects the most suitable fields for the filter. Next, the LLM processes the input — the event, the selected fields, and the detection rule — and generates three filter options along with an explanation for them. The explanation helps the analyst understand why these particular filters were suggested and make an informed choice.

Consider the following event in JSON format:

The LLM suggested three filter options that all contain the same command line fragment:

file_path: "\\WindowsPowerShell\\powershell.exe" AND filecmdline: "Get-VM -Name kafka\*"

filecmdline: "Get-VM -Name kafka\*"

filecmdline: "kafka*"

As in the previous example, two of the three output filters were valid. The last one was too broad to be usable. The analyst chose the first filter with minor edits:

file_path: "powershell.exe" AND filecmdline: "Get-VM -Name kafka\*"

Pros and cons of generating filters with an LLM

Using an LLM solved the problems of purely algorithmic filter generation: dependence on context and errors in string normalization. However, the single-request approach had its own drawbacks. First, it had no output validation. The LLM returned filters as-is, with no syntax check and no way to correct errors. Second, unlike in the algorithmic version, all filter generation tasks were handled by a single system prompt. As a result, a minor fix in one place could break the logic in another.

Using multiple AI agents

To address the problems of generating filters with a single model and a single system prompt, we tried distributing the tasks across different LLM agents. In this version, we brought in agents as early as the stage of selecting relevant fields. The chain includes four agents in total:

Selector: selects the relevant fields.

Generator: generates filters.

Validator: evaluates the generated filters. If the filters are found to be invalid, it returns the task to the generator. If the selected fields are found to be irrelevant, it starts a new field selection cycle. If the filters pass validation, or the limit on regeneration attempts is reached, the valid filters (or the best ones available) are passed to the analyst.

Commentator: analyzes the output filters and explains which field values were used and why.

For the following JSON event, the agents produce three valid filters based on the file path.

The filters differ in the additional parameters that support the detection:

file_path:"sysvol\\domain\\scripts\\logon.bat"

file_path:"sysvol\\domain\\scripts\\logon.bat" AND file_md5:"0x7..6E"

autorun_entry: "Group Policy\\State" AND file_path: "SYSVOL\\domain\\scripts\\logon.bat"

Pros and cons of the agent-based approach

LLM agents give us a system that can validate and correct filters. Its modular architecture also lets us tune and improve different stages of generation independently. However, this approach makes more LLM calls than the previous ones, so the system is slower. It also depends on access to a model, which may not be available in the organization’s isolated environment.

Evaluating the filter generation system

To evaluate how well the filter generation system works, we use two main metrics:

Approval rate. For each security alert, the system suggests three filters. If the analyst selects at least one of them, we count the generation as successful. For example, in the case below, the approval rate is 2/3.

False positive reduction rate (FP drop). This metric shows how much a filter helps reduce the number of false positives. It can only be measured over time, because we need to compare the number of false positive alerts received during a set period before and after the filter is deployed.

Below is a comparison of the three filter generation approaches by these metrics:

As the results show, LLMs significantly improve the efficiency of filter generation. At the same time, the LLM agentless and agent-based approaches perform almost identically. So we chose the simpler and faster option: an LLM with a single system prompt. As a result, we cut false positives by 99%, increased the number of filters generated per day by 28%, and made analysts’ alert handling 17% more efficient.

Takeaways

Practice has shown that filter generation can be automated effectively. We’ve looked at several options for automatically generating filters for false-positive security alerts: a purely algorithmic approach, an LLM-based approach, and an approach built on a group of LLM agents. All of them can generate valid filters and make the analyst’s work much easier, but each has its own pros and cons.

The algorithmic approach scored lower on the evaluation metrics, but in two-thirds of cases, it still produces filters that satisfy the analyst. It works especially well when there’s already a set of similar events to filter out, meaning enough context has accumulated. The algorithmic generator can also be deployed in any environment. Both standalone LLM and multi-agent LLM approaches show high accuracy, and their results differ only slightly, so the slower agent-based approach looks excessive at this stage. If an LLM is available, the best option appears to be a single model that handles several stages of the generation cycle.

Title: Cursor Removes Malicious Claude Code 2.1.313 Extension From Its Marketplace
Context: The disclosure identifies the distribution source behind a malware report initially attributed to Open VSX, where Socket’s investigation found no corresponding publication or...
Full Text:
Cursor has confirmed that a malicious Claude Code extension labeled version 2.1.313 was available through its extension marketplace on October 29, potentially affecting up to 5,000 users. The disclosure identifies the distribution source behind a malware report initially attributed to Open VSX, where Socket’s investigation found no corresponding publication or removal records.

OpenSourceMalware initially reported that a malicious version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension, 2.1.313, was published to the Open VSX registry. The analysis, written by Paul McCarty, described an unpacked macOS extension containing code that adds an SSH authorized key, attempts to establish a reverse SSH tunnel, and installs persistence. That article has since been substantially revised and no longer identifies Open VSX as the affected distribution channel.

The report also stated: “The provenance of the analyzed directory is not established.” It acknowledged that its findings do not independently demonstrate a compromise of Anthropic’s official distribution infrastructure. Socket has not obtained and analyzed the reported artifact.

OpenSourceMalware co-founder Jenn Gile’s initial LinkedIn post identified npm and Microsoft’s VS Code Marketplace as affected distribution channels. Cursor later confirmed distribution through its own marketplace.

Socket continuously monitors npm, Open VSX, and the VS Code Marketplace and automatically ingests newly published packages and extensions. Our ingestion systems did not capture version 2.1.313 from any of those registries, prompting us to investigate whether it had been publicly available.

Our review of registry records and its own ingestion logs has found no evidence that Claude Code version 2.1.313 became publicly available through Open VSX during the period examined. The version is also absent from the npm package’s current version and publication-time records.

These findings challenge reports that a malicious official release was briefly distributed and then removed. Open VSX’s public change feed records the neighboring releases, including all eight platform builds of each, but contains no publication or removal event for 2.1.313 in the window we reviewed. Public distribution of the reported artifact remains unsubstantiated.

Open VSX Has No Publication Record for 2.1.313 #

Open VSX provides a registry changes feed designed to track versions becoming available, being deactivated, and being removed. Its append-only history is intended to retain events even after a version is deleted or purged.

We examined 3,392 returned events beginning October 27, 2026. The latest event in that completed review was timestamped October 30 at 05:35:23 UTC. The results included:

ACTIVE events for all eight platform builds of 2.1.312.

ACTIVE events for all eight platform builds of 2.1.314.

No events for 2.1.313.

Under the documented behavior, a version becoming publicly available and subsequently being removed should leave a history. Its absence weighs against the explanation that 2.1.313 was simply published and quickly pulled.

Between October 27 and October 30 at 05:35 UTC, the same feed recorded 42 versions across 21 other extensions that were published and subsequently removed. Every version retained both events, including one removed approximately 90 seconds after publication. No corresponding publication or removal event appeared for Claude Code 2.1.313.

These observed removals show that even briefly available versions ordinarily leave a record. We found no such record for 2.1.313. Polling alone cannot exclude every short-lived event, which is why the registry’s retained change history is significant.

npm records also skip 2.1.313

We queried the npm registry metadata for @anthropic-ai/claude-code. Version 2.1.313 was absent from both the versions object and the time map.

npm’s metadata retains publication timestamps for unpublished versions in the package’s time record. For example, the malicious Axios releases 1.14.1 and 0.30.4 were removed following the March 2026 compromise, but their publication timestamps remain visible:

npm view axios time --json | grep -E '"(1\.14\.1|0\.30\.4)"'

The absence of 2.1.313 from Claude Code’s time record therefore weighs against the explanation that it was published to npm and quickly removed.

The adjacent entries were:

Version

Publication time in UTC

2.1.312

October 27, 2026, 18:36:10

2.1.314

October 30, 2026, 00:12:56

This provides no support for a malicious npm release at 2.1.313. We are not treating absence from the current registry response as an absolute guarantee that no administrative action or attempted publication occurred.

The public GitHub releases and changelog likewise skip 2.1.313. The 2.1.314 changelog we reviewed contains no explanation of the missing version or notice of this reported incident.

A skipped number is not, by itself, evidence of a security event. Within the range 2.1.260 through 2.1.314, the current npm and Open VSX catalogs also omit 2.1.262, 2.1.264, 2.1.279, 2.1.297, and 2.1.298. Those gaps do not establish what happened to any particular build.

The screenshot does not establish the download history #

The initial report’s screenshot shows 2.1.313 selected as latest, with a “Published 3 hours ago” label. The post displays a cropped version; the full-size original also shows the "Target Platforms" panel. It displays Linux and Windows download sizesthat match the public 2.1.314 builds at the displayed precision.

Platform

Screenshot labeled 2.1.313

Public 2.1.314 build

Linux x64

135.13 MB

Windows x64

136.07 MB

We checked these against the 2.1.314 registry metadata and download lengths. Open VSX’s interface rounds file sizes to two decimal places, so matching displayed sizes do not prove identical files or screenshot manipulation. The analyzed sample is also described as a macOS build, while the fully visible sizes above concern other platforms.

Screenshot published by OpenSourceMalware showing Claude Code 2.1.313 labeled as the latest release on Open VSX. Its displayed Linux and Windows download sizes match version 2.1.314.

The relative publication label does not establish three hours of continuous public availability. Open VSX distinguishes a version’s original timestamp from its availability transitions.

The screenshot raised questions about whether it documented an actual public listing. It shows 2.1.313 as the latest release, but its displayed Linux and Windows download sizes match 2.1.314, and we found no corresponding publication event in Open VSX’s change feed. These discrepancies led us to suspect the image was edited or created for illustrative purposes. It has since been removed.

Cursor Publishes Remediation Guidance #

Cursor’s security notice identifies the affected version, provides hashes for the malicious macOS and Windows packages, and includes indicators of compromise and remediation scripts. Cursor says it removed the extension, rebuilt its marketplace after rotating keys, and worked with the hosting provider to take the attacker’s server offline. It is contacting affected users directly.

For organizations assessing exposure, the key question is whether developers installed or updated the extension through Cursor’s marketplace during the affected window. Socket’s investigation found no corresponding publication or removal records for 2.1.313 in Open VSX, and no entry in npm’s publication history. Cursor’s confirmation establishes a separate distribution path and gives security teams a specific marketplace, version, and installation window to investigate.

Context: [2] While Darktrace has not observed direct evidence of CVE-2026-109618 or CVE-2026-109619 exploitation, on October 21st we observed a six-month high in detections consistent...
Full Text:
The disclosure of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 placed immediate pressure on organizations running PHP. Both vulnerabilities can allow unauthenticated remote code execution, including in products and appliances where PHP is embedded, and updates depend on third-party vendors [1].

Early guidance focused on patching internet-facing systems and monitoring for behavior associated with successful exploitation, including unexpected command execution, Webroot changes and outbound connections from PHP servers.

Darktrace observed widespread scanning across monitored environments involving hundreds of distinct source IP addresses that public reporting has associated with activity targeting the PHP vulnerabilities. The volume of scanning was significantly greater than the evidence available for successful exploitation. For analysts, that distinction is important. Scanning demonstrates interest in exposed infrastructure; establishing compromise requires evidence of subsequent behavior on the targeted system, including command execution, file modification or unexpected outbound communication.

PHP is not an isolated example. Imperva subsequently demonstrated remote code execution against a vulnerable Node.js build through malicious Brotli data, reproducing execution through compressed HTTP responses and configured request parsers. The same inputs were rejected by the patched runtime. Imperva linked its Node2Shell and PHP2Shell research to the increasing speed of vulnerability discovery and exploit development. [2]

While Darktrace has not observed direct evidence of CVE-2026-109618 or CVE-2026-109619 exploitation, on October 21st we observed a six-month high in detections consistent with zero-day exploitation activity, representing a 64% increase compared to historic data. This increase has not been confirmed as related to the PHP vulnerabilities. Darktrace’s behavioral approach is designed to detect anomalous activity without relying solely on rules written for a specific exploit. Comparable increases were observed around the Log4j disclosure and other globally significant vulnerability disclosures.

AI-assisted vulnerability research

The PHP disclosure arrives as AI systems have become more capable at vulnerability research [3]. OpenAI launched Daybreak in June 2026, combining GPT-5.5-Cyber, Codex Security and partnerships with security researchers and software maintainers. OpenAI says its models have been applied to discovering and generating patches for vulnerabilities in browsers, network infrastructure, FreeBSD and the Linux kernel. Darktrace joined the OpenAI Daybreak Cyber Partner Program in June to explore how OpenAI's cyber capabilities could be integrated within Darktrace products and services [4][10].

OpenAI reported in August that Codex Security Cloud had analyzed more than 30 million commits across more than 30,000 codebases. According to OpenAI, Cloudflare uses models accessed through Daybreak to investigate customer-authorized code and combines findings with live traffic and security signals to assess whether affected routes are active or receiving suspicious traffic, with proposed mitigations and patches remaining subject to customer review [5][6].

Faster discovery still leaves defenders with the work of locating affected software, testing fixes and completing remediation. The PHP case shows that gap clearly, particularly when vulnerable runtimes are embedded inside other products.

Enterprise agents as an attack surface

Darktrace Signal Labs has also examined how a trusted enterprise agent could be abused after an attacker has already obtained access to an environment. In a controlled simulation, researchers demonstrated that, in that post-compromise scenario, the Claude platform’s memory stores feature could be abused to establish a live C2 channel between an external operator and internal Claude Code agents. The external operator was able to dynamically assign network discovery, credential access, and data exfiltration tasks to the agents via this C2 channel. Detection of the agents’ activities relied on the correlation of process creation and network traffic activity from agent harness processes, alongside behavioral analysis to identify deviations from expected behavior. Darktrace has not claimed it observed this memory-store command-and-control technique in operational attacks [7].

AI-assisted attacks in Japan

Evidence from Japan indicates AI being used for vulnerability scanning and attacks outside controlled research. On 21 October, JPCERT/CC published findings from an investigation into recent unauthorized access incidents affecting organizations in Japan. JPCERT/CC states that it confirmed attackers had used AI to scan for known vulnerabilities and conduct attacks through APIs. According to JPCERT/CC, its examination of attack infrastructure found evidence of Android application analysis, API discovery and testing for weaknesses including server-side request forgery, and the infrastructure also targeted services intended for users outside Japan [8].

JPCERT/CC does not identify ARTEX by name in that publication. The named ARTEX attribution comes from separate investigations, including Microsoft's analysis of Storm-0940.

AI in offensive operations

Microsoft describes ARTEX as an open-source, multi-agent penetration-testing system capable of automating activity with limited human interaction. Microsoft reported that Storm-0940, which it assesses to be a China state-aligned actor active since 2021, used ARTEX against hundreds of organizations, and Microsoft attributed the ConnectWise supply-chain compromise [9].

Microsoft observed ARTEX accelerating scanning, reconnaissance, password spraying and OAuth application abuse. Several ARTEX-driven operations reached privileged cloud access less than three hours after initial targeting. Following the ConnectWise compromise, Storm-0940 attempted to authenticate to more than 2,250 tenants at rates of up to 2,900 attempts per minute [9].

Darktrace Threat Research found activity in its own telemetry involving infrastructure later associated with the campaign. On 13 October, Darktrace recorded failed authentication activity involving 144.172.64[.]128, one of the addresses Microsoft later identified as performing sign-ins and Microsoft Graph activity in ConnectWise customer environments. Darktrace analysis identified 65 failed authentication attempts in around 20 minutes.

The telemetry establishes repeated failed authentication from infrastructure later associated with the campaign. It does not establish ARTEX execution or successful compromise. At the time of observation, Microsoft's later attribution was unavailable. Analysts therefore had the behavior itself: repeated failed authentication from the same source over a short period, together with any related identity, application or network activity inside the environment.

Microsoft documented a wider password-spray campaign against 327 accounts across eight organizations between 10 and 14 October. It recorded more than 151,000 failed logons, including more than 111,000 on 11 October, but no successful authentication, token issuance, Graph call or directory change from that campaign. Microsoft also reported that most Storm-0940 targeting was unsuccessful [9].

Where the actor progressed beyond authentication, Microsoft observed service-principal sign-ins followed by Graph and directory operations. Activity included reconnaissance, application credential changes and attempts to modify privileges. Microsoft recommends correlating service-principal sign-ins with Graph activity, directory changes and resource access [9].

Behavior before attribution

The PHP and ARTEX cases begin with different information. PHP defenders knew which software required urgent remediation but initially had limited information about exploitation. Process execution, file modification and outbound communication could still provide evidence of compromise.

The PHP and ARTEX observations also illustrate the difference between volume and impact. Darktrace observed broad scanning around the PHP disclosure, while the ARTEX-associated infrastructure produced concentrated authentication activity. Neither observation independently demonstrates compromise and in each case examining the behavior that follows the initial interaction is the investigative clue.

The Darktrace ARTEX-related observation began with authentication behavior. Microsoft publicly attributed the source infrastructure eight days later. That attribution added context, but it did not change what had originally been recorded in the environment.

AI is now present at several points in this cycle. Daybreak applies models to vulnerability discovery and remediation. Darktrace Signal Labs demonstrated how a trusted enterprise agent could be co-opted in a controlled environment. JPCERT/CC confirmed AI-assisted vulnerability scanning and API attacks in recent incidents. Microsoft documented ARTEX being used by Storm-0940 in active operations [4][7][8][9].

Microsoft's findings also show why scale and impact must be assessed separately. One ARTEX-associated campaign produced more than 151,000 failed logons without successful access, while other operations reached privileged cloud access in less than three hours. Security teams have to distinguish high-volume attempts from activity that progresses through authentication, privilege changes and resource access.

The evidence required to assess these cases remains familiar: authentication records, process execution, application and directory changes, file activity and network communication. AI can increase the rate at which those behaviors occur. Defenders still need to establish their sequence and impact.

Title: A leak in the chain of command.
Context: Cisco has patched an actively exploited zero-day vulnerability affecting its ASA and Firepower Threat Defense firewall software. CISA warns that attackers are exploiting a VMware ESXi vulnerability that allows administrators to perform certain operations without generating audit logs.
Full Text:
DHS suffers a massive data leak. Researchers reveal Volt Typhoon’s sophisticated methods. Cisco patches a firewall zero-day. A suspected coordinated supply chain attack targets public GitHub repositories. Online scams overtake phishing. NIST shares post-quantum cryptography guidance. CISA warns a VMware ESXi vulnerability is under active exploitation. The Federal Election Commission takes systems offline. A Ukrainian national gets prison time for ransomware operations. Our guest is Yonald Chery, CTO from Technology Advancement Center (TAC), discussing securing operational technology in our critical infrastructure. Bitcoin mining gets you in hot water.

Today is Thursday October 29th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

DHS suffers a massive data leak.

A massive leak of Department of Homeland Security records has exposed information on more than 41,000 employees and contractors, potentially providing adversaries with a detailed roadmap of the department’s operations.

The archive, dubbed “Icepick,” was published by transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets. It reportedly contains data from DHS’s Okta identity management system, including employee contact information, reporting relationships, and access permissions for sensitive systems.

WIRED’s analysis identified references to undercover operations, surveillance programs, facial recognition tools, and investigative platforms. The records cover roughly one-seventh of DHS’s workforce, including thousands of ICE and Customs and Border Protection personnel.

Security experts warn the information could facilitate targeted phishing, impersonation, and intelligence gathering, particularly when combined with other leaked datasets.

DHS says it’s investigating a potential breach. Okta maintains its systems were not compromised.

The hackers, calling themselves the Department of Peace, framed the release as an act of government accountability.

Researchers reveal Volt Typhoon’s sophisticated methods.

For years, U.S. officials have warned that China’s Volt Typhoon hacking group poses an extraordinary threat to American critical infrastructure. Now, researchers are revealing the sophisticated methods behind those warnings.

As Kim Zetter writes in her Zero Day newsletter, Lumen Technologies’ Black Lotus Labs has uncovered what it calls Silent Train, a covert network of compromised routers, servers, and internet-connected devices that Volt Typhoon uses to infiltrate sensitive American networks.

The attackers construct elaborate chains of compromised devices, sometimes in less than two minutes, routing their activity through multiple countries before reaching their targets. Each chain is typically used for a single intrusion, then dismantled. The hackers erase logs, remove evidence, and disappear, sometimes after spending just minutes inside a network.

Researchers tracked more than 27 classes of compromised devices and identified at least four exploited zero-day vulnerabilities.

The targets include government agencies, defense contractors, telecommunications providers, military research institutions, and operators of energy, water, and transportation infrastructure.

Many victims are concentrated in Hawaii, California, and Texas, locations strategically important to U.S. military operations in the Indo-Pacific.

Researchers believe the campaign combines espionage with preparations for potential disruption during a conflict involving Taiwan. They’ve observed attackers stealing military-related documents, mapping networks, and collecting credentials that could provide future access.

And that access can persist long after the initial intrusion. Volt Typhoon sometimes returns weeks later using stolen credentials and entirely new routes.

The result is a carefully maintained network of potential access points into critical American systems, built to remain largely invisible until the attackers decide they need it.

Cisco patches a firewall zero-day.

Cisco has patched an actively exploited zero-day vulnerability affecting its ASA and Firepower Threat Defense firewall software. The high-severity flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-76418, allows unauthenticated attackers to remotely crash vulnerable devices with SSL VPN enabled, causing unexpected reboots and service disruptions. Cisco confirmed exploitation earlier this month but hasn’t identified the attackers or their targets. The company urges customers to install security updates immediately. Administrators unable to patch can mitigate the vulnerability by disabling secondary authentication on affected VPN tunnel groups.

A suspected coordinated supply chain attack targets public GitHub repositories.

Radware researchers have uncovered a suspected coordinated supply chain attack targeting 61 public GitHub repositories, including projects from Google, Brave, and Trivy. They identified 83 malicious submissions, most posted within just 43 minutes, using 74 GitHub accounts, many potentially compromised.

The attacker concealed malicious commands inside HTML comments in issues and pull requests. When vulnerable CI/CD workflows processed that content, the commands could execute automatically, attempting to steal environment variables, credentials, and access tokens.

Researchers confirmed malicious command execution in two cases but found no definitive evidence of stolen repository permissions or compromised downstream software.

The suspected objective was to gain access to repositories and potentially distribute malicious code through trusted open source projects.

Researchers recommend restricting workflow permissions and treating externally submitted content as untrusted.

Online scams overtake phishing.

Online scam detections doubled over the past year, overtaking phishing for the first time, according to Akamai’s latest State of the Internet report. Researchers recorded 6.4 million scams during the second quarter of 2026, including fraudulent stores, investment schemes, and payment scams.

Phishing also increased 61%, with AI helping criminals create convincing lures and launch shorter, more agile campaigns.

Meanwhile, a separate report from the Identity Theft Resource Center highlights the devastating human consequences. More than 80% of surveyed U.S. scam victims reported suicidal thoughts, while nearly nine in ten who sought institutional assistance received no response.

Many victims subsequently paid supposed recovery services, potentially exposing themselves to further fraud.

The findings illustrate both the growing industrialization of online scams and the troubling lack of support for their victims.

NIST shares post-quantum cryptography guidance.

NIST has released guidance to help federal agencies meet deadlines for transitioning sensitive systems to post-quantum cryptography. Under a June executive order, agencies must adopt quantum-resistant key establishment by the end of 2030 and digital signatures by the end of 2031. The guidance recommends prioritizing sensitive, long-lived data vulnerable to future quantum decryption, while allowing hybrid encryption approaches for particularly critical systems. NIST also urges agencies to assess their cryptographic supply chains, warning that meeting the deadlines will require immediate, coordinated action.

CISA warns a VMware ESXi vulnerability is under active exploitation.

CISA warns that attackers are exploiting a VMware ESXi vulnerability that allows administrators to perform certain operations without generating audit logs. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-41709, has been added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. CrowdStrike attributes earlier exploitation to the China-linked group Warp Panda, which reportedly used the zero-day to conceal activity during intrusions targeting U.S. organizations, including law firms. Despite its low severity rating, the vulnerability can significantly hamper forensic investigations. Federal agencies have two weeks to apply patches.

The Federal Election Commission takes systems offline.

The Federal Election Commission has taken several systems offline following reports of an attempted cyberattack, just days before the U.S. midterm elections.

The disruption affects electronic filing, campaign finance searches, and reporting tools, preventing organizations from submitting required disclosures detailing political spending. The FEC says it has identified an issue and is implementing a fix, but several services remain unavailable.

The timing is particularly sensitive, with record amounts of money flowing into congressional campaigns. Security experts warn that interruptions to financial disclosures could undermine transparency and public confidence.

Importantly, the FEC regulates campaign finance but does not administer elections. The incident has no direct impact on voting systems or how ballots are cast.

The agency says it’s working to restore services.

A Ukrainian national gets prison time for ransomware operations.

A Ukrainian national has been sentenced to nearly six years in a U.S. prison for his role in the Nefilim and Hive ransomware operations. Thirty-six-year-old Artem Stryzhak pleaded guilty to participating in attacks that encrypted victims’ systems and demanded ransom payments, including attacks against healthcare organizations during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Stryzhak joined Nefilim in 2021, agreeing to surrender 20% of his ransom proceeds in exchange for access to its malware. He later became an early Hive affiliate, participating in attacks against seven organizations, including healthcare providers and law firms.

The FBI helped one victim recover its files without paying.

Authorities are still searching for alleged Nefilim administrator Volodymyr Tymoshchuk. The State Department is offering up to $11 million for information leading to his arrest, conviction, or location.

Bitcoin mining gets you in hot water.

A company that previously turned space heaters into bitcoin miners now wants to bring cryptocurrency into your shower.

Heatbit has introduced Bitwater, an $899 replacement heating element that uses twenty bitcoin-mining chips to heat household water while generating cryptocurrency.

The idea is straightforward: Bitcoin mining produces heat, so why not put that heat to work? The company says Bitwater fits many conventional electric water heaters, operates without noisy fans, and sends mining proceeds directly to the homeowner.

The economics, however, are a little less refreshing.

A conventional heating element costs less than $30. Heatbit has shared estimates suggesting mining could generate roughly a dollar a day, potentially recovering the premium in about three years. But those returns depend on volatile cryptocurrency economics, hardware longevity, and household hot-water demand.

Shipments are planned for early 2027.

Our return on investment desk reports it would take over three hundred years of bitcoin mining to break even.

Whether Bitwater ultimately saves money remains uncertain. But at least your morning shower might finally contribute to your retirement portfolio.

Welcome to this week’s edition of the Threat Source newsletter.

“The darkest period of my life, so far, arrived the summer I was pregnant with my eldest son. The future was growing in me with all of its terrifying unpredictability, and I found myself anxious, unable to work and woefully at sea.” — Lauren Groff

I doubt Lauren had this maniacal infosec news cycle in mind when she wrote about the terrifyingly unpredictable future, but honestly, she’s got our current careers down cold. Let he who is not woefully at sea cast the first water balloon? I’ll work on it. Here we are with PHP taking up every available ounce of oxygen, Node.js adding its own spice to the sauce... and here’s me, staring my screen blankly, waiting for an original thought to leak out and onto this page. Not to worry, none have. There is simply nothing novel to say because the entire internet has it covered. In triplicate. With graphs and compelling statistics and AI-generated evil bad guy images galore.

These vulnerabilities are serious, and the remediations matter. Teams need to know what they run, find the affected systems, and get them patched and determine ways to secure systems that can’t be patched. I’m simply not going to add another dramatic headline to the stack or pretend there’s a clever new angle hiding in the margins. The thing I keep looping on is that the work underneath the headlines is familiar and it’s the real story. To defend your environment, you need a team that knows that environment, has enough time and expertise to investigate the telemetry, that can tell an anomaly from the usual benign noise, and take action. Yes, the right tools help, and without them you can’t do it — but the people doing the work are still what make those tools useful.

Give smart people enough room to do smart people stuff. This is the entire ballgame. Read it again: Give smart people enough room to do smart people stuff. Because a good response starts way before the headline. Know what you own, who owns it, what version is running, whether it can be reached from the internet, what identities can do what task on the device, etc. When a fix is available, make sure it actually reaches the system you meant to fix. If a system cannot be updated yet, give that exception an owner and a deadline. Reduce its exposure, add monitoring, and keep checking until the fix is in place. “We’ll get to it” is not a plan.

So, there may be nothing new to say about PHP this week, but the work is still worth talking about: Know your environment, take care of your team members, and keep paying attention when the weird thing stops being weird and starts becoming evidence. When the next headline arrives, help your teammate do the same.

“The only thing that makes life possible is permanent, intolerable uncertainty: not knowing what comes next.” — Ursula K. Le Guin

The one big thing

Cisco Talos has recently discovered "NIK C2," a new command-and-control framework that integrates AI directly into its attack chain. This Go-based Windows implant allows adversaries to dump credentials, stream keystrokes, and deploy screen-locking ransomware. It also uses an integrated OpenAI model to analyze harvested data on the fly. By hijacking the victim's own API keys to fund these requests, NIK C2 collapses data collection and exploitation into a single, continuous session.

Why do I care?

By embedding a live AI pipeline directly into the C2 loop, NIK C2 turns a compromised host into an active operational asset rather than a passive foothold. Because it processes data and generates context-aware payloads locally, it erases the offline processing delays that historically gave defenders a critical detection window. Furthermore, by piggybacking on the victim's OpenAI account, threat actors completely mask their infrastructure, leaving no attributable trace and complicating incident response.

So now what?

Defenders must embrace continuous behavioral vigilance. Ensure endpoint solutions monitor for unusual local proxy routing, unexpected PowerShell executions, and unauthorized access to browser databases or crypto wallets. Update your defenses using the ClamAV signature and indicators of compromise (IOCs) provided in the full blog.

Title: NIK C2 Malware Can Use Victims’ OpenAI Keys for AI Queries
Context: Talos said NIK C2 reshapes adversary tradecraft "by collapsing collection and exploitation into a single continuous session, effectively erasing the offline processing delays...
Full Text:
A new AI-enabled malware framework has been found that can fall back on victims' own OpenAI API keys for artificial intelligence requests, charging the usage to the victim while obscuring who made the requests.

Cisco Talos observed the command-and-control (C2) framework, dubbed NIK C2, in the wild, according to research published on October 29.

Its Go-based implant gave attackers remote access, credential theft, keylogging and surveillance capabilities, while an integrated OpenAI client let them send stolen data for AI analysis within the compromised session.

NIK C2 Routes AI Requests Through Victim Machines

The AI capability is built into the implant rather than requiring operators to process collected information separately. Talos said attackers could supply a prompt and model choice through the C2 panel, with the implant sending the request to OpenAI from the victim's machine and returning the response to the operator.

If the operator supplied no key, the malware read an OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable on the infected machine instead, which Talos called a deliberate design. An organization with an OpenAI API key configured on a compromised Windows system could therefore end up funding the attacker's AI requests.

Read more on AI API key abuse: Attackers Steal METR API Key and Burn $600,000 in AI Credits

Talos said OpenAI's billing system would charge the victim's payment method and its access logs would show the victim's key as the one making the requests, leaving no trace attributable to the attacker.

Malware Framework Combines Theft and Ransomware

Beyond its AI functionality, the Windows malware supported more than 52 commands covering credential theft, browser data collection, cryptocurrency wallets, Wi-Fi credentials, keylogging, screen capture and remote access. Talos said it also offered lateral movement and multiple defense-evasion capabilities.

The framework also contained a screen-locking ransomware module that displayed customized ransom demands in Bitcoin or the Tether stablecoin (USDT). Talos said the module encrypted no files, leaving no forensic trail of file-modification timestamps or encryption markers, and that a screen lock is considerably faster to deploy than file-encrypting ransomware.

The company said it observed at least three versions of the implant and found its infrastructure active during the research. That led it to assess with moderate confidence that NIK C2 is a fully functional framework rather than a proof of concept.

Talos said NIK C2 reshapes adversary tradecraft "by collapsing collection and exploitation into a single continuous session, effectively erasing the offline processing delays that historically granted defenders critical detection windows."
