Title: Threats Hidden in Replies: Threat Actors Deliver Malware and Credential Phishing in Email Threads
Context: By: Intelligence Team, Kahng An Recently, threat actors have been increasingly delivering malware or credential phishing attacks at the end of long email threads designed to...
Full Text:
By: Intelligence Team, Kahng An

Recently, threat actors have been increasingly delivering malware or credential phishing attacks at the end of long email threads designed to exploit a potential victim’s trust in an email contact. In this tactic, threat actors deliver malicious payloads at the end of seemingly normal email conversations after gaining the potential victim’s trust. These kinds of attacks, also known as email thread hijacking, exploit the recipient’s trust in the sender after several legitimate emails. Often these are legitimate email threads that threat actors respond to when accessing compromised email accounts. However, they can also be email threads intentionally started by the threat actor. In these latter cases, the emails start off as seemingly harmless messages that are used to build trust with a potential victim before delivering a malicious threat. While Cofense Intelligence has been tracking these campaigns as response-themed emails, the actual malicious email at the end of the thread is usually similar to simpler meeting invitation, document, or shared file-themed emails. As such, properly trained and aware recipients should be able to spot these threats that are embedded at the end of a conversation. This report is a high-level overview of some recent response-themed emails and some common campaign patterns to be aware of.

Key Points

Threat actors have been found delivering malware or credential phishing attacks as replies to email threads. These email replies can be found in both existing legitimate email threads and ones started by the threat actor.

Cofense Intelligence tracks these campaigns as response-themed Active Threat Reports (ATR), which outline the campaign’s spoofed brands, subject lines, and resulting malicious payloads.

Response-themed ATRs focus on IOCs (indicators of compromise) from the final malicious reply in an email thread.

Response-themed emails can be difficult to filter against because they are found within email threads that contain mostly non-malicious messages. Traditional email security solutions may trust long threads of seemingly legitimate emails and fail to block the final malicious payload.

Malware delivery was the predominant threat in Q1 2026 with 83.3% of response-themed ATRs being malware ATRs, but credential phishing was more prevalent in Q2 and Q3 2026 with 62.5% and 92.1% of total response-themed ATR volume in those quarters.

While response-themed emails have been increasing in popularity this year, response-themed emails are not a completely new tactic. They were previously seen in similar volume in Q1 2024 though were rarely seen by Cofense Intelligence throughout all the latter half of 2024 and almost all of 2025.

What Are Response-Themed Emails?

Cofense Intelligence tracks response-themed emails as any malicious emails that appear to be, or actually are, a reply to an email thread. These kinds of threats are notable because the vast majority of malicious emails are messages that are not contained within a thread. By delivering malware or phishing sites within replies to an email thread, threat actors are able to abuse pre-established trust that was formed over a series of seemingly legitimate back-and-forth messages. The ultimate goal of response-themed email campaigns is to establish a higher level of trust with a potential victim over a series of message replies (or abuse already established trust from a pre-existing email thread) and betray that trust with a standard malicious email lure. In short, response-themed emails are not necessarily any different from the typical malicious email except for this additional abuse of trust and the amount of time the threat actor devotes to developing this trust.

While the concept may seem basic, response-themed emails tend to be rarer compared to most other email themes. This is largely because replying within email threads requires a threat actor to either opportunistically use an existing email chain within a compromised account or intentionally target potential victims with seemingly legitimate email correspondence. These factors lead response-themed campaigns to be rarer and generally more targeted. Figure 1 shows the frequency of response-themed ATRs from Q1 2024 to Q3 2026.

Figure 1: Frequency of response-themed ATRs from Q1 2024 to Q3 2026.

The recent volume of response-themed emails is not unprecedented. Q1 2024 saw a similar amount of total response-themed email campaign volume to what was seen in Q2 2026. However, the majority of campaign threats during this time were credential phishing attacks instead of malware delivery. Response-themed emails quickly plummeted in volume after Q1 2024 and were not seen in any substantial volume until Q1 2026. From there, the quarterly volume of response-themed malware ATRs has remained relatively stable until Q3 2026, while the amount of credential phishing ATRs has continuously skyrocketed in Q2 and Q3 2026.

Campaign Characteristics

Generally, response-themed emails are only distinguished by the fact that they are malicious emails within email threads. While these kinds of campaigns may be more deceptive than most due to the social engineering aspects of building trust over multiple legitimate interactions, the lures themselves still use many common techniques from other email themes. For example, Figure 2 shows a campaign that resulted in a response that sends a meeting invitation link that actually delivers GoTo RAT, a legitimate remote access tool that is a part of the LogMeIn management suite and is frequently abused by threat actors as a remote access trojan.

Figure 2: ATR 416570 contains a response to a long email thread with a sudden invitation to a meeting. However, the embedded link to the purported meeting site delivers GoTo RAT instead. This figure shows only the final reply, which contains the malicious link. The preceding thread has been omitted for length.

Similarly, message notification lures are also commonly seen within response-themed campaigns. Figure 3 shows a secure message notification-themed email that contains an embedded link to a purported message center. However, the site then requests verification to open the secure message by either accessing a Microsoft account credential phishing site or downloading ConnectWise RAT, a legitimate remote access tool also known as ConnectWise ScreenConnect that is currently one of the most frequently abused by threat actors as a remote access trojan.

Figure 3: ATR 418145 contains a response to an email thread with a secure message notification. The embedded link directs to either a Microsoft-spoofing credential phishing site or a ConnectWise RAT download. This figure shows only the final reply, which contains the malicious link. The preceding thread has been omitted for length.

Conclusions

The cause for concern with these campaigns is not necessarily the malware or credential phishing payloads but the way the threat actors build up trust through legitimate emails. Response-themed emails, by their very nature of being within seemingly harmless email threads, seek to gain a potential victim’s trust through social engineering techniques. Compromised email accounts can be used to send links to supposed “important documents” that actually lead to a credential phishing attack. Threat actors can email a potential victim with harmless messages over the span of several hours or even days before attempting to send a “meeting invite” that downloads malware. In both of these cases, the threat actors are relying on betraying trust that was built up via an existing credible name or a series of seemingly normal interactions.

Thankfully, writing email replies still takes more effort from the threat actor than simply spamming out hundreds or thousands of similarly structured email templates across a list of victims. If written to a legitimate email chain, these would require access to a compromised email account that happens to have an email thread. The threat actor would then need to write a response with a hook that would be relevant to the thread (such as a meeting invitation). If the threat actor wants to start the email thread, then they would need to wait for a potential victim to respond and write replies to them. While email responses can be automated through generative AI solutions, allowing this campaign pattern to be scaled up to a broader potential attack surface, response-themed campaigns are generally limited to being highly targeted in nature, whether through opportunistically replying to existing threads in compromised email inboxes or creating new threads from scratch. These factors make response-themed emails rare compared to other campaign types.

For leadership, the core message is straightforward: a trusted sender and a familiar email thread are not necessarily proof that a message is safe. These kinds of attack patterns highlight the importance of carefully reading and assessing emails for potential threats, even within established email threads with known contacts. Any message within a thread may contain a malicious threat, so recipients should always stay aware of potentially manipulative messages that may be delivering unknown links, strange attachments, or other potential threats. A message that asks you to click a link, open an attachment, or log in deserves a second look no matter whose name is on it.

Mitigations

While traditional email security detections based off trusted senders, established contacts, and other known good signals may fail to filter these kinds of campaigns, email security solutions that continuously scan for suspect behavior and analyze malicious links and attachments in a sandbox environment may be the most reliable way of filtering these attacks. In particular, behavioral detections that flag sudden geographic shifts from the sender and potentially malicious requests may be better at handling this attack pattern.

Ultimately, the best defense against these kinds of attacks is training and awareness of potential email threats. While these campaigns feature their malicious payloads within email thread replies, they often include common phishing lures such as meeting invitations or documents that need to be reviewed. The only major difference is that response-themed emails can be more targeted and tailored to a potential victim based on responses within the thread and the amount of time involved in establishing and then exploiting trust. However, once the malicious email is sent, it will invariably be similar to what most malicious emails look like. With proper training and awareness of common email phishing techniques, recipients should be able to recognize potentially suspect emails. However, the real challenge is applying constant vigilance with familiar contacts or otherwise harmless emails. When receiving potentially malicious emails, consider validating the contents of the email out-of-band with the sender, especially if they are a known and trusted contact. While doing so, be sure to rely on contact information gathered from outside of the email itself because threat actors can also easily modify signature blocks as a part of their attack.

When developing better preventative measures against these attacks, consider implementing the following as a part of training and standard security operations:

Update employee security awareness training to reflect how these campaigns actually arrive: as replies inside existing email threads, often from a known contact whose account has been compromised, ending in a meeting invitation, a shared document or file link, or a secure message notification. Employees trained on real, current threats are more likely to pause before clicking, even when the message comes from a familiar name. Simulation exercises should reproduce this exact pattern, a malicious reply within an ongoing thread, rather than outdated generic examples.

Establish and enforce a software allowlist for remote access tools. Response-themed campaigns frequently deliver legitimate remote access tools that have been repurposed as malware, including ConnectWise RAT. Any remote access tool not on the approved list should be blocked from installing on corporate devices. Organizations without an allowlist should at minimum block the digital certificates associated with remote access tools they do not use.

Deploy enterprise password managers. When an employee follows a malicious reply to a credential phishing page, the password manager will refuse to fill credentials because the domain does not match the legitimate service. This gives a structural catch that works no matter how convincing the branding or how trusted the thread appears, and it complements employee training rather than replacing it.

Deploy email security that looks for behavioral anomalies inside otherwise trusted threads, rather than relying on sender reputation alone. Because these emails often come from legitimate or compromised accounts, the sending domain is frequently valid, so brand and domain mismatch checks catch little. Signals that do help include a known sender suddenly sending from an unusual location, or a long-running thread that abruptly introduces a link or attachment.

Use tools and software provided by Cofense such as Triage and Vision to prevent initial access and stop follow-on attacks. Triage gives security teams an in-depth breakdown of a reported phishing email, which makes a malicious reply buried in a legitimate thread easier to analyze and act on. Vision uses human insight and AI precision to quarantine and remove malicious emails from inboxes, including messages that reached users from a trusted or compromised sender.

Give employees a simple, one-click way to report suspicious emails, which is exactly what Cofense Triage and Vision are built for. Because these campaigns often target multiple recipients from the same infrastructure, an employee who reports a suspicious reply quickly gives security teams the chance to block that infrastructure before others click. A well-trained employee who flags a response-themed email is a detection tool no automated system can replicate.

Full Text:
On October 21, 2026, attackers published a malicious release of litellm, a popular Python proxy library for LLM providers with about 23 million weekly downloads. The malicious release, version 1.107.0, was available on PyPI and in LiteLLM's official Docker images for approximately two hours before being removed. It installed a credential stealer that runs whenever Python starts and also contained a second-stage remote access trojan (RAT) backdoor. The infostealer payload targets cloud, developer, AI-tool, browser and LiteLLM proxy credentials.

This marks the second supply chain compromise of LiteLLM in 2026, with the earlier incident (affecting versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8) being linked to TeamPCP activity by Datadog Security Research. No connection between the two compromises has been established at time of writing.

What happened

According to LiteLLM’s analysis of the incident, attackers used stolen GitHub CLI OAuth tokens from three engineers' accounts to launch LiteLLM’s private release workflow. At time of writing, it was not yet clear how the affected credentials were initially compromised.

The three stolen credentials were used to launch, approve and subsequently delete evidence of an unauthorized run of the legitimate build pipeline against a malicious fork, Berri-AI/litellm, whose name differs from the legitimate BerriAI/litellm fork by one hyphen. The similarity of the malicious fork’s name to the real project seems intended to evade casual detection by a human reviewer. The resulting wheels and images were published through LiteLLM's normal release channels and with seemingly legitimate build provenance that faithfully recorded the malicious fork as the source.

Payload analysis

The release adds three files to the victim Python installation’s site-packages directory:

cook.pth

cook.py

sitecustomize.py

Python runs .pth files and sitecustomize.py automatically every time the interpreter starts. Any Python process in the environment runs the malware, even if LiteLLM is never imported.

Credential stealer (cook.py): Collects secrets and sends them, encrypted with AES-256 and RSA-4096, to the lookalike domain www.litellm[.]dev/healthcheck.

Backdoor (sitecustomize.py): Every hour, checks a certain file hosted on a fixed GitHub repository (letters9813/pythonclient-test/main/domain.txt, now removed) for a domain, then downloads and runs Python code from it. Data exfiltration

Cloud: AWS, GCP and Azure credentials, including from instance metadata; Kubernetes, Docker, Vault and Terraform secrets

Developer: SSH, GPG and TLS keys, Git, npm and PyPI tokens, .env files, shell history

AI: LLM provider API keys, and sessions for Claude, Codex, Gemini, Cursor, Copilot and other AI coding tools

Browsers: saved passwords and cookies

LiteLLM proxy: If a database is configured, it queries the tables where the proxy stores upstream provider credentials.

What to do if you are affected

Manually remove the malicious cook.pth, cook.py, and sitecustomize.py from the site-packages directory.

Remove all code and data associated with the malicious litellm==1.107.0 release.

Revert to litellm==1.106.2, the latest safe version of the package.

From a clean machine, immediately rotate all affected credentials.

Audit relevant logs for use of exposed credentials during the exposure window.

Final thoughts

In this case, stolen developer tokens were used to point a trusted release pipeline at the wrong source. In order to ensure the validity of build provenance, it is essential to put in place adequate controls on which branches are eligible for building. Maintainers should lock release workflows to approved repositories and treat developer CLI tokens as the high-value secrets that they are.

Title: 8 eMudhra certificates are compromised. Here's what you need to know
Context: We immediately prioritized patching critical services across Cloudflare to protect our customers ahead of the public disclosure of the vulnerability
Full Text:
On October 19, 2026, at approximately 17:00 UTC, Cloudflare became aware that private keys associated with eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised. These certificates were widely trusted by browsers, operating systems, and also within Cloudflare. Because the keys themselves are weak, an attacker can create a forged certificate for any domain and use it to impersonate servers to intercept or modify traffic. This is a serious security incident with implications across the Internet. For reference, here is a link to more information about how SSL certificates work and why they are so critical to the operation of the Internet.

We immediately prioritized patching critical services across Cloudflare to protect our customers ahead of the public disclosure of the vulnerability. Our security review has not identified active exploitation of this issue on Cloudflare services.

We have released updates for the Cloudflare One Clients, also known as WARP or the 1.1.1.1 app, and Cloudflare Tunnel, also known as cloudflared. We have also deployed mitigations across our CDN, Developer, and Zero Trust products. If you are using Cloudflare Zero Trust with Gateway and an up-to-date client (see below), you are automatically protected.

Our response

We prioritized updating services that use public certificates to authenticate remote endpoints, including proxies connecting to origins and applications calling external APIs. In parallel, we updated shared trust stores, base images, and other shared foundations, providing a common mitigation path for services that inherit their certificate trust from those sources. We paired these updates with reloads, restarts, and image deployments needed to activate them. Applications with bundled or custom trust stores received separate assessment and updates. This work addresses certificate-based authentication, not a weakness in TLS’s encryption algorithms.

Teams across Cloudflare are presently working on further remediation. We are making progress, but there's much work still to be done. Some customers will need to take action on software or trust configurations that they operate, especially on their origin servers. The recommended actions are summarized below.

What customers should do

Developer guidance

For developers, look beneath the SDK.

An API client may delegate certificate verification to an HTTP library, a language runtime, the operating system, or a custom trust configuration. Updating the SDK alone may not change the underlying policy.

Once you patch, you may notice certificate errors in your dashboards. It's important to not resolve these errors by disabling verification. That would remove the authentication protection these updates are intended to restore.

This incident affects many software stacks that rely on the WebPKI for authentication. Mozilla’s Dennis Jackson has crowdsourced a list of commonly used packages that have been patched. We advise readers to upgrade as soon as possible. (Note that some of these may be indirect dependencies of your software stack, so look at the dependency tree.) Apply the relevant dependency updates, rebuild affected images, and confirm whether applications require a reload, restart, or redeployment.

Dennis Jackson’s test site provides browser checks, non-browser testing instructions, and package update information. Results apply to the verification path being tested, not every application on the device. Validate through the application’s actual TLS path. A successful browser test does not prove that a background service is protected. Neither does a curl test if the application uses a different verifier.

Timeline

The timeline of events so far is below.

Date and Time

Event

October 19, approximately 17:00 UTC

Cloudflare becomes aware of the compromise and begins assessment.

October 20, 02:00 UTC

Cloudflare One Client and WARP app security updates published across platforms.

October 20 09:15 UTC

Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) security update published.

October 20 19:20 UTC

CDN and server-side Zero Trust mitigations fully deployed.

Looking forward

The impact of this incident is not felt equally. Browser maintainers were able to remediate the issue with a flip of a switch. They of course have just one application to update, instead of hundreds, but they do have a neat trick up their sleeves: most browsers use quick-revocation mechanisms (like Chrome CRLSets). At Cloudflare we also use such a mechanism for some of our products. To bring it to more systems at Cloudflare and industry, we’re excited about projects like upki that understand a trust store can’t be a static list of root certificate authorities, but needs the ability to be quickly updated with information like revocation and certificate transparency keys.

Title: From Phishing to LLMjacking: Threat Actors Targeting Cloud Billing Accounts for LLM Usage
Context: Threat actors are not only using AI as a tool to conduct attacks, they are also compromising victim environments solely to abuse their finances for mass Large Language Model...
Full Text:
The Wiz Customer Incident Response Team (CIRT) has investigated a rising threat pattern in cloud environments: threat actors hijacking cloud billing accounts to fund unauthorized AI usage. Threat actors are not only using AI as a tool to conduct attacks, they are also compromising victim environments solely to abuse their finances for mass Large Language Model (LLM) execution, incurring hundreds of thousands of dollars in AI API charges.

Wiz CIRT has investigated multiple intrusions demonstrating this pattern, with this blogpost focusing specifically on campaigns targeting Google Cloud Platform (GCP) infrastructure. In these attacks, threat actors compromised privileged GCP user credentials and linked external, attacker-controlled GCP projects directly to the victim's internal billing accounts. Because the AI workloads were processed in foreign projects, prompt contents and model outputs remained completely hidden from the victim organization, leaving the nature of the mass AI usage unknown.

This blogpost details the full attack lifecycle observed across these intrusions, from the initial phishing and policy manipulation to cross-tenant project linking, and provides actionable threat hunting guidance to help organizations detect LLMjacking in their environments.

Initial Access: Phishing via Sponsored Search Ads

The attack began with a classic yet efficient phishing tactic. The threat actor purchased Google Search ads for common administrative search terms such as “google cloud” and “gcp”. When a user clicked the malicious ad, they were led through a Google Sites redirect to a fake Google login web page. Victim users with valid access to Google Console proceeded to input their account credentials and multi-factor-authentication (MFA) codes into the phishing page. The malicious site captured the user supplied credentials before seamlessly redirecting the user back to the legitimate Google authentication prompt. Forced to authenticate a second time, the user likely assumed the initial attempt was a minor glitch. In reality, the automated phishing kit immediately leveraged the harvested credentials to execute the first malicious login into the victim’s GCP environment from 212.73.134[.]136, the source IP address of the phishing kit. The threat actor then reauthenticated a few minutes later from a second IP address, which was later used for the rest of the GCP activity. Following reports of this activity, Google Ads has taken action to remove the malicious ad campaign.

Google automatically flagged the anomalous login attempt as suspicious and dispatched security alert emails to the user's inbox. However, to catch such intrusions early, organizations should not rely on user awareness alone, but ingest and monitor Google Workspace User Log Events for suspicious login flags and anomalous re-authentication triggers.

Persistence and Privilege Escalation: Disabling Guardrails and Externalizing Billing

Once inside the environment, the threat actor leveraged the compromised account’s excessive privileges to solidify their access, bypass organizational security controls, and prepare the billing architecture for external exploitation.

Enabling APIs and Minting Service Account Credentials

Rather than creating new infrastructure from scratch, the attacker targeted existing, low-usage GCP projects to:

Enable the Gemini API product

Create service accounts with Gemini API keys

Add the newly created service accounts to high privileged roles such as roles/ml.admin and roles/mcp.toolUser

Dismantling Organizational Policy Controls

To expand their reach without raising immediate alarms within internal domain governance, the threat actor deleted safety policies at the organization level, such as iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains. This action removed the guardrail that restricts Identity and Access Management (IAM) membership to verified company domains, enabling external, personal accounts to be granted access as well as high-privilege permissions.

Inviting External Threat Actor Accounts and Elevating Privileges

With domain restrictions lifted, the compromised user account was leveraged to add external actor-controlled Gmail accounts directly into the organization's billing account.

The threat actor also assigned administrative roles to the compromised users or the external accounts, such as:

roles/recommender.billingAccountCudAdmin on GCP projects

roles/billing.admin on GCP billing accounts

The role roles/billing.admin granted full control over the billing account, including the ability to manage permissions, attach external projects, and alter payment settings.

Linking Foreign Projects for Mass Exploitation

The threat actor linked external GCP projects directly to the victim’s internal billing account. This move established a cross-tenant access, allowing all API requests executed in the threat actors external projects to be automatically charged to the victim's billing account while keeping prompt payloads invisible to internal log monitoring.

Defence Evasion: Geographic Blending and Admin Lockout

Once initial access was secured, threat actors employed defense evasion techniques designed to avoid triggering location-based security alerts and prevent security teams from regaining control.

In each of the intrusions investigated, Wiz CIRT observed that after the initial login, subsequent threat actor activity shifted to originate from IP addresses geolocated within each victim organization's headquartered country, even when this did not match the compromised user’s actual physical location.

Additionally, after securing administrative control, the threat actors demoted pre-existing internal billing administrators from their administrative roles down to read-only billing viewers. This modification stripped legitimate administrators of their ability to revoke permissions or detach rogue projects directly from the console.

Impact: AI Resource Abuse

The primary objective of these intrusions was non-destructive financial exploitation - leveraging hijacked cloud infrastructure to offload the costs of high-volume LLM inference. Across the observed cases, the impact manifested as rapid billing surges driven by automated, large-scale Gemini API utilization.

Within 24 to 48 hours of initial access, victim organizations experienced unexpected charges reaching tens to hundreds of thousands of dollars in unauthorized Gemini API usage. This activity represented a sharp surge from the organizations' established baseline compute spend.

Because the threat actors linked external, attacker-controlled GCP projects directly to the victim’s billing accounts, all API key generation, prompt requests, and model outputs occurred entirely within foreign tenants. Consequently, while the victim organization carried financial responsibility for the API consumption, internal security and audit logs provided no visibility into the nature, content, or context of the AI workloads being executed.

Detection and Threat Hunting Indicators

To detect potential LLMjacking and unauthorized billing account manipulation in your Google Cloud environment, security teams should hunt for indicators across Google Workspace, GCP Admin Activity, and Cloud Billing audit logs. Wiz customers can review the Threat Intel Center advisory that includes the following indicators:

Review Google Workspace and GCP audit logs for activity from the indicators of compromise section below. Wiz customers can use this Cloud Events query.

Review GCP IAM for any users with external domains, especially non-corporate email providers such as @gmail.com. Wiz customers can use this Cloud Events query, and replace the domain.com with their own organization domain.

Review GCP audit logs for changes to organization policy controls, especially allowedPolicyMemberDomains, and IAM policy changes related to billing account administrators. Wiz customers can use this Cloud Events query.

Review GCP audit logs for unexpected Gemini API enablement, service account creation and service account API key creation in old projects Wiz customers can use this Cloud Events query.

Monitor abnormal cost surge in API usage, and potentially enforce spend cap budgets. Wiz Cloud Cost customers can detect abnormal AI usage per model and cloud provider by monitoring Cost Monitor Findings for Resource Anomalies.

Wiz Defend customers ingesting cloud logs such as Google Workspace will get Wiz Threats on the initial logins. Customers ingesting GCP audit logs will get Threats for the described activity.

If you experience a breach or any cloud security incident, contact Wiz CIRT for incident response support.

Title: The Risk of AI-Powered Antidetect Browsers in Online Fraud and Influence Operations
Context: Threat actors abuse these platforms, taking over accounts and using them for financial fraud, phishing and malware distribution
Full Text:
Key Findings

Antidetect browsers obscure the digital identity of their users, enabling a single operator to silently manage thousands of isolated accounts across multiple platforms (including Facebook, TikTok, Instagram, and YouTube), while evading detection systems that look for scams and coordinated inauthentic behavior.

Threat actors abuse these platforms, taking over accounts and using them for financial fraud, phishing and malware distribution. These accounts can also be used to coordinate influence operations, which becomes an even greater concern ahead of elections.

Social platforms primarily detect coordinated activity at the account and behavioral layer. Antidetect browsers run below the surface enabling them to remain undetected.

The three main antidetect browsers we discuss in this report are Kameleo, AdsPower, and MultiLogin.

These tools already use AI integration, from built-in automation templates to offering a dedicated MCP server that pipes LLM-generated content directly into pre-warmed account profiles at machine speed. Running a large-scale social media operation now requires only a credit card instead of a technical team.

Introduction

Antidetect browsers conceal their users’ digital identities, enabling a single operator or small team to simultaneously run thousands of isolated accounts across multiple platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Twitter/X, Discord, LinkedIn, Reddit, and many more, without triggering the detection systems employed by those platforms.

In this report, we highlight three main tools: Kameleo, AdsPower, and MultiLogin. We selected these specifically on the basis of documented references across underground forums and criminal marketplaces, indicating active adoption beyond their stated commercial purposes. Confirmed use cases include:

Account takeover operations in which session cookies harvested by infostealer malware are injected into clean browser profiles to assume control of banking accounts and cryptocurrency wallets without triggering authentication alerts.

Carding operations in which stolen payment credentials are tested across e-commerce platforms under the guise of distinct legitimate users.

Fraudulent loan applications submitted under fabricated identities.

Bulk creation of artificial accounts used to generate fraudulent advertising revenue at scale.

As documented in Anthropic’s September 2026 Threat Intelligence Report, attackers used antidetect browsers in a fraud campaign that targeted cryptocurrency exchanges and financial marketplaces. They combined antidetect browser profiles, residential proxies, automated CAPTCHA-solving, and identity-verification bypass tools to create large numbers of verified accounts while avoiding onboarding security checks. These accounts were later used in fraud operations.

The risk posed by antidetect browsers is greater because these accounts pass KYC verification, build legitimate activity histories, and appear benign during transactions. As a result, fraud detection systems that rely on user behavior or device identity often cannot identify these accounts as suspicious until after fraudulent activity has already occurred.

The antidetect browsers documented in this research are commercially available, legally registered platforms with documented legitimate use cases in digital marketing, e-commerce, and privacy protection. When deployed by threat actors, the same infrastructure that enables financial fraud at scale is equally applicable to Coordinated Inauthentic Behavior (CIB), the term used to describe organized manipulation campaigns in which false identities are central to the operation and adversarial methods are used to evade detection.

Meta’s most recent transparency reporting explicitly flagged this as a growing concern, with Russia, Iran, and China identified as the three leading sources of such activity globally.

The Identity Obfuscation Stack – How antidetect browsers defeat social media platform detection at every layer

Figure 1 – The five layers through which antidetect browsers defeat platform detection methods.

While antidetect browsers are not a new phenomenon, their threat potential has increased with the integration of AI. Previously, their operational impact was constrained by the manual effort required to run and maintain large account networks at scale. AI-assisted content generation, automated persona management, and machine-speed distribution pipelines now enables a single actor with a subscription and a prompt to do the work of a coordinated team.

In the following sections, we provide a technical breakdown of each tool, examining capabilities documented on their own platforms, underground forum references, and the specific features that position them as an emerging threat.

Figure 2 – Comparison of popular antidetect tools.

Defeating Platform Detection: The Identity Layer No Platform Can See

Companies like Meta, TikTok, and Google have spent billions of dollars building behavioral and identity detection systems to identify abuse of their platforms for scams, financial fraud, and coordinated inauthentic activity. Antidetect browsers are engineered to defeat every signal on which those systems rely.

Every antidetect browser uses fingerprint spoofing. When a browser connects to a website, it exposes dozens of identifying parameters that the website can collect to build a browser fingerprint, including canvas rendering output, WebGL vendor and renderer strings, font enumeration behavior, screen resolution, time zone, user agent, and hardware identifiers. Platforms cross-reference these signals to determine whether two accounts originate from the same device. Antidetect browsers intercept and fabricate each of these parameters individually, assigning a unique combination to every profile.

The criminal ecosystem surrounding these tools extends well beyond their commercial vendors. As seen in Figure 3, a threat actor on a Russian-language underground forum advertised an AiTM engine as a commercial service, with built-in functionality to export harvested session credentials directly into antidetect browsers. The post confirms that the pipeline from credential harvesting to antidetect-assisted account takeover is a documented, commercially available and actively traded workflow with dedicated tooling, published instructions, and an active buyer community.

Figure 3 – An AiTM engine advertised as a commercial service on a Russian-language underground forum, with built-in functionality to export harvested session credentials directly into antidetect browsers.

Kameleo

Modifying browser engines at the source level rather than applying surface overrides, Kameleo produces fingerprints drawn from real device signatures, making them significantly harder to flag as anomalous. Its adoption within criminal ecosystems is evidenced by its repeated appearance across the most active Russian-language hacking forums. As seen in Figure 4, Kameleo is listed alongside other antidetect browsers in a post by a proxy seller on an underground forum, advertising residential proxy services explicitly marketed for account farming, CAPTCHA bypass, and shield evasion against security systems including DataDome, the same platform for which Kameleo’s own blog publishes dedicated bypass guides.

Figure 4 – A proxy seller on an underground forum listing Kameleo as part of a complete operational stack. The service is explicitly marketed for account farming and bulk account management.

Kameleo’s engineering team published a guide detailing how to automate Facebook likes across multiple accounts simultaneously using precisely this fingerprint manipulation. As seen in Figure 5, evading platform detection is not a side effect but the tool’s primary operational value.

Figure 5 – Kameleo’s guide on how to automate Facebook likes across multiple accounts simultaneously using browser fingerprint manipulation.

Beyond fingerprinting, Kameleo suppresses WebRTC, a protocol that can leak a device’s real IP address even when a proxy is active, and provides explicit configuration options to prevent non-proxied UDP connections. The documentation frames this not as a privacy feature but as a counter to a known de-anonymization vector used by platform security teams.

At the session layer, Kameleo’s dedicated cookie injection API accepts complete cookie objects including session IDs, refresh tokens, and authentication flags, allowing a pre-authenticated session state to be inserted into a profile before it is launched. The platform sees the profile as an already-authenticated user, with no login event occurring to trigger anomaly detection. As independently documented by threat intelligence research and confirmed by security researchers, this workflow is established and active in the criminal ecosystem. Figure 6 shows a recruitment post on a Russian-language underground forum advertising a multifunctional infostealer with RAT capabilities explicitly designed to operate within antidetect browser environments, listing Kameleo, AdsPower, and MultiLogin among 21 compatible platforms capable of harvesting session cookies, authentication tokens, cryptocurrency wallets, API keys, and 2FA credentials.

Figure 6 – A recruitment post on a Russian-language underground forum lists 21 browsers including Kameleo, AdsPower, and MultiLogin as compatible platforms.

As seen in Figure 7, a threat actor on a Russian-language underground hacking forum explicitly introduces Kameleo as a component of Browser-in-the-Middle phishing kits targeting credentials across Google, Microsoft, Facebook, and financial platforms. In a Browser-in-the-Middle attack, the phishing server instructs the antidetect browser to create a new profile for the victim, assigned a residential proxy in their country and a clean device fingerprint. The victim’s credentials, entered on the phishing page, are passed in real time into the real login page of the target service through an automation framework. The target platform sees a login attempt from a consistent, locally coherent device with a residential IP address in the expected country, none of the signals that would trigger a security challenge or step-up authentication.

Figure 7 – A post on a Russian-language underground hacking forum introducing Kameleo as a component of Browser-in-the-Middle phishing kits targeting credentials across Google, Microsoft, Facebook, and financial platforms.

AdsPower

Chinese in origin and subsequently registered across multiple jurisdictions and localized into more than 20 languages, AdsPower applies fingerprint spoofing logic across more than 20 configurable parameters per profile and advertises a 99.2% ban avoidance rate. As seen in Figure 8, its proxy editor provides a built-in catalog of compatible third-party residential and rotating proxy providers, assignable directly within the profile creation interface. Figure 9 illustrates the granularity of fingerprint control available, with each profile’s WebRTC handling, time zone, geolocation, and language individually configurable to ensure the synthetic identity is consistent across every detectable signal.

Figure 8 – AdsPower’s proxy integration interface lists compatible third-party residential and rotating proxy providers available within the platform.

Figure 9 – AdsPower’s fingerprint editor displaying granular per-profile identity parameters including WebRTC, timezone and location derived from the assigned proxy IP.

The scale of AdsPower’s intended use is reflected in its pricing structure, with published tiers supporting up to 5,000 distinct profiles as seen in Figure 10, and enterprise arrangements available on request. As seen in Figure 11, its account editor supports platforms spanning social media, e-commerce, financial services, and professional networks including Facebook, Amazon, LinkedIn, X, PayPal, and Google.

Figure 10 – AdsPower’s pricing table reflects the intended operational scale, with enterprise tiers supporting more than 5,000 profiles available upon request.

Figure 11 – AdsPower’s account editor shows supported platforms available for bulk profile management, including Facebook, Amazon, LinkedIn, X, PayPal, and Google.

Scalability is further addressed through a built-in RPA engine and a dedicated Marketplace, as seen in Figure 12, offering pre-built templates for automated liking, commenting, direct messaging, follower scraping, and AI-assisted engagement across hundreds of profiles simultaneously. The multi-window synchronizer replicates identical actions across hundreds of profiles from a single input, while account warming automation builds synthetic activity histories over weeks to reduce platform suspicion before deployment.

Figure 12 – AdsPower’s RPA Marketplace lists pre-built automation templates for bulk account activity across major platforms, including automated liking, commenting, direct messaging, follower scraping, and AI-assisted engagement.

On the AI front, AdsPower advertises a dedicated Model Context Protocol server enabling direct integration with large language model workflows, creating a pipeline in which AI-generated content can be produced, injected into pre-warmed account profiles, and distributed across platforms in a fully automated sequence requiring no human involvement. A companion feature, the Cookie Robot, automates cookie warming on TikTok and Twitter/X accounts prior to operational use. The RPA Marketplace is the delivery mechanism for this pipeline, with ready-to-deploy workflows designed to operate in direct combination with AI-generated content, resulting in an end-to-end operation at a scale and speed previously associated only with state-sponsored actors.

As seen in Figure 13, AdsPower’s own published scraping guide explicitly acknowledges that scraping Facebook constitutes a violation of the platform’s terms of service and may result in legal action, before advising users that an antidetect browser can help bypass these limitations.

Figure 13 – AdsPower’s official scraping guide advises users that an antidetect browser can help bypass scraping limitations.

MultiLogin

MultiLogin operates as a fully featured antidetect browser platform, offering isolated browser profiles with unique device fingerprints covering canvas output, WebGL parameters, fonts, timezone, screen resolution, and user agent, with each profile maintaining separate cookies, local storage, and session data. The platform supports automation through Selenium, Playwright, and Puppeteer, enabling fully scripted, headless operation of multiple profiles simultaneously. MultiLogin has been referenced on Exploit, a Russian-language underground hacking forum, in a thread dedicated to antidetect browsers, indicating active discussion and adoption of the platform within criminal communities (see Figure 6).

MultiLogin extends its multi-account capability into the mobile layer through a phone farming infrastructure that replaces physical Android devices with cloud-hosted equivalents. Every cloud Android profile maintains its own persistent mobile device parameters, with proxies assigned per profile to control location and network identity. MultiLogin’s own documentation states that most account bans in phone farm environments occur due to multiple accounts sharing the same device signals, storage, or network patterns, and positions its product as the solution to this detection problem, an explicit acknowledgment that the platform is designed to defeat association detection at the mobile layer.

According to their website, virtual phone number provisioning through partner integrations enables SMS-based account verification without physical SIM cards or mobile devices. Each virtual number is paired with a mobile device fingerprint profile, enabling the rapid creation of large volumes of accounts that appear to originate from distinct mobile devices across different geographic locations.

MultiLogin maintains a dedicated web scraping solution page and publishes operational guides for scraping platforms including Facebook, LinkedIn, Amazon, and Twitter, with its built-in residential proxy infrastructure marketed as enabling scraping operations that bypass bot detection and IP-based rate limiting. Its stated use cases listed on its own website include ticket scalping automation, a practice explicitly illegal in multiple jurisdictions and prohibited by major ticketing platforms, with the platform’s infrastructure documented as tested daily against major ticketing services for compatibility. MultiLogin additionally lists AI Quick Actions Automation among its documented product capabilities, indicating a degree of AI integration into its operational workflow.

As seen in Figure 14, MultiLogin’s payment infrastructure accepts cryptocurrency alongside credit card payments and regional systems including SberPay and YooMoney. Notably, YooMoney has been designated on the OFAC Specially Designated Nationals list since April 2022 under Executive Order 14024 as a Sberbank subsidiary, and SberPay operates as a product of Sberbank, itself under comprehensive OFAC blocking sanctions since February 2022. The acceptance of these payment methods, alongside cryptocurrency, enables anonymous and potentially sanctions-non-compliant transactions. MultiLogin offers 24/7 support through dedicated Telegram channels staffed by human representatives and is tested daily against more than 50 major social media platforms to ensure continued compatibility. Taken together, MultiLogin’s mobile infrastructure, AI automation layer, scraping capabilities, criminal community presence, and payment infrastructure make it one of the most operationally complete platforms in this category.

Figure 14 – MultiLogin’s payment infrastructure accepts a variety of different payment services.

AI-Powered Campaign Infrastructure

The most consequential recent development is AI integration directly into the operational stack. AdsPower advertises a dedicated Model Context Protocol server enabling direct integration with large language model workflows, creating a pipeline in which AI-generated content can be produced, injected into pre-warmed account profiles, and distributed across platforms in a fully automated sequence requiring no human involvement. A companion feature, the Cookie Robot, automates cookie warming on TikTok and Twitter/X accounts prior to operational use, simulating browsing behavior to establish account credibility before the content distribution phase begins.

The RPA Marketplace mentioned in the previous section is the delivery mechanism for this pipeline. Available templates contain ready-to-deploy workflows maintained and updated by the vendor, designed to operate in direct combination with AI-generated content. This creates an end-to-end influence operation pipeline that requires no active operator presence once the campaign is initiated. The result is a single automated workflow that places coordinated influence operation capacity within reach of any sufficiently motivated actor, regardless of resources or technical expertise.

Web Scraping as Operational Intelligence

The web scraping capabilities documented across these platforms serve a function that extends well beyond data collection. Scraped data is the intelligence layer that makes the operation more precise. Several of the tools we reviewed maintain dedicated scraping solution pages describing capabilities including fingerprint rotation, CAPTCHA bypass, and headless browsing designed to extract data from platforms including LinkedIn, Amazon, Facebook, and Twitter while evading their anti-scraping defenses. As seen in Figure 13, the AdsPower published scraping guide explicitly acknowledges that scraping Facebook constitutes a violation of the platform’s terms of service and may result in legal action, before advising users that an antidetect browser can help bypass these limitations.

The combination of well-farmed personas and targeted scraping capabilities enables a precision influence operation at scale.

Workflow:

An artificial account, warmed up over several weeks of simulated activity, accumulates sufficient credibility to be accepted into a closed group on a social media platform.

Once inside, the platform’s scraping infrastructure extracts available information on every member, including names, profile data, religious affiliations, political interests, age, geographic markers, and engagement patterns.

The harvested dataset becomes the targeting intelligence for a bulk coordinated campaign, allowing artificial personas to engage each member with content calibrated to their specific profile, amplify narratives that resonate with the group’s demonstrated interests, and simulate the kind of peer validation that drives genuine behavioral change.

A Sophisticated and Professionally Maintained Ecosystem

The commercial availability of these tools reflects a fundamental shift in the influence-operation threat landscape: what was once the domain of well-resourced state actors and advanced persistent threat groups is now accessible to any motivated individual with a credit card. These are all professionally maintained, customer-supported, multilingual software platforms with pricing pages, knowledge bases, release notes, and dedicated sales teams. The only barrier to running a large-scale coordinated inauthentic operation is not a user’s technical sophistication but the need to pay a subscription fee.

The language coverage and market reach of these tools reflects the scale of their intended user base. AdsPower is available in 20 languages. MultiLogin supports English, Chinese, Russian, Vietnamese, and Portuguese, and is tested daily against more than 50 platforms. Kameleo maintains a public blog catalog of dedicated technical guides on bypassing Cloudflare bot detection, defeating DataDome, and solving Cloudflare Turnstile challenges, which are all security systems deployed specifically to identify and block automated or inauthentic browser sessions.

The customer support infrastructure surrounding these tools mirrors that of legitimate enterprise software, with MultiLogin offering 24/7 support through dedicated Telegram channels staffed by human representatives. As seen in Figure 14, MultiLogin’s payment infrastructure accepts cryptocurrency alongside credit card payments and regional systems including SberPay and YooMoney, both Russian payment services.

As seen in Figure 15, independent threat actors have developed and are actively selling purpose-built antidetect solutions on underground forums, complete with feature documentation, technical support, and monthly subscription pricing. This particular tool targets Android devices specifically, offering automated geolocation spoofing, device ID replacement, Wi-Fi environment manipulation, and Play Integrity bypass at 100 USD per month, reflecting the breadth of threat actor demand across different device categories and operational requirements.

As seen in Figure 16, the downstream commercial activity built on this infrastructure extends to farmed platform accounts advertised for sale on underground forums alongside explicit instructions to access them using antidetect browsers. Cryptocurrency is the default payment method. These posts confirm a mature commercial underground market in which these antidetect tools function as the operational backbone of a broader fraud and influence ecosystem.

Figure 15 – An antidetect tool designed for Android devices advertised on an underground forum, offers automated geolocation spoofing, device ID replacement, and Play Integrity bypass at 100 USD per month.

Figure 16 – Farmed Google Ads accounts advertised for sale on an underground forum.

Conclusion

The antidetect browser ecosystem represents a sophisticated, commercially mature, and increasingly AI-driven infrastructure that has fundamentally lowered the barrier to running scam and fraud operations, as well as coordinated inauthentic operations at scale. These commercially maintained tools are available in dozens of languages, backed by customer support teams, tested daily against the world’s largest social media platforms, and are now integrated with LLM pipelines that remove the human operator from the execution layer. The coupling of identity spoofing infrastructure, automated content distribution, and AI-assisted persona management represents a threat surface that platform detection systems may struggle to address, particularly in the context of elections taking place across multiple countries.

The infrastructure we documented is commercially available today. Its capabilities are not constrained by technical sophistication, national resources, or operational scale. The question is no longer whether these tools are being actively used for fraud, account takeover, and coordinated manipulation, but whether the detection, enforcement, and awareness frameworks across every layer of the ecosystem are prepared to counter them.

Recommendations

Security and threat intelligence teams:

The detection priority should shift from the account and behavioral layer, where these tools are already designed to appear invisible, to the network and infrastructure layer.

Indicators include residential proxy infrastructure operating at scale, WebRTC suppression patterns, anomalous cookie injection sequences, and known antidetect browser user agent strings in web traffic logs.

Account warming patterns, simulated by these tools over several weeks, may be indistinguishable from legitimate organic behavior without cross-referencing device fingerprint consistency over time.

Social media platforms:

Antidetectbrowser infrastructure should be treated as a first-class priority.

The capabilities operate below existing detection thresholds, and infrastructure-layer signals may be the only reliable detection surface available.

Platforms should consider actively acquiring and reverse engineering antidetect tools to map their proxy patterns, fingerprint rotation behaviors, and detection bypass mechanisms, and use those findings to recalibrate banning logic specifically against these tools’ TTPs.

CISOs and companies:

The risk posed by antidetect browser infrastructure extends well beyond influence operations.

Silent account takeover using cookie injection workflows can bypass multi-factor authentication without generating a login event.

Organizations are advised to review whether their session monitoring infrastructure can detect pre-authenticated session anomalies, and to incorporate antidetect-specific attack scenarios into red team exercises and threat models.

Threat actors can leverage antidetect browsers to replicate victim device fingerprints and geolocation to execute unauthorized transactions without triggering behavioral anomaly detection.

Fraud detection systems that rely on device consistency and session continuity signals should be specifically reviewed for resilience against fingerprint spoofing and session injection at the identity infrastructure layer.

Title: Is the ad a scam? How to tell before you click
Context: Also known as malvertising, a click on this kind of ad will exploit browser/software vulnerabilities or trick you into unwittingly installing malware via an app download
Full Text:
Fraudulent ads have been around for about as long as the advertising industry. Today, they often reach you through social media feeds, apps and search results you use every day, and the platforms showing them can also (inadvertently) help build them. In September, the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) asked whether platforms should be required to stop impersonation scam ads from ever reaching consumers. Its concern is the ad tools that those platforms offer to advertisers. They can generate the copy, images and video, and optimize who sees the result, regardless of whether the ads are legitimate or not.

In Europe, nearly one trillion scam ads were served to social media users in 2025, generating an estimated £3.8 billion in revenue for these platforms. In the US, data is harder to come by, although Meta alone projected 10% of its 2024 revenue would come from ads for scams and banned goods, amounting to a staggering $16 billion.

For consumers, the message is clear: you might trust the platform, but you can’t trust the ads on it.

What do scam ads look like?

Scam ads could appear on search engine pages, e-commerce marketplaces and shopping sites, mobile apps and games, video sites, messaging platforms and a host of other websites. But perhaps the biggest risk comes from social media sites. Nearly a third (30%) of people who reported losing money to a scam last year said it started on social media.

They could include advertising that:

Impersonates a legitimate company and leads to a phishing site designed to mimic the real version

Offers special deals on goods for a limited time, as a way to create a sense of urgency

Offers investment opportunities, often in cryptocurrency ventures, that promise high returns with no downside

Impersonates customer support for legitimate companies like banks

Promises mega giveaways of cash and prizes which only require the user to share personal and financial information to access

Scares the victim with fake security warnings that their computer or device is infected

Engages the victim with clickbait such as outrageous news stories with sensational headlines

What’s the end goal?

These ads serve various purposes. Some may be outright malicious. Also known as malvertising, a click on this kind of ad will exploit browser/software vulnerabilities or trick you into unwittingly installing malware via an app download. Others are designed to persuade you into handing over personal information via prize giveaways, questionnaires and other phishing-style pages. This could subsequently be used to commit identity fraud.

Another category of scam ads will target your finances more directly. They may ask for money to invest in a fictitious scheme, pay for a non-existent product, or hand over money to pay a fake fee, for example. In some cases, the scam ad may take you to a fake e-commerce site which covertly harvests your card details.

While these efforts are often digital, beware too of calling phone numbers on ads. They might put you through to a scam call center where the operatives will be trained to relieve you of your money and/or personal/financial information. This is often what happens if you get swindled by a fake security alert.

Banks hate these scams because, in jurisdictions like the UK, they are responsible for reimbursing customers for “authorized push payment” (APP) losses in some instances. They have long argued that social media platforms in particular should do more to police this content, and to compensate victims. However, in the US and elsewhere, social media companies aren’t legally bound to do so, despite profiting from the ad revenue.

This may change, of course, depending on the outcome of the FTC’s rulemaking, which is at its earliest stage. It says it may consider forcing platforms to vet advertisers, monitor posted ads, investigate scams, remove fraudulent advertising, and pursue disciplinary action, among other measures.

Scam-ad red flags: what to look out for

In the meantime, the best you can do is to spot the warning signs of a scam and steer well clear of suspect ads. You should be able to spot them by looking out for a few common red flags that include:

Urgent language encouraging you to act quickly. This rushes us into making decisions that otherwise we may not make, like sharing our personal information.

Too-good-to-be-true offers that trigger our fear of missing out. These are often presented as time-sensitive in order to ramp up the urgency.

Any requests for sensitive personal information, which could help fraudsters build a profile of us with which to use for identity fraud. It could be details as innocuous as email/home address, phone number and full name.

Phone numbers on ads that will probably route you to a scam call center. Most legitimate companies funnel support issues through digital channels initially.

Pressure to download software in order to fix an ‘issue’ with your computer/device.

Sensational news designed to tantalize and persuade you to click through.

Celebrity endorsements for products and services for sale (sometimes deepfaked), or investment opportunities.

What happens if I’ve fallen victim to a scam ad?

If you’ve clicked through on a scam ad or called the number, and then downloaded something, handed over some personal/financial information, used your card to buy something, or made a bank transfer, don’t panic. Also:

Don’t reply to any further messages from the scammer and monitor your accounts for suspicious activity.

If relevant, contact your bank or card provider immediately and tell them what happened. They should be able to freeze your card or account while they investigate. If you’ve made a transfer, it will fall under an APP fraud claim. Card payments may be eligible for a chargeback.

If you’ve handed over passwords, change them immediately on the relevant site and anywhere else you’ve reused them. Switch on two-factor authentication (2FA) for these sites and consider using a password manager to store strong, unique credentials for every account.

If you’ve downloaded anything, run a scan using security software from a reputable provider. And ensure your operating system and all applications are all up to date.

Preserve evidence of the scam where possible. This includes the ad itself, and any URLs, screenshots, emails/messages, payment records or correspondence with the scammer. It will help if you’re able to proceed with a reimbursement claim.

Report the ad to the platform that showed it, using its built-in reporting option, and report the scam to the authorities, e.g. the FTC (US) or Report Fraud (UK).

Scam ads are getting easier to generate thanks to AI, and can look increasingly professional, even including video content. That puts more pressure on you to spot the warning signs. Stay safe.

Frequently asked questions (FAQs)

Why are there so many scam ads on Facebook and Instagram?

Scammers place them there to get maximum exposure, knowing the platforms don’t police their content rigorously. They may want your personal/financial information, or to trick you into buying a non-existent product. They may even want to con you into a fake investment.

How can I tell if an ad is a scam?

It might use urgent language and too-good-to-be-true offers, potentially endorsed by celebrities. It may ask for sensitive personal information, or feature phone numbers that take you to a call center where operatives will ask for the same details or urge you to download remote access software. It might claim your PC is infected with malware and pressure you into taking action. It could even deliver sensational news designed to encourage click throughs.

Can I get my money back if I paid through a scam ad?

Social media companies are not required by law to compensate users that may have been defrauded. But depending on where you live you may be able to file an APP claim with your bank. If you’ve made a card payment, you may be able to file a chargeback claim.

What should I do if I’ve fallen victim to a scam ad?

Don’t panic. Preserve the evidence and stop any communication with the scammer. Monitor your accounts for suspicious activity. Change any passwords you’ve shared and switch on 2FA. Contact your bank or card provider, tell them what happened, and ask them to freeze your bank account/card. If you’ve downloaded anything, run a security scan and ensure your operating system and software are all up to date. Report the ad to the platform and the scam to the authorities.

Title: Beyond Passwords: How Attackers Abuse Device Code Authentication
Context: As the digital threat landscape continues to shift and threat actors exploit new attack vectors, practicing good cyber hygiene and staying informed about emerging threats remain...
Full Text:
By: Adriane Andaya, Cofense Phishing Defense Center

The Cofense Phishing Defense Center (PDC) has analyzed several emails that may look like ordinary spam to the untrained eye. Threat actors attempt to mimic routine corporate emails and blend into everyday inbox traffic. As aware of the common phishing tac tactics grows, threat actors are turning to techniques such as device code phishing. To understand how this technique works, it is important to understand what access codes are and how they differ from the common username-and-password method of authentication. Access codes are temporary codes that are entered instead of the users’ credentials on devices that are requesting authentication. While this method can simplify sign-ins, attackers can abuse it. If a victim completes the sign-in process, they may unknowingly authorize the threat actor’s session, which potentially grants access to the account and associated resources.

Figure 1: Fake bid invitation email

Cofense PDC analysts have handled several of these malicious emails that use subjects designed to capture the recipient’s interest. As illustrated in Figure 1, the email appears to be a regular bidding invitation, but when the recipient clicks on the link to view the project details, they’re redirected to a fake login page and prompted to enter their email. Microsoft branding is used to make the page appear more trustworthy.

Figure 2: Syncfusion phishing login page from the embedded URL

Figure 3: Spoofed Mimecast device enrollment page

As shown in Figure 2, the threat actors leveraged familiar brands such as Syncfusion and Microsoft to give the phishing page an appearance of legitimacy. The attack then proceeds after the victim has entered their email address. As seen in Figure 3, a very convincing spoofed Mimecast page adds another layer of legitimacy, encouraging the victim to enroll their device under the guise of an IT policy.

It is important to note that despite these familiar brands being used, the URL in the address bar does not match any of these brands’ registered domains. This mismatch should be an immediate red flag. By incorporating well-known brands, threat actors exploit familiarity to increase the likelihood of a successful phishing attempt.

Figure 4: Access code generation

Figure 5: Microsoft pop-up window

Figure 4 shows that a code will be generated, and a button to “view the document” will be presented to the user, which opens a Microsoft window (Figure 5) prompting the user to enter the code to allow access. Microsoft warns that entering the code will grant the originating application or device access to the account without requiring the user’s password and may bypass the protection normally provided by MFA. The second warning advises users not to enter codes from unverified sources. If a code from an untrusted source has been entered, it must be treated as an account compromise, and you must immediately notify your IT department. You can also take these steps to prevent or minimize the account breach:

Change the account password.

Sign out of all active sessions or revoke existing sessions.

Review recent account activity for suspicious or unauthorized access.

Review authorized applications and remove any unfamiliar or suspicious entries.

Re-verify registered security and MFA methods.

Check for unauthorized account changes, including sent emails, deleted items, forwarding rules, recovery addresses, or other modified settings.

This tactic targets decision-makers, management-level personnel, and key figures, but anyone can fall victim to this phishing campaign. It is crucial to verify any agreement, contract, or other related documents, especially if they are from an unfamiliar sender. In some cases, even familiar emails have been compromised and have been used to send emails that contain malicious URLs or attachments. To prevent your account from being compromised, you must check for any suspicious signs on the website you will be redirected to before entering any credentials.

As the digital threat landscape continues to shift and threat actors exploit new attack vectors, practicing good cyber hygiene and staying informed about emerging threats remain essential. While no security measure can eliminate all risks, staying vigilant and adopting safe digital habits can go a long way toward keeping you and your credentials secure.

However, as sophisticated tactics like device code phishing demonstrate, individual awareness alone is not enough. Organizations also need the ability to detect and respond to threats that slip past traditional security controls. Cofense combines real-world threat intelligence, AI-driven detection, and human expertise to help organizations identify and respond to these evolving phishing threats.

Learn how Cofense can help strengthen your organization's phishing defenses: https://cofense.com/platform.
